tasks.label: Demonstrate systems for customers and explain details, such as the causes and consequences of false alarms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential install hand-off: after finishing a burglar/intrusion system in a single-family home, the technician sits with the homeowner at the keypad or app, walks through arming/disarming and entry-delay behavior, user codes and duress code, and explains what typically triggers false alarms (pets, drafts moving blinds, unlocked doors, forgotten codes, kids) and the consequences (police dispatch, municipal false-alarm fines, permit revocation, monitoring-center verification calls).

Small-business/commercial handover: technician briefs the owner and several staff on opening/closing procedures, partitioned arming, panic and hold-up buttons, how to cancel an accidental trip with the central station passcode, and the cost and ordinance consequences of repeat false dispatches.

Fire alarm system demonstration to a building owner, property manager, or facility maintenance staff (often around acceptance testing): explaining the FACP annunciator, alarm vs. supervisory vs. trouble signals, silence/reset, sensitivity and dust/steam/cooking-induced nuisance alarms, and the fire-department response and fee consequences of unwanted alarms.

Pre-sale or upgrade demonstration at the customer's premises or in a showroom: showing camera views, doorbell/video verification, smart-lock and app features on a demo board or live equipment, and answering questions about reliability and false-alarm rates before the customer buys.

Follow-up coaching after a false alarm or during a service call: technician (or the same installer by phone/app screen-share) reviews the event log with the customer, identifies the cause, re-explains correct operation, and describes the fine/dispatch consequences if it recurs.

tasks.label: Test and repair circuits and sensors, following wiring and system specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Periodic (annual/semi-annual) inspection and testing of a commercial fire alarm system in an occupied office, school or hospital: functional-testing smoke/heat detectors with canned smoke from ladders or poles, testing pull stations and notification appliances, checking SLC loop voltages and trouble/supervisory circuits at the FACP, then correcting faults found - cleaning or swapping a detector head, re-terminating a loose conductor, replacing an end-of-line resistor - and re-verifying against the system spec.

Residential service call on a burglar/fire alarm: diagnosing a zone trouble or false alarm by metering door/window contacts and PIR motion sensors, tracing 22/18 AWG runs through attic, crawlspace or basement joists, splicing a damaged or rodent-chewed wire, replacing a failed contact or sensor, and verifying the zone at the panel and with central station.

Small commercial site (retail store, restaurant, bank branch): troubleshooting an open, short or ground fault on a burglar alarm or access/CCTV circuit - work behind counters, above drop ceilings and in back-of-house rooms while staff and customers are present - repairing terminations, replacing a keypad or sensor, and re-testing the loop.

New construction / renovation commissioning: pre-testing newly pulled cable (continuity, insulation resistance, loop resistance, polarity) in a partially built building, finding miswires, reversed pairs or runs damaged by other trades, repairing splices and device terminations per the wiring diagram, and verifying each addressable device.

Large industrial or institutional plant: diagnosing addressable loop faults, duct detectors, sprinkler flow/tamper switches and relay modules interfacing elevators and HVAC in mechanical rooms and at height; metering circuits, replacing modules or a control panel board (sometimes bench-repaired in the shop), and re-testing per specification.

sources.system: Cell Doctor
sources.title: Automatic solar cell diagnosis and treatment | Journal of Intelligent Manufacturing
sources.claim: Cell Doctor is an automated production-line cell in which a robotic arm loads solar cells, an electroluminescence station diagnoses defects, a laser station repairs (isolates/cuts) them, and an I-V characterization station verifies the result - a full autonomous diagnose-repair-verify loop on an electrical device in a purpose-built cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated diagnosis and repair of a defective electrical device. It transfers to 'test and repair circuits and sensors' because the system localizes an electrical fault against specification, performs a physical corrective action, and re-verifies electrically - the same test/repair/verify cycle, at finer precision than alarm wiring, in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: Takaya APT-1400F / APT-1600FD flying probe test systems

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated in-circuit/continuity testing of wired assemblies. It transfers to the 'test circuits ... following wiring and system specifications' half of this task: the machine probes conductors, measures resistance/continuity/component values against a stored specification and reports the specific faulty net.

sources.system: Ersa HR 600 XL / HR 600/3P automatic rework system

tasks.label: Feed cables through access holes, roof spaces, or cavity walls to reach fixture outlets, positioning and terminating cables, wires, or strapping.

instances.label: Residential retrofit in an occupied single-family home: drill access holes through top plates/baseboards, fish alarm/camera cable from the attic or crawl space down a cavity wall to a device outlet, avoiding existing wiring, insulation and fireblocks, then position, strap and terminate conductors at the device and keypad/panel.

New-construction rough-in in a framed house or light commercial shell: bore studs and joists, pull fire alarm/security cable through bored holes and roof-space runs to each box location, staple/strap per code, leave service loops, terminate at devices and the fire alarm control panel.

Retrofit of an occupied commercial facility (office, school, hospital, retail): run plenum-rated cable above suspended ceilings, through wall sleeves, cavity walls and existing conduit, support with J-hooks, drop to device boxes and terminate at devices and the head end, working around occupants and existing MEP.

Head-end/closet work: dress in, position, label, strap and terminate dozens of incoming conductors on fire alarm control panel terminal strips, initiating-device circuits, power supplies and punch-down blocks in an electrical or telecom room of a controlled facility.

Industrial/large-site work: pull cable through EMT conduit runs, cable tray and block/cavity walls in a warehouse, plant or parking structure (often from lifts or ladders), including exterior wall penetrations for cameras, then terminate at devices and enclosures.

instances.label: Trouble call on a commercial/institutional fire alarm system (office, school, hospital): the FACP shows a ground fault or open on an initiating/notification circuit. Tech opens the panel, reads trouble codes, meters and isolates loop segments, opens device backboxes and above-ceiling junction boxes on a ladder to find a loose terminal screw, nicked conductor or corroded splice, in an occupied building.

Scheduled periodic inspection/maintenance visit (NFPA 72) at a commercial site: walk the building examining each initiating device, notification appliance, conduit and raceway, check panel and battery terminations for tightness and corrosion, verify circuit supervision, and document deficiencies such as loose connections or damaged insulation.

Residential security/fire system service call where the fault is a wiring or termination defect: tech traces hardwired zone circuits with a meter from the panel in a closet/basement to door and window contacts, checks splices in attic, crawlspace and basement joists, and finds a loose terminal, a chewed or nicked conductor, or a corroded splice.

Residential service call where the reported trouble is not a simple conductor fault: intermittent false alarms or supervisory trouble caused by misaligned contacts, sensor placement, moisture, insects/pests, RF interference or an aging device; requires in-situ judgment across a cluttered, occupied home to determine what is actually wrong.

Exterior/site security work (CCTV, card readers, gates, perimeter detection): examine weather-exposed cable runs, conduit and weatherproof enclosures on rooftops, poles, building exteriors and parking areas for water intrusion, UV-degraded or rodent-damaged insulation and loose or corroded terminations, working from a ladder or lift in whatever weather is present.

Shop/bench examination in the contractor's facility: a removed control panel, keypad, camera or pre-terminated cable assembly is placed on the bench and examined to locate a faulty connection, bad solder joint or damaged insulation before reinstallation.

Trouble/false-alarm diagnostic call at a commercial or institutional site: interpret the panel trouble code, measure battery, charger and loop voltages/resistance with a meter, isolate a bad device, wiring fault or ground fault, correct programming at the keypad/panel, replace the failed battery or device, and retest until the system is clear.

Pre-test and commissioning on a new-construction or renovation jobsite: with the building still under construction (dust, trades working, temporary power), verify each installed device point-by-point against programming, sound notification appliances, test the panel's standby battery calculation and set, and correct punch-list faults before the AHJ acceptance test.

Shop/bench test at the contractor's facility: bench-test a replacement or returned control panel, keypad, siren or standby battery on a workbench with a power supply and meter before it goes to a job — verify default programming, key function, sounder output, and battery capacity.

Occupied commercial/institutional building (office, school, hospital, retail) service or system upgrade: drilling through top plates, studs and rated walls above a suspended ceiling grid, from a ladder in an occupied corridor or room, with dust control, protection of finishes, and firestopping of penetrations.

tasks.label: Inspect installation sites and study work orders, building plans, and installation manuals to determine materials requirements and installation procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential new-install survey: technician walks an occupied single-family home or apartment, checks door/window counts and construction, panel and keypad locations, attic/crawlspace/basement cable routes, existing wiring and Wi-Fi coverage, reviews the work order and equipment manuals, and determines the device/materials list and how the install will be run.

Small occupied commercial retrofit (retail store, restaurant, clinic, small office): survey ceiling type and plenum, existing conduit/legacy panel, sprinkler/HVAC interfaces and egress paths, compare against the work order and manufacturer installation manuals and local code, and produce the device counts, cable types/lengths, mounting hardware and installation sequence.

Large new-construction or major-renovation commercial/institutional job (school, hospital wing, office tower): study stamped fire alarm shop drawings, riser diagrams, submittals and panel manuals, then walk unfinished floors amid other trades to verify conditions, sleeve/penetration locations and coordination conflicts, and generate material pull lists and a rough-in installation plan.

Industrial, warehouse or campus facility addition (plant, distribution center, data center): survey high-bay/racked or hazardous areas, existing detection and suppression tie-ins, plant electrical standards and access constraints, and determine specialty materials (conduit, seals, beam detectors, mounting) and the installation procedure with the facility's permitting rules.

Service/trouble or upgrade call at a mixed residential or small-business site: inspect the existing installed system and its documentation, diagnose what is present versus what the work order specifies, and determine replacement parts, compatible devices and the procedure needed to complete the repair or upgrade.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous jobsite documentation. It shares the mobility and perception needed to traverse an installation site, but it delivers scans/imagery, not a determination of materials requirements or installation procedures from work orders, plans and manuals, so the transfer covers only a sub-step of this task.

instances.label: Residential new-construction rough-in: in an unfinished single-family house with open wood framing, the installer drills stud/joist penetrations, pulls alarm, keypad and detector cable, and staples it flat to studs and joists at code intervals and near boxes, using a hand stapler on a ladder among other trades' debris and materials.

Shop/prefab work in the contractor's warehouse: assembling raceway and conduit sub-assemblies, backboards and riser assemblies on benches before delivery, including fastening cable to plywood backboards with staples, in a fixed-layout shop with standard tools.

instances.label: Residential intrusion install: after mounting PIR motion detectors and glassbreak sensors in furnished rooms of a private home, the installer sets pulse count / sensitivity on DIP switches or a pot inside each detector housing (pet immunity, drafts from HVAC registers, sunlit windows) and configures the matching zone/sensor options at the wall-mounted alarm keypad, then walk-tests each room and re-adjusts.

Small commercial intrusion install (retail store, office suite, small warehouse): installer keys sensor sensitivity, pulse count, entry/exit and swinger-shutdown options into the wall-mounted programming keypad of the control panel, tuning for high ceilings, shelving, roll-up doors and HVAC air movement per the manufacturer's tables; verifies by walk test with a partner watching the keypad.

Addressable commercial fire alarm commissioning: per-device smoke detector sensitivity/alarm thresholds (day-night settings, less sensitive settings for dusty warehouse or kitchen-adjacent areas, drift compensation) entered device-by-device through the fire alarm control panel keypad/LCD menus; panels are frequently pre-programmed on a shop bench before installation.

Nuisance-alarm service call at an as-found site (home, restaurant, garage): technician diagnoses why a detector false-alarms (steam, dust, sunlight, insects, pets, forklift heat), climbs a ladder to the ceiling- or high-wall-mounted unit, lowers sensitivity via switch/pot or lens mask, or reprograms the sensitivity at the keypad, and retests in place.

Large institutional site (hospital, school, airport, campus): bulk sensitivity programming for hundreds of addressable initiating devices at the panel, coordinated with field walk-tests, sensitivity-report printouts and AHJ acceptance testing across occupied corridors and rooms.

sources.system: MATT (Smart Device Test Automation Robot)
sources.title: MATT the Smart Device Test Automation Robot | Adapta Robotics
sources.claim: MATT is a commercially sold device-test robot that autonomously actuates physical buttons, switches and control knobs on a device fixtured in its work area, using AI computer vision to read the device display and confirm the resulting state.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated functional testing of fixtured electronic devices. Entering a programming/sensitivity sequence on an alarm keypad or FACP keypad is the same physical act — multi-key presses on a small keypad plus reading an LCD to confirm the entered value — and the same class of small switches (DIP switches, rotary/pot adjustments) that MATT actuates on devices held in a bench fixture.

sources.system: OptoFidelity TOUCH

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated keypress/touch testing of a fixtured device. Alarm keypad programming requires the same precision (individual keys on a small keypad) and display-based verification; the demonstrated positioning accuracy far exceeds what pressing an alarm keypad key requires.

tasks.label: Inspect completed work to certify that maintenance meets standards and that aircraft are ready for operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Airline line maintenance: after a defect rectification or component change (wheel/brake, LRU, hydraulic line, pack valve) at the gate or line hangar, the certifying technician verifies the installation hands-on — correct part and hardware, torque marks, safety wire, connector and clamp security, no FOD left behind — runs an operational/leak check, closes panels and cowls, and signs the aircraft off as ready for the next flight, under departure-time pressure.

Heavy check (C/D check) in an MRO hangar: an inspector performs buyback and final inspections of other mechanics' completed work — structural repairs and rivet patterns, corrosion treatment, sealant, wiring and system reinstallation — often inside wing tanks, wheel wells and belly areas before panel closeout, cross-checking each work card and stamping the package before the certificate of release.

General/business aviation repair station or FBO hangar: an A&P/IA inspects completed annual, 100-hour or repair work on a piston single, light twin or turboprop — control rigging and cable tension, cotter pins, engine controls, brake and fuel lines, run-up and leak check — on aircraft of many different makes, ages and modification states, then makes the airworthiness release entry.

Post-repair / post-paint exterior verification in a hangar: after a skin repair, lightning-strike repair or repaint, the technician performs a general visual inspection of the airframe exterior, locates and records any remaining damage or defects relative to structural stations, and documents that the exterior condition meets standards.

Engine/component shop bench work: final verification of a repaired piece-part (turbine blade, combustor liner, vane, machined fitting) — dimensional/geometry measurement against drawing tolerances and crack/NDT check after the repair — before the part is accepted and tagged for return to service.

Field or off-airport work: certifying completed maintenance on an aircraft away from a maintenance facility — an AOG repair at an outstation ramp, agricultural or utility helicopter maintenance at a landing strip or job site, or military/field expedient repair — with improvised access, weather exposure and no fixed layout.

instances.label: Line-maintenance transit/daily check on the ramp or at the gate: walkaround of a parked airliner in ambient weather, kneeling under the aircraft to check main and nose gear struts for oleo extension and hydraulic weepage, tire wear/cuts/pressure, brake wear-pin indicators, gear pins and doors, and eyeballing pneumatic deice boots and probes for damage; findings written up before departure.

Scheduled base/heavy check detailed inspection in a hangar: opening access panels and gear doors, climbing into wheel wells and wing/keel bays with flashlight and mirror to inspect hydraulic tubing, hoses, actuators and fittings for leaks, chafing, corrosion and cracks, checking gear pins/bushings/torque links for wear and play, and reservoir/accumulator levels and pressures per task cards.

Troubleshooting a specific reported defect: pilot writes up a hydraulic quantity loss, gear indication, or deice boot fault; technician pressurizes the system or cycles the gear on jacks, traces fluid trails through confined structure, feels/wipes lines to localize the leaking fitting or seal, and pressure-checks the deicer boot for holes.

Back-shop/component-shop inspection of a removed part: landing-gear cylinder, axle, brake or actuator disassembled and cleaned, inspected on a bench and in an NDT booth (fluorescent penetrant, magnetic particle, eddy current) for cracks, plus dimensional/wear and corrosion assessment against manual limits before repair or scrap disposition.

Exterior airframe/structural damage inspection in the hangar or on the apron: general visual inspection or post-event (lightning strike, hail, ground bump) survey of fuselage skin, wings, control surfaces and fairings for cracks, dents, burn marks, missing fasteners and paint/coating damage, with defects mapped and sized against allowable damage limits.

tasks.label: Conduct routine and special inspections as required by regulations.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Line-station routine check at the gate/ramp (preflight, transit, daily/weekly): walkaround of the parked aircraft checking skin and panel security, tire condition and pressure, brake wear pins, strut extension, hydraulic/oil/fuel leaks, engine inlet and fan blades by hand, lights, probes and drains, plus associated servicing checks, under time pressure between flights and in whatever weather is present.

Exterior general visual / conditional damage inspection of the airframe skin - post-lightning-strike, hail, bird-strike or ground-equipment contact, or the scheduled exterior GVI/dent-and-paint survey during a check - performed on an aircraft parked in a maintenance hangar or on a ramp stand, covering fuselage, wings, empennage and nacelle surfaces and mapping/sizing any damage found.

Scheduled base-maintenance check (A/C check) zonal and detailed inspections in a hangar: open access panels and fairings, enter wheel wells, wing and belly bays, inspect structure, wiring, ducts, control cables and rigging, cabin/cargo compartments and floor structure, and carry out associated operational/functional checks of systems per task cards.

Engine internal (gas-path) inspection required by the maintenance program or a service bulletin: borescope of the installed engine through access ports to examine compressor and turbine blades, combustor liner and vanes, or equivalent crack/distress inspection of engine modules and components in an engine shop.

Special non-destructive inspection required by an airworthiness directive or service bulletin - eddy current, ultrasonic, penetrant or thermography - on a structural area (lap joint, fitting, spar) on the aircraft, or on components removed to a shop (landing gear parts, discs, composite panels), with recorded accept/reject results.

General aviation or business-aircraft annual / 100-hour inspection in a small repair-station hangar: remove cowlings, seats and inspection panels on a one-off aircraft configuration, run compression checks, inspect engine mounts, control cables and pulleys, corrosion-prone areas and hardware, then reassemble and record findings.

tasks.label: Replace or repair worn, defective, or damaged components, using hand tools, gauges, and testing equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Line maintenance at the gate/ramp: technician replaces a defective line-replaceable unit or worn part on a turnaround-pressured aircraft (main wheel/tire, brake unit, position light, air data or proximity sensor, cabin/seat item), working outdoors on the apron with stands, hand tools, torque wrenches, safety wire, and a functional test after installation.

Scheduled base/heavy check in an airline or MRO hangar: remove and replace worn or defective systems components on the airframe (hydraulic actuators, pumps, valves, ducts, bleed components, cargo/flight-control hardware), often in confined access areas (wheel wells, belly, pylon, cabin floor) reached by lifts and stands, followed by rigging, leak/functional checks and gauge readings.

Structural repair in a hangar or military depot: drill out corroded/cracked fasteners, remove a damaged skin panel, bracket, or doubler, fit and drill the replacement, install and seal fasteners, and inspect the finished repair to the structural repair manual.

Component repair-station bench work: a removed LRU (hydraulic actuator, fuel or pneumatic valve, wheel-and-brake assembly, starter/generator) is disassembled on the bench, worn seals, bearings, bushings and discs are measured with gauges and replaced, then the unit is reassembled and functionally tested on a test stand before return to service.

Engine parts repair shop: worn or damaged engine airfoils and hardware removed at teardown (compressor/turbine blade tips, leading edges, vanes) are restored on benches and machines — measuring wear, removing damaged material, adding material by weld/clad, and blending/grinding back to the manual dimensions before reassembly.

General aviation shop or small operator hangar: replace worn or defective components on piston/turboprop aircraft of many different types and ages — cylinders, magnetos, exhaust, brake linings, tires, control cables, vacuum pumps — with improvised access, non-standard hardware, and a run-up/functional check afterwards.

tasks.label: Inspect airframes for wear or other defects.

General aviation / business aircraft annual or 100-hour airframe inspection in a small repair-station or FBO hangar: inspection panels opened, then examination of skins, control surfaces and hinges, cables, pulleys, tube or spar structure, fabric or composite skins and hardware for wear, corrosion and cracks.

Damage assessment away from a maintenance base: aircraft or helicopter parked outdoors at an outstation, a remote strip or an austere flight line, inspected in ambient weather and lighting after ground-handling damage, a hard landing or a suspected strike.

tasks.label: Check for corrosion, distortion, and invisible cracks in the fuselage, wings, and tail, using x-ray and magnetic inspection equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled exterior structural survey during a hangar check: technician on stands/lifts walks the fuselage, wings and empennage looking for corrosion blistering, skin dents/distortion, loose or cracked fasteners and skin cracks, tap-tests suspect areas, marks and writes up findings on the task card.

Detailed on-aircraft NDT at designated structural locations per AD/service bulletin or the NDT manual: portable eddy-current or ultrasonic probes run over lap joints, stringers, spar caps and fastener holes after access panels are removed; instrument calibrated on reference standards, indications interpreted, findings documented.

In-situ radiographic inspection on the aircraft: portable x-ray source and imaging plate/DR panel positioned on both sides of a structure (lap joint, control surface, wing box area) in a cordoned radiation exclusion zone in the hangar or on the ramp; exposures made, images read for cracks, corrosion thinning and trapped water.

Magnetic particle inspection of ferromagnetic parts removed from the aircraft (landing-gear components, steel fittings, bolts, shafts) at the NDT shop's wet horizontal bench: clean, magnetize, apply fluorescent suspension, view under UV in a darkened booth, evaluate and mark indications, demagnetize and document.

Internal / confined-area corrosion and crack inspection: entering wing fuel tanks, the belly bilge, cargo floor beam bays or the empennage interior after removing panels, insulation blankets and sometimes seats/floor, using flashlight, mirror and borescope plus spot NDT in cramped, poorly lit spaces.

sources.system: Donecle / Mainblades inspection drones (Delta TechOps, Jet Aviation, United)
sources.title: Aircraft Inspections With Drones Accelerate Toward Next Evolution | Aviation Week
sources.claim: Autonomous inspection drones (Donecle, Mainblades) are in airline/MRO service for exterior general visual and lightning-strike inspections, but the deployed workflow has technicians review every captured image; AI is not yet qualified to close out task cards.
sources.transferJustification: Drone GVI covers the same objects (fuselage, wings, tail exterior) and defect classes (lightning strikes, dents, cracks) as this task's visual portion, but it delivers imagery rather than an accepted inspection finding.

sources.transferJustification: Same inspection target (aircraft exterior skin) and defect types (damage, lightning strike) as the visual part of this task; it is data capture with automated detection, not subsurface x-ray/magnetic inspection.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: fluorescent penetrant inspection of aero components. tasks.label: Measure parts for wear, using precision instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Component/accessory or landing-gear overhaul shop: a technician measures removed hardware on a bench against overhaul-manual serviceable limits — bearing journals, bushings, pistons and actuator bores, gear teeth, seal lands, splines — using outside micrometers, dial bore gauges, telescoping gauges, calipers, dial indicators and go/no-go gauges, recording dimensions on a work card.

Engine overhaul shop: turbine and compressor airfoils, discs, seals and shrouds are measured for erosion, tip loss, creep growth, chord/thickness loss and clearance dimensions during module teardown, using micrometers, blade gauges, CMMs and optical scanners, dispositioned against engine manual limits.

General-aviation / piston-engine shop: cylinder bore taper and out-of-round, valve guide ID, crankshaft journal and rod bearing dimensions measured during top or major overhaul with telescoping gauges, dial bore gauges and micrometers; small shop, parts cleaned and brought to a bench.

Airline base maintenance / heavy check: parts pulled off the aircraft (control-surface hinge bushings, attach pins and bolts, brake linings, wheel bearings, actuator rod ends) are carried to a hangar bench and measured with micrometers, calipers and pin gauges to decide serviceability before reinstall.

In-situ measurement that requires the assembled aircraft: control-surface free play with a dial indicator, tire tread depth with a depth gauge, brake wear-pin protrusion with a scale under applied pressure, oleo strut extension, cable diameter/wear with go-no-go gauges, flap track and hinge play — mechanic working under/around a parked aircraft on the ramp or in a hangar, often in confined access.

On-wing internal and structural measurement: borescope measurement of compressor/turbine blade erosion, tip rub and nick depth through engine access ports; ultrasonic skin thickness and corrosion depth, and dent depth mapping on the airframe from stands or a lift.

sources.system: Mitutoyo MiSTAR robotic measurement cell at Méca-Précis (with Engineering Data)
sources.title: Robotic Metrology Drives Process Improvements at Méca-Précis – Metrology and Quality News
sources.claim: A commercially installed robotic metrology cell combining a multi-axis articulated robot, a Mitutoyo MiSTAR CMM and a 20-pallet store performs full dimensional inspection of aerospace and satellite components autonomously inside a glass safety enclosure.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: production dimensional inspection of aerospace metal parts. Wear measurement in overhaul is the same physical act — locating features on a metal part and reading dimensions to a few microns against limits — on comparable objects at comparable precision; only the limit table differs.

sources.system: Q-Span Gauging System
sources.developer: newScale Robotics (Novanta) with Universal Robots UR3e
sources.title: Robots Need Dexterity to Work With Bore Gauges | Automated Bore Gauge
sources.claim: A commercial collaborative-robot gauging workstation picks small machined parts and takes measurements with standard bore gauges, bore micrometers and a robotic caliper, combining several instrument readings per part in one automatic sequence.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated QC gauging of machined parts with the same hand instruments (bore gauge, bore micrometer, caliper) an aircraft mechanic uses to measure wear; same instruments, same part sizes, same read-to-limit output.

sources.system: ZEISS ScanBox Series 5 / 5110 with ATOS 5 for Airfoil
sources.title: ZEISS ScanBox Series 5: inspection integrated into production
sources.claim: A robot-loaded, enclosed optical 3D measuring machine is sold specifically for gas-turbine airfoil inspection, measuring a turbine blade in minutes and a complete blisk in under an hour.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: dimensional inspection of turbine airfoils. Blade wear disposition in overhaul is decided from exactly these dimensions (chord length, thickness, leading/trailing-edge radius, tip), which the cell measures to metrology accuracy.

sources.system: AI-guided white light robot inspection

sources.claim: GE Aerospace has deployed articulated industrial robots carrying white-light optical scanners that scan high-precision engine parts during off-wing MRO visits, producing a digital record of each part's condition; the first such inspectors went into service in autumn 2024 on high-pressure turbines.

sources.system: AutoInspect
sources.title: Digital inspection procedure for engine components industrialized | Aviation Pros
sources.claim: Lufthansa Technik industrialized AutoInspect, a robot-based optical measurement procedure for engine components that is in productive use in its Hamburg engine shops.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated robotic optical metrology of engine components in an MRO shop cell. It establishes that a robot can position a precision sensor over overhaul hardware to production standards; the disposition output (crack vs. dimensional limit) differs but the sensing and positioning problem is the same.

sources.system: Robotic white light interferometry rework inspection system

sources.title: Automated assessment for grinding spots on aircraft landing gear components using robotic white light interferometry
sources.claim: A robotic white-light-interferometry system positions the sensor over aircraft landing gear components to make 3D measurements of reworked areas, replacing manual inspection with micrometers and gauges; an exemplary rework inspection validated the approach.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional assessment of landing-gear component surfaces that mechanics currently measure with micrometers and gauges to decide return to service — the same objects, precision and serviceability decision as wear measurement.

sources.system: Mainblades and Donecle inspection drones; Iris DentCheck (Donecle + 8tree)
sources.title: Aircraft Inspections With Drones Accelerate Toward Next Evolution | Aviation Week
sources.claim: Autonomous inspection drones are approved and in service in airline hangars and outdoors for visual aircraft surface inspection, but the drone-mounted precision dent-measurement product remains pre-market and drone vendors question measurement accuracy from a flying platform.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to bound, not support, on-aircraft precision measurement: deployed hangar robots perform visual inspection, while quantitative dent/thickness measurement on the installed airframe is not yet an accepted robotic capability.

tasks.label: Remove or install aircraft engines, using hoists or forklift trucks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled turbofan engine change on a narrow-body airliner (CFM56/LEAP/V2500) in an airline or MRO hangar: aircraft on wheels/jacks, cowls opened, mechanics disconnect fuel, hydraulic, bleed-air, electrical and control interfaces, rig a bootstrap hoist or engine change stand, break torque on the mount bolts, lower the ~5,000-9,000 lb engine to a dolly, then hoist and mate the replacement QEC engine, torque mounts, reconnect and leak/ops check.

Unscheduled line-maintenance engine change performed outdoors on the ramp or a remote stand (AOG), narrow- or wide-body, with a mobile crane or engine change trailer, working around wind, temperature, lighting and limited access, on a tight turn-time.

General aviation piston engine (Lycoming/Continental, 250-500 lb) removal and installation in a small FBO/repair-station hangar: cowling removal, disconnecting baffles, controls, fuel/oil lines, wiring and exhaust, lifting with a cherry-picker hoist, then installing the overhauled/replacement engine on shock mounts, reconnecting and rigging controls.

Turboprop or helicopter powerplant (PT6, T700, etc.) removal/install in a military or corporate hangar or on the flightline: overhead or portable hoist, drive-shaft/gearbox alignment, torque-critical mount hardware, plumbing and harness reconnection in a tightly confined engine bay.

Engine shop / build-up work: handling a bare or QEC engine with an overhead crane or forklift between shipping stand, build-up stand and test-cell mount inside an engine overhaul facility, bolting the engine to the stand/mount and connecting instrumentation before or after an aircraft install.

sources.system: 'Alfred' rotor assembly robot (Pratt & Whitney / RTX, Eagle Services Asia)
sources.title: Robot Assembles Aircraft Engines | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: The most advanced deployed aerospace engine-assembly robot found is Pratt & Whitney's 'Alfred' at Eagle Services Asia in Singapore, which works autonomously inside a fenced 26x20-ft cell handling high-pressure compressor rotors into an oven and a hydraulic stacking system - engine component assembly, not attaching an engine to an aircraft.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: jet engine module assembly. It does not transfer - the robot handles fixtured rotor modules presented on dedicated tooling inside a fence; it does not lift a complete engine onto an airframe pylon/mount, torque mount bolts, or connect fuel, hydraulic, pneumatic and electrical interfaces.

sources.system: Airbus seat installation robot
sources.title: Meet the versatile Airbus robot automating aircraft seat installation
sources.claim: In the most structured aerospace setting available - an Airbus final assembly line - the newest installation robot announced is for fitting cabin seats, with the first two units due at the A321 FAL in late 2026; engine installation on the FAL remains a manual hoist operation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: installing large components into an aircraft inside a purpose-organized assembly line. It does not transfer - seats are light, rail-guided cabin items; the evidence shows aerospace assembly-line robotics has not reached engine removal/installation, and autonomy of the seat robot is not established.

sources.system: Rolls-Royce FLARE snake robots / Remote Boreblending Robots
sources.title: Robots Swarm inspecting your airplane engines – IEEE Future Directions
sources.claim: Engine OEM robotics effort in MRO is directed at in-situ inspection and repair inside the engine precisely to avoid the manual engine removal-and-remount operation; no robotic system is described as performing the removal or reinstallation itself.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: on-wing engine maintenance. It does not transfer - these are small in-engine crawlers/boreblending tools, partly remotely operated, with no lifting, mating or connection capability for a whole powerplant.

tasks.label: Service and maintain aircraft and related apparatus by performing activities such as flushing crankcases, cleaning screens, and or moving parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: General-aviation piston engine oil service in an FBO/repair-station hangar: cowling removed, warm oil drained from the crankcase, oil suction screen and/or spin-on filter removed and cleaned (filter cut open and media inspected for metal), gaskets replaced, new oil added to spec, drain plug and filter torqued and safety-wired, ground run and leak check, logbook entry.

Line servicing of fluid levels on a transport-category aircraft at the gate or in a hangar: check engine oil sight gauges/IDG oil, hydraulic reservoir quantity, and replenish with the correct fluid via the servicing panel or pressure-fill connection to the required level.

Deeper fluid-system servicing on a transport or turboprop aircraft: open cowl/access doors and panels, replace hydraulic and engine oil filter elements, drain and refill gearbox/IDG oil, purge and bleed the system, torque and lockwire fittings, clean up spillage, sign off.

Scheduled airframe lubrication per the lube chart in a hangar: locate dozens of grease fittings on landing gear, gear doors, flap/slat tracks, control surface hinges and bellcranks (some reached from stands, in wheel wells, or with the aircraft on jacks), couple a grease gun to each zerk, pump until fresh grease purges, wipe excess, oil cables and rod ends, cycle the mechanism to verify free movement.

Cleaning and replacing screens and filters: induction/inlet air filters, fuel strainers and screens, ECS/hydraulic filter screens; removing the item from the aircraft or component, washing it in solvent or an ultrasonic tank, drying, inspecting for contamination, and reinstalling with new seals and lockwire.

Cleaning of the aircraft and engine areas as part of servicing: exterior wash of the airframe in a hangar or wash rack, degreasing the belly, engine nacelle and landing gear areas after fluid work, and wiping down worked-on areas before inspection.

tasks.label: Test operation of engines and other systems, using test equipment, such as ignition analyzers, compression checkers, distributor timers, or ammeters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-maintenance operational engine run on the aircraft: technician boards/straps in or works with a run crew on a ramp or run-up pad, starts the engine, advances through idle/power-assurance points, watches EGT/ITT/N1/RPM/oil pressure and vibration on cockpit and portable instrumentation, checks for leaks and correct accessory operation, shuts down and documents results.

Piston-engine cylinder differential compression check and ignition checks in a general-aviation shop/hangar: cowling opened, spark plugs removed, compression tester adapter threaded into each cylinder, prop positioned at TDC and held, dual gauge readings taken per cylinder, plus magneto timing/ignition-analyzer checks and mag drop verification.

Electrical/charging system testing with multimeter, clamp ammeter and load bank: verify generator/alternator output current and voltage, battery capacity and load, bus voltages, continuity and resistance of circuits and bonding, on an aircraft in a hangar or at the gate.

Avionics and instrument functional testing with ramp test sets: pitot-static/air-data test set, transponder/ADS-B ramp tester, nav/comm test equipment connected to the installed systems at the gate or in the hangar, running required test profiles and comparing indications to tolerances.

Hydraulic, pneumatic and fuel-system operational tests on the aircraft: hydraulic mule or engine-driven pumps pressurize the system, gauges and pressure/flow instrumentation record readings while gear, flaps, brakes or thrust reversers are cycled, checking actuation times, pressures and leaks in a hangar.

Shop/test-cell testing of removed engines or components after overhaul: engine mounted on a stand or thrust frame in an enclosed test cell and run through an acceptance test schedule, or a removed component (pump, actuator, LRU, generator) tested on a dedicated test bench to spec.

sources.title: Advanced Technology Center | Lycoming Engines
sources.claim: Lycoming's Advanced Technology Center runs aviation piston engines in 16 automated production test cells that execute performance checks and control the test functions automatically, with data acquisition — i.e., machine-run engine operational testing of the same engines GA mechanics test.

sources.title: Advanced Tech Services | Lycoming
sources.claim: Lycoming's test cell and flight-stand services list automated test cycle control and ..., with dynamometer power checks, in-cylinder pressure analysis and full-load performance sweeps executed on engines mounted as they would be in the airframe.

sources.title: Turbine Technology: The Small Turbine Engine Test Cell | Aviation Pros
sources.claim: Rolls-Royce's turbine engine test cells in Indianapolis, built with Atec dynamometers and the UMACS monitor-and-control system, run production/overhaul acceptance certification test cycles and mission-simulation cycles automatically, with humans supervising rather than driving each throttle movement.

tasks.label: Assemble and install electrical, plumbing, mechanical, hydraulic, and structural components and accessories, using hand or power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Line/base maintenance on an in-service transport aircraft at a gate or line hangar: remove and install an accessory or line-replaceable unit (hydraulic pump, actuator, valve, generator, starter, wheel/brake, pneumatic duct). Work is through access panels and in confined bays, with flexible hoses, B-nuts, electrical connectors, torque values, cotter pins/lockwire, followed by an operational check and sign-off, under turnaround time pressure.

Heavy check or structural mod in an MRO hangar: fit and install structural components and accessories — skin patch/doubler, stringer or frame repair pieces, angles, brackets, intercostals, fairings and access doors — including trimming to fit, drilling and countersinking, deburring, sealant application and installing solid rivets, Hi-Loks or bolts to spec with hand and power tools.

Electrical installation during heavy check, retrofit or STC mod: mount avionics units, racks, lights, sensors and switch panels; route, clamp and tie wiring harnesses through the fuselage, cockpit and E&E bay; terminate and mate connectors; install bonding/grounding straps; then continuity/functional test.

Plumbing installation: install hydraulic, fuel, oxygen and pneumatic tubing, hoses, fittings, filters and valves on the aircraft or on an engine build-up stand — aligning rigid tube runs, starting and torquing B-nuts without cross-threading, fitting seals and clamps, safety-wiring, then servicing and leak-checking the system.

Component/back-shop bench work in an MRO shop: build up or reassemble an accessory, module or subassembly (engine compressor rotor or module, hydraulic actuator, valve, pump, wheel-and-brake, gearbox) from cleaned/inspected parts on a fixture or stand — installing seals, washers and nuts, applying staged torque sequences with calibrated tools, and documenting the build before test.

General aviation/corporate shop: install engine accessories, exhaust and control components, avionics, interior parts and plumbing in a wide mix of small piston and turbine airframes, often one-off configurations with non-standard, aged hardware and improvised access, in a small shop or on the ramp.

tasks.label: Maintain, repair, and rebuild aircraft structures, functional components, and parts, such as wings and fuselage, rigging, hydraulic units, oxygen systems, fuel systems, electrical systems, gaskets, or seals.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On-aircraft removal/replacement and repair of functional components and systems in a hangar or on the line: hydraulic actuators, pumps and valves, fuel pumps/lines, oxygen bottles and regulators, gaskets and seals. Mechanic opens access panels, disconnects lines and wiring, breaks torque on possibly corroded or lockwired fasteners, fits the replacement, torques, safety-wires, then leak/ops checks. Overhead, kneeling and confined-access positions on a live aircraft.

Airframe structural repair performed on the aircraft: assess a dent, crack, corrosion or impact damage on fuselage/wing skin per the SRM, drill out rivets, cut out damaged skin or composite/honeycomb, fabricate and fit a doubler or bonded patch, install fasteners or cure the patch, seal, and refinish. Work at height on stands, often inverted or in tight bays.

Back-shop bench overhaul/rebuild of a removed unit (hydraulic actuator, servo valve, pneumatic or fuel component): disassemble a used unit with unknown wear, clean, inspect against CMM limits, replace every O-ring, gasket and seal, reassemble to torque, then functional/leak test on a bench test stand and certify.

Shop refurbishment of removed parts by machining and surface processes: paint/coating strip, blasting, blending and grinding of worn surfaces, weld/clad build-up, abradable seal removal and reapplication, re-machining to print for engine and airframe parts in the parts shop.

Electrical system repair: troubleshoot and repair wiring harnesses, chafed wires, splices, connector pins and terminal lugs, bonding/grounding straps, in avionics bays, behind cabin sidewalls and floor panels, and in wing/belly areas with restricted reach.

Rigging and mechanical adjustment: rig flight control cables to tension and travel specification, adjust pushrods, bellcranks and turnbuckles, adjust door, flap and landing gear mechanisms, then perform functional and duplicate inspection checks on the aircraft.

tasks.label: Measure the tension of control cables.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Annual or 100-hour inspection of a light piston GA aircraft (Cessna/Piper) in a maintenance hangar: technician removes inspection panels and reaches into wing roots, the tail cone and under the cabin floor to clamp a mechanical tensiometer (correct riser/anvil set for 1/16"-3/16" cable) on aileron, elevator, rudder and trim cables, reads deflection, converts via the chart with ambient-temperature correction, and records tension against the maintenance manual range.

Base/heavy maintenance check on a transport-category airliner or regional jet in an airline hangar: tension checks on rudder, elevator, stabilizer-trim and spoiler cables routed through under-floor bays, the wheel well, fuselage crown and the vertical stabilizer; requires stands or lifts, opening many access panels, confined-space entry, and a second technician holding controls in neutral while the reading is taken.

Rigging verification after a cable, pulley, bellcrank, turnbuckle or control-surface replacement: repeated measure-adjust-measure cycles, taking tensiometer readings at several stations along each cable run in the airframe until every cable in the interconnected system falls within limits at the specified temperature.

Helicopter, business jet, agricultural or vintage aircraft cable tension check performed on an outdoor ramp/flight line or in an operator's hangar: cramped access along tail booms, control tunnels and pylons, varied non-standard cable routings, ambient temperature correction, sometimes with the tensiometer applied overhead or at awkward angles.

Component shop/bench work: newly fabricated, swaged or overhauled control cable assemblies and control quadrants checked in a rigging jig or bench fixture, where tension is applied and verified (pre-stretch/proof-load and rig-to-spec) with a tensiometer or load cell before installation.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: measuring the tension of steel spokes in a laced wheel. Transfer to measuring flight-control cable tension is close in the objects and precision involved (thin steel tension members carrying tens of kgf/lbf, read to a specified tolerance) and the environment matches the E1 counterfactual exactly: the tension member is presented fixtured to a purpose-built machine, which senses tension and reports a number without a human applying the instrument.

tasks.label: Obtain fuel and oil samples and check them for contamination.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Light/GA piston aircraft, preflight or 100-hour/annual inspection on an outdoor ramp, tie-down row or GA hangar: mechanic crouches or kneels under each wing and at the gascolator, pushes a clear plastic tester into each spring-loaded quick-drain sump (often 5-13 points), catches fuel, holds it to the light to judge color, water droplets, sediment and smell, redrains until clear, then also pulls the engine oil dipstick to check oil condition. Aircraft is parked wherever it happens to sit; weather, lighting and access vary.

Transport-category aircraft at a gate or in a maintenance hangar: scheduled water-drain check of wing and center fuel tank sumps using the aircraft drain tool/hose into a clear container or bucket, inspecting the drawn fuel for free water, particulates and microbiological growth before it is dumped or logged; work done overnight or during a turn, around ground support equipment and other crews.

Engine, gearbox or APU oil sample for spectrometric/trend oil analysis (SOAP): open a cowl fastener or access door, draw warm oil through a sampling valve or via a tube-and-pump/syringe into a labeled bottle at a specified point in the drain, cap, label, log the hours, and send to the lab; performed in a hangar or on the flight line on turbine or piston engines.

Shop-side check of the drawn samples at a bench or small fluid lab in the maintenance facility: shake and settle the sample, do a clear-and-bright visual, apply water-detecting paste/capsule or a free-water detector, run a filter-patch or particle count where required, and record and report the result against limits.

Austere or field conditions: helicopter at an off-airport landing site, agricultural aircraft at a private grass strip, or deployed military flightline; fuel drawn from aircraft sumps and from drums/bowsers with a tester jar and water-detecting paste, oil sampled from the engine, all in wind, rain, dust or darkness with no fixed layout or facility support.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: drawing an oil sample from in-service oil-filled equipment through a drain/sampling port into a sealed bottle. Same objects (viscous lubricating/insulating oil, small valve port, sample bottles), same precision class (vision-guided docking to a port a few centimetres across), and the same waste-flush-then-collect sequence used for aircraft engine oil sampling.

tasks.label: Examine engines through specially designed openings while working from ladders or scaffolds, or use hoists or lifts to remove the entire engine from an aircraft.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On-wing borescope inspection of a commercial turbofan (compressor, combustor, HPT/LPT blades) through the engine's borescope ports: technician on a maintenance stand/ladder in an airline hangar or at a gate, hand-inserts and articulates a video probe, motors the rotor, measures and dispositions blade damage against AMM limits, records findings.

Line-maintenance visual examination of an engine through cowl doors and access openings/panels (fan case, accessory gearbox area, thrust reverser) from a ladder or work stand at the gate or in the hangar: looking for leaks, chafed lines, cracks, loose hardware, FOD, and writing up discrepancies.

General-aviation piston engine at a small FBO/repair-station shop: borescope of each cylinder through spark-plug holes and visual examination through cowl openings during an annual/100-hour inspection, cowling partially opened, work done off a low stand or stepladder.

Removal of a transport-category engine from an aircraft in a hangar or on the ramp: disconnect fuel, hydraulic, pneumatic and electrical interfaces, open cowls/thrust reverser, rig a bootstrap hoist or engine change lift, unbolt mounts, lower engine onto a transport dolly.

Removal of a small piston or turboprop engine in a shop using an engine hoist/overhead crane: disconnect controls, lines and wiring at the firewall, attach lifting sling to hoist, pull the engine off the mount and set it on an engine stand.

MRO engine shop: assembled QEC-built or bare engine mounted on a build stand or in a test cell, inspected through borescope ports and access openings before/after test runs, technician working from a platform or ladder around the stand.

instances.label: General-aviation piston engine ground run at an FBO/maintenance base: after cylinder or ignition work, or in response to a pilot squawk of roughness, the technician starts the engine on the ramp or run-up pad and listens through idle, mag checks and full power for misfire, roughness or valve-related noise, cross-checking EGT/CHT and RPM to call out which cylinder/valve is at fault.

Turbine (turbofan/turboprop/turboshaft) engine ground run at an airline line station or MRO run-up area: technician listens from the cockpit and from outside for abnormal sounds — bearing whine, rumble, blade rub, bleed/air leak whistle, surge — while monitoring instruments, to confirm or clear a reported defect before release to service.

Localizing a noise on a running engine mounted on the aircraft: technician moves around the aircraft and listens at cowl openings, exhaust, induction and accessory section at idle and low power, has a helper vary throttle, and compares the two engines of a twin to distinguish an exhaust leak, sticking/burned valve, induction leak or accessory noise.

Post-overhaul or post-repair acceptance/break-in run of an engine mounted on an instrumented test stand or in a shop test cell: technician runs the prescribed power schedule while listening for abnormal noise and watching instruments, and signs off or rejects the engine.

Away-from-base or field engine run: helicopter landing zone, agricultural or remote strip, unimproved parking, aircraft on grass or gravel with ambient wind and weather; the technician listens to the operating engine to diagnose a defect or judge airworthiness for the ferry/next flight.

instances.label: Base/heavy maintenance in an MRO or depot hangar: drilling out the rivets and fasteners around a cracked or corroded fuselage/wing skin section and cutting the defective skin out, working on the assembled aircraft from stands and lifts, on curved surfaces and in varied orientations, without nicking the underlying structure.

Removing an individual seized, sheared or damaged fastener (screw, hi-lok, bolt) by centre-punching and drilling it out so a defective part or panel can come off; occurs on the aircraft at the gate/ramp or in the hangar and on components in the shop, in awkward one-off locations under time pressure.

Composite/bonded structure: cutting and milling out damaged skin plies and honeycomb core (scarfing) on a radome, fan cowl, control surface or on the aircraft's composite skin, to reach and remove internal damage/water ingress before a patch repair.

Confined or obstructed access: drilling out fasteners, drilling access holes and cutting out defective parts inside wing fuel tanks, wheel wells, tail cones, belly bays or on an installed engine, working overhead or lying in tight spaces with hand drills and punches.

Cabin/interior modification: reconfigure seats and seat tracks, install IFE/Wi-Fi equipment, monuments, stowages, lighting and placards to a new LOPA drawing inside the cabin of an in-service aircraft.

Bench/component-level modification in a back shop: modify a removed part or subassembly per drawing or engineering order — drill a new hole pattern, install nutplates, bushings, doublers or reinforcement angles, trim/rework and seal a panel, bracket or cowling held in a fixture on a bench.

tasks.label: Clean engines, sediment bulk and screens, and carburetors, adjusting carburetor float levels.

instances.label: Annual/100-hour inspection on a single-engine piston GA aircraft in an FBO or repair-station hangar: with cowling removed, degrease and clean the installed engine (cylinder fins, case, baffles, exhaust, accessory area) using solvent spray, brushes and rags, masking magnetos/alternator/air filter, then dry and wipe down so leaks can be spotted.

Oil and fuel system screen service on a piston aircraft in a hangar: cut safety wire and remove the oil suction/pressure screen and the gascolator (fuel strainer) sediment bowl and screen, wash the screens in solvent, inspect for metal/debris, install new gaskets, reinstall, torque and re-lockwire, then run up and leak-check.

Carburetor overhaul on the bench in a shop: disassemble a removed float-type aircraft carburetor, clean body, jets, bowl and passages (solvent/ultrasonic, air blow-out), replace gaskets and needle/seat, set the float level to the manufacturer's dimension with a gauge (bending the tab), reassemble, leak/flow check.

In-situ carburetor work on an installed piston engine, working under the cowl with awkward access: drain and remove the bowl, clean the inlet screen and sediment, verify/adjust float level and needle seating, reinstall with new gasket, safety-wire, and perform a ground run-up check.

Turbine/turboprop line or hangar maintenance at an airline or corporate operator: perform an on-wing engine core/compressor water or foam wash of an installed engine — rig the wash cart and manifold at the inlet, fit covers/plugs, motor the engine through the wash and rinse cycles, then dry-motor and restore the engine.

Engine overhaul/MRO shop: clean the disassembled engine's parts before inspection — crankcase halves, cylinders, gears, hardware, or turbine airfoils and cases — using degreasing tanks, spray washers, ultrasonic consoles or blast/waterjet stripping, then rinse and dry to inspection cleanliness.

tasks.label: Install and align repaired or replacement parts for subsequent riveting or welding, using clamps and wrenches.

instances.label: Heavy-check/MRO hangar, airframe sheet-metal repair: a mechanic positions a fabricated repair doubler or replacement skin section over damage on a fuselage, wing surface or control surface, trial-fits it to the contour, transfers/match-drills holes, and holds it with clecos, C-clamps and sheet-metal fasteners so it can be riveted. Access is often overhead or from stands, and each damage site is one-off.

Confined interior structural replacement in the hangar: replacing a cracked stringer, frame section, floor beam, rib or bulkhead fitting inside a wing box, fuel tank or fuselage interior. The mechanic crawls or reaches into a congested cavity, hand-fits and shims the replacement, aligns it to existing hole patterns, and secures it with clamps and wrenches for riveting.

Backshop/bench work on a removed component: an exhaust stack, engine mount tube, duct, bracket, cowl or fairing is set up in a jig, vise or weld fixture; the repaired or replacement piece is positioned, aligned to fit-up tolerance and clamped or tacked so a certified welder can weld it, or so it can be riveted.

Line maintenance or general-aviation shop: replacing a damaged access panel, fairing, skin patch or bracket on an aircraft parked on the ramp or in a small hangar, aligning holes to existing structure and holding the part with clamps and screws/wrenches before final fastening, often under time pressure and variable weather.

Military depot or heavy structural modification: fitting large replacement structural parts (wing skin panel, longeron, splice fitting, doubler kit) onto an aircraft or major assembly supported in jigs/stands, aligning to drilled hole patterns with locating pins, clamps and wrenches ahead of riveting or welding.

tasks.label: Accompany aircraft on flights to make in-flight adjustments and corrections.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-heavy-maintenance functional check flight on an airliner (airline or MRO): the mechanic rides the jumpseat, works the FCF card with the flight crew, monitors systems and gauges, cycles switches, circuit breakers and valves, moves through cabin, cargo hold and avionics bay to check for leaks, noises, smells and temperatures, makes the in-flight adjustments possible at altitude, and records findings so the aircraft can be returned to service.

Post-maintenance or acceptance test flight on a business jet or turboprop at a small MRO or corporate flight department: the mechanic flies along to chase an intermittent squawk (autopilot/rigging, pressurization, avionics, vibration, fuel imbalance), operates and adjusts systems in flight, replicates the fault, and decides what still must be rigged on the ground.

Helicopter maintenance test flight (EMS, offshore, utility, law-enforcement or police unit): the mechanic/crew chief aboard monitors vibration, rotor RPM, hydraulic pressures and engine parameters, tends test/HUMS equipment, makes in-flight setting adjustments and calls the iteration of ground trim-tab/track-and-balance corrections between hops.

Ride-along 'flying mechanic'/crew chief on ferry, charter or cargo flights to stations without maintenance support: accompanies the aircraft, handles in-flight problems (resets, cabin/galley/environmental systems, pack or bleed faults, securing loose items), and repairs the aircraft at the outstation so it can continue.

Flight-test or special-mission ride-along at a manufacturer, modification center or survey/air-ambulance operator: the technician aboard tends instrumentation racks and the modified systems under test, makes in-flight adjustments and reconnections to keep the test points valid, and logs anomalies.

tasks.label: Locate and mark dimensions and reference lines on defective or replacement parts, using templates, scribes, compasses, and steel rules.

instances.label: Hangar sheet-metal shop bench: mechanic lays out a flat replacement part (doubler, patch, filler, angle) on aluminum stock from an SRM drawing or shop template - establishes a datum from the stock edges, scribes trim/cut lines, bend tangent lines, rivet centerlines and hole centers to about 1/32 in, on an ordinary bench with rule, square, compass and scribe.

Shop bench: transferring an existing pattern onto a replacement part - the removed damaged skin, doubler or the mating structure is used as the template; mechanic aligns and clamps it to the new part, marks through the existing holes, then scribes reference/centerlines and edge-distance lines on the new part so the pattern matches the airframe exactly.

Maintenance hangar, work on the installed aircraft: laying out and marking on structure in place - the trim/cutout boundary at a specified offset around a damaged skin area, rivet layout for a patch, blend-out limits, or reference lines on an installed component; curved skins, overhead or confined access (wheel well, wing underside, inside fuselage), aircraft on jacks or stands.

Component/accessory or engine overhaul shop: marking dimensions and reference lines on machined or cast parts - engine case, bracket, fitting, blade or bushing - on a bench or surface plate using steel rule, height gauge, compass and scribe, to lay out machining, drilling or inspection reference datums on curved or three-dimensional parts.

Line maintenance at the gate/ramp, outdoors and under turnaround time pressure: mechanic locates a dent, corrosion patch or lightning-strike area, measures it against allowable-damage limits and marks its boundary and reference dimensions on the skin for assessment, deferral or later repair.

Cabin, cockpit or equipment bay interior: plastic film draped over seats, carpet, sidewall panels, instrument panels or avionics racks to protect them from dust, sealant, hydraulic fluid or paint while a structural or systems repair is made in a cluttered, confined interior.

Line maintenance at the gate or on the ramp: technician quickly tapes plastic film over an open panel, a damaged window or around a temporary skin/composite patch to keep debris, sealant or weather off adjacent structure, under time pressure and outdoors.

tasks.label: Clean, strip, prime, and sand structural surfaces and materials to prepare them for bonding.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Heavy-maintenance/MRO hangar, bonded repair on installed structure: mechanic locally removes paint and primer from a damaged area of a composite or aluminum skin (flap, fairing, radome, fuselage panel), masks the surrounding area, sands/abrades the bond area to the required finish, solvent-wipes, and applies bonding primer. Access is from stands or staging, often vertical or overhead; the damage geometry and location differ every time and the surrounding structure must not be damaged.

Composite or sheet-metal back shop: a removed component (control surface, access panel, honeycomb sandwich assembly, blade, duct) is on a bench or trestle; the technician strips the coating, sands the faying/bond surfaces, cleans with solvent, and primes them before an adhesive-bonded doubler or patch is laid up.

Bond shop / clean-room bench work on small parts and repair materials: doublers, brackets, splice plates and metal details are degreased, abraded or grit-blasted, chemically treated, and sprayed with thin bonding primer (e.g., BR-127 class) within the specified time window before bonding.

Prep of installed structure in confined or interior locations: inside the fuselage cabin/cargo bay, wheel wells, or inside a wing bay — cleaning, scuff-sanding and priming a small area so a doubler, bracket, insulation blanket or interior panel can be bonded. Poor lighting, limited hand access through openings, adjacent systems to protect.

Line maintenance / flight-line or small line hangar: quick surface prep for a small bonded patch, bonded repair or sealant application under turnaround time pressure, with portable hand tools, variable ambient conditions, and the aircraft parked as found.
