sources.claim: A KUKA six-axis robotic workcell at an automotive manufacturer grips automotive glass panels, inspects the primer edge with machine vision, applies urethane, and decks the panels for installation in a vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic urethaning and decking of vehicle glass in a plant cell. It links the adhesive application and the glass-setting steps in one automated cell, the same sequence a glass installer performs on a replacement windshield.

tasks.label: Allow all glass parts installed with urethane ample time to cure, taking temperature and humidity into account.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Replace all moldings, clips, windshield wipers, or other parts that were removed prior to glass replacement or repair.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Windshield replacement finished in an auto-glass shop bay on a common late-model sedan/SUV: snap the cowl vent panel back over the base of the glass engaging a row of push clips (replacing broken clips), reinstall both wiper arms on splined shafts at the correct park position and torque the nuts, refit A-pillar/roof-edge moldings and the interior mirror/rain-sensor cover, then check fit, sweep and wind noise.

Same windshield reassembly performed as a mobile job in the customer's driveway, an office parking lot or curbside: cowl panel and clips, wiper arms, exterior moldings and mirror cover reinstalled on the vehicle parked as found, on uneven pavement with variable weather, wind and lighting, tools carried from the van.

Door (side) glass replacement, usually in the shop: reseat the vapor barrier, reconnect window-switch/speaker harness connectors, hang and press the interior door trim panel onto its hooks and ~10 clips, refit the belt weatherstrip/outer molding, screws and mirror trim, then verify window travel and absence of rattles.

Back glass or quarter glass job in the shop: refit interior hatch/pillar trim panels and their clips, reinstall the rear wiper arm and nut cover, exterior reveal moldings, reconnect defroster spade terminals and the rear washer hose, reinstall third-brake-light or cargo trim.

Chip/crack repair or an ADAS windshield job where only small parts were removed: reinstall rain-sensor and camera covers, mirror cover, cowl seal and, if removed for access, the wiper arms; frequently done mobile at the customer's location.

Heavy truck, bus, RV or older gasket-set vehicle at a fleet yard or roadside: reinstall the rubber gasket locking strip, chrome reveal molding and large wiper arms/blades, often with corroded pinch welds and stiff, deformable rubber trim.

sources.system: ABB Dynamic Assembly Pack for Final Trim and Assembly
sources.title: Dynamic Assembly Pack sensors enable ABB to automate trim assembly
sources.claim: ABB's Dynamic Assembly Pack is a commercial functional module that lets industrial robots install trim parts (dashboards, carpets, seats inside the body; doors, bumpers, wheels outside) onto car bodies moving on a conveyor or AGV, using gripper-mounted vision plus force-control sensors to find attachment points to millimeter precision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic installation of exterior/interior trim parts (bumpers, doors, dashboards) onto a vehicle body in a line workstation. Transfers to refitting cowl panels and moldings after glass work: same class of clipped/bolted plastic and trim parts, same millimetre alignment against a car body, with vision and force feedback compensating for body position variation.

sources.system: Visumatic Cobot Clip Inserter (UR10 + VIM-700)
sources.title: Cobot Clip Inserter | Visumatic Industrial Products
sources.claim: Visumatic sells a turnkey collaborative cell (UR10 plus VIM-700 clip feeder) that automatically inserts plastic push clips into an automotive interior trim part held in a sensorized fixture, installing clips in a set order, monitoring insertion depth and logging each insertion to qualify the assembly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated insertion of automotive plastic push clips into a trim panel in a fixture. The clips and moldings a glass technician re-installs are the same fastener class, and the cell demonstrates seating them to verified depth without damage when the workpiece is fixtured and the clips are presented.

sources.system: Radix Controls vision-guided lug-nut fastening cell (Cognex In-Sight + robot nutrunner)
sources.title: Vision-guided robot fastens wheel lug nuts | Vision Systems Design
sources.claim: A deployed plant application by Radix Controls uses Cognex vision to locate each wheel on a roughly positioned vehicle on a moving assembly line and then drives a robot-held nutrunner into position to torque the lug nuts within about 40 seconds.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: vision-guided fastening of nuts on a vehicle whose exact pose varies. Refitting a wiper arm requires seating it on a splined shaft and torquing a retaining nut — comparable object scale, torque and pose-uncertainty handling, in an assembly-line cell.

sources.system: Innovative Automation roof ditch molding clip assembly cell
sources.title: Robotic Automation Systems | Innovative Automation
sources.claim: Innovative Automation built a production robotic cell in which a dial-table fixture holds an automotive roof ditch molding while one robot notches it and a second robot places the retaining clips into their required positions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic assembly of clips to an exterior automotive molding in a fixtured cell. Same part family (long flexible exterior molding plus snap clips) and precision as the moldings and clips replaced after glass work.

sources.system: ABB OmniVance Plastics Assembly Clipping Cell
sources.title: OmniVance™ Plastics Assembly Clipping Cell | ABB
sources.claim: ABB markets the OmniVance Plastics Assembly Clipping Cell as a standardized robotic cell that clips a wide range of automotive plastic assemblies — instrument panels, center consoles, fuel ..., door panels — together in the same production cell, using a SCARA SmartFeeder with integrated vision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic clipping of automotive plastic trim assemblies with model changeover in one cell. Shows that clip engagement across differing part geometries is handled in purpose-built cells, the mixed-model aspect of re-installing clips and moldings on varied vehicles.

sources.system: Figure 02 humanoid
sources.title: Successful test of humanoid robots at BMW Group Plant Spartanburg
sources.claim: Figure's humanoid worked ten-hour shifts for about ten months in BMW's Spartanburg plant, autonomously removing and precisely positioning sheet-metal parts into fixtures for more than 30,000 X3 vehicles.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sustained autonomous precise part placement into fixtures on an automotive production floor. Supports that dexterous part-fitting is achieved in machine-built plant settings, but only with parts presented and fixtures defined — not on arbitrary customer vehicles.

sources.system: SmartBay robotic service bay (and RoboTire tire-changing system)
sources.title: Automated Tire unveils AI robot to solve tire shop staffing shortage | Fox News
sources.claim: Robotic service-bay automation that works on customer vehicles in ordinary shops is limited to wheel and tire work: Automated Tire's SmartBay uses computer vision and machine learning ... change tires, balance wheels and inspect vehicles in a service bay with limited human oversight; no comparable system re-installs trim, clips, moldings or wiper arms.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated work on customer vehicles inside a service bay. Cited to bound the E2 claim: shop-floor vehicle robots exist only for the rigid, standardized wheel/hub interface, and nothing in this class handles flexible moldings, hidden clip receptacles or wiper linkages.

tasks.label: Remove broken or damaged glass windshields or window glass from motor vehicles, using hand tools to remove screws from frames holding glass.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-shop bay: cracked/laminated windshield on a late-model passenger car driven into the service bay. Tech removes wiper arms, cowl panel and A-pillar moldings with hand tools (screws, clips), protects paint/dash, cuts the cured urethane bead with a wire tool or cold knife around the full perimeter, disconnects rain/humidity sensor and camera bracket, then lifts the glass out with suction cups without damaging pinch weld, paint or trim.

Mobile service at a customer's driveway, street parking or office lot: same bonded windshield removal performed outdoors on a vehicle parked as found, variable ground, lighting and weather, limited access on one side, tools carried from the van.

In-shop door/side window replacement after a break-in or crack: tempered glass often already shattered. Remove door trim panel screws and clips, peel the vapor barrier, unbolt/unclip the glass from the regulator, extract remaining glass pieces and vacuum shards from the door cavity and interior.

Mobile call for a shattered back glass or quarter glass at a customer site: tempered glass in fragments with defroster/antenna tabs and a bonded or gasket-set perimeter; remove interior trim and headliner edge, cut out remaining bonded glass or gasket, and clean thousands of shards from the cargo area and body channels.

Fleet yard, dealership lot or job site: glass removal on a commercial truck, bus, RV or heavy equipment cab — larger gasket-set or bonded panes, ladders/lifts needed, mixed fastener types, vehicle positioned wherever it sits on institution-controlled premises.

sources.system: Glass Bot / QuarterMaster bonded glass removal system
sources.title: Glass Bot — Bonded Glass Removal Systems
sources.claim: The most automated glass-removal product in the auto-glass trade is the Glass Bot, a technician-mounted, remote-controlled wire-tensioning cut-out system; the human still sets the anchors, threads the wire, removes trim and lifts the glass, so no autonomous robot performs the removal.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (cutting bonded automotive glass free), but the device is a hand-placed, remote-controlled power tool covering only the urethane-cutting sub-step, so it cannot substantiate autonomous completion of the whole instance.

sources.system: Glass Bot
sources.title: Glass Bot Available for Easy Glass Removal
sources.claim: The Glass Bot has been marketed since 2007 as a hand tool alternative for windshield removal, confirming its role as a technician-operated device rather than a robot.

sources.system: Glass Bot Apex Corner Tool
sources.title: Glas Bot System Gets New Accessory
sources.claim: Accessories added to the Glass Bot in 2014 still only guide the cutting element along the glass perimeter; the system automates the cut path, not the disassembly of trim or the extraction of the glass.

sources.system: SEDA Windshield Cutter / glass removal equipment
sources.title: Windshield cutter - SEDA International
sources.claim: In vehicle dismantling, the equivalent product is a hand-held windshield cutter operated by a worker; even destructive, quality-insensitive glass removal in recycling yards is not automated by a robot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = cutting bonded windshields out of end-of-life vehicles in a dismantling facility (a purpose-built industrial setting). It is human-held and human-guided, so it shows the E1-style setting is served by manual tools, not autonomous machines.

sources.system: FANUC R-2000iA windshield priming/handling cell
sources.title: Glass Windshield Handling Robot - FANUC R-2000iA Adds Primer to Automotive Windshields
sources.claim: Industrial robots in fenced OEM cells handle and prime new windshields and apply adhesive for installation, but these cells work on unused glass presented on racks and do not cut cured urethane, disassemble wipers/cowl/trim, or handle broken glass on an in-service vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robotic windshield installation/handling in OEM glazing cells. Transfer fails: the cell handles intact new panes in fixtures, whereas removal requires perimeter cutting of cured adhesive, fastener/trim disassembly and shattered-glass handling on a used vehicle body, none of which is demonstrated.

tasks.label: Replace or adjust motorized or manual window-raising mechanisms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-shop replacement of a failed power window regulator on a common late-model car or SUV in a service bay: pry off the interior door trim panel and disconnect switch/harness connectors, peel back the vapor barrier, lower and support the glass, unbolt the glass from the regulator clamps, drill out or unbolt the regulator rivets/nuts, work the old cable-drum or scissor regulator out through the door access hole, fit and secure the replacement, reconnect, cycle and align the glass, then reinstall the panel without breaking clips.

Mobile service call at a customer driveway, street parking spot, or employer parking lot: the same regulator/motor replacement performed on the vehicle as found, outdoors, with variable light, weather and access, tools staged from a van, often on a door with broken tempered glass fragments inside the cavity that must be vacuumed out first.

Adjustment work in the shop after a door-glass replacement or a complaint of a binding/off-track window: reseating the glass in the regulator clamps or channel, squaring the glass in the run channels, setting up/down travel stops, lubricating tracks, and re-initializing the power window auto-up/anti-pinch function, then verifying smooth full-travel operation and seal.

Older vehicle, work truck or fleet van with a manual crank regulator or an early power unit: corroded or seized fasteners, rusted rivets to drill out, brittle trim clips and non-standard door internals with no factory access holes, sometimes requiring improvised fixes and refitting of a used or universal regulator.

Diagnosis and replacement of just the window motor, switch, or door module: testing switch and motor circuits, removing the motor from the regulator, installing the new motor/switch, and running the programming/normalization procedure so one-touch and anti-pinch operate to spec.

sources.system: PHA Czech door module assembly line (Rockwell Automation controls)
sources.title: PHA Czech Deploys New Door Module Assembly Line and EOL Test Stations
sources.claim: Automated supplier assembly lines build window regulator door modules (pulley riveting, drum winding, regulator and motor assembly) in a fixtured factory line - manufacture of new modules, not removal/replacement of a regulator inside an existing vehicle door.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is factory manufacture of new window-regulator modules. It does not transfer: the repair task requires disassembling a used vehicle door (trim clips, harnesses, corroded fasteners), extracting a broken regulator through an access hole and aligning existing glass, none of which this line performs; the split between automated and manual stations is also not established.

sources.system: Bluewrist 3D vision guided robotic windshield installation
sources.title: 3D Vision Guided Robotic Windshield Installation
sources.claim: Vision-guided industrial robots insert automotive glass into car bodies on factory assembly lines, in a fixtured production cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is factory windshield decking (placing new glass on a known body on a conveyor). It does not transfer to replacing or adjusting a window-raising mechanism: there is no disassembly, no blind work inside a closed door cavity, no fastener removal, and no glass-to-regulator clamping or travel adjustment.

sources.system: KraussMaffei door panel assembly/trimming robot cell (for Yanfeng)
sources.title: These Robots Can Assemble Two Vehicle Door Panels in Only 40 Seconds
sources.claim: Robotic cells assemble and clip new interior door trim panels at a Tier 1 interiors supplier's technology centre, working on new parts presented in fixtures.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is assembling new door trim panels in a fixture. It does not transfer: the repair task requires prying an already-installed panel off a vehicle without breaking clips and then working inside the door shell, which this cell never does.

sources.system: Collaborative robotic unscrewing/screw-collection cell for EoL EV batteries
sources.developer: Wuhan University of Technology / University of Birmingham
sources.title: Robotic Removal and Collection of Screws in Collaborative Disassembly of End-of-Life Electric Vehicle Batteries
sources.claim: Robotic disassembly of automotive assemblies (EV battery packs) remains research-stage and human-robot collaborative, with robots unscrewing reliably only when geometry is known in advance.
sources.transferJustification: Closest published robotic disassembly of automotive hardware. It does not substantiate this task: it is a semi-automated laboratory cell working on flat, open, pre-characterised packs, not autonomous teardown and rebuild of a vehicle door with clips, harnesses, glass and confined blind access.

tasks.label: Remove moldings, clips, windshield wipers, screws, bolts, and inside A-pillar moldings and lower headliners in preparation for installation or repair work.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mobile auto-glass job at a customer's home: technician works in a driveway, carport or on the street beside a late-model passenger car. Prep for windshield replacement means lifting/removing wiper arms (retaining nut plus taper break), unclipping and lifting the plastic cowl panel, pulling side moldings and A-pillar trim clips, and freeing the top edge of the headliner — all without cracking plastic or scratching paint, in whatever weather and lighting is present.

Mobile job in a commercial parking lot or fleet yard (office lot, apartment lot, contractor yard): vans, pickups and SUVs parked among other vehicles, uneven pavement, limited access to one side. Same prep sequence — wiper arms off, cowl and moldings unclipped, screws/bolts removed, interior A-pillar trim popped and headliner edge lowered — with parts bagged for reinstallation.

In-shop bay at an auto-glass shop: common late-model sedan/SUV driven onto a flat bay floor. Straightforward prep — wiper arms removed with a puller, cowl fasteners and clips released, retaining moldings removed, ADAS camera cover and rearview mirror trim taken off — before urethane cut-out.

In-shop job on a vehicle requiring deeper interior disassembly: A-pillar trim with airbag-tethered clips removed, sun visors and grab handles unbolted, and the headliner front edge dropped several inches to clear the glass; also encapsulated moldings and rain/light sensor brackets transferred. Requires knowing model-specific clip locations and avoiding airbag and wiring damage.

Collision-center or older/damaged vehicle: rusted or seized cowl screws, broken and missing clips from a prior repair, adhesive-bonded reveal moldings, glass shards and bent pinchweld. Prep involves extracting stripped fasteners, cutting or drilling out corroded bolts, and salvaging or substituting damaged clips.

Heavy truck, bus, RV or specialty/classic vehicle in a shop or yard: gasket-set or bolted-in glass, large chrome or rubber moldings, exterior visor and mirror brackets to unbolt, interior panels to drop; work performed from ladders or stands on a large, non-standard body.

sources.system: RoboTire robotic tire-changing system
sources.title: Discount Tire testing RoboTire system for use in stores | Tire Business
sources.claim: RoboTire's four-arm robotic cell, installed in Discount Tire stores, autonomously locates and removes lug nuts and takes wheel/tire assemblies off customer vehicles in a retail service area; this is the closest deployed case of a robot removing fasteners and parts from customer vehicles, but it is confined to large standardized steel lug nuts at a fixtured wheel hub and involves no plastic trim, clips or interior work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wheel removal from a customer vehicle in a shop. It shows robots can find and undo standardized exterior fasteners on varied vehicles in an E2 facility, but the auto-glass prep task requires damage-free release of plastic snap clips, wiper-arm tapers, A-pillar trim and a flexible headliner inside the cabin — object types, compliance control and workspace that this system does not address, so it cannot substantiate completion of the prep instance.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Automated Tire's SmartBay is a robotic service-bay machine that changes and balances tires in a standard 12-foot bay; notably it was engineered specifically to avoid unbolting lug nuts and removing the wheel, indicating that robotic fastener/part removal on customer vehicles remains the hard part of shop automation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tire service on customer vehicles in a shop bay. It is the most recent robotic vehicle-service system in a human facility, yet it deliberately leaves wheels bolted on and performs no trim, molding or interior disassembly, so it does not substantiate the glass-prep removal steps.

sources.system: DeMoBat automated battery disassembly cell (KUKA KR Quantec + Fraunhofer IPA software)
sources.title: Fraunhofer tests disassembly of disused electric car batteries with robots | heise online
sources.claim: In the DeMoBat project a KUKA industrial robot under Fraunhofer IPA control autonomously loosens screws, opens sealing joints ... on end-of-life EV battery packs inside a fenced industrial disassembly cell — automotive-component disassembly, but on fixtured packs of known geometry rather than trim on an assembled car.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic disassembly of an automotive assembly (screws, joints, cables) in a purpose-built cell. It is the best E1 evidence for robotic unfastening of car components, but the workpiece is a rigid pack presented in a fixture with a priori geometry; it does not cover wiper-arm removal, damage-free prying of plastic clips and moldings, or lowering a headliner inside a vehicle cabin.

sources.system: Survey of robotic disassembly (assessment of DeMoBat and related systems)
sources.title: Vision-Guided Dual-Arm Humanoid Robotic Disassembly of End-of-Life 18650 Lithium-ion Battery Packs
sources.claim: A 2026 survey of robotic disassembly characterizes the DeMoBat automotive work as feasible only because geometric uncertainty was removed — the packs' geometry was known in advance — underscoring that robotic automotive disassembly has not been shown on variable, as-found vehicle assemblies.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as the DeMoBat item; cited to bound the transfer, since auto-glass prep involves model-to-model variation, corroded fasteners and hidden clips rather than a priori known geometry.

sources.system: Autonomous e-waste disassembly robot demonstrator (iDEAR-type cell)
sources.title: Robots to the rescue: Automated disassembly for e-waste recycling | Tech Xplore
sources.claim: A Fraunhofer-developed e-waste disassembly demonstrator performs unscrewing, levering, cutting and extraction fully autonomously, but on small electronic products (e.g., removing a motherboard from a computer) in a laboratory/industrial cell, not on vehicle bodies or interior trim.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous unscrewing and levering during product disassembly. The objects are small bench-top electronics on a fixtured pallet; scale, reach into a car cabin, damage-free plastic-clip release on painted bodywork and handling a large flexible headliner are outside what is demonstrated, so it cannot substantiate this task's instances.

tasks.label: Install new foam dams on pinchwelds, if required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-shop windshield replacement on a late-model passenger car in an auto-glass or collision shop bay: after the old glass is out and the residual urethane trimmed, the tech cuts a self-adhesive foam dam strip to length and presses it along the pinchweld flange, butting the ends and keeping it inboard of the urethane path.

Mobile windshield replacement at the customer's driveway, street parking, or office lot: vehicle sits as parked, variable light, wind, dust and temperature; the tech kneels/leans over the cowl to press the foam dam onto the pinchweld before applying urethane.
In-shop back glass, quarter glass or vent glass replacement where a foam dam/spacer is required on a tight, curved pinchweld with limited hand access around trim clips and defroster tabs.

In-shop replacement on an older vehicle, work truck, van or RV with a corroded, previously repaired or irregular pinchweld: rust spots primed, dam trimmed and fitted around clips, notches and uneven residual urethane so it seats flat.

On-site fleet or dealership work performed in a dealer service bay or fleet yard controlled by the customer institution: several similar vehicles glazed in sequence, foam dam applied to each pinchweld to a standard procedure.

sources.system: RoboTape System for 3M Tape (Innovative Automation)
sources.developer: Innovative Automation / RoboTape (Barrie, Ontario) with 3M and Beckhoff controls
sources.title: A Tight Bond: Automated Industrial Tape Dispensing Systems | Machine Design
sources.claim: RoboTape (Innovative Automation, with 3M) is a commercial robotic system in which a robot-mounted head peels, cuts to length and presses adhesive foam tape onto parts with varying geometries inside an enclosed work cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic application of adhesive foam sealing tape to automotive parts. A foam dam is a self-adhesive foam strip laid along a contour and pressed down, cut to length with butted ends — the same object class (3-16 mm foam strip), the same millimetre-level placement precision, and the same press-and-cut motion as this task.

sources.system: Arnold Machine windshield glass assembly cell (multi-robot, 3D vision) at Carlex
sources.title: Automotive Windshield Glass Assembly - Arnold Machine
sources.claim: A Fanuc-robot automation cell built by Arnold Machine for glass maker Carlex handles automotive windshields through primer, urethane and perimeter-seal/locating-pin installation, using 3D vision to cope with glass edge and curvature variation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: installing the perimeter seal on an automotive windshield in a robotic cell. The perimeter seal serves the same dam/spacer function at the glass-to-pinchweld joint, on the same workpieces, at the same tolerance; only the substrate (glass edge vs. body flange) differs.

sources.system: SONDERHOFF FIPFG mixing and dosing systems with linear robot (FERMAPOR K31)
sources.title: Formed-In-Place-Foam Gasketing (FIPFG) Technology - Henkel Adhesives

tasks.label: Install rubber channeling strips around edges of glass or frames to weatherproof windows or to prevent rattling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Auto glass shop service bay, late-model car: during windshield replacement the tech fits the new perimeter molding/gasket (U-channel or clip-in reveal molding) around the edge of the replacement windshield, trims it to length at the corners, and seats it so the glass beds without wind noise; vehicle is a customer car of unpredictable make/model/condition parked in the bay.

Mobile service at a customer driveway, street, or employer parking lot: same job of fitting rubber channeling/molding around the edge of the replacement windshield or back glass, done outdoors beside the customer's vehicle in variable weather, light, and ground surface, with only a van's worth of tools and parts.

Shop bay, classic car, heavy truck, RV or bus: one-piece rubber gasket with locking strip installed around a windshield opening — gasket fitted to the glass edge, roped or pressed into the pinchweld flange, lock strip inserted, corners custom trimmed and sealed on a body with rust, tolerance variation, and no standard fixturing.

tasks.label: Cut flat safety glass according to specified patterns or perform precision pattern making and glass cutting to custom fit replacement windows.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop bench/cutting table: a specified pattern already exists (shop pattern library, catalog spec, or DXF) for a flat piece — heavy-truck door or vent glass, bus/RV/marine flat lite, classic-car flat windshield half. Worker lays out the pattern on flat laminated or annealed safety-glass stock, scores and breaks the shape, seams/polishes the edges and drills or notches for hardware. Indoor, controlled shop conditions.

Shop bench: the customer's old flat lite (intact but cracked, or taped back together) is used as the pattern. Worker traces its outline onto new flat safety glass, cuts the shape including radiused corners, grinds/seams the edges to match, and reproduces holes and notches. Indoor shop.

Shop bay with the vehicle present: precision pattern making from the opening itself — a street rod with a chopped top, a custom or vintage body where no glass or pattern survives. Worker makes a posterboard/plywood template from the channel, judges glass line and channel depth, transfers to glass, cuts, then trial-fits in the frame and trims/grinds repeatedly until it seats in the gasket.

Mobile/field call at a job site, farm or fleet yard: excavator, dozer, tractor or truck cab flat lite. The broken piece or a known cab pattern is available, so the worker cuts flat safety glass to that pattern on the van's bench (or cuts it at the shop from the pattern), seams the edges, and fits it to the gasket. Outdoors, variable weather and footing.

Mobile/field call where nothing survives to copy: the cab or door glass is blown out and no pattern exists. Worker measures the opening in place, makes a template on site, cuts flat safety glass, then trial-fits and trims to the frame. Outdoors, uneven ground, variable light and weather.

tasks.label: Hold cut or uneven edges of glass against automated abrasive belts to shape or smooth edges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Auto glass shop bench: technician cuts flat laminated glass to a pattern for an older car or light-truck door/vent window, then holds each cut edge against a water-fed abrasive belt sander mounted on the bench, seaming the perimeter smooth before fitting the lite.

Small or intricate pieces: vent glass, small quarter lights, mirror glass and template-shaped pieces with tight curved edges, some below 300 mm across, shaped on the belt to match a pattern and then dressed so the edge seats in the channel.

Mobile/field job at a customer's site (farm yard, fleet lot, body-shop driveway): tech trims and smooths a rough cut edge with a portable belt/edge sander set up in or beside the van, in variable light, weather and footing.

tasks.label: Cool or warm glass in the event of temperature extremes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mobile replacement job in winter (customer driveway, apartment lot, roadside), ambient near or below freezing: technician warms the new windshield/backlite (delivered cold on the van rack) and the bonding area gradually with a heat gun, warm-air blower, heated blanket or the vehicle's own heater so the glass reaches the urethane manufacturer's application window without thermal shock cracking.

Mobile job in summer heat/direct sun (glass and body panels well above 120 F): technician cools the replacement glass and the pinchweld area - moves the vehicle into shade, uses a canopy/tarp, runs the A/C, lets the glass sit out of the sun - so the glass is not too hot to prime, handle, or set when the urethane is applied.

In-shop replacement in cold weather: replacement glass arrives from an unheated delivery truck or outdoor/unheated rack storage and is brought into the heated bay to warm and acclimate (and the urethane cartridge is warmed) before priming and setting; glass must come up to temperature evenly and without cracking.

In-shop work in hot weather: glass stored in a hot warehouse or sun-exposed rack, or a vehicle driven in with sun-soaked glass, is cooled in the shaded/air-conditioned bay until the glass surface is within the adhesive's and the technician's working temperature range before install.

Chip/crack repair temperature conditioning on the vehicle (mobile or in shop): the installed windshield is warmed to drive off moisture and bring the glass into the resin's cure window on a cold day, or shaded/cooled after sun exposure so resin does not cure prematurely, before injection and UV curing.

roles.description: Diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul automotive vehicles.

tasks.label: Follow checklists to ensure all important parts are examined, including belts, hoses, steering systems, spark plugs, brake and fuel systems, wheel bearings, and other potentially troublesome areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealership or franchise service bay: technician performs the standard multi-point inspection alongside an oil change/tire rotation. Vehicle on a hoist; opens hood to check fluid levels/condition, battery, air filter, serpentine belt and coolant/vacuum hoses; underneath measures brake pad and rotor condition, checks exhaust, CV boots, steering linkage and suspension for play, tugs wheels for bearing play, measures tire tread and pressures, checks lights and wipers; records green/yellow/red results in the shop system.

Complaint-driven systematic inspection at an independent shop: customer reports a noise, vibration, leak, or rough running. Technician follows the system-specific checklist — road test, then on the lift checks steering/suspension play with a pry bar, spins and rocks wheels for bearing noise/play, traces fuel and brake lines for leaks, and on older gasoline vehicles removes and reads spark plugs and inspects ignition components.

State safety and/or emissions inspection at a licensed inspection station: statutory checklist covering brakes (often pad/lining thickness or roller-brake test), steering and suspension, tires, exhaust, glass, wipers, horn, lights, plus OBD scan; technician signs and certifies the result.

Used-vehicle reconditioning or pre-purchase inspection at a dealership or independent shop: 100+ point checklist on an unfamiliar, sometimes high-mileage vehicle — road test, undercarriage rust and leak survey, brake and fuel system, belts and hoses, spark plug/ignition condition on older cars, wheel bearing and steering play, fluid condition, with a written condition report and cost estimate.

Fleet or high-volume lane preventive-maintenance inspection (rental, delivery vans, municipal, rideshare fleets) at a fleet garage: standardized PM checklist on uniform vehicle types at high throughput — fluids, belts/hoses, brakes, tires, steering/suspension, leaks — logged to a fleet maintenance system.

Mobile inspection away from a shop: mobile technician performs a checklist inspection in a customer driveway, office parking lot, or seller's location, with no lift, jack and hand tools only, in variable weather and lighting.

tasks.label: Test and adjust repaired systems to meet manufacturers' performance specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-repair verification drive on streets around the shop to confirm objective function against spec: brakes stop straight and firm, ABS/traction and transmission shift behavior normal, no warning lamps or new codes after the fix.

Road test to confirm a subjective customer complaint is resolved after repair (clunk over bumps, vibration at speed, pull, intermittent drivability), in traffic and over varied surfaces, deciding whether further adjustment is needed.
Shop bay/alignment rack: after steering or suspension repair, measure camber, caster and toe, adjust tie rods and cam bolts to OEM spec, center the steering wheel and reset the steering-angle sensor.

Shop bay: after sensor/module/engine-management repair, connect a scan tool, clear codes, run OEM functional and actuator tests, perform relearns and sensor calibrations (throttle, crank, steering angle, ESP, ADAS camera/radar), and confirm live data within spec.

Shop bay: fluid/pressure system verification after repair — evacuate and recharge A/C to the specified refrigerant weight and check pressures/vent temperature; bleed brakes including ABS unit and leak/pedal check; cooling system pressure test.

Shop bay, under hood/vehicle: mechanical adjustment and verification with hand tools after engine or accessory repair — belt tension and pulley alignment, valve lash, throttle body clean and idle relearn, retorque of fasteners, vacuum/exhaust leak checks on an aged, corroded vehicle.

Fleet, rental or loaner check-in/check-out damage inspection at a depot, airport return lot or fleet yard: compare the vehicle's current condition against its baseline, log new body damage, tire and underbody issues, and record findings so damage repairs and chargebacks can be processed.

tasks.label: Align wheels, axles, frames, torsion bars, and steering mechanisms of automobiles, using special alignment equipment and wheel-balancing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine four-wheel alignment on a late-model, good-condition car/CUV in a dealership or tire-store alignment bay: drive onto the rack, mount targets/clamps, compensate and measure, adjust front toe (and rear toe/camber where adjustable) at clean, free-turning tie rods and cam bolts, center the steering wheel, reset the steering angle sensor, print before/after report.

Alignment on an older, high-mileage or salt-belt vehicle: jam nuts, cam bolts and adjusting sleeves are corroded or seized and need penetrating oil, heat or a torch; some angles are not factory-adjustable so aftermarket camber bolts, slotted struts or shims must be installed; pre-alignment inspection often reveals worn tie rod ends or ball joints that must be replaced before the vehicle can be set to spec.

Wheel balancing as part of tire service: each newly mounted tire/wheel assembly is placed on the spin balancer, measured, and clip-on or adhesive weights are applied at the indicated positions, then the assemblies are installed and torqued.

Vibration-complaint work on the customer's used wheels: scrape off old adhesive weights and residue, clean corroded bead seats and hub faces, run road-force measurement, decide whether to match-mount (re-index the tire on the rim), re-index the wheel on the hub, or condemn a bent rim, then rebalance and road-test.

Light truck/SUV chassis work: adjusting torsion bars or ride height before alignment, aligning lifted or heavily accessorized pickups with aftermarket control arms/eccentrics, working under a loaded chassis with long-reach tooling.

Alignment after collision or suspension repair: measure thrust angle and axle setback, check unibody/frame reference dimensions, determine which components are bent versus adjustable, straighten or refer for structural repair, then set the geometry.

tasks.label: Repair, reline, replace, and adjust brakes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Front (or all-four) disc brake pad and rotor replacement on a passenger car or light truck in an independent/dealer shop bay: vehicle on a lift, wheels off, caliper and bracket bolts removed, piston retracted, worn pads and rust-bonded rotor removed, hub cleaned, new rotor/pads/hardware installed, bolts torqued to spec, fluid level checked, pedal bedded and road-tested.

Rear brake service in a shop bay: drum reline (drum pulled, shoes, return/hold-down springs, star-wheel adjuster and hardware replaced, drum measured, brakes adjusted) or rear disc with parking-brake caliper requiring piston wind-back or electronic parking brake service mode via scan tool, then park-brake adjustment.

Hydraulic brake repair in a shop bay: replacing a seized caliper, wheel cylinder, flexible hose, steel line (cut, bend, flare, route and clip) or master cylinder, then bleeding the system by pressure/vacuum or scan-tool ABS bleed procedure, checking for leaks and verifying pedal.

Inspection, measurement and adjustment work in a shop bay: measuring pad/shoe thickness, rotor thickness and runout, resurfacing rotors on a lathe, cleaning and lubricating caliper slides and hardware, adjusting drum brakes and parking-brake cable, brake fluid exchange, and documenting findings.

Heavily corroded or difficult job in a shop bay (rust-belt or fleet/heavier light-duty vehicle): seized caliper slide pins or bracket bolts, snapped bleeder screws, rotors requiring heat, hammer or puller, drums seized to hubs, damaged fasteners extracted and threads chased before new parts go on.

Mobile brake service at the customer's home driveway, workplace parking lot or roadside: no lift, vehicle jacked and on stands on uneven or sloped pavement, limited tooling, weather and bystanders present, pads/rotors replaced and road-tested on public streets.

tasks.label: Repair, replace, or adjust defective fuel injectors, carburetor parts, and gasoline filters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: General repair shop bay: replace one or more failed port fuel injectors on a late-model gasoline engine. Tech removes engine cover, intake ducting, wiring connectors and fuel rail bolts, extracts carbon-seized injectors from the head/manifold bores, fits new O-rings and clips, torques the rail, then pressurizes the system, checks for leaks, clears codes and road-tests.

Shop bay, GDI or light-truck diesel: replace high-pressure direct injectors. Requires removing intake/valve cover or turbo piping, replacing high-pressure lines, using a slide-hammer puller on stuck injectors, cleaning the bore, fitting new copper/Teflon seals to spec, torque-to-angle, then programming injector trim codes and verifying no leaks.

Vehicle on a lift or in a bay: replace a gasoline filter - either an inline frame-rail canister with corroded quick-connect fittings, or an in-tank filter/strainer requiring the tank to be drained and dropped or an access panel cut, with fuel spill containment and a post-repair pressure test.

Shop bay, on-vehicle fuel system service: hook a pressurized canister or induction machine to the fuel rail test port/throttle body, run the engine through a cleaning cycle, replace filters or rail seals as needed, and adjust idle/fuel pressure, verifying with a scan tool and fuel pressure gauge.

Bench work on injectors already removed: mount them in a flow bench, run leak/spray-pattern and flow tests, disassemble pintle caps, filter baskets and O-rings, ultrasonic-clean and back-flush, reassemble with new seal kits, re-test for flow matching, then reinstall on the vehicle.

Older/classic vehicle or small light-duty engine in a shop: overhaul or adjust a carburetor - remove it, disassemble the float bowl, jets, needle and seat and accelerator pump, clean passages, install a rebuild kit, reinstall with a new base gasket, and set float height, idle mixture and choke by ear and with a vacuum gauge.

sources.claim: RoboTire, the most advanced deployed robotic system in US vehicle service, is installed in tire retail stores where it removes, lifts and installs wheel-and-tire assemblies on customer cars; its scope is wheels only, with technicians operating the cell and handling balancing/TPMS work.

It does not transfer to fuel injector, filter or carburetor work, which requires under-hood/underbody disassembly of varied, corroded, small-clearance components and leak-tight reassembly.

tasks.label: Align vehicles' front ends.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine front-end/four-wheel alignment in a dealership, tire-chain or independent shop bay: tech drives the customer car or CUV onto the alignment rack, mounts targets (or uses a touchless rack), checks tire pressure and ride height, then sets total and individual toe (and camber where an adjuster exists) by loosening jam nuts and turning tie-rod sleeves, centers the steering wheel, prints the before/after report and road-tests. Fasteners release with normal hand tools.

Alignment on an older, high-mileage or rust-belt vehicle whose adjusters are corroded or seized: penetrating oil, torch or induction heat, breaker bars and vise-grips on the tie-rod sleeve, frequently ending in replacing a seized inner/outer tie rod or cam bolt before the toe can be set; boot clamps and dust boots must not be twisted or torn.

Alignment done as part of, or right after, suspension/steering or collision repair: pre-alignment inspection for worn ball joints, bushings and bent parts; angles out of factory range so the tech installs shims, offset cam-bolt kits, slotted strut plates or adjustable aftermarket parts, re-measures and iterates until caster/camber/toe and thrust angle are in spec.

Alignment on a lifted or modified light truck/SUV, or a front axle alignment on a heavy-duty or fleet truck in a fleet garage: non-stock specs, adjustable control arms, axle shims/king-pin geometry, drag-link adjustment for steering-wheel centering, work performed on a heavy-duty rack or drive-on pit.

Alignment on a late-model ADAS-equipped car where the alignment must be followed by a steering-angle-sensor reset and a static forward-camera/radar calibration referenced to the thrust line, using targets set at measured distances in the calibration bay plus a scan-tool session.

tasks.label: Repair and service air conditioning, heating, engine cooling, and electrical systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Electrical system diagnosis and repair in a dealership or independent shop bay: customer car with a no-start, intermittent warning light, parasitic battery drain, or dead accessory circuit. Tech pulls codes with a scan tool, back-probes connectors, reads wiring diagrams, measures voltage drops, traces and repairs chafed harness wire or corroded connector, replaces a sensor/relay/module, reprograms as needed, verifies the fix.

A/C repair in a shop bay: complaint of no cooling. Tech performs a performance test with gauges, leak-detects with UV dye or electronic sniffer, then replaces failed components (compressor, condenser, hose, orifice/expansion valve, receiver-drier) in a crowded engine bay, recovers/evacuates/recharges refrigerant to spec with PAG oil, and verifies vent temperature.

Engine cooling system repair in a shop bay: overheating or coolant leak. Tech pressure-tests the system, removes belts/covers/hoses, replaces thermostat, water pump, radiator, cooling fan, or hose, refills with the correct coolant, vacuum-fills and bleeds air, and road/idle-tests for temperature and leaks.

Routine electrical/HVAC component service in a shop bay: 12V battery test and replacement (hold-down, terminals, battery registration), alternator or starter replacement, headlight/bulb, fuse, blower motor or resistor replacement, cabin filter, coolant top-off or refrigerant top-up service on a customer car.

Mobile or roadside/fleet-yard service: mechanic works on a vehicle in a parking lot, driveway, or fleet yard — jump-start and battery replacement, alternator swap, hose or thermostat repair, wiring fix — with variable ground, weather, lighting, and no lift.

Interior HVAC repair in a shop bay: heater core, evaporator, or blend-door actuator replacement requiring partial or full dash/console disassembly, disconnecting harnesses and HVAC ducting, then reassembly and verification of heat and airflow.

sources.system: RoboTire tire-changing system

Cited to bound, not extend, capability: lug nuts are standardized, externally exposed, and presented at a known height, whereas AC/cooling/electrical repair requires diagnosis, engine-bay disassembly, varied corroded fasteners, hoses, and connectors. Performance does not transfer.

tasks.label: Troubleshoot fuel, ignition, and emissions control systems, using electronic testing equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Check-engine-light / driveability complaint on an arbitrary customer vehicle in a dealership or independent shop bay: connect a scan tool at the DLC under the dash, pull DTCs, freeze-frame and live data, then run hypothesis-driven pinpoint tests under the hood (DMM back-probing of sensor/injector/coil circuits, lab scope, wiggle tests) to identify the failed component, connector or wiring and write up the finding.

Cylinder-specific misfire / ignition fault in the bay: identify the misfiring cylinder from scan data, remove coil-on-plug units and plugs, capture secondary-ignition or coil-current waveforms, run injector pulse and relative-compression (amp-clamp) tests to distinguish a bad coil, plug, injector, wiring fault or mechanical problem.

Fuel-supply diagnosis on a vehicle in the bay: attach a pressure gauge at the rail Schrader or an inline adapter, run static/dynamic pressure and volume tests, current-ramp the in-tank pump with a scope and amp clamp, check the pressure regulator, filter, relay and pump circuit; often requires access under the vehicle on a lift.

Emissions-control diagnosis in the bay: hook a smoke machine to the EVAP service port and visually hunt a leaking hose, canister, vent valve or filler neck under the vehicle; functionally test purge and vent solenoids; evaluate O2/AFR sensor, catalyst-efficiency monitor and EGR operation with the scan tool.

Intermittent fault that will not set a hard code: rig scope leads or a datalogger into the cabin, road-test the vehicle in traffic under the customer's complaint conditions (cold start, hills, hot restart), capture the event, then review the data to narrow to a root cause.

Mobile / fleet-yard / roadside diagnosis: technician drives to a customer lot, fleet yard or breakdown location and performs the same fuel, ignition and emissions troubleshooting with a portable scan tool, meter and pressure gauge outdoors, in weather, with no lift and limited lighting.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: end-of-line ignition-system testing. The diagnostic output — which cylinder's plug, coil or wiring is at fault, derived from electrical waveform analysis — is the same output a technician produces in a misfire diagnosis, on the same components.

tasks.label: Test drive vehicles and test components and systems, using equipment such as infrared engine analyzers, compression gauges, and computerized diagnostic devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Diagnostic road test on public streets for a powertrain/drivability complaint (hesitation, misfire under load, stalling, poor shift quality): tech drives the customer's car in traffic, loads the engine, monitors scan-tool live data, reproduces the symptom.

Diagnostic road test on public streets for a chassis/NVH/brake complaint (clunk over bumps, vibration at 60 mph, pull under braking, intermittent noise): tech drives varied surfaces, listens and feels, and localizes the fault by seat-of-the-pants judgment.

Post-repair verification test drive: after a repair the tech takes the vehicle on a short street loop or around the dealership lot to confirm the complaint is gone, no warning lamps return, and brakes/steering/shifts behave normally.

Computerized diagnostic session in the service bay: connect a scan tool to the vehicle's diagnostic connector under the dash, pull DTCs and freeze frame, stream live data, run bidirectional actuator/system self-tests, clear codes and verify readiness.

Under-hood/under-car component and system testing in the bay with meters and gauges: battery/charging test, sensor and circuit voltage/resistance checks with DMM or scope, fuel pressure, vacuum, injector, emissions analyzer or brake performance checks across a varied customer fleet.

Engine mechanical testing: remove spark plugs/injectors in a crowded engine bay, thread in a compression or cylinder leak-down gauge, disable ignition/fuel, crank the engine, record per-cylinder values and compare.

tasks.label: Test electronic computer components in automobiles to ensure proper operation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealer or independent shop bay: technician connects a scan tool to the under-dash OBD-II port of a customer vehicle, runs a global module scan and module self-tests, verifies each control module communicates on the bus, and reports which modules are operating properly.

Pinpoint in-vehicle testing of a suspect module: locating and back-probing the module's harness connector (often behind trim, under the dash, or in the engine bay) with a DMM/oscilloscope to check power, grounds, reference voltages and CAN/LIN waveforms, deciding module vs. circuit fault.

Bench or post-repair verification: a removed ECU/BCM checked on a bench with a breakout box and power supply, or a newly installed/reprogrammed module functionally verified after flashing, calibration or configuration, before the car is released.

Intermittent or condition-dependent complaint that can be reproduced by exercising the system: engine running or vehicle on rollers, running ABS/ESP/ADAS actuator and function tests and logging data until the failing electronic function is identified.

Open-ended intermittent fault only appearing on the road or under wiggle/thermal stress: technician road-tests with a logger, performs wiggle and load tests, and reasons from symptom history to localize a failing module or connection.
Mobile/fleet-yard/roadside diagnosis: technician goes to a parking lot, driveway or roadside breakdown, connects a scan tool and tests modules on a vehicle in an uncontrolled outdoor setting.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: production electrical/functional test of automotive control modules. Same objects (automotive ECUs and their connectors/circuit nodes), same output (pass/fail on proper operation), with the module fixtured and presented to the tester as an E1 setting would present it.

tasks.label: Maintain cleanliness of work area.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift floor cleaning of the open bay floor and drive aisles in a dealership or independent repair shop after vehicles are moved out: sweeping/scrubbing up dust, grit, dropped fasteners, cut zip-ties and shop dirt on sealed concrete, working around lift posts, columns and parked equipment.

Fluid spill cleanup inside a working bay: engine oil, coolant, ATF or brake fluid dripped or spilled next to and under a vehicle on a hoist, with a drain pan, tool cart, jack stands and air hoses in the way; spread absorbent granules or oil-dry, let it soak, sweep it up, dispose of it as regulated waste, then degrease the stain so the floor is not slick.

Wiping down the workbench and tool cart with rags/degreaser and putting away the tools used on the job: sockets, wrenches, torque wrench, scan tool, specialty pullers returned to the correct drawer/foam slot; staging cores, new parts and packaging; clearing greasy fingerprints and metal shavings from the bench top.

Waste handling around the bay: used oil filters into the filter crusher/drum, oily rags into the covered rag bin, drained fluids to the waste-oil tank, cardboard and part boxes broken down to the recycle bin, old rotors/exhaust to the scrap bin, take-off tires stacked or moved to the tire rack.

Periodic deep clean of the work area: degreasing built-up oil film under and around the lift, wiping down the hoist arms, jack stands, oil-dispensing reel, creeper and bench legs, pulling debris out of tight spaces between the lift posts, wall and cabinets before a shop inspection or dealer audit.

Mobile/roadside service cleanup: after a repair in a customer driveway, parking lot or roadside, gather tools and hardware off the ground, sweep or absorb any fluid spilled on asphalt, bag the trash and old parts, and load everything back in the service van, on uncontrolled ground and in whatever weather.

tasks.label: Overhaul or replace carburetors, blowers, generators, distributors, starters, and pumps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair-shop bay, light vehicle on a lift: diagnose-confirmed starter motor replacement. Tech removes splash shields/heat shield, disconnects battery, works blind above/below the engine, breaks loose corroded bolts and the battery-cable nut, swaps the unit, torques, reconnects, and verifies cranking.

Repair-shop bay: alternator (generator) replacement on a car or light truck. Serpentine belt released, connectors and bracketry removed in a crowded engine bay, sometimes intake or subframe components displaced for access; new unit installed, belt routed, charging output verified.

Repair-shop bay: pump replacement involving fluids — water pump (drain coolant, remove pulley/timing cover, scrape gasket surface, refill and bleed), in-tank fuel pump module (relieve pressure, drop tank or cut access), or power-steering pump (line fittings, flush and bleed).

Shop bench work: overhaul/rebuild of a removed unit — carburetor on a classic, collector, or small/utility engine (disassemble, remove welch plugs, clean passages, install kit gaskets/needle-seat, set float, adjust mixture) or distributor/starter rebuild (bushings, brushes, solenoid), then bench test.

Fleet or heavy-duty truck shop: replace a turbocharger/supercharger ('blower'), air compressor, or injection pump on a diesel engine — hot, oily, heavy components, oil and boost plumbing, torque-critical fasteners, engine run-in check.

Mobile mechanic or roadside/parking-lot job: starter, alternator, or fuel pump replaced on a customer's driveway or lot with jack stands, portable tools, weather and lighting as found, no lift or fixed layout.

sources.system: SmartBay

It touches no engine or driveline components.
sources.transferJustification: Nearest deployed robot in a US repair-shop bay (same E2 setting); cited to show that even the most standardized shop job (wheels/tires) is only partly automated and provides no capability for unbolting and swapping starters, alternators, distributors or pumps.

sources.system: automotive service robots (survey of RoboTire and similar point solutions)
sources.title: Robots are primed to replace auto mechanics (or are they?) | Electronics360

sources.transferJustification: Directly surveys robots for automotive maintenance and repair, the occupation and task in question; establishes absence of a system covering component overhaul or replacement.

sources.system: HRC disassembly cell (2x KUKA LBR iiwa 14 R820, nut-runner, Schunk vice)
sources.developer: Autonomous Remanufacturing Laboratory, University of Birmingham
sources.title: An experimental human-robot collaborative disassembly cell - ScienceDirect

sources.transferJustification: Turbocharger teardown is the disassembly half of a 'blower' overhaul on a fixtured bench (the E1 counterfactual for instance 4/5); cited to show the demonstrated capability requires a human collaborator and stops short of cleaning, part replacement, reassembly and test.
