sources.system: Engine Component Robotic Assembly System (oil pump housing cell)
sources.title: Engine Component Robotic Assembly System | Midwest Engineered Systems
sources.claim: Industrial robotic cells assemble new engine components — e.g. an oil pump housing assembly cell where a robot picks housings from a conveyor pallet, loads a fixture and presses parts — demonstrating E1 assembly of new, uniform parts rather than removal or overhaul of used units.
sources.transferJustification: Assembly of new pumps in a fixtured cell is the manufacturing counterpart of pump replacement; cited to delimit capability — it starts from clean, uniform, presented parts and never removes a failed, corroded unit from a vehicle, so it does not transfer to overhaul or replacement.

tasks.label: Tune automobile engines to ensure proper and efficient functioning.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled tune-up on a modern 4-cylinder gasoline car in a dealer or independent shop bay: open hood, remove engine cover and intake ducting, unplug and pull ignition coils, extract old spark plugs from deep wells, inspect them, install new pre-gapped plugs to torque spec, replace engine air filter, reassemble, clear/verify codes with a scan tool and road test.

Tune-up with difficult access or complications: transverse V6/V8 where the rear bank requires removing the intake manifold or wiper cowl, seized/carbon-welded or broken plug extraction with penetrant and extractor tools, replacement of failed coils or plug wires, injector cleaning, all on a customer's used, dirty vehicle in a bay or on a lift.

Driveability-complaint 'tune': hook up scan tool in the cabin, read codes and live data, test misfire/fuel trim, then perform the corrective physical work (clean throttle body or MAF sensor, replace a sensor or coil), apply an ECU calibration/software update, run idle and throttle relearn, and verify on a road test.

Older carbureted or distributor-equipped vehicle (classic car, light truck, small utility engine): set ignition timing with a timing light while the engine runs, set dwell/points, adjust idle speed and idle mixture screws, adjust valve lash, replace cap, rotor and plugs, and verify by ear and with a tachometer/exhaust analyzer.

Performance calibration tune of a modified engine in a tuning shop's chassis-dyno cell: strap the vehicle to the rollers, connect wideband AFR and calibration interface, run repeated power pulls and steady-state points while iteratively adjusting fuel, spark and boost maps, then validate the final calibration.

Fleet/heavy-duty scheduled engine tune in a fleet garage: valve lash and injector height adjustment or injector replacement on a diesel, ECU calibration update, forced DPF regeneration, filter changes, performed on the vehicle in an institution-run maintenance shop.

sources.system: HORIBA ADS EVO Automatic Driving System (and predecessor ADS-7000)
sources.title: ADS EVO Automatic Driving System - HORIBA
sources.claim: HORIBA's ADS EVO is a commercially sold driving robot that physically actuates a vehicle's pedals, steering and gear selector to operate the car unattended through prescribed drive cycles inside a chassis dynamometer test cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated operation of a vehicle on a dynamometer. Dyno tuning requires exactly this physical act (running the engine through load/speed points on rollers); the robot replaces the human operating the controls during the tuning pulls.

sources.system: AVL CAMEO 5 with AVL PUMA test-bed automation and engine/vehicle test-bed actuators
sources.title: AVL CAMEO 5™ | AVL
sources.claim: AVL CAMEO 5 is a commercially deployed test-bed automation/calibration product that runs Design-of-Experiments measurement campaigns on engine and powertrain test beds and optimizes ECU calibration parameters unattended, commanding the test-bed actuators (dynamometer load, throttle/actuator set points) that physically exercise the engine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated engine control calibration on a test bed. This is the same activity as a dyno tune - iteratively varying fuel, spark/injection and boost parameters at measured operating points until an optimized map is produced - performed by the test cell rather than by a technician.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Automated Tire's SmartBay is a robotic platform installed in a conventional service bay that changes tires and performs vehicle inspection with one technician supervising up to three bays; it represents the current frontier of shop-floor service robotics and is limited to wheel/tire work, not under-hood engine service.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wheel/tire service in a human service bay. It does NOT transfer to engine tuning - the work is at the wheel hub with standardized lug patterns and fixed presentation, whereas tuning requires disassembling varied under-hood packaging, handling connectors and fragile plugs, and diagnosing running behavior.

sources.system: RoboTire System
sources.title: RoboTire installs its first system at Discount Tire - The Robot Report
sources.claim: RoboTire's robotic cell was installed in Discount Tire retail stores to remove and install wheel/tire assemblies, showing that deployed automotive-service robots in human shops are confined to the wheel-off/wheel-on portion of service.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fastener removal/installation on a customer vehicle in a service shop. Transfer to engine tuning fails: lug nuts are large, uniform and externally presented, while tune-up fasteners, coil connectors and plug wells are buried in vehicle-specific under-hood packaging.

sources.system: Robotic disassembly cell for autonomous remanufacturing (turbocharger dismantling)
sources.developer: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and project partners (Journal of Remanufacturing)
sources.title: Journal of Remanufacturing - robotic disassembly as key enabler of autonomous remanufacturing
sources.claim: Research disassembly cells have demonstrated autonomous unscrewing and dismantling of used automotive components (e.g., an automotive turbocharger, EV battery packs) by industrial robots in fixtured laboratory cells, but only for single components brought to the robot, not for servicing an assembled vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous removal of threaded fasteners from used automotive hardware in a fixtured cell. It substantiates isolated sub-steps only; it does not substantiate a whole tune-up (varied under-hood access, electrical connectors, torqued plugs in deep wells, running verification).

tasks.label: Repair or replace parts such as pistons, rods, gears, valves, and bearings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Wheel/hub bearing replacement on a customer car in a repair-shop bay: vehicle on a lift, remove wheel, caliper, rotor and ABS sensor, often fighting corroded or seized fasteners, then either bolt on a hub unit or press the old bearing out of the knuckle and a new one in, torque to spec and verify no noise/play.

Cylinder-head / valvetrain work in a shop bay: remove head from an in-service engine, disassemble valve springs and keepers, replace valves, seals, guides, rockers/lifters or camshaft, lap or check seats, reassemble with new gasket and torque-to-yield sequence, verify no leaks or misfires.

Engine bottom-end repair/rebuild: pull the engine or drop the pan, remove rod caps and old rod/main bearings or a scored piston and rod, measure journals and bore clearances (plastigage/micrometer), fit new pistons, rings, rods and bearings, torque and verify oil pressure and compression.

Transmission, transfer case or differential internals rebuilt on a bench after removal: split the case, pull worn gears, synchros, clutch packs and press-fit bearings off shafts, set pinion depth/backlash and preload with shims, reassemble and road-test for noise and shift quality.

Ancillary rotating-component replacement in a shop bay: idler and tensioner pulley bearings, water pump, alternator/AC-clutch bearings, CV joints and axle shafts on the vehicle, working in a crowded engine bay around hoses, brackets and wiring.

Mobile or fleet field repair of the same components (mobile mechanic, fleet yard, roadside, farm/heavy-duty): work done on uneven ground or a gravel lot, with jacks or portable lifts, variable weather and lighting, and only the tools carried on the truck.

sources.system: Honda Manufacturing of Alabama automated engine assembly line (92 robots)
sources.title: Honda launches new automated engine assembly line in Alabama - Made in Alabama
sources.claim: A production engine plant runs a fully automated, robotic piston/connecting-rod installation process on new engine blocks in a fixtured, purpose-built line - i.e. the install half of 'replace a piston' is automated for new parts in a machine-built setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory installation of pistons/rods into engine blocks. It shares the objects (pistons, rods, bearings) and precision of the install step of this repair task, but it works on new, clean, dimensionally known parts presented by a fixtured line; it does not remove worn parts, judge wear, or handle used, carboned or corroded assemblies.

sources.system: DeMoBat robot disassembly cell (KUKA robots, Fraunhofer IPA)
sources.title: New technologies for the disassembly of electric vehicle batteries and motors - Fraunhofer IPA
sources.claim: Automated disassembly of used automotive assemblies (battery packs and electric drive units) has been demonstrated only in a research robot cell, with vision to find screws; feasibility was shown at demonstrator level rather than as a deployed repair process.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic disassembly of used automotive units. It is the closest evidence for the 'remove the worn part' half of this task, but it targets recycling of e-drive units and battery modules in a purpose-built cell, not measurement-driven repair and reassembly of ICE valvetrain, gear or bearing assemblies to service spec.

sources.system: Autonomous Remanufacturing Laboratory robotic disassembly demonstration (pin removal)
sources.title: Disassembly demonstration key to robotic remanufacturing - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Robotic disassembly for remanufacturing - including removal of press-fit pins of the kind found in internal combustion engines - is still at the level of laboratory demonstrations addressing basic uncertainty handling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic removal of interference-fit components during remanufacturing. It bears directly on removing worn pistons, gears and bearings, and shows the state of the art is single-operation lab demonstrations, not whole component-replacement jobs.

sources.system: SmartBay autonomous tire-changing platform
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The frontier of robotic automation inside human vehicle-service bays is wheel and tire service, and even that is run with an operator supervising the bays; no in-bay system replaces internal drivetrain or engine components.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic wheel/tire service in a shop bay. It shows shop-bay robots exist but are restricted to a single standardized wheel-level operation with the wheel left on the car; it does not transfer to removing calipers, hubs, heads or gearcases and replacing internal bearings, valves or gears.

tasks.label: Diagnose and replace or repair engine management systems or related sensors for flexible fuel vehicles (FFVs) with ignition timing, fuel rate, alcohol concentration, or air-to-fuel ratio malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealer or independent shop bay: flex-fuel pickup/SUV in with MIL on and a stored code (e.g., P0171 lean, P0135 O2 heater). Tech verifies complaint, hooks up scan tool, reads freeze frame and fuel trims, pinpoint-tests with DMM/scope, condemns a comparatively accessible sensor (upstream O2, MAF, TPS), removes and installs the new part, clears codes, drive-cycle verifies.

Shop bay, hard-access component: flex-fuel alcohol-concentration sensor in the fuel line under the vehicle, or crank/cam position sensor behind the engine or under the intake. Requires lift, shield/intake removal, rusted fasteners and fuel quick-connects, blind connector unplugging in tight quarters, then reassembly, torque, leak check and verification.

Intermittent driveability complaint (stumble, hard start after E85 fill) with history-only or no codes: road test with scan tool/scope recording, wiggle-testing harness and connectors, voltage-drop and ground tests, locating a chafed wire, corroded pin or bad ground; solder/heat-shrink repair or connector terminal replacement, then re-verification.

PCM/ECM failure or corrupted calibration: unbolt module, release and remate multi-pin locking connectors, install replacement, then J2534 flash/programming, VIN and immobilizer/security relearn, idle and fuel-trim relearn, and post-repair verification.

Alcohol-concentration/fuel-quality fault: confirm actual ethanol content with fuel composition test, drain and flush a contaminated tank, clean or replace the flex-fuel sensor and filter, reset the ethanol learn/calibration, refill and verify adaptive relearn.

Mobile/fleet service call: technician diagnoses and replaces an engine-management sensor on a flex-fuel fleet vehicle in a customer parking lot, yard or roadside, with a portable scan tool, hand tools and no lift, in ambient weather.

sources.system: Figure 02
sources.developer: Figure AI (with BMW Group Plant Spartanburg)
sources.title: F.02 Contributed to the Production of 30,000 Cars at BMW
sources.claim: The most advanced humanoid deployment in the automotive sector is autonomous pick-and-place of new sheet-metal parts into welding fixtures on a BMW assembly line — no diagnosis, disassembly, or fastening of used vehicle components.
sources.transferJustification: Cited as the frontier of humanoid manipulation on vehicles; transfer FAILS — the task is placing new, racked parts into fixtures, with none of the fault isolation, electrical pinpoint testing, fastener removal from a used vehicle, or connector demating this task requires.

sources.system: RoboTire System
sources.title: RoboTire Installs First Tire Changing Robots at Discount Tire Store
sources.claim: A deployed robotic system works inside human repair-shop service bays, but only removes, lifts and installs wheel/tire assemblies; it performs no fault diagnosis and no under-hood or underbody component replacement.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = tire/wheel service in a shop bay (E2 setting). Transfer FAILS: lug nuts on an exposed wheel face are large, standardized and externally accessible, whereas engine-management repair requires diagnosis plus small fasteners, fuel lines and multi-pin connectors deep in an occluded engine bay.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: AI robot changes your tires and balances them too
sources.claim: A newer robotic service-bay platform is claimed to handle tire changes, balancing and inspections with limited human oversight, but it is an unveiling of a single-purpose tire system, not engine diagnosis or repair.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = automated tire service in a dealership bay. Transfer FAILS: no evidence of diagnostic reasoning, electrical testing or removal/installation of engine sensors; autonomy is a vendor claim from a product unveiling.

sources.system: NIO 4th-generation battery swap station
sources.title: Nio CEO Says Battery Swap Station Target Won't Be Met as Focus Shifts to Next-Gen
sources.claim: Autonomous robots do remove and install a major vehicle component on customer vehicles at scale, but only through a purpose-designed swap interface with fixed geometry in a purpose-built station, with no diagnosis involved.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = autonomous unbolting/installation of a vehicle component in an E1 station. Transfer FAILS: the swap interface is engineered for machine access on a handful of known models, whereas this task needs fault isolation and removal of arbitrary, corroded, occluded sensors across many model years.

sources.system: Skill-based robotic wire-harness connector installation system
sources.title: Automotive Wire Harness Connector Installation Using Skill-Based Robotic Programming
sources.claim: Even the isolated sub-step of mating an automotive electrical connector is a research problem: a state-of-the-art skill-based robotic system reached only 76.7% success on a fixtured car door, far below the reliability a shop would accept.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robotic connector insertion, an unavoidable sub-step of replacing any engine-management sensor or module. Performance in a fixtured lab cell is well below worker quality, so the sub-step does not carry over even at E1.

sources.system: Kinetic Hubs / Kinetic Vision
sources.title: Kinetic Announces Opening of Three New ADAS and Autonomous Vehicle Service Hubs Across Phoenix and Los Angeles
sources.claim: The most robotics-forward US aftermarket service network uses AI, vision and robotics for ADAS calibration and programming, yet certified human technicians remain in the loop for diagnosis and repair.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = robot-assisted vehicle sensor calibration/programming in a service facility. Transfer FAILS: the robotics position calibration targets and run software routines while human technicians perform diagnosis and any physical repair.

tasks.label: Tear down, repair, and rebuild faulty assemblies, such as power systems, steering systems, and linkages.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steering/suspension linkage overhaul in a general repair-shop bay: vehicle on a lift, tech removes rusted/seized fasteners on control arms, tie-rod ends, ball joints and sway-bar links, presses out and installs bushings/joints on a shop press, reassembles to torque spec, and verifies with an alignment/road test.

Power-steering system repair: rack-and-pinion or steering gear and pump removed from the vehicle, disassembled/resealed or replaced on a bench, hoses and fittings renewed, unit refitted, system filled, bled and leak-tested in a shop bay.

Engine (power system) internal repair or overhaul: engine pulled or worked in-vehicle, heads/timing set/oil pan removed, worn bearings, gaskets, chains, valve components inspected and measured, machining farmed out or done in-house, engine rebuilt to torque/clearance spec, filled and run-tested in a shop bay.

Automatic transmission / transaxle / differential / transfer case: unit dropped out of the vehicle, torn down on a bench in a transmission or driveline specialty shop, clutches, seals, bearings and valve-body parts inspected and replaced, unit reassembled, reinstalled, filled and road-tested.

Smaller bolt-on assemblies rebuilt or resealed on the bench in a shop: brake calipers, CV axles/driveshafts, water pumps, turbochargers, starters/alternators, hydraulic and A/C components — teardown, clean, inspect, replace worn internals with a kit, reassemble and refit.

Field/mobile work: fleet yard, roadside, or customer driveway with no lift — assembly (e.g., steering linkage, axle, pump, drivetrain component) removed and rebuilt or swapped with portable tools, on uneven ground, variable weather and lighting, and with limited access.

sources.system: Human-robot collaborative disassembly cell (KUKA LBR iiwa 14 R820, nut-runner and gripper)
sources.developer: University of Birmingham Autonomous Remanufacturing Laboratory (D.T. Pham group)
sources.title: An experimental human-robot collaborative disassembly cell - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: The closest laboratory analogue to bench teardown of an automotive assembly is a human-robot collaborative cell that disassembles a turbocharger, with two KUKA LBR iiwa arms working alongside a human operator who performs the tasks the robots cannot; it covers disassembly only, not inspection, repair or rebuild.
sources.transferJustification: Turbocharger teardown is a bench teardown of a faulty automotive assembly, the first sub-step of this task; it shows the state of the art stops at disassembly in a lab cell and still requires a human operator, so it cannot substantiate whole-task completion.

sources.system: CAD-to-POMDP probabilistic robotic disassembly planner (research prototype)
sources.title: From CAD to POMDP: Probabilistic Planning for Robotic Disassembly of End-of-Life Products
sources.claim: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life products remains a research problem; as of late 2025 the disassembly of returned products is still performed predominantly by hand, and published systems are planning prototypes rather than deployed teardown-repair-rebuild machines.
sources.transferJustification: Directly addresses robotic disassembly of end-of-life mechanical products, the teardown step of this task, and establishes that even that step is not routinely automated.

sources.system: Robotic battery-pack disassembly line
sources.title: Automated disassembly line aims to make battery recycling safer, faster | ORNL
sources.claim: A robotic system for tearing down spent EV battery packs exists only as a laboratory demonstration line aimed at recycling; it disassembles packs to cell level but does not inspect, repair and rebuild a serviceable assembly.
sources.transferJustification: EV battery pack teardown is a modern automotive assembly teardown with comparable fasteners and connectors; the demonstration is disassembly-for-recycling only, so it does not carry over to repair and rebuild.

sources.system: Robotic EV battery pack disassembly workcell (case study on Fiat 500e pack)
sources.title: Robotics for electric vehicles battery packs disassembly towards sustainable remanufacturing | Journal of Remanufacturing
sources.claim: In a study of robotic disassembly of a production EV battery pack (Stellantis Fiat 500e), variability of real components defeated general automation and a human operator outperformed the automated solution on tasks such as connector removal.
sources.transferJustification: Same class of work (teardown of a used automotive assembly with fasteners, clips and connectors) and shows the automation gap persists even with the unit brought to a fixed cell.

sources.system: Experimental robotic cell for EV-LiB module disassembly
sources.title: An experimental robotic cell for the disassembly of electric vehicle battery modules | Journal of Remanufacturing
sources.claim: As of 2025 automated teardown of EV battery modules is still a fenced prototype cell demonstrating a disassembly process only, addressing safety and cost, not a production system that rebuilds serviceable assemblies.
sources.transferJustification: Purpose-built (E1-style) cell for teardown of an automotive assembly; it is the strongest E1 analogue found and still covers only disassembly, at prototype maturity.

sources.system: SmartBay autonomous tire-changing system
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced robotic system actually working in US service bays performs tire changing under technician supervision; no comparable deployed system tears down, repairs and rebuilds vehicle assemblies.
sources.transferJustification: Wheel/tire service in a repair-shop bay is the nearest deployed automation to this task; it handles standardized lug fasteners and a single known interface only, and does not include teardown of internal assemblies, wear inspection, part selection or rebuild, so it does not transfer.

tasks.label: Plan work procedures, using charts, technical manuals, and experience.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Disassemble units and inspect parts for wear, using micrometers, calipers, and gauges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Brake service in a shop bay: raise the vehicle, remove wheels, unbolt caliper and bracket, remove pads and rotor as needed, measure rotor thickness with a brake micrometer, check runout with a dial indicator and pad thickness with a gauge, compare to discard specs.

Engine internal teardown in a repair or machine shop: pull cylinder head/oil pan, remove pistons, rods and crank, then measure bore diameter and taper with a dial bore gauge, journals with a micrometer, bearing clearance with plastigage, deck warp with straightedge and feeler gauges.

Automatic transmission, transfer case or differential overhaul on a bench: split the case, remove clutch packs, planetaries, shims and bearings, measure clutch plate and steel thickness with calipers, endplay and ring-gear backlash with a dial indicator, bushing wear against spec.

Bench teardown of a small bolted accessory unit of a standard type (starter, alternator, water pump, turbocharger, brake caliper, hub/bearing assembly): unbolt the housing, separate parts, measure shaft, bore, brush or piston dimensions with micrometer/caliper and judge reuse vs replace.

Partial disassembly on the vehicle during diagnosis/inspection: pull valve cover or wheels, check valve lash with feeler gauges, timing-chain stretch, camshaft lobe lift with a dial indicator, wheel-bearing/ball-joint play, tread depth gauge; reassemble and report findings.

Mobile or fleet field work: same disassembly and gauge checks performed in a customer driveway, parking lot or fleet yard from a service truck, with variable ground, lighting and weather and no fixed equipment.

sources.system: AgiProbot (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology)
sources.title: AgiProbot: Automating Components Disassembly Process For Remanufacturing Purposes - DirectIndustry e-Magazine
sources.claim: KIT's AgiProbot research project runs a purpose-built cell that automates disassembly of used automotive starter motors, plus an AI inspection station (rotary table, robot arms, cameras) that assesses the condition of returned cores; difficult cores are still routed to humans.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: remanufacturing teardown and condition inspection of automotive starter motors. Same class of bolted automotive unit, same unscrewing and part-separation operations and reuse-vs-scrap judgment a technician makes on the bench, in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: DeMoBat robot demonstration platform (KUKA KR QUANTEC)
sources.title: New technologies for the disassembly of electric vehicle batteries and motors - Fraunhofer IPA
sources.claim: Fraunhofer IPA's DeMoBat project built a robot-based demonstration platform that automatically disassembles EV battery packs and electric drive units, with image processing that recognizes screws and connections and 3D-camera success checks after each disassembly step.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated teardown of automotive assemblies (battery packs, e-drive units) in a fixtured cell. Demonstrates autonomous fastener removal and part separation on real automotive units, i.e. the disassembly half of this task, at E1.

sources.system: Marposs M110 automatic gauging machine
sources.title: MARPOSS automatic measuring machine for inspection of shaft-like components
sources.claim: Marposs M110 is a commercial automatic gauging machine that loads, measures and classifies crankshafts, camshafts and transmission shafts to production tolerances in a fully automatic cycle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic dimensional gauging of the very parts a technician micrometers (crank, cam and transmission shafts). Micron-level contact gauging with pass/fail classification is the measurement-and-judgment half of this task, but only on parts presented fixtured to the machine.

sources.system: SmartBay (Automated Tire Inc.)
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced deployed shop-floor wheel/tire automation is only semi-automated: Automated Tire's SmartBay changes tires with the wheels left on the vehicle and still needs an operator for several steps, and provides camera-based brake insights rather than micrometer measurement; the earlier wheel-removing RoboTire went bankrupt.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated wheel/tire service in a shop bay, the closest deployed vehicle-side automation. It shows that no deployed system removes brake calipers or takes micrometer wear measurements on a vehicle in an E2 shop.

sources.system: Robotic disassembly systems (industry review; no single named system)
sources.title: Automation in remanufacturing: how robots are extending product lifecycles
sources.claim: Trade review of remanufacturing automation reports robotic disassembly is only beginning to emerge and that seized bolts, deformed parts and ... still block automation, with most remanufacturing work remaining with skilled human technicians.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: industrial teardown of used units. Establishes the demonstrated ceiling of disassembly automation for worn, corroded automotive cores, which bounds engine and transmission teardown judgments.

sources.system: Human-robot collaborative disassembly cell (KUKA LBR iiwa 14 R820), Autonomous Remanufacturing Laboratory
sources.title: An experimental human-robot collaborative disassembly cell - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: State-of-the-art research cells for tearing down an automotive unit (turbocharger) are human-robot collaborative: two KUKA LBR iiwa cobots with nut-runner and gripper work alongside an operator because of the variability of end-of-life cores.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: teardown of an automotive unit in a fixtured cell. Shows that even for a small unit the demonstrated cell requires an operator, bounding claims of autonomous whole-unit teardown.

sources.system: SRC engine remanufacturing process (manual disassembly)
sources.title: Reman Process — Springfield Remanufacturing Corporation
sources.claim: In industrial engine remanufacturing, complete engine teardown to individual components is still performed by skilled human personnel.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: engine teardown and inspection at industrial scale in the most structured available setting; documents that no automated system performs it, supporting E0 for engine teardown even under the E1 counterfactual.

tasks.label: Change spark plugs, fuel filters, air filters, and batteries in hybrid electric vehicles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Engine (and cabin) air filter replacement on a hybrid at a dealership or independent shop bay: release hood latch, open hood, unclip or unscrew the airbox lid, work intake ducting aside, lift out the dirty element, seat the new one, re-secure clips; cabin filter behind the glovebox.

Spark plug replacement on the gasoline engine of a hybrid (Prius, Camry/RAV4 Hybrid, Escape Hybrid) in a shop bay: remove engine cover and intake tubing, unplug ignition-coil connectors, unbolt and lift coils, extract old plugs with socket/extension from deep wells (sometimes carbon-seized), verify gap, torque new plugs to spec, reassemble.

12V auxiliary battery replacement in a hybrid in a shop bay: locate the battery (engine bay, trunk well, or under a seat), pull trim/cover, unbolt terminal clamps in the correct order, remove hold-down bracket, lift out a 30-45 lb battery from a tight tray, install and torque the replacement, reconnect vent tube, restore/re-register vehicle electronics.

Fuel filter / fuel-system filter service on a hybrid: depressurize the fuel system, then either replace an in-line filter under the vehicle on a lift or drop/open the in-tank pump-and-filter module under the rear seat, manage fuel spillage, replace seals, reassemble and leak-check.

High-voltage traction battery pack or module replacement on a hybrid in a shop bay: de-energize and pull the service plug, remove rear seat/cargo trim, disconnect HV cables and cooling duct, unbolt and extract the pack, install the replacement, torque HV terminals, verify isolation and clear codes.

Mobile/roadside service call: 12V battery or air filter replacement performed at a customer's driveway, apartment parking lot, or workplace lot, with the vehicle parked as found, variable lighting and weather, no lift or shop fixtures.

sources.system: Comau automated range-extender engine assembly line (vision-guided cobots)
sources.developer: Comau (line for Li Auto range-extender engines)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory installation of new spark plugs into bare, fixtured cylinder heads. It shares the object (spark plug) and torque precision, but not the service instance's removal of engine covers, coil connectors and used plugs from an engine inside a vehicle, so it does not substantiate the whole service instance.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced automotive service-bay robot unveiled by mid-2026 automates only tire changing, and even that is semi-automated: a human operator still removes the used tire, positions the new tire, connects the air line and mounts balance weights; it avoids lug nuts entirely by leaving wheels on the car.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine service-bay work on a customer vehicle (tire replacement). It marks the state of the art for robots working on assembled vehicles in a shop; since even exterior wheel work still needs a human in the loop, it gives no support for under-hood consumable replacement.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic wheel removal/installation on customer vehicles in a service bay; cited only as negative context on the maturity of service-bay robotics.

sources.title: Robotic Disassembly Platform for Disassembly of a Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicle Battery: A Case Study
sources.claim: A laboratory robotic cell with four industrial robots demonstrated autonomous, vision-guided, non-destructive disassembly of a plug-in ... battery pack into modules, including unscrewing jammed fasteners; it is a case-study prototype whose limitations are reported, and it covers teardown only, not installation of a replacement in a vehicle.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic fastener removal on vehicle battery hardware; cited to show the capability is research-stage, bearing on whether removal-and-replace service work could be completed at worker quality.

tasks.label: Rewire ignition systems, lights, and instrument panels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Exterior lighting circuit repair in a shop bay: rodent-chewed or corroded headlight/taillight/trailer wiring on a customer vehicle on a lift or floor. Tech traces the fault with a wiring diagram and DMM, cuts out damaged conductors, strips/crimps or solders new pigtail or splice, seals with heat-shrink, re-looms and secures the harness, refits the lamp assembly, and verifies all lighting functions.

Behind-the-dash / instrument panel wiring repair in a shop bay: remove kneebolster, trim, cluster or partial dash; find chafed wire, melted connector body, or broken terminal in the body/IP harness; depin and replace terminals or splice in new wire, repair the connector, retape the bundle, reassemble the interior, and confirm gauges, warning lamps and accessories work.

Ignition/starting-circuit wiring in a shop bay: repair or replace ignition switch harness pigtail, lock-cylinder wiring, coil or plug-wire harness, or repaired starter/immobilizer circuit wiring; includes steering column disassembly on some vehicles, splicing, security-system relearn, and start/run verification.

Add-on and accessory wiring in a shop bay: trailer brake-controller and 7-pin harness, auxiliary or upfitter lighting, remote start, or replacement lamp modules. Tech routes new wire through firewall grommets, taps or fuses circuits, crimps/solders terminals, loom-wraps and zip-ties runs to factory routing, and load-tests the added circuits.

Major harness work in a shop bay: partial or full harness replacement after collision, engine-bay fire, flood, theft damage, or on a restoration/older vehicle. Extensive removal of interior/engine-bay components, routing a new harness through the body, connecting dozens of connectors and grounds, and full functional check-out over several hours.

Field rewiring away from the shop: mobile/roadside tech or fleet-yard mechanic repairing lighting, trailer, or ignition wiring in a customer parking lot, driveway, jobsite or fleet yard, working on the ground with hand tools in variable weather and lighting.

sources.system: Dual-arm wire harness assembly system (Tampere University, Journal of Manufacturing Systems vol. 83)
sources.title: A dual-arm robotic system for automated multi-branch wire harness assembly in automotive industry - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: State-of-the-art research dual-arm robot for automotive wire-harness assembly works on a fixtured lab workbench building NEW harnesses and achieves only 55% and 73% success on two multi-branch harness processes — far below worker-quality reliability, and it does no fault diagnosis, splicing, or vehicle disassembly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic assembly of automotive wire harnesses. It is the closest robotic work to rewiring (same objects: automotive wires, connectors, tape), so its limits bound what a robot could do on the harder in-vehicle repair version of the task.

sources.system: UR5e behavioral-cloning connector insertion study
sources.title: Behavioral Cloning for Robotic Connector Assembly: An Empirical Study
sources.claim: Even in high-volume vehicle production, wire harness assembly remains largely manual; robotic work is confined to lab studies of single connector insertions on a fixtured bench with a UR5e arm.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mating automotive wire-harness connectors. It shares the objects and precision of rewiring; the paper documents that even this narrow sub-step is not industrially automated, so the full repair task is not either.

sources.system: Nissan / University of Tennessee wiring harness robot
sources.developer: University of Tennessee Tickle College of Engineering with Nissan North America
sources.title: Automotive's Automated Robot - Tickle College of Engineering
sources.claim: The most publicized attempt to automate automotive wiring is a university/Nissan prototype that inserts wires into connectors on a bench; harnesses produced held about 50 wires versus hundreds in production vehicles, and it is aimed at possible mass production years away.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembling vehicle wiring harnesses. Same wires/connectors as rewiring; the prototype status and 50-wire scale show no system can handle in-vehicle harness work at production scale.

sources.system: Robotic disassembly platform for PHEV battery pack (KUKA-based cell)
sources.developer: University of Birmingham / collaborators (MDPI Batteries case study)
sources.title: Robotic Disassembly Platform for Disassembly of a Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicle Battery: A Case Study
sources.claim: Robotic disassembly research on vehicle assemblies reports that disconnecting cable harnesses, removing cable ties and handling snap-fit connectors remain unsolved for autonomous robots, requiring destructive cutting or human help.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic removal of wiring from an installed vehicle assembly, i.e. the disassembly half of a rewiring job. Failure here shows the removal step of rewiring cannot be done robotically even in a fixtured cell.

sources.title: BMW Group deploys Figure 03 humanoid after tests with previous version - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced humanoid robots deployed in automotive plants perform sheet-metal part insertion for welding, not electrical wiring or repair work.

sources.claim: Automation that has actually reached the vehicle service bay is limited to wheel removal/refitting with robot arms under technician supervision; no service-bay system performs electrical harness repair.

tasks.label: Install, adjust, or repair hydraulic or electromagnetic automatic lift mechanisms used to raise and lower automobile windows, seats, and tops.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Independent or dealership service bay: replace a failed power window regulator/motor on a customer sedan or SUV. Tech verifies the complaint, pries off the door trim panel and pulls back the adhesive vapor barrier, unbolts the glass from the sash, supports the glass, unbolts/drills rivets on the old regulator, feeds the new assembly through the door aperture, reconnects the harness, cycles and aligns the glass, reinstalls trim without broken clips or rattles.

Service bay: diagnose and correct a power window/seat electrical or adjustment complaint without full mechanism replacement - test switch, motor, master switch, ground and module with scan tool/DMM, replace switch or motor, clean/realign glass run channel or seat track, lubricate, and perform the auto-up/anti-pinch or seat memory relearn procedure.

Service bay: repair a power seat lift/track mechanism - disconnect battery and airbag/occupant-sensor connectors, unbolt and remove the seat from the vehicle, replace the seat motor, transmission cable, gearbox or bent track, clear jammed debris, reinstall to torque spec, reconnect and clear seat-module/airbag codes, verify all axes travel.

Service bay: convertible top or hydraulic lift mechanism work - diagnose a leaking hydraulic pump/cylinder or slow top, replace pump, hoses or lift cylinder, bleed the system, then adjust top linkage, cables, latches and header alignment so the top seals and cycles correctly.

Mobile/roadside service at a customer's driveway, workplace parking lot or curbside: window regulator or motor replacement, or securing a dropped window, working outdoors from a van in variable light and weather with no lift or fixed equipment.

sources.system: Automated Tire SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced robotic system deployed in US automotive service bays performs tire/wheel changing and inspection under technician supervision; no service-bay robot performs interior mechanism disassembly or repair.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (wheel service in a repair shop). Cited to mark the frontier of shop-floor service robotics: it works on external, standardized wheel geometry with a dedicated fixture and does not involve door/seat/top disassembly, harness handling, or mechanism adjustment, so it does not transfer to this task.

sources.system: Figure 02
sources.title: BMW successfully tests humanoid robots at Spartanburg plant
sources.claim: Humanoid robots in automotive settings have autonomously performed single part-insertion steps into fixtures on a plant line, not multi-step disassembly and repair of installed vehicle mechanisms.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automotive manufacturing part insertion in a fenced/plant cell). Does not transfer: the demonstrated step is placing a new sheet-metal part into a purpose-built fixture, whereas this task requires diagnosing a fault and disassembling a used vehicle door or seat and refitting and adjusting a mechanism.

sources.transferJustification: Related task (new-component manufacturing of window regulators/door modules). sources.title: Robotic Removal and Collection of Screws in Collaborative Disassembly of End-of-Life Electric Vehicle Batteries
sources.claim: Robotic disassembly of automotive assemblies (unscrewing fasteners from EV battery packs) remains a semi-automated, human-collaborative research capability rather than an autonomous repair capability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic disassembly of used automotive hardware). Shows the state of the art is lab-scale, human-collaborative unscrewing of accessible fasteners on a fixtured pack - far short of the confined-space door/seat teardown, harness work and mechanism adjustment this task requires.

tasks.label: Conduct visual inspections of compressed natural gas fuel systems to identify cracks, gouges, abrasions, discoloration, broken fibers, loose brackets, damaged gaskets, or other problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Triennial/after-incident detailed CNG fuel system inspection on a heavy-duty vehicle (transit bus, refuse truck, Class 8 tractor) with roof- or back-of-cab cylinder packs, in a fleet maintenance garage. Technician uses ladder/roof access, removes shields, covers and access panels, inspects 4-10 composite cylinders over all surfaces (mirrors/lights for undersides), straps, brackets, high-pressure lines, fittings, PRDs and vent tubes; classifies gouges/abrasions/broken fibers by damage level, documents findings and affixes an inspection label.

Detailed CNG fuel system inspection of a light- or medium-duty vehicle (bi-fuel pickup, van, shuttle) on a lift in a shop bay: remove tank shields and access panels, inspect underbody- or cargo-mounted cylinder(s) all around for cracks, gouges, discoloration and broken fibers, check brackets/straps, gaskets, high-pressure lines and fittings, perform leak check, document and label.

Routine visual check of readily accessible, exposed CNG fuel system components on the underbody and exterior of a light-duty CNG van or pickup during a PM or pre-service walkaround in a shop bay - no shields or panels removed: look for chafed or cracked fuel lines, loose or corroded brackets, damaged shields, discoloration and evidence of leaks.

Same routine PM-level check but extending to engine-bay CNG plumbing (regulator, high-pressure lines, fittings, gaskets) under an opened hood, plus a soap-solution or electronic methane leak check of joints.

Damage-triggered inspection after a collision, fire exposure, dropped/struck cylinder or reported gas odor, at a fleet garage or body shop: judgment-heavy assessment of cylinder and system condition against CGA C-6.4 damage levels, often requiring partial removal of cylinders or components for bench inspection and a condemn/return-to-service decision.

Mobile/field inspection at a customer yard, remote depot, fueling site or roadside: inspector travels to vehicles parked outdoors on uneven ground in variable weather and lighting, works from a ladder or on the ground with hand tools and a flashlight to inspect cylinders, shields, brackets and lines.

It substitutes for the technician's eyes on the same class of objects (lines, brackets, shields, fasteners) at similar scale, so it transfers to the accessible-component portion of a CNG fuel system visual check, though it cannot open shields or engine bays.

tasks.label: Repair or rebuild transmissions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: General repair shop / dealership: remove and replace a failed automatic transmission in a customer vehicle. Vehicle on a lift; disconnect battery, shift cable, wiring harnesses, cooler lines, driveshaft/axles, exhaust and crossmember; unbolt torque converter through the inspection window and bellhousing bolts; lower on a transmission jack; swap over sensors/mounts; install reman unit, refill, relearn adaptives, road test.

Shop bay: in-vehicle repair of transmission components without full removal — valve body or solenoid pack replacement, shift solenoids, speed sensors, pan/filter and fluid, output-shaft and pan gasket leaks, mount and linkage replacement, plus scan-tool adaptation reset and road-test verification on a wide mix of makes and mileages.

Transmission specialty shop bench overhaul: tear down a used automatic unit on a rebuild stand, clean and air-check circuits, inspect gears, bushings, pump and drums for wear, measure clutch clearance and end play, select shims/steels, replace clutches, bands, seals and hard parts, reassemble to spec, then dyno or road test.

Shop bay: manual transmission/transaxle work — remove the gearbox to replace clutch kit, flywheel, pilot and throw-out bearings; or bench work replacing synchros, bearings and shift forks inside the case; reinstall, bleed hydraulics, verify shift quality.

Awkward or off-site variants: heavy 4WD pickups, vans and body-on-frame vehicles with rusted fasteners and tight access, or fleet/mobile service performed in a customer yard, parking lot or roadside where the vehicle is jacked on uneven ground and tooling is limited.

sources.system: Symbio Robotics SymbioDCS-controlled six-axis robots on Ford transmission assembly line
sources.title: Artificial Intelligence Enables Robots to Assemble Transmissions | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: Six-axis industrial robots, guided by Symbio's AI software, assemble new automatic transmissions (including installing heavy components such as torque converters) on a fenced production line at Ford's Livonia transmission plant.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory assembly of NEW transmissions from known parts in dedicated fixtures. Transfer to 'repair or rebuild transmissions' does not hold: it omits removal from a vehicle, teardown of a contaminated used unit, wear inspection, clearance measurement and selective part replacement, and it depends on part presentation designed for the cell.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced automotive service-bay automation unveiled as of May 2026 changes tires with the wheels still on the vehicle and is only semi-automated: a human operator must remove the used tire, position the new one, connect the air line and mount balance weights.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine under-vehicle service work (tire replacement) in a repair-shop bay. It is far simpler than transmission repair — no fastener removal, no diagnosis, no internal component work — yet still requires a human for several steps, bounding what shop robots can do today.

sources.system: Robotic disassembly systems for remanufacturing (literature survey)
sources.developer: authors of 'Redefining End-of-Life: Intelligent Automation for Electronics Remanufacturing Systems' (arXiv)
sources.title: Redefining End-of-Life: Intelligent Automation for Electronics Remanufacturing Systems
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed/preprint survey of remanufacturing automation states that disassembly of used products remains the hardest, bottleneck stage for automation because returned units vary and their condition is uncertain; robotic disassembly systems are still research-stage rather than deployed production equipment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated teardown of used products in remanufacturing, the core of a transmission rebuild. The survey shows the state of the art is experimental cells for simpler products, with no deployed system tearing down and rebuilding used powertrain units.

tasks.label: Rebuild parts, such as crankshafts and cylinder blocks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Short-block / engine rebuild in a repair shop bay: tear down a used engine (corroded, seized or over-torqued fasteners, varied engine families), degrease and clean parts, inspect and measure bores, journals and deck for wear, deglaze or hone cylinders, fit new bearings, rings and pistons, check clearances with Plastigage/micrometer, torque main and rod caps in sequence, verify the assembly turns freely.

Machine-shop reconditioning of a cleaned cylinder block: locate and bore cylinders to the next oversize (or sleeve), deck the block flat, hone to final bore size and crosshatch finish on shop boring/honing machines, verify size with bore gauge.

Crankshaft reconditioning in the machine shop: inspect a used crank for cracks and straightness, mike the mains and rod journals, set it up in a crankshaft grinder and grind journals to a uniform undersize, chamfer oil holes, polish journals, re-check size and taper.

Cylinder head rebuild / valve job: disassemble the used head (spring compressor, keepers, seals), clean and pressure-test, replace worn guides and seals, cut or grind valve seats and valve faces, check concentricity and seal, reassemble springs/retainers/keepers and check installed height.

Bench rebuild of used subassemblies in the shop: brake calipers and master cylinders (hone bore, new seals/pistons), differentials (set pinion depth, backlash, preload with shims), transfer cases and manual transmissions, starters/alternators, water pumps and hydraulic units — teardown, inspect, replace worn parts, reassemble and test.

Reconditioning rotating friction surfaces on shop machine tools: resurface brake rotors and drums on a bench lathe and machine flywheels/pressure plate surfaces to spec, checking thickness, runout and finish against minimum-thickness limits.

sources.claim: Rottler's H85AXY CNC vertical honing machine hones all cylinders of a complete V-block, including automatic rollover of the block, in an unattended automatic cycle — the honing step of rebuilding a cylinder block.

sources.system: Hengga brake disc automatic production line

sources.system: Robotic disassembly research (University of Birmingham / RECODE programme)
sources.title: Robotic disassembly and remanufacturing automation (IEEE)
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed robotics work as of 2022 characterizes disassembly of used products (the first step of any rebuild) as still hard to automate because returned cores vary in condition and require dexterous, contact-rich manipulation; published demonstrations remain lab-scale (e.g., robotized removal of press-fitted pins).
sources.transferJustification: Teardown of a used engine, head, caliper or differential is exactly the disassembly step this literature evaluates; it establishes that no fielded robotic system performs it.

tasks.label: Retrofit vehicle fuel systems with aftermarket products, such as vapor transfer devices, evaporation control devices, swirlers, lean burn devices, and friction reduction devices, to enhance combustion and fuel efficiency.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Independent repair/speed shop: customer's used car on a lift or with hood open; tech installs a bolt-on air/fuel enhancement device (e.g., intake 'swirler'/vortex insert, fuel-line magnet/inline device) — loosen clamps, remove intake tube or fuel hose section, fit device, re-clamp, check for vacuum/fuel leaks, clear codes, test drive.

Dealer or independent shop: retrofit of evaporative-emissions/vapor-transfer hardware (aftermarket charcoal canister, vapor transfer valve and hose kit, purge solenoid) — route hoses under hood and along underbody, secure clamps and brackets, splice or plug electrical connectors, then smoke-test the EVAP system and verify no DTCs.

Fleet maintenance facility: same efficiency retrofit kit (inline fuel device, lean-burn/fuel-management module, friction-reduction device) installed across a run of near-identical vans or light trucks, one vehicle at a time on a bay lift, with pre/post fuel-economy documentation.

Specialty conversion shop: larger fuel-system retrofit such as an LPG/CNG or lean-burn conversion kit — mount tank/regulator, run fuel lines and fittings, tee into existing fuel and vacuum lines, mount and wire the controller, leak-test and calibrate on a scan tool.

Mobile/roadside mechanic: installs a bolt-on fuel-saving device in a customer's driveway, parking lot, or job site — no lift, uneven ground, weather, tools carried in a van, vehicle condition unknown until arrival (rust, prior modifications).

tasks.label: Use handtools, such as screwdrivers, pliers, wrenches, pressure gauges, or precision instruments, as well as power tools, such as pneumatic wrenches, lathes, welding equipment, or jacks and hoists.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-bay component removal and replacement on a truck or bus in a fleet/dealer shop: alternator, water pump, air compressor, injectors, turbo, starter. Mechanic works in a crowded engine bay or under the chassis, breaks loose corroded/seized fasteners with hand and pneumatic wrenches, disconnects hoses, harness connectors and clamps, scrapes gaskets, installs the new part and torques to spec.

Wheel-off/wheel-on service in the shop: truck raised on a lift or jacks, pneumatic impact wrench used to remove lug nuts on hub-piloted dual wheels, heavy wheel-and-tire assemblies pulled and reinstalled (rotations, replacement of pre-mounted assemblies, wheel removal for access), lug nuts torqued in sequence to 450-500 ft-lb.

Tire and brake system work beyond wheel R&R: demounting/mounting a 22.5 in. truck tire on the rim with a heavy-duty changer and bars, plus brake jobs - pulling drums or rotors, replacing shoes/pads, S-cam bushings, slack adjusters, wheel seals, adjusting and measuring lining.

Bench or stand overhaul of a used unit: tearing down an engine, cylinder head, transmission, injector or hydraulic pump; cleaning carbon and corrosion; measuring wear with micrometers, dial bore gauges, feeler gauges and pressure gauges; honing/lapping; reassembling with torque wrench to spec and pressure-testing.

Welding, cutting and grinding repair: welding cracked brackets, mounts, exhaust and frame members, torch-cutting and grinding, fabricating and fitting reinforcement plates. Much of it done in position on the vehicle; some on removable parts clamped at a bench or table.

Mobile/roadside service call: technician works on the shoulder, at a customer yard, or under a trailer in the field with a service-truck tool kit - changing a wheel, replacing an air line or brake chamber, chasing an electrical fault, jump starting - in traffic, weather and uneven ground.

tasks.label: Inspect brake systems, steering mechanisms, wheel bearings, and other important parts to ensure that they are in proper operating condition.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Periodic-maintenance / DOT-style annual inspection of a Class 8 tractor or trailer in a fleet shop bay, on a lift or over a pit: measure drum-brake lining thickness through the inspection port, check drums for cracks/heat checking, measure pushrod applied stroke at 90-100 psi on each chamber, check slack adjusters, air lines and chambers for chafing/leaks, check steering gear, drag link, tie-rod ends and kingpins for play, check hub oil level/seal leakage and wheel-bearing endplay, and write up defects.

Complaint-driven diagnostic inspection in the shop (driver reports pulling brakes, wander, growl or hot hub): road test, jack an axle, rock the wheel top-and-bottom and side-to-side, use a pry bar on kingpins and tie rods while a second person turns the wheel, sometimes pull a drum or hubcap to inspect bearings and seals, then determine the cause.

Wheel-off component inspection during a brake reline or hub service: examine removed drums/rotors for scoring, cracks and out-of-round, measure drum ID, inspect S-cam bushings, springs and backing plate, inspect greasy used bearing cones, cups and races for spalling, brinelling and discoloration, check the seal and spindle, and decide reuse vs. replace.

Scheduled inspection of a transit or school bus at an agency garage inspection lane/pit on a standardized fleet: brake lining and stroke checks, air system leak-down and low-pressure warning test, steering play at the wheel, suspension and wheel-end checks, recorded on the agency's PM form.

Quick screening/intake condition check of a unit entering the yard or shop: walkaround and drive-through look at tires, visible brake components and hub-end leakage, undercarriage damage, air leaks and missing parts, generating a defect list that decides whether the unit goes to a bay.

Field or roadside inspection: mobile technician at a customer's gravel yard, a truck stop, a construction site or the highway shoulder crawls under the unit with a flashlight and creeper to check brakes, steering linkage and wheel ends, often in weather, mud and poor lighting.

tasks.label: Raise trucks, buses, and heavy parts or equipment using hydraulic jacks or hoists.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fleet or dealer heavy-truck shop: technician drives a Class 6-8 straight truck or tractor into a bay and raises it on a permanent lift (in-ground, four-post drive-on, or two-post frame-engaging), positioning adapters/arms at the frame lift points, raising to working height and engaging the mechanical locks before PM service or under-vehicle repair.

Shop floor without a full lift: technician rolls a hydraulic floor jack or places a bottle jack under an axle, spring seat, or frame rail of a loaded or partly loaded truck, raises one corner or one axle, chocks the remaining wheels and sets jack stands for wheel, brake, hub or suspension work.

Component handling in the shop: rigging chains/slings or a transmission jack, engine hoist, jib or overhead bridge crane to lift a heavy part (engine, transmission, differential, drive axle, battery pack, dual wheel/tire assembly) out of or onto a truck and set it on a stand or bench, working in tight clearance around the chassis.

Component handling in the shop where the part is a standardized, precisely located module (e.g., a swappable battery pack, a complete wheel assembly, an engine on a pallet) lifted at fixed attachment points with a hoist and set into a cradle or rack.

Transit or motorcoach garage: raising a full-size 12-18 ton bus with a set of four to six portable mobile column lifts positioned at each wheel (or in-ground piston hoists), synchronizing the columns and setting stands before under-bus work.

Field/roadside service call: jacking a loaded truck or trailer on a highway shoulder, gravel yard or customer site with a bottle or air jack on uneven, unprepared ground, chocking wheels and cribbing to raise an axle for a tire, wheel-end or brake repair.

tasks.label: Adjust and reline brakes, align wheels, tighten bolts and screws, and reassemble equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fleet or dealer truck shop: relining/replacing brakes on a tractor or trailer axle — chock and lift the unit, pull the wheel/tire assemblies and brake drums, remove worn, road-grimed S-cam shoes, return springs, anchor pins and rollers, install relined shoes and hardware, repack/replace wheel seals, reassemble hub and drum, remount wheels, and set the slack adjuster; also includes air-disc pad and rotor changes on newer tractors and transit buses in a depot bay.

Scheduled PM/DOT inspection service in a shop bay with the truck or bus on a lift or over a pit: measure and adjust air-brake pushrod stroke/slack adjusters, re-torque U-bolts, spring hangers, driveline and exhaust fasteners found loose, replace missing bolts, and reassemble guards, shields, panels and covers before release.

Reassembly of a major component after overhaul in the shop: an in-frame or out-of-frame diesel engine rebuild on a stand (pistons and cylinder liners installed, cylinder head set and head bolts torqued in sequence and angle, manifolds, covers, accessories refitted), or a transmission/differential put back together to torque spec.

Wheel-off service in the shop: removing and reinstalling heavy truck/bus wheel and tire assemblies (steel or aluminum, 100-250 lb) on hub-piloted studs, running up and torquing 10 lug nuts to 450-500 ft-lb in a cross pattern, and re-torque after road test.

Wheel alignment work in a shop alignment bay: setting steer-axle toe (and checking camber/caster, adding shims) on a tractor or bus with laser/computerized alignment heads, and squaring drive or trailer axles by adjusting torque rods or slider alignment on a used, often corroded chassis.

Mobile/roadside service call: a service truck responds to a disabled tractor-trailer on a highway shoulder, truck stop lot or customer yard — adjust brakes, replace a brake chamber or slack adjuster, tighten loose fasteners and reassemble components in the open, in traffic, weather and mud, with only what is on the service truck.

tasks.label: Attach test instruments to equipment, and read dials and gauges to diagnose malfunctions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fleet or dealer truck shop bay: a Class 8 tractor comes in with a driver complaint or lit dash lamp. Mechanic opens the cab, plugs a laptop/scan tool into the 9-pin J1939 (or OBD) connector under the dash, pulls active and inactive fault codes, runs guided diagnostic routines and actuator/cylinder cutout tests, and interprets live data to identify the failing component.

Electrical diagnosis in the shop: mechanic attaches DMM leads, clamp ammeter, or oscilloscope probes to batteries, starter/alternator circuits, ground straps, sensor and ECU harness connectors (often back-probing seals in a cramped, greasy engine bay or under the dash), runs voltage-drop, load and waveform tests and reads the meter to isolate an open, short, or failing sensor.

Pressure/flow instrumentation on the vehicle: threading gauges or transducers into fuel filter housing / rail test ports, hooking air-brake test gauges to service and supply lines, fitting a cooling-system pressure tester, hydraulic gauges on a PTO circuit, exhaust backpressure or turbo boost taps; running the engine or charging the air system and reading the dials against spec to diagnose the fault.

Off-vehicle bench or test-stand work in the shop: removed injectors on an injector/pop test bench, starter or alternator on a bench tester, turbo or air compressor checked on a stand, or a rebuilt diesel engine rigged onto a dynamometer test stand with instrumentation for a run-in and performance check.

Mobile/field service call: technician drives a service truck to a roadside shoulder, customer yard, quarry or construction site, works outdoors in weather with limited light and awkward access, hooks up a scan tool and gauges to a disabled bus or truck to determine whether it can be repaired on the spot or must be towed.

Like the mechanic's task, the machine must couple instrumentation/media lines to an engine's ports and take running measurements to judge whether the unit is faulty; the workpiece (a diesel engine) and the fluid/pressure connections are the same class of objects the mechanic connects gauges to, but the engine is presented fixtured on a pallet.

sources.system: KS Engineers engine test beds (carousel/pallet system with automatic docking)

tasks.label: Perform routine maintenance such as changing oil, checking batteries, and lubricating equipment and machinery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled PM ('A'/'B' service) on a Class 8 tractor in a fleet maintenance shop: truck driven into a bay or onto a lift, engine oil drained (10-14 gal) via drain plug, spin-on oil and fuel/water-separator filters removed and replaced to torque, sump refilled and level verified, 20-40 chassis grease fittings (kingpins, tie-rod ends, driveline U-joints, slack adjusters, fifth wheel) greased until purge, batteries load-tested and terminals cleaned, coolant/DEF/washer topped off.

Transit or school bus PM in a municipal/contractor bus garage, worked from a pit or lift: large-sump engine oil and filter change, transmission/hub fluid checks, lubrication of door, suspension and chassis fittings, battery-compartment slide-out inspection and load test, fluid top-offs, all on a fixed fleet of a few bus models on a mileage-based schedule.

Field/mobile routine service by a lube or service truck at a customer yard, quarry, or jobsite: oil and filter change plus full grease-up of a vocational truck, dump truck, or off-road diesel machine, done outdoors on uneven ground with the machine parked where it stopped, variable weather, dirt and mud, no lift.

Battery service in the shop: pulling the battery box cover or slide-out tray on a truck or bus, load-testing 2-4 group-31 batteries, cleaning corroded terminals and tightening cable clamps, and lifting out and replacing failed 60-70 lb batteries, then verifying charging-system output.

Scheduled lubrication-only service: greasing every lube point on a tractor, trailer, or piece of equipment (kingpin, fifth wheel plate, spring pins, S-cam bushings, slack adjusters, landing gear, bogie slider) at the required interval, with no fluid change involved.

sources.system: RoboTire tire-changing system
sources.title: RoboTire installs system at Detroit Garage - The Robot Report
sources.claim: RoboTire's autonomous tire-changing system, using a six-axis arm with vision, gripper and torque wrench, is installed and operating in retail tire service bays (Discount Tire, Detroit Garage), changing four tires on customer vehicles in about 25 minutes.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wheel/tire replacement on customer vehicles in a human service bay. It is the closest deployed robot doing fastener work on arbitrary vehicles in a shop, and it shows the current frontier: a fixed arm servicing one standardized, outward-facing interface (lug nuts at a known hub) after a VIN lookup. It does not reach under a chassis, does not remove drain plugs or seized spin-on oil filters, does not handle hot waste oil, and does not couple a grease gun to dozens of varied zerk fittings, so it does not substantiate completion of a PM oil-change/lube service.

sources.system: Robotic Fuelling System (RFS)

tasks.label: Examine and adjust protective guards, loose bolts, and specified safety devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Annual DOT/FMCSA periodic inspection and PM service on a tractor or straight truck in a fleet maintenance bay: walk-around and under-vehicle examination of protective guards (splash guards/mud flaps, fan and belt guards, driveline/PTO shields, heat shields), safety devices (lights, mirrors, horn, wipers, seat belts, reflectors, emergency kit, underride guard) and fasteners; tighten loose bolts, re-secure or realign guards, and adjust devices as defects are found on a dirty, corroded in-service vehicle.

School bus or transit bus safety-device check and adjustment in a district/transit garage: operate and adjust emergency exit doors, hatches and buzzer switches, stop arm and crossing gate linkages, handrails and barriers, wheelchair lift interlocks and gates; tighten seat, barrier and handrail bolts to spec and re-adjust switch travel until each device passes the state inspection checklist.

Wheel-end fastener service on a lifted truck or bus in a shop bay: check wheel nuts on all positions including inner duals for looseness, re-torque to specification after a wheel-end or brake job, and flag stretched or damaged studs.

Post-repair fastener/torque verification on chassis and driveline in a shop bay: spring U-bolts, driveshaft flange bolts, exhaust and air-intake clamps, bumper and rear underride guard bolts, battery box and fuel tank straps; locate the specified fasteners under the vehicle on a lift and torque them to spec.

Engine and accessory guard/safety-device work on a truck or a stationary/marine diesel: fit, align and secure fan shroud, belt guard, coupling or PTO guard and heat shields so they clear rotating parts, and verify engine protection/shutdown devices and emergency stops operate; bend or shim brackets as needed.

Roadside or field service call: mobile mechanic at a roadside, customer yard or job site secures a dragging mud flap, loose heat shield or guard, tightens fasteners found loose, and checks the affected safety devices so the vehicle can be released to service, in weather and without lift access.

tasks.label: Inspect, test, and listen to defective equipment to diagnose malfunctions, using test instruments such as handheld computers, motor analyzers, chassis charts, or pressure gauges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fleet or dealer shop bay: a Class 8 truck or transit bus comes in with a fault lamp, derate or driveability complaint. Tech connects a laptop/handheld diagnostic computer to the J1939/OBD port, pulls active and inactive codes, runs guided/bidirectional tests, probes circuits with a multimeter, and isolates the root cause (sensor, harness, injector, aftertreatment, ECM).

Shop bay, engine-internal mechanical/performance fault: knock, misfire, rough running, low power, excess blowby. Tech listens with a stethoscope, does cylinder cut-out tests, hooks up pressure gauges (oil, fuel rail, boost, crankcase) and interprets the readings to identify the failed internal component.

Shop or depot lane condition check on a truck/bus: hunting fluid leaks (oil, coolant, fuel), air-system leaks with the system charged, undercarriage damage, corrosion, tire wear and mismatches; output is a defect list for the write-up.

Scheduled PM service or DOT/FMCSA annual inspection in a fleet shop: full checklist with measurements - brake lining thickness, pushrod stroke, air loss rate, steering/kingpin play, exhaust and frame checks, lights - plus a road test to confirm complaints.

Roadside or on-site breakdown: mobile service tech diagnoses a no-start, air leak, DPF derate or electrical fault on a shoulder, in a customer yard, quarry or jobsite, with a handheld computer, gauges and hand tools, in weather and with no lift.

Component-level bench diagnosis in the shop after removal: injectors on a fuel-injection test bench, turbocharger, starter/alternator on a tester, or an engine on a stand/dyno; run the test cycle and judge pass/fail and failure mode.

sources.system: KUKA fully automated cold test stand (BMW Hams Hall)
sources.title: Fully automated cold test stand | KUKA Global
sources.claim: KUKA built fully automated cold-test benches at BMW's Hams Hall engine plant that automatically make mechanical and electrical connections to the engine (intake, exhaust, oil chamber, all sensors/actuators, ECU), run the test, and detect faults in valve-train and camshaft noise using laser and microphone systems.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: end-of-line engine cold test. It is the same act as the human task - connecting test instrumentation to an engine, motoring it, and listening/measuring to identify which internal component is at fault - on the same class of object (an assembled combustion engine), but in a purpose-built fixtured cell.

sources.system: Polytec laser vibrometer engine cold test / injector test

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated NVH fault identification on fixtured engines and injectors. The diagnosed fault modes (camshaft damage, valve clearance, high-pressure pump faults, injector performance) are the same ones a diesel technician chases by ear and with gauges.

sources.claim: Siemens Simcenter Anovis is an end-of-line sound/vibration test system that automatically identifies anomalies and performs pass/fail checks on engines (cold and hot test), turbochargers and transmissions on production test benches.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated acoustic/vibration fault detection on powertrain units in fixtured test benches; the same 'listen to the running unit and name the defect' function as the technician, applied to engines and turbochargers.
