tasks.label: Rewire ignition systems, lights, and instrument panels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Fleet maintenance shop bay: tractor or trailer with inoperative marker/tail/turn lights from chafed or corroded wiring. Tech probes circuits with a test light/multimeter, locates the fault along frame rails or in the trailer nose box, cuts out the damaged section, strips, crimps or solders and heat-shrinks splices, re-routes and clips/ties the harness, then verifies all lamps and flash rates.

In-cab instrument panel work: remove dash trim, gauge cluster, and knee bolster; trace broken or shorted wires behind the dash by blind reach in a confined footwell; replace a damaged connector body or terminal pin, run new lead(s) through grommets to a switch, gauge, or body controller; reassemble the dash and confirm all gauge/telltale function.

Ignition/starting-circuit rewiring in a shop bay: replace ignition switch wiring, start relay/solenoid leads, or heavy-gauge battery cables and ground straps in the engine bay and along the frame. Includes cutting cable to length, installing and crimping lugs, cleaning corroded terminals, torquing studs, loom and tie-down, then crank and voltage-drop testing.

Mobile/roadside repair at a customer yard or highway shoulder: rewire a trailer 7-way plug, ABS power lead, or a torn light harness outdoors on gravel or pavement, in weather, with the truck at whatever angle it stopped, using hand tools from a service truck; splice, seal, secure, and test before the unit rolls.

Bench and retrofit work in the shop: fabricate or modify a harness for an LED lighting conversion, auxiliary lamps, or a replacement instrument panel circuit — measure and cut wire, strip, crimp terminals into connector housings, loom and tape — then install the finished harness in the bus or truck, route it through the firewall, connect and test.

sources.system: Dual-arm wire harness assembly system (Tampere University, task-level programmed dual-arm robot)
sources.developer: Tampere University (Malvido Fresnillo et al., Journal of Manufacturing Systems)
sources.title: A dual-arm robotic system for automated multi-branch wire harness assembly in automotive industry
sources.claim: State-of-the-art autonomous dual-arm robotic wire-harness assembly, run on a fixtured assembly platform in a lab/industrial testbed, completes complex multi-branch harness routing only 55-73% of the time — far below acceptable shop-repair reliability, and only for building new harnesses rather than repairing installed ones.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is factory assembly of vehicle wire harnesses — the same deformable-wire manipulation, connector mating, and routing skills a truck mechanic needs. Because even this easier, fixtured, fixed-product version is unsolved, it cannot substantiate repair rewiring.

sources.system: Robotized wire harness assembly (state of the art, surveyed systems)
sources.developer: Chalmers University of Technology et al. (systematic literature review)
sources.title: A Systematic Literature Review of Computer Vision Applications in Robotized Wire Harness Assembly
sources.claim: Academic review of robotized wire harness assembly states that routing a harness inside a car body is done manually; robotic work is confined to isolated sub-steps on fixtures, not in-vehicle wiring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is installing wiring inside a vehicle body on a production line — the closest industrial analogue to in-vehicle rewiring. The review reports it remains manual, so it cannot substantiate robotic completion of rewiring.

sources.system: Robotic electrical cable connector (ECC) disassembly systems (state of the art)
sources.developer: University of Bologna (Carricato et al.), MDPI Robotics
sources.title: Robotic Disassembly of Electrical Cable Connectors: A Critical Review
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed critical review finds that non-destructive robotic removal of electrical cable connectors remains unresolved, with accessibility, motion planning, and extraction still at an early stage — the disassembly half of any rewiring job.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is unplugging and removing installed cabling from a vehicle assembly — a prerequisite step of rewiring. Its unresolved status means no cited system can perform the removal portion of a rewire autonomously.

sources.system: Q5D SQ25W / CY1000 wiring automation robots
sources.title: PRODUCTRONICA 2025: Q5D showcases vehicle headliner where wiring automation using a 5-axis robot has replaced conventional wire harnesses
sources.claim: Commercially available robotic wiring cells lay and terminate wire directly onto new components such as vehicle headliners inside a purpose-built machine enclosure; they manufacture new wired parts from a CAD program and do not diagnose or repair wiring already installed in a vehicle.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is automated production of wiring on a vehicle component in an E1 cell. It transfers only to fabricating new wiring on a fixtured new part, not to fault-tracing, splicing into legacy circuits, or installing wiring in a truck.

sources.system: SmartBay (Automated Tire Inc.); RoboTire
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay
sources.claim: The frontier of deployed robotics in vehicle service bays is wheel/tire handling and inspection with rigid, standardized components; even these systems still need an operator for steps like connecting the air line, and no deployed service-bay robot performs electrical wiring repair.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is a different vehicle-service operation in the same E2 shop bay. It does not transfer: wheels are rigid, standardized, externally accessible objects, whereas rewiring requires fault diagnosis, deformable-wire manipulation, and blind confined-space work.

tasks.label: Test drive trucks and buses to diagnose malfunctions or to ensure that they are working properly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-repair or post-PM verification road test: after a brake job, engine/aftertreatment repair or scheduled service, the technician drives the truck a few miles on public streets and highway, watches gauges and dash lamps, checks brake feel, steering, shift quality, and returns to sign the vehicle off as roadworthy.

Diagnostic road test to reproduce and characterize an open-ended customer complaint (clunk over bumps, vibration at 55 mph, wandering steering, intermittent hesitation or shift flare, air leak, HVAC or ABS lamp), often with a scan tool logging live data; output is a symptom characterization pointing to a root cause.

Low-speed function check confined to the shop lot or fleet terminal yard: build air, roll the truck forward and back, apply service and parking brakes, engage gears, check steering and clutch, listen for leaks or knocks before returning the unit to service.

Transit or school bus road test after repair: driving the bus around the depot and out on the route at service speeds to verify powertrain, brake, suspension and body systems behave normally under load and over route conditions.

Loaded / high-load performance test of a heavy truck for complaints of power loss, engine derate, overheating, poor fuel economy or transmission slippage — pulling a loaded trailer up a grade at highway speed while monitoring temperatures, boost and engine data.

sources.system: STÄHLE SAP2000 Modular autopilot / steering and shift robots
sources.title: STÄHLE GmbH | ADAS & Autonomous Vehicle International
sources.claim: STÄHLE supplies commercially deployed autopilot, steering and shift robots that drive vehicles through test programs on chassis dynamometers (exhaust, endurance, acoustics, R&D) and on proving grounds — i.e., a machine occupies the driver's seat and operates pedals, shifter and steering through the test cycle without a human driver.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-driven dynamometer test cycles. The robot performs exactly the driving actions of a test drive (throttle, brake, clutch, shifting, steering) on the same class of vehicle, with the vehicle brought to the machine, which is the E1 form of this task.
