tasks.label: Disassemble units such as water pumps, control valves, and compressors so that repairs can be made.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench teardown of a standardized freight air-brake control valve (AB/ABD/ABDX/DB-60 service and emergency portions) at a component/COT&S reconditioning shop: a few high-volume model families, remove pipe-bracket and cover bolts, split portions, lift out diaphragms, springs, slide valves and check assemblies, lay parts out undamaged for cleaning and inspection; typical road grime and some stuck fasteners.

Bench teardown of assorted smaller auxiliary units in a transit/passenger or locomotive component shop - water pumps, magnet and control valves, governors, air dryers, regulators, small motor-driven pumps - across many models and fleets, low volume each, aged and partly corroded, parts must be preserved for reuse and kept matched.

Heavy unit teardown in a shop bay: air compressors (locomotive/transit), HVAC compressors, blowers and gear units. Hoist or jib crane needed, cast housings, seized or galled fasteners sometimes needing heat/impact tools, press-fit bearings, pistons and shafts requiring pullers, gaskets that tear and must be scraped.

In-place/on-car disassembly on a repair track, pit or shop track: stripping components while attached to or under the car - brake valve portions on pipe brackets, under-car pumps and reservoirs, air lines - working overhead or kneeling in confined space, variable weather and lighting, uncoupling piping before stripping the unit.

Tank-car and specialty fluid-system valve teardown (bottom outlet valves, angle valves, safety relief valves) at a tank car repair shop: product residue and hazmat precautions, heavy corrosion and scale, frozen fasteners requiring torch, impact wrench or drilling, condition varies unit to unit.

tasks.label: Measure diameters of axle wheel seats, using micrometers, and mark dimensions on axles so that wheels can be bored to specified dimensions.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume freight-car wheel shop: used axles, demounted from wheelsets and cleaned, arrive on a conveyor/rack line. The repairer sets a 6-8 in. OD micrometer over each wheel seat, takes readings at several points and planes, checks taper and out-of-round against AAR limits, and stencils or chalks the seat diameter on the axle so the mating wheel bore can be sized for the interference fit.

Axle reclaim/machining cell: after the wheel seat has been turned or ground on a CNC axle lathe, the finished seat diameter is gauged (at the machine or an adjacent gauge stand) with a micrometer and the resulting dimension is recorded and marked on the axle for the wheel borer.

Transit/passenger rail car maintenance shop, lower volume and mixed axle types: an axle sits on stands or a roller cradle in a shop bay; the repairer wipes the seat, measures the diameter with a micrometer against the axle drawing/spec, and marks the dimension in paint or chalk before the wheel is bored and pressed.

Small contract, short-line or locomotive shop with mostly manual tooling: a crane sets an older, sometimes rusted or nicked axle on V-blocks; the repairer stones/deburrs the seat, measures with a micrometer (often several repeat readings), judges whether the seat is reclaimable, and hand-marks the dimension.

Pre-mount verification: axles already marked are pulled from staging racks before pressing; the repairer re-measures the wheel seat with a micrometer, confirms the mark matches the gauged value and the bored wheel's size, and corrects or re-marks the dimension if it disagrees.

tasks.label: Test electrical systems of cars by operating systems and using testing equipment such as ammeters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled periodic electrical inspection/test of a transit or commuter rail car in an agency maintenance shop: power the car up, operate lighting, doors, HVAC, PA/communications and control circuits, measure voltages and currents with a multimeter/clamp ammeter, check battery and charger output, record results and flag out-of-spec circuits.

Fault-driven troubleshooting in the shop of a defect reported in a defined circuit (dead door circuit, blown fuse, HVAC contactor not pulling in): read the schematic, open control cabinets and underfloor boxes, operate the system while probing terminals with a meter to isolate the failed wire, relay or contactor.

Fault-driven troubleshooting of an open-ended or intermittent electrical problem: chafed or corroded wiring under the carbody, water ingress, a fault that appears only when the car moves or is cold; requires exploratory probing, flexing harnesses and connectors while watching the meter, and judgment about where to look next.

Bench test of a removed electrical component or line-replaceable unit (door controller, HVAC inverter, battery charger, relay/contactor panel, blower or traction motor) at a shop test bench or test stand: hook it to the test set, energize it, run the test sequence, measure current, resistance and insulation, and pass or fail the unit.

Outdoor yard or repair-track electrical checks on freight cars and consists: test end-of-train device battery/charge and radio link, ECP or trainline continuity and cable/connector integrity, lighting and wiring on specialty cars; done on ballast between cars, in heat, cold, rain or at night, in a railroad-controlled yard.

Post-repair/overhaul high-voltage and load testing: megger/insulation-resistance tests on traction motors, cables and high-voltage circuits, withstand-voltage checks, and current-draw or load testing of propulsion, auxiliary power and battery systems on a car in the shop or on a depot test track.

sources.transferJustification: Same task content as the O*NET task at unit level: the machine operates rail car electrical systems and measures electrical parameters to produce an accepted pass/fail result; only the fixturing (mating the interchangeable test adapter) is presented to it.

tasks.label: Replace defective wiring and insulation, and tighten electrical connections, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Transit/commuter rail car inside an agency maintenance shop: a fault is traced to a chafed, burned or corroded wire in an under-car junction box, conduit run, truck cable or door/HVAC circuit. The repairer works from a pit or platform in confined space, cuts out the bad section, pulls new wire through existing conduit/loom, crimps lugs, re-insulates with heat shrink/tape, torques terminals, re-ties the bundle and continuity-tests the circuit.

Locomotive or passenger-car electrical locker/control cabinet in the shop: replacing individual defective wires on relay panels and terminal boards per schematic, replacing chafed insulation and sleeving on cab and control-circuit leads, and tightening loose terminal-block and stud connections found during inspection. Work is done on the car, in a crowded aged cabinet with as-found wiring.

Component/bench work in the shop's electrical rebuild room: a removed standardized component (junction box, terminal board, contactor/relay panel, marker-light assembly, traction-motor lead box) has its old leads removed and is rewired to the print with new wire, crimped lugs/ferrules, new insulation, terminals torqued, then bench tested.

Scheduled preventive-maintenance electrical connection check: going over battery box posts, terminal boards, junction-box studs and ground straps on a standard fleet car, torquing every electrical connection to spec and re-taping/sleeving where insulation is worn; largely repetitive fastener work on known, standardized hardware.

Freight car, refrigerated/intermodal unit or mine car handled on a repair track in a railroad-controlled yard: replacing damaged EOT/marker light or telemetry wiring, reefer control wiring, or heater-pad leads; work outdoors on ballast beside the car with a mobile tool cart, in whatever weather, on cars of many different builders and ages.

Mobile/field repair away from the shop: bad-order car on a customer siding, industrial spur, mine haulage track or wayside; the repairer arrives by truck, works on uneven ballast or mud in variable light and weather, and must improvise routing and splices to get the car moving.

sources.system: WAGO Cabinet Wiring Robot (Wiring Bot)
sources.title: More Efficient Control Cabinet Wiring | WAGO
sources.claim: WAGO's commercially offered Cabinet Wiring Robot automatically prepares conductors (cut, strip, crimp, print) and wires control-cabinet clamping points inside a purpose-built robotic station, i.e. new-build wiring in an E1 cell rather than repair of existing wiring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated installation of wire into terminal points of an electrical enclosure. It shares objects (stranded conductors, ferrules, terminal blocks) with rail-car electrical wiring, but it wires a new, CAD-defined mounting plate presented empty in a purpose-built cell; it does not locate, remove or replace defective wiring in an as-found used assembly.

sources.system: Averex wiring centre (portal robot)
sources.title: Automated Control Cabinet Wiring Solution for Scalable Renewable Energy Systems (SpringerLink)
sources.claim: The Kiesling/Rittal Averex portal wiring robot cuts, strips, crimps, routes wires through cable ducts and connects them to components on the mounting rail of a control cabinet — a fully automated purpose-built wiring machine for new panel build.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic routing and termination of wires in an electrical enclosure. Objects and precision are comparable to rail-car control-cabinet wiring, but the machine works on a fixtured, empty mounting plate to a known CAD plan and has no demonstrated ability to diagnose, extract, or replace a defective wire in existing wiring.

sources.claim: Schweitzer Engineering Laboratories runs deployed Robotiq screwdriving workcells with UR cobots that autonomously drive torque-controlled screws in electrical equipment assembly, scaled from a pilot cell to 27 production ... and about 1.4 million screws per year.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: torque-controlled fastening of screws in fixtured electrical assemblies. sources.system: Railcar Inspection Portal (RIP)

sources.transferJustification: Context, not capability transfer: it documents that deployed rail-yard automation detects defects without acting physically on the car, so it cannot support any positive judgment for wiring replacement.

sources.system: robotized wire harness assembly (literature review)

sources.title: Overview of Computer Vision Techniques in Robotized Wire Harness Assembly: Current State and Future Opportunities
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed review work reports that wire-harness operations — the closest industrial analogue to replacing wiring and terminating connections — are still performed manually by ..., with robotized versions confined to research and narrow cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembly and termination of wiring. Cited as negative/context evidence that even in the far more structured automotive setting the manipulation of wires is not automated end-to-end, reinforcing the negative judgments for as-found rail-car wiring repair.

tasks.label: Install and repair interior flooring, fixtures, walls, plumbing, steps, and platforms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Freight car exterior appurtenances on a yard repair track: broken/bent sill steps, ladder rungs, grab irons, hand-brake platforms and running boards. Worker inspects the damage against AAR rules, torch-cuts or gouges off the damaged part and old welds/rivets, grinds and preps, fits the replacement in the correct gauge/position, welds or bolts it, and inspects. Outdoors, weather exposed, many car types.

Freight boxcar/gondola interior in a car shop: replace damaged wood decking or nailable steel floor sections, patch or replace interior lining and side wall panels, re-fasten sheathing. Involves demolition of rotted/splintered planks, cutting stock to fit around posts and door openings, nailing/bolting/welding, and cleanup inside a dark, confined car body.

Passenger/transit car interior overhaul in a heavy-maintenance shop: strip out floor covering and rotted subfloor, install new subfloor and adhered floor covering, refit wall/ceiling panels, seat pedestals, luggage racks, handrails, stanchions and trim; align, shim and fasten hundreds of varied fittings in a narrow car body.

Passenger car plumbing in a shop: diagnose and repair leaks; replace toilets, retention/water tanks, valves, sinks, and piping in cramped restroom modules and under-car spaces; cut, fit and seal pipe runs, pressure test, verify no leaks.

Mine cars and specialty cars at a mine shop or industrial repair facility: repair hopper/car body interiors and liners, replace tank car walkways, running boards, safety platforms and ladders; heavy corroded steel, abrasive-worn surfaces, cutting and welding.

Field/road repair at an industry siding, customer plant track, or in a standing consist: mobile repair truck work to replace a broken step or grab iron, straighten a bent platform, or patch a floor so the car can move; ballast underfoot, no fixtures, uncontrolled surroundings and weather.

sources.system: Path Robotics AW-3 / AW-5 autonomous welding cells
sources.title: Path Robotics raises $100M to automate welding - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Path Robotics sells AI welding cells that scan steel parts, generate weld paths and weld autonomously in fabrication shops without programming; this covers arc welding of fixtured steel parts but not damage assessment, removal of the old component, fit-up or fastening of railcar appurtenances.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous arc welding of variable steel weldments inside a fenced cell. It is the closest capability to welding a replacement step or platform onto a car, but it welds parts presented to it and does not cut off damaged parts, prep corroded surfaces, position appurtenances to AAR gauge, or bolt/rivet them, so it cannot complete the whole repair instance.

sources.system: ROBEL Rail Automation ROBOT (two FANUC arms on a rail wagon)

sources.claim: ROBEL's rail-mounted FANUC robot system detects rail and switch defects and repairs them autonomously by welding, milling and grinding — autonomous steel weld repair, but on track infrastructure, not on rail car bodies, floors, fixtures or plumbing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous defect-adaptive steel repair (material removal plus weld deposition plus grinding). Objects differ fundamentally — continuous rail head and switch components with fixed geometry versus replacing fabricated railcar steps, platforms, floors and fixtures — so the capability does not carry over to installing replacement parts on a car.

sources.system: Alstom Hornell Plant 4 automated welding robots

tasks.label: Repair window sash frames, attach weather stripping and channels to frames, and replace window glass, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Transit/commuter passenger car in the shop: replace a vandalized or cracked side-window glazing panel (laminated glass or polycarbonate). Worker removes interior trim and retaining strips/screws, extracts the damaged pane and old rubber channel, cleans and inspects the frame, fits a new channel/weather strip and pane, refits retainers, checks for rattle and water leakage.

Locomotive or cab-car window: replace a cracked windshield or cab side window in the locomotive shop, including cutting out bonded urethane or removing a locking gasket, cleaning and priming the frame, setting heavy laminated safety glass, and resealing.

Heavy overhaul bench work: window sash assemblies removed from the car are stripped of old glazing rubber and glass, the frame is repaired (straightened, corroded members or rivets replaced, screw holes retapped), then reglazed with new channel and glass.

Bench build-up of a replacement window unit from new components: a clean/new sash frame is fitted with new glazing channel and weather stripping and a new pane is set and secured, producing a finished unit ready to install in the car.

Sealing repairs on the car in the shop: strip worn weather stripping and glazing channel from window and door frames, clean off old adhesive/residue, and fit new stripping and channels to stop leaks and wind noise.

Field repair in the yard or at a terminal track: broken window on a car in service is temporarily boarded/replaced outdoors on the track, working from a ladder or platform in ambient weather with hand tools carried to the car.

sources.system: Tecauma robotic glazing cell (glazing robot on assembled window)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory glazing of window sashes. Comparable objects (glass panes, sash frames with glazing channels) and comparable precision to setting a new pane in a rail car window frame; it shows the capability exists only where the sash is presented fixtured on a purpose-built line.

tasks.label: Align car sides for installation of car ends and crossties, using width gauges, turnbuckles, and wrenches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Heavy body repair on a damaged freight car (gondola, boxcar, hopper) inside a railcar repair shop: sides bowed in or spread out from impact or overloading; the repairer rigs turnbuckles/chain jacks and porta-power between sides or to floor anchors, applies heat where needed, repeatedly checks inside width and squareness with width gauges and tape, pulls the sides to AAR tolerance, then holds them while a new car end or replacement crossties are fitted and welded. Iterative, force- and judgment-heavy on used, corroded, plastically deformed structure.

Program (fleet) rebuild work in a shop on a series of like cars, e.g. re-ending or re-siding a run of gondolas: cars staged on a rebuild stand with standard jigs and a repeatable procedure, side sheets/posts new or reconditioned, alignment consists mostly of setting and holding the two sides to gauged width with turnbuckles and wrenches while the new end and crossties are positioned and welded.

Repair-track or field repair in a rail yard or at a customer siding: localized alignment of a bent side stake, top chord or side sheet so a replacement crosstie or patch end can be installed; portable come-alongs/turnbuckles, wrenches, tape and width gauge; outdoors on ballast, weather and lighting variable, car sometimes still loaded, restricted access alongside adjacent tracks.

Transit or passenger rail car body work in a transit maintenance shop: aligning carbody side frames/posts back to dimension for installation of an end bulkhead, cross member or crosstie during collision repair or a mid-life overhaul; tighter tolerances than freight, work done around installed wiring, ducting and interior fittings.

Mine car or small industrial/plant car repair at a mine shop or industrial plant shop: sides bent from dumping and rock loading pulled back to gauge with turnbuckles and wrenches, then ends and crossties bolted or welded in; small heavy cars, dirty, rough conditions, minimal fixturing.

Functionally the same operation as aligning car sides for car ends/crossties — machine sets and holds the width, joining follows — but on lighter sheet-metal parts presented new in a fixtured cell.

sources.title: Implemented projects | Robotic Complex for Metro Car Roofs | Techvagonmash

sources.title: Automated Laser Welding Cell for Rail Car Wall Panels | Midwest Engineered Systems

sources.transferJustification: Directly adjacent task: fabrication of rail car side wall panels. Establishes that in current railcar automation the robot's role is welding, while dimensional positioning of large panel components remains manual.

tasks.label: Repair car upholstery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Transit/commuter car maintenance shop: repairer pulls a damaged seat cushion or seat back (torn or slashed vinyl/moquette, burned or worn spots) of one of several fleet seat models, strips the old covering by pulling staples/hog rings, inspects and patches or replaces the foam and burlap, fits and stretches a new cover over the pan, staples/hog-rings and trims it, and refits the cushion to the seat frame.

In-car spot repair in the shop or yard: repairer works in the aisle of a rail car, replaces or heat-patches a slashed vinyl seat insert, re-glues a lifted seam or loose armrest pad, and re-secures the trim without removing the seat from the car; access is cramped between seat rows and adjacent seats/panels must not be damaged.

Fleet refurbishment batch in the shop: dozens of identical seat cushions/backs of one standard model are rebuilt to a single spec — new fire-rated foam on a standard pan, pre-cut/pre-sewn cover stretched, stapled and trimmed — repetitive, high-volume, uniform parts and materials.

Upholstery/trim shop bench work: repairer takes a pattern from a worn cover, lays out and cuts vinyl, moquette or leather, and sews the panels, welts, boxing and zippers into a complete replacement seat cover on an industrial sewing machine, matching the existing cover's shape and stitch detail.

Locomotive cab and miscellaneous interior trim: repair of the engineer's/fireman's seat cushion and backrest in the cab, plus armrest pads, headrest covers, sleeper-car mattresses and padded wall/bulkhead panels; varied one-off items, often repaired in place in a confined cab or vestibule.

Mobile/field repair away from the shop: repairer meets a car at a customer siding, station platform or outdoor storage track and makes a quick upholstery fix (patch a torn seat, re-secure a cover) with hand tools and portable kit, in weather and with no fixed layout or equipment.

sources.system: Dvolu automated upholstery cell (Fanuc M-710iC + machine vision + laser trimming)
sources.developer: Dvolu (Fanuc Authorized System Integrator) / Fanuc America
sources.title: Fanuc-powered robotic cell automates furniture upholstery process
sources.claim: A deployed, vision-guided Fanuc M-710iC robotic cell built by integrator Dvolu autonomously picks seat cushions from pallets and stretches, staples, trims and palletizes upholstery coverings in a purpose-built furniture-plant work cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is upholstering seat cushions in furniture manufacturing. Objects (foam seat cushions, upholstery fabric), the operations (stretch, staple, trim a cover onto a cushion pan) and the required precision (wrinkle-free stretch, clean staple line) match rebuilding a standardized rail seat cushion when identical cushions are presented fixtured on pallets in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Duncan Aviation upholstery shop automation (CNC leather cutter, 5-axis CNC foam machine, computerized sewing machines, patterning software)
sources.title: Evolving Aircraft Upholstery Methods | Duncan Aviation
sources.claim: In a large seat-refurbishment (MRO) upholstery shop, automation is limited to CNC cutting of cover material and foam, patterning software and computerized stitching/quilting machines; the seat itself is disassembled to the frame and reassembled by hand at adjustable tables.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is seat re-upholstery in an aircraft MRO shop — the closest industrial analogue to rail seat re-covering (same materials, same strip/refit sequence). It shows that even the most automated re-upholstery shops automate only cutting and stitching sub-steps, while teardown, cover fitting and reassembly remain manual.

sources.system: Sewbot autonomous sewing workline
sources.title: The return of the Sewbot! | Innovation in Textiles
sources.claim: Softwear Automation's Sewbot worklines sew flat sewn goods such as t-shirts autonomously in factory worklines using vision-guided fabric steering; the technology is confined to flat panel sewn goods, not three-dimensional shaped covers or repair work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is automated garment sewing. It bounds what autonomous sewing can do today — flat, standardized panels fed in a purpose-built workline — and does not extend to patterning and assembling a shaped seat cover from a worn original.

sources.system: KSL/PFAFF robotic 3D sewing head and KL 500 robotic sewing cell
sources.title: A new era begins – Dürkopp Adler Group at Texprocess 2019
sources.claim: Robot-assisted industrial sewing cells (PFAFF Industrial / KSL) demonstrate fully automatic 3D sewing of automotive interior trim (slush skins on dashboards) and CNC turning-head sewing units with vision, shown as trade-fair applications in purpose-built cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robotic sewing of automotive interior trim. It shows robotic sewing exists only for fixed, pre-programmed seams on known parts in dedicated cells, which does not carry over to patterning and sewing a replacement rail seat cover taken from a worn original.

roles.title: Motorboat Mechanics and Service Technicians
roles.description: Repair and adjust electrical and mechanical equipment of inboard or inboard-outboard boat engines.

tasks.label: Start motors and monitor performance for signs of malfunctioning, such as smoke, excessive vibration, or misfiring.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outboard-powered boat on a trailer or rack in a marine dealership service bay/yard: tech hooks up flush muffs or drops the lower unit in a test tank, starts the outboard, watches the telltale stream and exhaust smoke, listens for misfire/rough idle, feels vibration, runs it through idle and mid-range while watching gauges/diagnostic laptop.

Inboard or sterndrive boat in the shop with the engine hatch open, water supplied by hose/muffs: tech starts the engine, monitors idle quality and throttle response, looks for smoke, oil/fuel/coolant leaks, water flow, abnormal vibration and misfire, restarts after each adjustment.

Freshly rebuilt or repaired engine/powerhead run on a shop test stand or dynamometer before installation: start, break in, run through load and rpm points while monitoring oil pressure, temperature, smoke, knocking and vibration.

On-water sea trial after a repair: boat launched at a ramp or run from the slip, engine started and run up on plane and to wide-open throttle on a lake/river/coastal water with waves, traffic and weather, while judging smoke, vibration, misfire and rpm under real propeller load.

Mobile/dockside service call: boat in a customer's slip or on a trailer in a driveway, cramped and cluttered access, tech starts the engine in situ to reproduce a reported symptom and monitors it for smoke, vibration or misfiring.

sources.system: Simcenter Anovis end-of-line test system
sources.title: Going from hot and cold testing of engines to a robust end-of-line testing system for electrified vehicles - Simcenter
sources.claim: Siemens' Simcenter Anovis end-of-line test system, integrated into production test benches, performs automated cold and hot testing of internal combustion engines, using vibration, sound, speed, temperature and torque sensors with automatic pass/fail checks and fault-pattern detection.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: end-of-line hot test. It is the same act as this task - the engine is run and judged for signs of malfunction (abnormal vibration, noise/misfire patterns) - performed on a fixtured engine with automatic pass/fail and root-cause indication rather than by a technician's ear and eye.

sources.system: JW Froehlich hot test stands (SOLVISO/SOLCOR measurement and control)
sources.title: Combustion engines - JW Froehlich Maschinenfabrik GmbH
sources.claim: JW Froehlich has built more than 335 hot test stands in which a complete combustion engine is fired on fuel and measured without load and under gradually increasing loads, with highly automated media supply and guided parameterization.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: production hot test / run-in of an assembled engine. Same physical act as the instance - starting a complete piston engine and monitoring it under load for faults - with the engine presented fixtured to the machine, as an E1 setting would present it.

sources.system: AVL Engine TS EOL Hot / AVL PUMA 2 testbed automation
sources.title: Engine/Hybrid Production | AVL
sources.claim: AVL supplies end-of-line loaded hot test systems and quality-audit test systems for gasoline, diesel and CNG engine production lines, providing automated performance testing of every assembled engine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: EOL hot test of a newly assembled engine. The machine starts and loads the engine and verifies it against limits, i.e. running an engine and detecting malfunction, at 100% of production volume in engine plants.

sources.system: RIGAL multi-parameter test bench
sources.title: Multi-parameter test bench - RIGAL - Assing - automatic / for marine engine / mechanical
sources.claim: The Assing RIGAL test bench, offered with an automatic operating mode, tests both outboard and inboard marine ..., with a water tank housing the outboard and a sealed transmission connecting its shaft to the dynamometer, simulating all operating modes.
sources.transferJustification: Directly marine: the same engines this occupation services (outboard and inboard) are started and run automatically in a water tank against a dynamometer while parameters are measured, which is the fixtured-engine form of starting a motor and monitoring its performance.

sources.system: JW Froehlich cold test field for gasoline engines (AGV-fed test stands)
sources.title: Cold test field for gasoline engines - JW Froehlich Maschinenfabrik GmbH
sources.claim: In a seven-stand engine test field built by JW Froehlich for a German OEM, autonomous guided vehicles bring engines to the test stands and hand them over automatically, with optical crankshaft position detection aligning the drivetrain before the engine is pulled in and bolted to the stand.
sources.transferJustification: Supports the E1 counterfactual rather than the test itself: it shows that presentation, alignment and fixturing of the engine to the test machine is itself automated in purpose-built engine test facilities, so the instance can arise with no human loading step.

tasks.label: Document inspection and test results and work performed or to be performed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Mount motors to boats, and operate boats at various speeds on waterways to conduct operational tests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outboard repower/new-motor hang in a dealership rigging bay: a 300-600 lb outboard is hoisted onto the transom of a boat sitting on a trailer or lift, set to the correct height on the transom bracket, through-bolted and sealed, propeller fitted and fasteners torqued to spec. Hull shape, transom thickness and bolt pattern vary boat to boat.

Inboard or sterndrive engine installation at a boatyard: engine craned through a deck hatch onto the stringer beds, aligned to the shaft coupling or transom assembly to a few thousandths of an inch, mounts bolted and torqued, engine secured in a cramped, irregular bilge.

Post-repair sea trial on a public waterway: technician leaves the slip or launches from a public ramp, runs the boat from idle through cruise to wide-open throttle among other traffic, wind and chop, watching RPM, temperature, oil and water pressure, feeling for vibration, testing shifting, steering and trim, checking the bilge for leaks, then judges pass/fail and returns, docks or retrieves on the trailer.

Combined repower and water test: technician hangs and rigs a new outboard in the shop, trailers the boat to a ramp, launches, runs the break-in and performance test on the lake or coastal water, then adjusts engine height or propeller pitch and re-tests until the boat hits its target WOT RPM and speed.

Short in-water operational check in the marina basin or in the shop test tank: engine run at idle and low speeds in and out of gear, cooling telltale/water pump flow verified, shifting, alarms, charging and idle quality checked before the boat is released to the customer.

sources.system: Fori Automation Chassis Marriage Systems with Auto/Multi-Fasten stations
sources.title: Auto & Multi-Fasten Chassis Marriage - Fori Automation
sources.claim: Fori Automation supplies turnkey automotive chassis marriage (engine/powertrain-to-body decking) systems with automatic multi-fastening stations in which automated slides with torque tools or robots fasten all spindles simultaneously on a fixtured, purpose-built line; over 500 such systems supplied in 20 years.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automotive powertrain 'marriage'/decking. It is the same physical operation as mounting a motor to a boat - a heavy (hundreds of kg) propulsion unit is positioned against a fixtured structure to a set height/position and through-bolted to torque - performed in a purpose-built line where the workpiece is presented in a known position, so it transfers to the E1 counterfactual of motor mounting.

sources.system: ROFA fully/semi-automatic marriage stations
sources.title: Fully and semi automatic marriage stations - ROFA Industrial Automation Group
sources.claim: ROFA supplies fully and semi-automatic marriage stations for joining chassis and drive train to the vehicle body, using robots with EC screwdrivers and NC axes for the screwing operations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated powertrain-to-body joining. Comparable object mass and bolt-torque precision to hanging an outboard or bolting an inboard to its beds, and the environment (fixtured body, presented powertrain, fenced line) is exactly the E1 counterfactual for mounting a motor to a boat.

sources.system: SuperFlow SF-Black Widow engine dynamometer with electric throttle actuator and WinDyn
sources.title: SF-Black Widow Engine Dynamometer - SuperFlow
sources.claim: Commercial engine dynamometer test cells run engines through prescribed speed and load profiles automatically: an electric throttle actuator drives the throttle from the control system and the software executes pre-scripted acceleration sweeps, step and steady-state tests and engine break-in cycles while logging hundreds of channels.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: running a marine engine through its speed range for an operational/break-in test. When the work is brought to the machine (engine docked on the test stand), the machine itself actuates the throttle and load and records the performance data that the technician's low-speed water test is meant to obtain.

sources.system: Outboard marine engine dynamometer and emissions test cell automation (LabVIEW/cRIO)
sources.developer: DMC, Inc. for an outboard engine manufacturer
sources.title: Outboard Marine Engine Dynamometer and Emissions Test Cell Automation | DMC, Inc.
sources.claim: A world-leading outboard marine engine manufacturer's dynamometer and emissions test cells were automated with LabVIEW/CompactRIO, including CAN communication with the engine ECU, though the client specifically required an operator-controlled manual mode rather than automated test sequences.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: outboard engine operational testing in a purpose-built cell. Shows such cells exist for exactly these engines, but the cited installation keeps a human operator in control, so it is treated as non-autonomous context only.

sources.system: SM300 / SM300-NG autonomous command system
sources.title: SM300-NG: Class-Approved Autonomous Command System | Sea Machines
sources.claim: Sea Machines' SM300/SM300-NG is a class-approved, vessel-agnostic autonomous command system retrofitted to workboats and uncrewed surface vessels that takes full control of a vessel's steering and throttle for a planned voyage, with collision avoidance and remote command; it is fielded on commercial and defense vessels.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous navigation of a powerboat on open water. It covers only the helm-and-throttle portion of a sea trial; no evidence was found that it performs or evaluates an engine operational test, launches/retrieves a boat, or inspects for leaks and abnormal vibration.

sources.system: Simrad AutoCaptain Autonomous Boating System
sources.title: Simrad Marine Electronics Unveils Simrad AutoCaptain - A Breakthrough in Autonomous Boating Technology :: Brunswick Corporation
sources.claim: Brunswick's Simrad AutoCaptain, launched at IBEX in October 2025, performs autonomous docking, undocking and short-distance maneuvering of recreational boats integrated with Mercury propulsion, working in unfamiliar marinas rather than only previously mapped locations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: low-speed boat handling in a marina. Relevant to the dockside/basin operational check because it shows machine control of a boat in a marina, but it does not run or evaluate an engine test.

tasks.label: Repair engine mechanical equipment, such as power tilts, bilge pumps, or power take-offs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Power trim/tilt repair on a sterndrive or outboard, boat on a trailer or lift inside a marina/dealer service bay: technician diagnoses whether the fault is the trim motor, solenoid/relay, hydraulic pump, or a leaking ram, removes salt-corroded fasteners and hoses, replaces or rebuilds the unit, refills and bleeds fluid, and cycles the drive to verify full travel and hold.

Bilge pump / bilge system repair with the boat in a service bay or on a lift at the yard: technician works head-down through a narrow hatch into a wet, cluttered bilge, removes a failed pump and float switch, cuts and re-clamps discharge hose, splices and seals wiring, remounts the pump, and tests both automatic and manual operation.

Engine-driven accessory / power take-off repair on an inboard engine in a cramped engine compartment: raw-water pump, PTO clutch, power-steering or hydraulic pump — technician gets access around stringers and exhaust, removes belts/couplers, replaces impellers, seals, bearings or the whole accessory, re-times/aligns, and runs the engine to check pressure, leaks, and noise.

Mobile/dockside service call on a customer's boat at a slip, mooring, or in a driveway: same trim-tilt or bilge-pump style repair, but performed with the boat afloat and moving, limited tools, poor lighting, unknown boat layout, and no controlled premises.

Bench repair of a component already removed from the boat (trim/tilt hydraulic pump, tilt motor, bilge pump, PTO clutch pack): technician clamps the unit in a vise or fixture, disassembles it, inspects for wear, corrosion and scoring, decides repair-vs-replace, fits a seal/o-ring or brush kit, reassembles to torque, and pressure/function-tests it on the bench rig.

sources.system: BEAM-1 (Battery disassembly Autonomous Mobile Manipulator)
sources.title: Revolutionizing Battery Disassembly: The Design and Implementation of a Battery Disassembly Autonomous Mobile Manipulator Robot (BEAM-1)
sources.claim: BEAM-1 is an autonomous mobile manipulator that perceives, plans and removes many types of bolts from end-of-life EV battery packs in a lab/industrial disassembly setting; it performs only fastener removal, not fault diagnosis, component replacement, reassembly, or functional testing of a repaired assembly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic unscrewing during teardown of a used, corroded product. It is the closest demonstrated analogue to marine repair, but it covers only fastener removal on one product family in a controlled cell; it does not substantiate diagnosing a faulty trim pump or bilge pump, replacing seals/impellers, reassembling to torque, and verifying operation, so it cannot support a positive judgment for this task.

sources.system: Experimental robotic disassembly cell for EV battery modules
sources.developer: University of Birmingham group (Journal of Remanufacturing case study)
sources.title: An experimental robotic cell for the disassembly of electric vehicle battery modules
sources.claim: An experimental fenced robotic cell was built to disassemble EV battery modules; it is a reconfigurable purpose-built (E1) prototype limited to destructive and non-destructive teardown of one product class, with no repair, reassembly, or functional verification, and prior manual work is noted as variable and hard to automate.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated teardown of a used mechanical/electrical assembly inside a purpose-built cell. It shows the frontier of E1 remanufacturing automation is single-product teardown; it does not show condition-dependent diagnosis, part replacement, reassembly and test of a repaired unit, so it cannot substantiate completion of a bench rebuild of a marine trim pump or bilge pump.

tasks.label: Perform routine engine maintenance on motorboats, such as changing oil and filters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Four-stroke outboard oil-and-filter change at a marine dealership service shop, boat on a trailer or lift: pull the cowling, drain via the pan plug or vacuum-extract through the dipstick tube, break loose and spin off the used cartridge/spin-on filter, oil the new gasket and torque it, refill to spec, run the engine on muffs, verify level and check for leaks.

Sterndrive or inboard gasoline engine oil-and-filter change with the boat in the water at a marina slip: open the engine hatch, work in a cramped bilge/engine box, vacuum-extract oil through the dipstick tube, reach a remote or awkwardly mounted spin-on filter with a strap/cap wrench, contain drips over water, replace fuel/water separator, top off and check.

Scheduled service on a larger inboard diesel cruiser or twin-engine sportfish at a boatyard or dock: oil and filter change on both mains plus generator, several fuel filters and racor water separators, transmission/gear oil, priming and bleeding fuel system, running the engines up to temperature and re-checking levels.

Mobile service call at a customer's private dock, backyard lift, or driveway/dry-stack lot: technician brings extraction pump, filters and oil to an unfamiliar boat in uncontrolled conditions (weather, tight dock access, boat rocking), performs oil and filter change, and carries away waste oil.

High-volume routine servicing of a standardized fleet (rental/livery boats, tour or patrol boats, dealer pre-delivery) at the operator's facility: identical engine models serviced back-to-back on lifts or racks, oil and filter, gear lube, fuel filter, documented per an interval checklist.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The most advanced robotic automotive service-bay system publicly launched (SmartBay, May 2026) automates tire changing/balancing and inspection only, and still requires a human operator to handle the tires; no fluid or filter servicing is offered.
sources.transferJustification: Closest related task: robotic servicing of a vehicle inside a service bay. It shows the frontier of in-bay service robotics is wheel/tire work with human assistance; nothing in it covers draining used oil, unscrewing a used oil filter, or refilling to a checked level.

sources.system: UR10 cobots at Ford Craiova plant
sources.title: Dispensing Robots for Precise Robotic Dispensing | Universal Robots
sources.claim: Cobots deployed on an automotive assembly line dispense grease and fill new engines with oil, i.e. only the fill sub-step of an oil service, performed on fixtured engines presented in known position.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: filling an engine with oil on an assembly line. It substantiates only automated oil dispensing into a fixtured new engine; it does not cover draining used oil, removing/replacing a filter, or verifying level on a used engine.

sources.system: ROBOFUEL
sources.title: SCOTT making ROBOFUEL refuelling system progress with AHS mining truck fleets - International Mining
sources.claim: A robotic arm autonomously couples a fuel nozzle to mining haul trucks in a purpose-built refuelling station, using vision and sensing, without an operator.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous machine-side fluid transfer to a vehicle. It shows robots can locate and couple to a standardized fluid port on a large vehicle in a purpose-built bay, but involves no threaded-fastener removal, no used-fluid extraction, and no filter replacement.

sources.system: Autofuel robotic refuelling arm
sources.developer: Autofuel (Denmark), pilot at Neste station, Finland
sources.title: This Robotic Arm Will Refuel Your Car So You Don’t Have To
sources.claim: Robotic car refuelling exists only as a single pilot station and requires the vehicle to be fitted with a special fuel cap, indicating that even simple robotic fluid service on consumer vehicles depends on vehicle modification.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated fluid servicing of a consumer vehicle. It bounds the state of the art: pilot-scale, requires a purpose-fitted cap, and adds fluid only — far short of an oil-and-filter change on a varied marine engine.

sources.system: SEDA DrainTower / ModuleOne depollution stations
sources.title: Vehicle drainage system - Recycling Product News
sources.claim: The industry-standard equipment for extracting engine oil and other fluids from vehicles (ELV depollution drain towers) is operator-driven suction/drilling equipment in a purpose-built station, not an autonomous robot.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: draining engine oil from a vehicle. The closest commercial fluid-extraction technology is a human-operated tool station with unclear/no autonomy, so it cannot support a positive judgment for an autonomous oil change.

tasks.label: Replace parts, such as gears, magneto points, piston rings, or spark plugs, and reassemble engines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tune-up part replacement on an inboard or sterndrive gas engine while it sits in the boat: boat on a trailer or lift in the dealership service bay, technician reaches into a cramped engine box, pulls coil/plug wires, removes eight fouled or partly seized spark plugs, gaps and torques new ones, replaces thermostat/fuel filter, and reassembles covers and hoses.

Powerhead / short-block internal repair on a bench or engine stand in the shop: outboard powerhead or inboard block torn down after a scored-cylinder failure, replace pistons, piston rings, rod/main bearings, gaskets and seals on a salt-exposed used engine, check bore and ring gap, then reassemble to factory torque sequences.

Lower unit / sterndrive gearcase rebuild on the shop bench: split the housing, press off and replace worn forward and pinion gears, bearings, clutch dog and seals, shim pinion depth, set backlash within spec, reassemble and pressure-test.

Ignition and electrical component replacement on older two-stroke outboards in the shop: pull the flywheel, replace magneto points/condensers, coils, stator or CDI pack behind corroded fasteners and brittle wiring, reassemble the flywheel and timing plate, and reset timing.

Bolt-on component replacement in the boat at the shop: water-pump impeller kit, fuel pump, starter, alternator, exhaust manifold/riser or gimbal bellows on a sterndrive, working over the transom or through an access hatch, and reassembling the drive/engine after the swap.

Field service at a marina slip, launch ramp or customer's driveway: mobile technician replaces plugs, a fuel pump, impeller or ignition coil on a boat in the water or on a trailer, kneeling in a wet cockpit with variable weather, lighting and access, then reassembles and test-runs the engine.

sources.system: MWES robotic connecting rod assembly cell (ABB IRB6700 + IRB140)
sources.title: Robotic Assembly System for Engine Connecting Rods
sources.claim: Turnkey robotic cells assemble new engine components (piston connecting rods) end-to-end in a fenced industrial cell: robots load fixtured rods, pick and lubricate bolts, and apply closed-loop final torque with only an operator loading blanks.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory assembly of engine internals. It shows robots can torque engine fasteners and handle pistons/rods, but only with new, identical parts arriving fixtured on pallets; it does not cover teardown of a used, corroded marine engine, inspection/measurement, or model-to-model variation.

sources.system: MWES engine component robotic assembly system
sources.title: Engine Component Robotic Assembly System | Midwest Engineered Systems
sources.claim: A second MWES cell robotically assembles engine oil-pump housings from feeders into fixtures with press-fit and inspection steps, in a fenced cell with an operator only loading part feeders.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated sub-assembly of engine components. Comparable small parts and press/torque precision, but every input is a new part presented by a feeder in a purpose-built cell, not a worn assembly being repaired.

sources.system: Robotic disassembly platform for PHEV battery packs (Autonomous Remanufacturing Laboratory)
sources.title: Robotic Disassembly Platform for Disassembly of a Plug-In Hybrid Electric Vehicle Battery: A Case Study
sources.claim: Autonomous robotic disassembly of used products is still a laboratory case study: a vision-guided platform unscrews fasteners on a plug-in hybrid battery pack, handling jammed screws and swapping nutrunner adapters.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic teardown of a used, bolted assembly — the closest analogue to removing worn engine parts. It remains a lab demonstration on one product family and does not establish worker-quality teardown and reassembly of varied marine engines.

sources.system: Autonomous Remanufacturing Laboratory robotic pin-removal system
sources.title: Engineers demonstrate key step in robotic disassembly - University of Birmingham
sources.claim: Robotic disassembly of machines such as internal ... is characterized by its own researchers as ad hoc and lacking robustness to the uncertainties inherent in disassembly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: removing press-fit pins, an operation the authors note is common in internal combustion engines. Establishes that even single disassembly primitives were research-stage, so it cannot support completion of a full engine part-replacement job.

sources.system: N25A-T023 Robotic Manipulation Learning for Repair of Marine Diesel Engines (TRACLabs Phase I)
sources.developer: Office of Naval Research / TRACLabs Inc.
sources.title: Navy - 25.A STTR - Robotic Manipulation Learning for Repair of Marine Diesel Engines
sources.claim: As of the 25.A solicitation, autonomous robotic repair and maintenance of marine diesel engines is an unmet Navy research objective, funded only at Phase I feasibility level.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the task domain (marine engine repair by robot); cited as context showing the capability is a solicited research goal rather than a demonstrated system, so it supports no positive judgment.

sources.system: RoboTire automated tire-changing system
sources.title: Tire Changing Robot Installed at Second Discount Tire Store
sources.claim: The closest deployed automotive-service robot changes wheels in retail tire stores; it is limited to wheel fasteners and wheel handling, not engine internals.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fastener removal/installation on customer vehicles inside a human service facility. Transfer fails for this task: it addresses one standardized fastener pattern on an exterior wheel, not diagnosis, teardown, measurement and reassembly of engine internals in a cramped compartment.

tasks.label: Idle motors and observe thermometers to determine the effectiveness of cooling systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Customer boat on its trailer in the dealership service bay or yard; tech connects a garden hose/flush muffs to the raw-water intake, turns the key, idles the outboard or sterndrive for several minutes, watches the dash temperature gauge or scan-tool coolant reading, spot-checks the thermostat housing and exhaust with an IR thermometer, and judges whether the cooling system holds normal operating temperature.

Inboard or sterndrive-powered boat in the water at the shop's dock or a marina slip; tech opens the engine hatch, starts the engine, lets it idle to operating temperature, monitors the helm gauge and scan-tool coolant temperature, checks raw-water pump flow and exhaust discharge, and decides whether cooling is adequate.

Post-repair verification in the service bay after replacing an impeller, thermostat, heat exchanger or hoses: engine run at idle on a water supply until the thermostat opens, temperatures read at several points and compared against spec, then signed off as repaired.

Rebuilt or removed engine run on an in-shop run stand, water-brake dyno or test tank with instrumentation attached; engine idled during break-in while coolant and exhaust temperatures are watched to confirm the cooling circuit works before installation.

Mobile service call at a customer's private dock, boat ramp or driveway on an overheating complaint; tech idles the engine as found (in the water or on muffs), watches gauges and takes IR readings in cramped, uncontrolled conditions to judge cooling effectiveness.

sources.system: SIMPRO engine hot test benches
sources.title: SIMPRO - HOT TEST: Engine Hot Test Benches (datasheet)
sources.claim: Commercially supplied engine hot-test benches run production engines in a cell where pallets and trolleys carry matchplates that make the fluid and electrical connections, with conveyors circulating pallets automatically; no-load benches exist specifically for running (idling) tests.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: end-of-line hot test of an assembled engine. It is the same physical act as the rated task - the engine is run and its coolant temperatures observed to decide whether the cooling circuit performs - with the engine fixtured and its services docked by the cell rather than hooked up by a mechanic.

sources.system: SIMPRO engine hot test benches
sources.title: SIMPRO - HOT TEST: Engine Hot Test Benches (datasheet)
sources.claim: The same hot-test cells instrument engine coolant inlet and outlet temperature (plus oil, exhaust and turbo temperatures) as standard measurement channels, so the cooling-system readings the mechanic takes are acquired and evaluated by the machine.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task: the accept/reject decision in a hot test rests on coolant temperature staying within limits, which is exactly the judgement 'effectiveness of the cooling system'.

sources.system: Test Control engine test cell control software (cell computer, throttle actuator, dynamometer)
sources.developer: Industrial Test Control & Automation (Test Control Ltd, UK)
sources.title: Engine Test Cell Control Software - Test Control
sources.claim: Deployed engine test cells (four cells used for engines from the production line and engines returned by customers) run engines through pre-defined schedules with a cell computer driving the throttle actuator and dynamometer, with no human interaction; key signals including temperatures are monitored continuously against alarm limits and a faulted engine is shut down automatically.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated run testing of production and customer-returned engines. It covers the whole rated act - machine-controlled starting and running of the engine and machine observation of temperature channels against limits - including engines returned from service.

sources.system: Power Test PowerNet LT data acquisition and control with Power Test engine dynamometers
sources.title: Engine Data Acquisition - PowerNet LT - Power Test, LLC
sources.claim: Engine dynamometer control packages sold to rebuild facilities and the marine market run fully automated test patterns with four engine temperature sensors (engine, oil, fuel, air), configurable alarm values, and automatic throttle and load control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dyno run test of a marine engine in a test cell. Same engines (marine inboards and sterndrives), same measurement (temperature channels during a controlled run), with the engine mounted to the machine.

sources.system: Power Test marine dynamometers
sources.title: Marine - Industries Served by Power Test, Inc.
sources.claim: Power Test markets these dynamometer test systems for marine propulsion engines, used to validate new, remanufactured or repaired engines in a test cell before the vessel is used.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes that the automated test-cell route applies to marine engines specifically, i.e. the workpiece of this occupation, including repaired engines.

sources.system: End-of-line engine test stands with automatic docking systems
sources.developer: industry-standard practice at OEM engine plants
sources.title: Engine test stand - Wikipedia
sources.claim: At end-of-production-line engine test stands the engine changeover is automatic and fluid, electrical and exhaust connections are made and broken by docking systems, so the work is presented to the machine without a human making the hookups.
sources.transferJustification: Supports the E1 counterfactual: in a purpose-built setting the engine arrives fixtured with its cooling, fuel and electrical services docked automatically, which is how this task would begin at E1.

sources.system: Spot with thermal payload and autonomous inspection missions
sources.title: Autonomous Detection of Combustible Gas - Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Legged inspection robots autonomously patrol industrial facilities capturing thermal images and reading analog gauges on scheduled missions, i.e. the 'observe the thermometer' half of the task is autonomous in a structured facility - but no cited system starts an engine, rigs cooling water, or works inside a boat's engine compartment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous temperature and gauge observation on a fixed route in an institution-controlled plant. It substantiates only the observation step, not starting and idling a boat engine, so it cannot carry an E2 judgment for a whole instance.

tasks.label: Inspect and repair or adjust propellers or propeller shafts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Boat on a trailer or lift in a marine dealership/marina service yard: technician pulls the cotter pin and castle nut, removes the propeller from an outboard or sterndrive shaft (often corroded or with a spun hub, sometimes needing a puller or heat), inspects blades, hub, thrust washer and shaft splines for dings, line wrap and wear, then installs the same or a replacement prop with grease, new hardware and correct torque.

Customer complains of vibration or poor performance: technician inspects the prop and shaft on the boat, checks blades for bends/cupping loss, checks shaft runout with a dial indicator, tests for a slipping hub, decides between repair, re-pitch or replacement, and verifies the fix on a sea trial/tachometer test.

Inboard boat hauled at a boatyard: technician works under the hull to pull the propeller with a puller, withdraws the shaft, inspects it for bend, wear and corrosion at the cutless bearing and packing, replaces the cutless bearing/packing, refits the shaft and prop, and realigns the engine coupling with feeler gauges/dial indicator.

In-water service at a slip or ramp: technician (or diver) inspects the prop while the boat floats, cuts away fishing line and weed from the prop shaft and seal area, checks for damage, and in some cases swaps the prop in the water.

Mobile service call at a customer's driveway, dock or launch ramp: technician inspects a damaged propeller and swaps it for a spare or new prop using hand tools, with no shop equipment beyond a toolbox.

Bench/prop-shop reconditioning of a damaged aluminum or stainless propeller: measure pitch/diameter and blade geometry, straighten bent blades, weld missing material, grind and blend to profile, restore pitch and cup, balance and polish.

tasks.label: Adjust carburetor mixtures, electrical point settings, or timing while motors are running in water-filled test tanks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealer/marina service shop: carbureted 2-stroke outboard (e.g., 1990s 90 hp) clamped to the test-tank stand after a carburetor rebuild; tech runs it in the water-filled tank and sets the low-speed/idle mixture screws on each of 2-3 carburetors plus idle speed, judging by tachometer, exhaust smoke and engine sound, then verifies clean acceleration off idle.

Shop test tank: ignition timing / 'link and sync' on a carbureted outboard - timing light on the flywheel, loosen locknuts and set idle timing and maximum spark advance stop screws, synchronize throttle plates to spark advance per the service manual, re-verify running at several throttle positions.

Inboard/sterndrive gasoline engine (MerCruiser or Volvo Penta V6/V8 with 2- or 4-barrel carburetor) run on a test tank/water supply in the shop bay: set idle mixture screws with a vacuum gauge and set base timing by loosening the distributor hold-down and rotating the distributor while reading a timing light, working in a crowded engine compartment.

Older breaker-point ignition: dwell/point setting adjusted with a dwell meter and Allen wrench through the distributor window while the engine runs in the tank (or point gap set to spec, then dwell verified running), followed by a re-check of timing.

Troubleshooting run: engine will not hold a tune or runs rough in the tank; tech iterates across mixture, idle and timing adjustments while diagnosing other causes (air leak, fuel restriction, weak spark, worn reeds), deciding when adjustment is inadequate and further repair is required.

tasks.label: Set starter locks and align and repair steering or throttle controls, using gauges, screwdrivers, or wrenches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealer/marina service bay, boat on a trailer or lift: technician adjusts mechanical shift and throttle cables between the binnacle/side-mount control and the outboard or sterndrive — loosens jam nuts, turns barrel adjusters, sets idle and WOT stops, then verifies neutral detent, no gear creep, and full throttle plate travel with the engine running on muffs or in a test tank.

Service bay: repair/replacement of mechanical steering — pull a seized rotary or rack steering cable out of the conduit through the console and transom, grease and install the new cable, connect the link arm to the engine tilt tube, torque hardware, and verify smooth lock-to-lock travel and centered helm.

Service bay or lift: hydraulic steering service — top up and bleed helm and cylinder, chase weeping fittings and O-rings, check/adjust cylinder-to-engine and twin-engine tie-bar alignment, then verify lock-to-lock with no air and no leaks.

Service bay: set the starter lock (start-in-gear protection) on a newly rigged engine/control — position and screw down the neutral-start switch or shift-interlock plunger to spec, and verify the engine cranks only with the control in neutral.

Service bay: diagnose an intermittent starter-interlock fault on an older boat — probe the harness, key switch, lanyard stop and neutral switch with a multimeter, find corrosion/worn switch, replace and re-set the interlock, verify.

Dockside or launch-ramp service call: on a customer's boat floating in a slip, free and adjust a binding throttle/shift control or steering, working in a cramped console/bilge on a moving deck, in wind, spray and whatever weather is present, with only the tools carried aboard.

tasks.label: Disassemble and inspect motors to locate defective parts, using mechanic's hand tools and gauges.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealer/marina service shop: outboard powerhead teardown. Motor on an engine stand in a service bay; tech removes cowling, flywheel, starter, carbs/EFI, cylinder head and exhaust plate, then splits the crankcase; uses micrometers, dial bore gauge, feeler gauges and a straightedge to check bore taper, piston/ring wear, scoring from a lean seizure, head warpage; identifies which parts are defective and writes the estimate.

Shop bench: lower unit / gearcase or sterndrive drive teardown after a water-in-oil or hard-shift complaint. Remove gearcase, press out shafts and bearings, inspect gears, clutch dog, seals and water pump impeller, check bearing preload/backlash with dial indicator and shim gauges, decide which components are replaceable versus scrap.

Boatyard/service bay: inboard or sterndrive engine partially disassembled in the hull. Boat on a trailer, lift or blocks; tech works in a cramped, greasy, varying engine compartment removing exhaust manifolds/risers, heads or oil pan around hoses, wiring and bilge water; inspects for corrosion, water intrusion and cracks with gauges, borescope and compression tester; many fasteners are corroded or seized.

Mobile/field service at a customer's dock, slip or driveway: technician arrives with a hand-tool kit, works from a dock finger or the boat's cockpit (sometimes afloat with motion and weather), pulls a powerhead cover, drops a lower unit, or removes a starter/fuel system to locate the defect on the spot.

Shop bench: small subassembly teardown — carburetors, fuel pumps, power trim/tilt units, starters, alternators, thermostat/water-pump housings. Small screws, delicate diaphragms and springs, corroded aluminum castings; inspect jets, seals, brushes and bushings with gauges to find the defective component.

tasks.label: Adjust generators and replace faulty wiring, using hand tools and soldering irons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inboard engine compartment / bilge of a customer boat in a marine dealership service bay: technician traces a chafed, corroded or heat-damaged section of engine harness, cuts out the bad run, splices in new marine-grade wire with a soldering iron and adhesive heat-shrink, re-looms and re-clamps it, working overhead and by feel in a cramped, oily space.

Charging-system service on the boat in the shop bay: load-test the alternator/generator output, adjust belt tension and pulley alignment, adjust or replace the voltage regulator, renew corroded output leads and battery cable lugs (crimp plus solder), then re-test output at the batteries.

Helm/dash and accessory circuit rewiring aboard the boat: replace faulty wiring to gauges, ignition switches, bilge pumps and nav lights; pull new wire behind panels, through conduits and stringers, terminate and solder connections, verify circuit operation.

Dockside or afloat service call: repair failed wiring and adjust an onboard genset/charging system in a damp, cramped engine room while the vessel is in the water, with motion, weather and no lift access.

Bench rebuild/adjustment of a removed alternator, generator or starter at the shop workbench: disassemble with hand tools, diagnose brushes/diodes/regulator, replace and solder internal leads, reassemble and bench-test output.

Bench fabrication of replacement wire assemblies to a known specification (battery cables, engine harness pigtails, sensor leads): cut, strip, terminate and solder lugs/connectors with heat-shrink, ready for installation.

tasks.label: Repair or rework parts, using machine tools such as lathes, mills, drills, or grinders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the marine service shop, dressing and cleaning up a metal part with a bench grinder, wire wheel or die grinder: knocking nicks and dings off a propeller blade or shaft, cleaning corrosion and old gasket material from a mating surface, grinding down a weld or a proud edge so a bracket seats. Part is held by hand or in a vise; quality judged by eye and by trial fit.

Lathe work in the shop: turning a scored prop shaft, coupling or pump shaft to clean it up, machining a bronze bushing or sleeve to size, facing a spacer, cutting a keyway seat or thread. Worker measures with mic/caliper, chucks and dials in the part, takes cuts to a fit dimension.

Drill press or hand-drill work on a removed part at the bench: drilling and tapping new mounting holes in a bracket, engine mount, transom plate or exhaust flange; enlarging or re-drilling a hole; drilling out a rivet or clean bolt; countersinking and deburring.

Working on the engine in the boat or on the stand: extracting broken, snapped or salt-seized fasteners (manifold studs, riser bolts, head studs) by center-punching, drilling out the stud, using extractors, and repairing the threads by tapping oversize or fitting a thread insert. Cramped bilge/engine-bay access, corroded and unpredictable material, no fixturing.

Mill or surfacing machine work in the shop: resurfacing an exhaust manifold, riser or cylinder head mating face that is warped or corroded, milling a slot or flat, boring or line-boring a housing back to size.

One-off fabrication or duplication of a small part that is no longer available: measuring the broken original or the space it fits, cutting stock on a bandsaw, then drilling, milling and grinding an adapter, shim, spacer or bracket to fit.

sources.system: Renishaw OSP60 / SPRINT adaptive machining
sources.title: Adaptive machining (Renishaw capability note, OSP60 / SPRINT)
sources.claim: Renishaw's OSP60 on-machine scanning probe with SPRINT technology lets a CNC machine tool scan an individual workpiece and automatically generate and load a cutting toolpath adapted to that part's true measured form, enabling automated adaptive machining of parts that differ from nominal.
sources.transferJustification: Reworking a worn or damaged marine part on a lathe/mill is machining to a fit dimension on a part whose true form differs from nominal; adaptive machining is that same operation (scan actual form, adapt cut) on comparable metal parts to comparable tolerances, inside a machine tool enclosure.

sources.system: Renishaw OSP60 / SPRINT copy-cut

sources.transferJustification: Fabricating a replacement for an unavailable marine part is duplication of an existing/broken original in metal stock; copy-cut performs exactly that measurement-to-toolpath-to-cut sequence automatically.

sources.system: FerRobotics Active Contact Flange (ACF / ACF-K) robotic grinding end effectors

sources.claim: FerRobotics supplies force-controlled robotic grinding, sanding, polishing and deburring end effectors (Active Contact Flange) that equip industrial robots and cobots to perform surface material removal on varied workpieces with constant contact force and tolerance compensation, in continuous production.

tasks.label: Mount, balance, change, or check condition or pressure of tires.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealership/independent shop service bay: replace a worn tubeless tire on a street bike (sport, cruiser, touring). Lift the bike on a table lift, remove brake caliper/chain adjusters/axle/spacers/ABS sensor ring, pull the wheel, break beads and demount the old tire on a motorcycle tire changer, strip old weights, mount the new tire respecting rotation arrow and balance dot, seat beads, inflate, balance with stick-on weights, refit wheel, torque axle, set pressure.

Routine check of tire pressure and condition during a service, safety inspection, or pre-delivery inspection in the shop: locate the valve stem behind spokes/brake disc on each wheel, gauge and adjust pressure, measure tread depth, inspect sidewalls for cracks/plugs/embedded nails, judge wear pattern (cupping, flat-spotting, squaring) and advise replace or pass.

Wheel-only work at the bench: customer or another shop drops off loose motorcycle wheels (or a tire plus wheel). Mechanic demounts the used tire, cleans the bead seat, mounts and inflates the new tire, and static/dynamic balances it with weights; no work on the bike itself.

Off-road / dual-sport tube-type tire change in the shop: stiff knobby tire, inner tube and rim lock, spoked rim. Bead breaking, tire irons or changer with bead-holding tools, inserting and inflating the tube without pinching, positioning rim lock and valve, rebalancing rarely required.

Scooter, moped, or small-wheel bike: 10–13 inch rims, tires with very tight beads, wheel access obstructed by bodywork, exhaust, or a single-sided swingarm; often requires removing plastics or the muffler before the wheel comes off, then demount/mount on a small-rim changer and refit.

Field work: roadside, customer driveway, rally, or race paddock. Plug or patch a punctured tire, set pressures for track/weather with a portable gauge and compressor, or swap a wheel/tire on a stand or the ground, with uncontrolled surface, weather and lighting.

tasks.label: Replace defective parts, using hand tools, arbor presses, flexible power presses, or power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealership or independent shop service bay: customer motorcycle on a lift, technician replaces routine wear parts — brake pads/rotors, chain and sprockets, tires/tubes, cables, levers, filters, spark plugs, battery — on a wide mix of makes, models and years, dealing with dirt, corroded or over-torqued fasteners, thread lockers, and torque specs.

Engine/drivetrain internal parts: engine or transmission removed or partially disassembled on a bench, replacing pistons, rings, valves and guides, cam chain, clutch plates, gaskets and seals; requires measurement, torque sequences, correct orientation of small parts, and clean reassembly.

Bench press work on removed components: pressing out worn wheel bearings, steering-head races, swingarm/linkage bushings and fork bushings with an arbor or hydraulic press and drivers/fixtures, then pressing in the new parts to correct depth without distortion.

Chassis, bodywork and electrical component replacement: forks, shocks, handlebars, fairings and plastics with dozens of varied fasteners, plus switchgear, regulator/rectifier, ECU, harness connectors and lighting — cable routing, connector unplugging, plastic clips and delicate trim.

Field/mobile powersports work: replacing parts on ATVs, UTVs, dirt bikes and scooters at a customer's driveway, a race paddock, or roadside — bike supported on uneven ground, limited tooling, weather and lighting as found.

Fleet/rental depot: standardized fleet of scooters, mopeds or shared e-mopeds serviced repeatedly in a warehouse-style facility, swapping the same brake pads, tires, controllers or batteries across identical units.

sources.system: RoboTire (4th-generation tire changing system)
sources.title: AI-powered RoboTire can change 4 tires twice as fast as a human | Fox News

sources.transferJustification: Related task: replacing wheels/tires on cars. Shows deployed autonomous fastener removal and part swap, but only for lug-nut wheel interfaces on cars in a purpose-built bay platform; motorcycle part replacement involves different attachment methods and far greater model variability.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous removal of fasteners from used vehicle hardware. Demonstrates that reliability without part-specific teaching, and speed, are both far below what a shop technician's part replacement requires.

tasks.label: Dismantle engines and repair or replace defective parts, such as magnetos, carburetors, or generators.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dealership or independent shop service bay: top-end work on a modern street bike. Bike on a lift; remove tank, exhaust, coolant lines and cam cover; pull cylinder head; inspect/lap valves, replace guides, seals and head gasket; reassemble to torque spec and cam timing.

Shop bench work on fuel/induction components of older bikes, ATVs and small-displacement machines: remove carburetor(s), disassemble, clean varnished jets and passages, replace needle/seat, floats, diaphragms and o-rings (or fit a replacement carb/throttle body), reinstall and synchronize.

Shop bay replacement of engine-mounted electrical parts: stator/magneto, rotor-flywheel pulled with a puller, ignition coil/pickup, starter motor or charging generator. Drain oil, remove side cover, unroute and re-route harness, reseal cover and refill.

Full engine-out overhaul in a shop: drop engine from frame, mount on stand, split crankcases, replace crank bearings, rings, pistons, gears/shift forks; measure clearances and shim, reassemble, reinstall in frame and run-in.

Powersports/race shop repeat top-end rebuilds on the same few dirt-bike models: piston, rings, wrist pin, cylinder swap or replate, base/head gaskets, torque sequence; done on a dedicated bench with model-specific tooling and service manual specs.

Mobile or trackside repair: mechanic works from a van in a customer driveway, at a race paddock, or on a trail; engine components removed and replaced (carb, stator, top end) with improvised support, variable lighting, weather and no fixed layout.

sources.system: Birmingham robotic disassembly testbed (peg/pin extraction, RECODE programme)
