roles.title: Tire Repairers and Changers
aliases: Commercial Tire Service Technician (Commercial Tire Service Tech)
roles.description: Repair and replace tires.

tasks.label: Unbolt and remove wheels from vehicles, using lug wrenches or other hand or power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail tire store / auto service bay: a passenger car, SUV or light pickup (Prius- to F-150-class) is driven in and put on a lift; the changer breaks loose and removes 4-6 OEM lug nuts per wheel with an impact wrench and pulls each wheel off the hub for new tires, rotation, or a flat repair. Standard wheels, no complications.

Same shop bay, but the removal is complicated: a locking lug nut needing the customer's key socket, corroded/over-torqued/rounded nuts or a snapped stud, or an alloy wheel rust-seized to the hub that must be struck, heated or pried off; sometimes aftermarket/oversized wheels or dually-pickup rear wheels.

Mobile or roadside light-vehicle service: the tech jacks a car or light truck in a customer driveway, office parking lot, or highway shoulder, breaks the nuts loose with a cordless impact or lug wrench, and removes the wheel to fit a spare or take the tire for repair. Uneven ground, weather, live traffic.

Commercial tire center or fleet garage: medium/heavy truck, trailer or bus wheels - 8-10 stud hub-piloted duals torqued to ~450-500 ft-lb, 100-150 lb steel or aluminum assemblies removed with a 1-inch impact gun and a wheel dolly, often after jacking the axle on the shop floor.

Roadside heavy-truck service call: service truck responds to a blown drive or trailer tire on a highway shoulder or truck stop lot; tech jacks the axle and removes the dual wheel(s) at the site in traffic and all weather.

Off-the-road equipment at a mine, quarry, farm or construction yard: loader, haul truck or tractor wheels with multi-piece rims and very large flange nuts, removed with a torque multiplier or hydraulic gun and handled by a tire manipulator/handler machine on unimproved ground.

sources.system: RoboTire automated tire-changing system
sources.developer: RoboTire, Inc. (assets/patents later assigned to The Reinalt-Thomas Corp. d/b/a Discount Tire)
sources.title: Discount Tire pilots automated tire changing system | Chain Store Age
sources.claim: RoboTire's robotic system, installed in a Discount Tire retail service bay in Fountain Hills, AZ, removes lug nuts, lifts and removes wheel/tire assemblies from customer passenger vehicles and reinstalls them; store technicians operate the system and do TPMS/balancing.

sources.system: RoboTire tire changing system (4-arm cell)
sources.title: RoboTire installs another system with Discount Tire - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The deployed RoboTire cell uses four robotic arms around the lifted vehicle: two smaller arms remove and refit the lug nuts, two larger arms lift the wheels off the car; a second system was installed at a Discount Tire store ..., TX.

sources.system: RoboTire with Zivid 2 M70 robot-mounted 3D camera
sources.title: RoboTire's automated wheel-changing system - Case Study (Zivid)
sources.claim: Vendor case study of the deployed system states the robot-mounted 3D vision plus AI makes RoboTire fully autonomous, locating shiny wheel nuts and removing the wheel from the ... at millimetre accuracy across varied vehicles and wheel types.

sources.system: RoboTire tire changing system
sources.title: From Manual to Robots: RoboTire's Impact on the Tire Shop Floor - Tire Review
sources.claim: RoboTire's CEO reports four systems active in US shops (two Discount Tire stores, an independent dealer, a Detroit garage), 99% reliability, and a supported vehicle range of Prius to F-150 only, with Class A trucks a future goal.

sources.system: RoboTire automated guidance system
sources.title: Tire-changing startup RoboTire files for Chapter 7 bankruptcy - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Trade press describing RoboTire's guidance (and its Feb 2024 Chapter 7 filing) confirms the robot independently finds the wheel and selects socket/positioning rather than being teleoperated.

sources.system: Kal Tire WheelJaws (and remote-controlled Kal Clamp)
sources.title: WheelJaws redefines mining tire removal safety - Heavy Equipment Guide
sources.claim: State-of-the-art aid for large off-the-road/mining wheel removal is a mechanical clamp fitted by the technician that holds the wheel assembly while the last lug nuts come off - an assist device, not an autonomous wheel-removal robot.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: The newest shop automation (SmartBay, unveiled May 2026) deliberately avoids this task: it changes tires with the wheels left bolted to the vehicle, so it does not demonstrate unbolting and removing wheels.

tasks.label: Place wheels on balancing machines to determine counterweights required to balance wheels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail tire store / general service bay: after new passenger-car or light-truck tires are mounted, the tech lifts each 45-75 lb wheel-tire assembly off the changer, slides it onto the balancer shaft with the correct centering cone, tightens the quick-nut, sets or auto-senses rim dimensions, spins it, and reads the required weight amounts and positions. Four wheels per vehicle, mixed 15-22 in steel and alloy rims, floor cluttered with tires and tools.

Vibration-complaint or rotation rebalance: used assemblies pulled off a customer vehicle, dirty, corroded, old clip and tape weights still attached; some aftermarket or lug-centric wheels needing flange-plate adapters; often a road-force balance with a load roller to diagnose a ride disturbance.

Commercial truck / fleet tire shop: 22.5 in steel or aluminum drive and steer wheels with tires weighing 100-250 lb, hoisted with a lift assist onto a heavy-duty balancer; also large trailer, ag and industrial wheels needing special adapters.

Mobile tire service: balancer bolted into a service van or a portable unit used at a customer's driveway, a roadside breakdown, or a fleet yard; uneven ground, weather, poor lighting, wheel lifted into the van and spun there.

High-volume wholesale/prep work: distribution center, dealership prep area, or custom wheel-and-tire package line, balancing dozens of new same-size assemblies in batches, staged on carts or a roller conveyor beside the balancer.

sources.system: Schenck RoTec wheel assembly lines / fully automatic balancing station
sources.title: Wheel Assembly Lines: individual & complete solutions | Schenck
sources.claim: Schenck RoTec's production wheel assembly lines include fully automatic balancing stations in which a handling robot loads the wheel-tire assembly into the balancing device with precise positioning; the station measures unbalance and automatic applicators fit adhesive or clip weights in the correct planes. These are commercial OEM production lines (fenced, conveyor-fed cells).

sources.system: Hofmann AWS-R automatic wheel balancing machine in a wheel assembly line
sources.title: Wheel Balancing Machines - dynamic balancing | Hofmann: the Original!
sources.claim: Hofmann's AWS fully automatic two-plane wheel balancing machines measure static and dynamic imbalance of complete car wheels up to 50 kg in about 9 seconds, clamping the rim automatically in the centre bore, running mixed wheel types, and are integrated into automatic wheel assembly lines with correction stations.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: automatic determination of the counterweights needed to balance a mounted wheel-tire assembly, with machine loading and clamping in place of a human placing the wheel on a shop balancer.

sources.system: TIREBOT tire-workshop collaborative robot
sources.developer: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia (research prototype, tire-workshop equipment partner)
sources.title: TIREBOT: A collaborative robot for the tire workshop - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: TIREBOT, a cobot validated in a real tire workshop, was designed only to lift and transport wheels between stations; the researchers state that operating the workshop machines remains a human job.
sources.transferJustification: Directly about the shop workflow of moving wheels to the balancing machine; shows the machine-loading and measuring step was left to the human.

sources.system: RoboTire robotic tire-changing system at Discount Tire
sources.title: Discount Tire testing RoboTire system for use in stores | Tire Business
sources.claim: RoboTire's system, installed in Discount Tire stores in 2022-2023, removed wheels from the vehicle and carried assemblies to the tire changer and balancer, but a human operator oversaw the changing and balancing operations; the company filed Chapter 7 in January 2024.
sources.transferJustification: Closest in-shop robotic system to this task; shows wheel transport was robotic while balancer operation stayed with the human operator.

sources.system: SmartBay robotic service bay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Automated Tire's SmartBay, unveiled May 2026, is a robotic service-bay platform that changes tires without removing the wheel and balances the wheel on the vehicle; the first generation is explicitly semi-automated, with an operator required to position the new tire, connect the air line and mount the balance weights, and it was described as ready to deploy rather than deployed.
sources.transferJustification: Reaches the same output (required counterweights) in a shop bay, but never places a wheel on a balancing machine and is a semi-automated, newly unveiled first generation with per-cycle operator involvement.

sources.system: AutoW8t automated wheel weight application system
sources.title: Automated wheel and tire balancing | Automotive Manufacturing Solutions
sources.claim: Automated wheel-weight application systems for balancing tire-wheel assemblies are used in automotive assembly plants, with robotic application of cut-to-weight adhesive weights on high-speed production lines.
sources.transferJustification: Downstream half of the same balancing operation on tire-wheel assemblies in a purpose-built plant line, corroborating that the measure-and-correct loop is automated at E1.

tasks.label: Identify tire size and ply and inflate tires accordingly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail tire store service bay: after mounting new passenger/light-truck tires, the tech reads the sidewall (e.g., 225/65R17 102H, load range SL/XL) and the door placard, inflates each tire to seat the beads, then sets final pressure; wheels come off the vehicle and go on a tire changer, mixed vehicle mix all day.

Courtesy pressure check / top-off in the shop or service drive: TPMS light, seasonal check, or post-rotation; tech identifies tire size and load rating on all four (sometimes mismatched or aftermarket) tires, checks with a gauge and adds or bleeds air to the correct pressure while the tires stay on the vehicle.

Commercial truck/bus/trailer tire service at a fleet or truck-tire shop: identifies load range/ply rating (e.g., 295/75R22.5 Load Range G, 14-ply equivalent) and rim type, inflates to 100-120 psi in a safety cage or with a remote-fill chuck, checks matched duals.

Roadside or mobile service call: service truck responds to a flat or low tire on a highway shoulder, parking lot, or customer driveway; tech identifies the tire size/ply on an unfamiliar vehicle and inflates from the truck's compressor in traffic, weather, and uneven ground.

Agricultural / OTR / industrial tires: tractor, loader, skid-steer or forklift tires at a farm, yard, or heavy-equipment shop; tech identifies ply/star rating and inflates large-volume tires to comparatively low but critical pressures, often with liquid ballast or multi-piece rims.

sources.system: 3defacto Wheel Assembly Machine (WAM) line, incl. Inflation Station
sources.title: Wheel Assembly Machines - 3defacto
sources.claim: 3defacto's fully automated wheel assembly line automatically detects wheel size for tires/rims fed on conveyors and inflates the assembled wheel with a self-selecting inflation bell to within ±0.1 bar, for wheel sizes 15-58 inches across automotive, commercial vehicle and agricultural applications.
sources.transferJustification: Same task elements: machine determines the tire/wheel size and fills to the specified pressure; objects are the same passenger, truck and ag tires a tire changer inflates.

sources.system: Bohnenkamp fully automated wheel assembly machine (developed with 3DEFACTO)
sources.title: Fully automated wheel assembly from 20 to 52 inches - Bohnenkamp SE
sources.claim: Bohnenkamp AG commissioned the 3defacto-built fully automatic assembly machine at its Osnabrück facility; it mounts and fills commercial-vehicle, agricultural, earthmoving and industrial wheels from 20 to 54 inches to within ±0.05 bar of target pressure without set-up time, one wheel every 70 seconds.
sources.transferJustification: Deployed production use of automatic inflation to a target pressure on truck and agricultural tires, the same objects and pressure precision a tire changer must achieve.

sources.system: Schenck RoTec wheel assembly lines / tire inflation bells
sources.date: 2025 (current product documentation; VentuoVal robot cell in operation since summer 2024)
sources.title: Wheel Assembly Lines: individual & complete solutions | Schenck
sources.claim: Schenck RoTec supplies fully automatic, robot-assisted wheel assembly lines whose inflation bells inflate passenger car, SUV and commercial-vehicle tires with compressed air, with vision systems detecting tire/rim markings for correct orientation.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers the inflate-to-specification step for car, SUV and truck tires in an automated line, with machine vision handling tire identification/marking detection.

sources.system: SmartBay
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Automated Tire's SmartBay, the current in-shop robotic tire-change platform for dealerships and tire shops, still requires a human operator to connect the air line and inflate the tire; the company says full automation of mounting, airing and balancing is only a possible future version.

sources.system: RoboTire robotic tire-changing system
sources.title: Automated Tire decloaks with new autonomous tire-changing SmartBay - The Robot Report
sources.claim: RoboTire, the robotic wheel-changing system installed in Discount Tire stores in Arizona and Texas, went bankrupt (Chapter 7) more than two years before May 2026; its robots scanned the VIN and wheels and removed/installed wheels, with tire mounting and inflation performed on a separate Hunter tire changer operated by a technician.
sources.transferJustification: Closest in-shop (E2) robotic system for tire work; establishes that in-shop robots handled wheel removal/installation, not autonomous identification and inflation, and are no longer operating.

sources.system: Scanflow AI tire sidewall scanning
sources.title: Best TIN Scanning Methods for Tire Manufacturers 2026
sources.claim: Machine-vision OCR systems that read embossed tire sidewall markings (TIN/DOT code, brand, size) with industrial cameras and deep learning are in commercial use for tire manufacturing and scrap-tire intake.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated reading of tire sidewall codes. It substantiates only the 'identify tire size/ply' element; it is software vision, so the inflation judgment rests on the robotic lines cited above.

tasks.label: Raise vehicles, using hydraulic jacks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail tire store service bay: technician drives a passenger car or small SUV into the bay, rolls a hydraulic floor jack (or swings two-post lift arms) to the manufacturer's pinch-weld/frame jack points, raises the vehicle to working height, and secures it on stands or lift locks before pulling wheels.

Shop bay, awkward vehicle: full-size pickup, cargo van, lowered sports car, lifted 4x4 with aftermarket kit, or an EV with a battery skid plate; technician must pick non-standard lift points, use pucks/adapters or a bottle jack, and raise one corner or one side without crushing rockers or pinching the battery case.

Mobile/roadside light-vehicle service call: highway shoulder, parking lot, or customer driveway; ground may be sloped, cracked, gravel or soft; technician chocks wheels, positions a floor or bottle jack from the service truck under the jack point, and raises the vehicle enough to swap the wheel while traffic passes.

Commercial truck, bus, or trailer tire service inside a fleet garage or truck-stop service bay: technician positions a 20-ton hydraulic bottle or air/hydraulic jack under the axle housing or frame rail, raises the dual assembly clear of the floor, and cribs or stands it before removing the wheels.

Heavy-vehicle roadside call or off-road equipment in the field: blown drive tire on an interstate shoulder, or a tractor/loader/skid-steer tire on a farm or construction site; jacking on dirt, mud or gravel with cribbing under the jack base, in weather and without shop lighting.

tasks.label: Glue tire patches over ruptures in tire casings, using rubber cement.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail tire/auto service shop bay: passenger or light-truck tire dismounted from the wheel and placed on a stand or spreader; tech probes the puncture, reams/skives the injury channel, buffs the inner liner with a low-speed rasp, brushes on self-vulcanizing rubber cement, waits for tack, positions a combination patch-plug centered over the rupture, stitches it down, seals the edges, then remounts and balances.

Commercial truck tire service center: 22.5" steel-belted casing on a tire spreader; tech locates a nail hole or larger rupture, skives out damaged cord and fills with repair gum, cleans and buffs the liner, applies vulcanizing cement, and cements/stitches a reinforced repair unit of the correct ply-rating over the injury, sometimes followed by a heat-cure section repair.

Retread plant repair station: nail-hole-detected casings arrive from inspection on spreaders; worker systematically preps and cements repair units over each marked injury inside the casing before the casing moves on to buffing/cushion gum/tread application; high repetition, standardized casings and repair materials.

Mobile/roadside commercial tire service: service truck dispatched to a fleet yard, dock apron, or highway shoulder; tire dismounted at the site, injury located and patched with cement and a repair unit on the ground or on the truck's tailgate, in variable weather, lighting, and surface conditions, under time pressure.

Farm, OTR, or industrial tire repair (field or heavy-tire shop): large agricultural, loader, or earthmover tire with a sizeable rupture or sidewall cut; injury cleaned and skived, large area cemented, and a heavy reinforced patch or section repair applied and stitched, often with the tire lying flat or wedged and requiring the worker to climb into or under it.

tasks.label: Replace valve stems and remove puncturing objects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tire shop service bay, non-TPMS wheel (older car, trailer, spare, farm/lawn wheel): with the tire bead broken or the tire off the rim, the tech pulls the old rubber snap-in valve stem out with pliers or a valve puller, cleans the bore, and pulls/presses in a new stem before the tire is remounted.

Tire shop service bay, TPMS-equipped passenger/light-truck wheel: replace the valve service kit (grommet, nut, core, cap) on a clamp-in sensor, or replace a snap-in sensor valve stem, torque the retaining nut to spec, and confirm no leak — the dominant modern case at new-tire installation.

Flat repair in a shop: inflate/inspect the tire, find the leak with soapy water or by sight, locate the embedded nail, screw, staple or glass shard in the tread, pull it out with pliers, then ream and install a plug-patch from inside; sometimes finding no object or finding an unrepairable sidewall injury.
Commercial truck / farm / OTR wheel in a fleet garage: replace a large-bore or clamp-in metal valve stem, valve extension or hose on a dual-wheel assembly, torque the nut, and leak-check.

Commercial truck / farm / OTR tire, fleet garage or yard: pick and pry stones, nails, bolts and other debris out of deep tread grooves during inspection or before retread casing prep, marking injuries that penetrate.

Mobile / roadside service call in a customer driveway, parking lot, or highway shoulder: locate and pull the puncturing object from the tire, plug or patch it, or replace a leaking/broken valve stem, with the wheel on the vehicle or on the ground, in whatever weather and lighting is present.

tasks.label: Apply rubber cement to buffed tire casings prior to vulcanization process.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Passenger/light-truck tubeless puncture repair in a tire shop service bay: after the injury channel is prepared and the inner liner is buffed around it, the tech brushes vulcanizing rubber cement over the buffed area of the demounted casing (tire lying on a bench, floor or repair stand), lets it flash off to tack, then applies the patch/combination unit.

Commercial truck tire spot/nail-hole repair in a truck tire service center or fleet shop: casing held open on a spreader or repair stand, larger buffed area on the inner liner cemented with a brush or dauber (sometimes two coats), then patch applied and the tire cured or chamber-cured.

Retread plant cementing station: a buffed truck casing arriving on a monorail/spreader is coated over its whole buffed crown and shoulders with rubber cement (bonding solution) in a ventilated cementing booth before cushion gum and precured tread are applied and the tire is cured.

Section repair of a truck or OTR casing in a shop/retread plant repair station: the hand-skived, irregular, often deep cavity plus the surrounding buffed area is cemented in coats (inside cavity and outer surface) before repair gum filling and vulcanization.

tasks.label: Hammer required counterweights onto rims of wheels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Retail tire store / general service bay: passenger-car or light-truck wheel is dismounted and spun on a shop wheel balancer; the technician reads the imbalance value and position from the balancer display, picks the correct one-piece clip-on weight from the weight tray, positions it on the rim flange at the indicated clock position and drives it on with a wheel-weight hammer, then re-spins to verify zero residual imbalance.

Same shop, but an alloy or custom wheel with a cosmetic finish: coated/clip-on weights of the correct clip profile must be seated on a narrow or curved flange (often the inside flange, sometimes hidden behind spokes) without chipping paint, clearcoat or the machined face; weight type and placement plane are chosen for fit and appearance.

Mobile / on-site service: technician works from a service van at a customer driveway, fleet yard or roadside; the wheel is balanced on a portable or van-mounted balancer (or on-vehicle) and clip weights are hammered onto the rim in the open, on uneven pavement and in variable weather and lighting.

On-vehicle finish/match balancing: after off-car balancing leaves residual vibration, the wheel is spun while mounted on the car and correction weights are hammered onto the accessible rim flange with the assembly on the hub.

Mobile/roadside or on-site fleet service: technician at a customer yard, truck stop shoulder, or job site sprays soapy water on an inflated tire still on the vehicle (or on a spare laid on the ground), often in poor light, wind, cold, or rain, to find which tire leaks and where.

Farm, quarry, or industrial service: large agricultural, OTR/earthmover, or skid-steer/forklift tires (well above 24.5" bead), leak-checked with soapy water on site or in a bay; mud- and stone-caked surfaces, tire often too big for any test tank.

Vehicle-side prep during the same wheel service: with the wheel off, the worker scrapes/wire-wheels rust scale and old friction debris from the hub mounting face, brake drum face and stud area (drum and hub still on the axle, vehicle on a lift or jack) so the wheel seats flat before reassembly.

Wheel refinishing/reconditioning shop or truck-wheel recon line: the bare wheel is sandblasted or shot-blasted all over to strip old coating, oxidation and corrosion to bare metal as preparation for painting/powder coating before the tire is reassembled onto it.

Mobile/roadside or on-site fleet service from a service truck: rim cleaned with hand scraper, wire brush or air die grinder at the customer's yard, a highway shoulder, or a jobsite, in whatever weather and lighting exist, with only the tools carried on the truck.

tasks.label: Separate tubed tires from wheels, using rubber mallets and metal bars or mechanical tire changers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tire store / dealership service bay: technician demounts a standard passenger-car or light-truck tire (14–20 in. steel or alloy wheel, almost always tubeless, occasionally an older tube-type trailer or classic wheel) by deflating, breaking both beads and levering the tire off on the shop's mechanical tire changer, rim undamaged and TPMS intact.

Same shop bay but a difficult passenger/light-truck wheel: low-profile or run-flat tire, 20–24 in. custom polished alloy, stiff sidewalls needing bead-press/helper arms and sometimes hand bars and a rubber mallet to free a rusted bead, with zero tolerance for rim scratches.

Commercial truck tire shop: Class 6–8 medium/heavy truck or bus wheel, including tube-type assemblies with tube, flap and lock/side ring, demounted on a heavy-duty hydraulic truck tire changer or with bead breaker, metal bars and mallet; 100–250 lb assemblies, high stored energy, ring safety procedure.

Bench or floor work on small tube-type tires: lawn and garden, wheelbarrow, hand-truck, ATV, trailer and motorcycle wheels, worked with rubber mallet, tire irons and a small changer; the inner tube must be deflated, worked out without pinching, inspected and reused or replaced.

Agricultural / OTR service: large tube-type tractor, implement or loader tire, often calcium-filled and caked in mud, laid flat at a farm yard or in a heavy service bay, beads broken with hydraulic bead breaker and long metal bars, tube pulled out, rim rust cleaned.

Mobile/roadside service call: technician works from a service truck at the roadside, a fleet yard, or a job site, demounting a damaged passenger or truck tire on uneven pavement or gravel in whatever weather, using a truck-mounted changer or bars and mallet.

tasks.label: Patch tubes with adhesive rubber patches or seal rubber patches to tubes, using hot vulcanizing plates.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tire shop bench: technician cold-patches a light-truck, ATV or farm-implement inner tube whose puncture has already been marked — buffs the butyl around the hole with a rotary rasp to the right depth without perforating it, brushes on vulcanizing cement, waits for tack, peels the backing, centers and stitches a rubber patch, then re-inflates and re-checks for leaks.

Tire shop: hot vulcanizing plate repair of a large truck, tractor or OTR inner tube — buff and clean the area, position an uncured gum patch, clamp the tube between the heated plate and pressure pad with correct alignment and pressure, run the cure cycle, release and inspect the bonded patch.

Shop bench: small tube from a bicycle, motorcycle, lawn/garden or hand-truck wheel — thin, highly floppy tube; scuff the marked spot with sandpaper, apply cement or a self-vulcanizing peel-and-stick patch, press firmly, verify seal in a water tank.

Mobile/field service: tube from an agricultural tractor, skid-steer or off-road truck tire is patched at the customer site — farmyard, job site or roadside — with a portable buffer, cement and cold patch or a portable vulcanizer, in dirt, wind, variable light and cramped working positions.

Shop: complex tube repair — long tear, boot/reinforced section repair, or damage near the valve stem — requiring skiving/feathering the edges, cementing, layering multiple or oversized patches, and a longer vulcanizing cure with careful pressure control; judgment needed on whether the tube is repairable at all.

sources.transferJustification: Closest industrial analogue to the task: buffing rubber and bonding a vulcanized rubber repair patch to a rubber article, done inside a purpose-built plant. It indicates that even in the most structured rubber-repair setting, robotic patch application is not an available capability; the project explicitly targets human assistance, not replacement.

tasks.label: Inflate inner tubes and immerse them in water to locate leaks.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-equipment tube at a general tire/service shop: lawn mower, wheelbarrow, hand-truck or garden-tractor tube pulled from the tire, valve chucked to shop air, partially inflated, then dunked and rotated section by section in the shop's water tub until a bubble stream shows the pinhole, which is marked with crayon before deflating.

Motorcycle/ATV/scooter tube at a powersports or bike shop: thin tube inflated slightly, submerged in a test tank, rotated fully and the valve base checked, one or more small punctures (or a rim-side chafe pair) located and marked, then handed off for patching.

Agricultural tractor or large implement tube at a farm-tire dealer: bulky heavy tube (e.g., 18.4-38) inflated and worked through a large tank or trough in sections, often with a hoist, looking for chafe holes, valve-stem leaks and multiple pinholes; each leak marked.

Heavy truck, industrial or aircraft tube-type assembly at a commercial tire center: tube (with flap) inflated to test pressure and immersed in a large test tank, or the whole mounted assembly dunked; leak point located and marked; higher pressures and safety cage/tank handling involved.

Mobile/field service call at a farm yard, roadside, construction or mine site: tube removed on uneven ground in variable weather, inflated from the truck's air line and dunked in a stock tank, barrel or bucket (or wetted with soapy water where no tank exists) to find the leak, which is marked on the spot.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic inflation of tire/wheel assemblies on an assembly line. It covers the 'inflate' half of this task on comparable rubber tire components at comparable pressures, in a purpose-built machine cell, but does not itself perform the water-immersion leak search.

sources.title: A Machine Vision–Based Automated Wheel Leak Detection System Using Real-Time Object Detection in the Water Leak Testing Process
sources.claim: A machine-vision system integrated with an industrial water ... in automotive wheel manufacturing automatically detects the bubbles emitted by a pressurized part submerged in the water tank in real time, replacing the operator's visual bubble inspection, with 100/100 correct classifications in operational trials.

Same physical procedure, same water-tank environment, and the same precision demand (resolving the bubble source on the part surface); the workpiece is a rigid wheel rather than a limp tube, so transfer holds only where the tube is presented fixtured, as an E1 setting would present it, and at automotive-wheel scale.

tasks.label: Assist mechanics and perform various mechanical duties, such as changing oil or checking and replacing batteries.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Full oil-and-filter change on a customer's passenger car or light truck in a tire/quick-lube shop bay: drive the car in and lift it (or use a pit), position a drain pan, break loose and remove the drain plug, drain hot oil, replace the crush washer and re-torque the plug, locate and unscrew the spin-on or cartridge filter (often stuck, awkwardly placed, and different on every model), oil the new gasket and install to spec, remove the underhood fill cap, pour 4-8 quarts, check the dipstick, run the engine and check for leaks, reset the maintenance reminder, and dispose of the used oil and filter.

Battery service on a customer vehicle in the shop: load-test the battery and charging system with a tester clamped to the posts, then if it fails, open the hood, disconnect terminal clamps (often corroded, sometimes needing a puller), remove the hold-down bracket or J-bolt, lift a 35-50 lb battery out of a tight engine bay, wire-brush the tray and cable ends, set and secure the new battery, torque the terminals, verify start and charging, and register the battery to the vehicle where required.

Assisting a mechanic on a job in the bay: positioning and lifting the vehicle, holding a component or exhaust hanger while the mechanic bolts it, handing specific tools and sockets on request, removing and reinstalling splash shields and fasteners under direction, topping or bleeding systems while the mechanic works, pumping the brake pedal, and cleaning up spills, cores, and scrap around the lift.

Quick-service items on a customer car in the bay: replace wiper blades, swap engine and cabin air filters, replace burned-out bulbs, top off washer fluid, coolant, and power steering fluid, grease chassis fittings on older vehicles, and check/adjust tire pressures — each item on a different make and model with a different latch, clip, and access path.

Parts and materials runner work in the shop: fetch the correct filter, battery, case of oil, or wheel from the stockroom shelves, carry it to the correct bay and stage it beside the lift, and haul used oil jugs, core batteries, and scrap tires out to the waste area.

Mobile/roadside service call with a service truck: at a customer's driveway, a fleet yard, or the shoulder of a road, jump-start or replace a battery, top off oil or coolant, and assist the road mechanic — working around traffic, weather, uneven ground, and whatever vehicle is there.

tasks.label: Clean and tidy up the shop.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-shift floor cleaning of the service bays, walkways and door aprons at a tire store or truck-tire shop: sweeping/scrubbing rubber dust, tread shavings, tracked-in grit, spilled mounting-lube water and small litter off a concrete or epoxy floor, working around parked vehicles, lifts, hoses and equipment.

Tidying the work area: gathering scattered hand tools, impact sockets, torque sticks, pry bars, valve tools and wheel-weight boxes and returning each to its cart, drawer or pegboard; coiling air hoses, rolling floor jacks and jack stands back to the wall, stacking cones and hubcap trays.

Clearing tires and wheels: collecting used/scrap tires left around the bays, carrying and stacking them onto the scrap pile, cage or disposal trailer; restacking take-off wheels and returning unsold inventory tires to the correct rack slot in the back room.

Waste handling: emptying shop and lobby trash cans, tying and replacing liners, flattening cardboard boxes and gathering tire wrappers, banding and packaging, then hauling everything out to the dumpster or recycling bin in the lot.

Wipe-down and front-of-house tidying: wiping grease and lube spatter off the tire changer, balancer, air lines, benches and service counter, restocking supplies, and straightening/cleaning the customer waiting area and restroom.

Spill cleanup: an oil, coolant, gear-lube or bead-lube spill in a bay or under a lift, requiring absorbent granules or pads to be spread, swept up and bagged, then the area degreased and mopped, often in tight space under a raised vehicle.

tasks.label: Clean sides of whitewall tires.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Tire shop service bay: after mounting and installing new whitewall tires on a customer's car, the changer sprays whitewall cleaner on the installed tires (car on a lift or on the floor), scrubs the white sidewalls with a stiff brush to remove mounting lube, crayon marks and the protective film residue, rinses/wipes, and checks appearance before handing the car back.

Mount-and-balance station: loose wheel/tire assemblies (or bare tires) on the bench or balancer. The worker cleans the white sidewall of each assembly - protective coating, bead lube, storage dust, scuffs - before installation, display or seasonal storage.

Heavily soiled or yellowed/oxidized whitewalls, typically on a collector car, long-parked vehicle or older customer car: repeated dwell-and-scrub passes with whitewall cleaner and abrasive pad/stiff brush, taking care not to cut through the thin white rubber layer or damage adjacent black rubber, wheel finish or paint.
Shop inventory/used-tire area: batch cleaning of whitewall sides on used or stored tires before resale or display, dozens of loose tires handled at a time, dirt and road film only.

tasks.label: Wind large springs with upward motion of arm.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential torsion spring replacement: technician stands on a ladder in a homeowner's attached garage, sets the new spring(s) on the shaft above the door header, inserts winding bars in the cone and winds 7.5-8 full turns with repeated upward strokes of the arm, then locks the cone set screws and checks door balance. Cluttered garage, variable headroom, live stored energy of several hundred lb-ft.

Residential service/tune-up call: door is out of balance or drifts, technician adds or removes a quarter to half turn on the existing torsion spring(s) with winding bars from a ladder, re-tightens set screws and re-tests balance by hand.

New-construction or replacement door installation at a residential/light-commercial jobsite: unfinished garage, debris, other trades working, temporary lighting; springs wound to the door manufacturer's turn count after the door, shaft and drums are set.

Commercial sectional or loading-dock door at a warehouse or industrial plant: heavier and often multiple/larger torsion springs at 10-16 ft, worked from an extension ladder or scissor lift amid racking, piping and dock traffic; higher winding torque and more turns.

Rolling steel service door or coiling grille at a retail store, school, or fire station: spring tension set inside the barrel via the tension wheel/winding bars per the manufacturer's turn chart, working overhead from a ladder or lift inside an occupied building.

sources.system: Bespoke Machines Ltd automatic spring tensioner / setting machine for roller blind torsion springs
sources.title: Spring Tensioner for Roller Blind Springs UK Supplier
sources.claim: A purpose-built automatic setting machine built by Bespoke Machines Ltd applies pre-tension to torsion springs in a roller-blind assembly plant, i.e., a machine that winds a torsion spring into an assembly under machine control in a fixtured station.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: pre-tensioning a torsion spring inside a roller-blind tube assembly. It is the same physical act as winding a door counterbalance spring (rotating one end of a helical torsion spring through a prescribed angle to store energy in a shaft assembly) performed by a machine in a purpose-built station; the difference is scale of torque, which is covered by the servo torsion drives cited separately.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying controlled multi-turn rotation and high torque to a fixtured torsional element. Winding a large door torsion spring is exactly this - a prescribed number of full turns against several hundred Nm of reaction torque - so the drive capability and turn-count precision transfer directly once the shaft assembly is fixtured.

sources.system: Universal Robots cobot nut-running cells (UR+ nut-runner kits)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: torque-controlled fastener tightening on a fixtured assembly. Securing the two set screws that lock a wound winding cone to the torsion shaft is the same operation on comparable steel hardware at comparable torque, and is the step that converts spring rotation into an accepted, safe counterbalance.

Residential or light-commercial garage door opener/operator repair: replace a stripped gear-and-sprocket kit, logic board, capacitor, belt/chain, trolley or safety photo-eyes on a unit mounted overhead, working from a ladder; reconnect low-voltage wiring, reset travel limits and force, and test safety reverse.

Commercial overhead sectional, rolling steel door or dock equipment repair at a warehouse/loading dock: replace commercial springs, cables, bearings, barrel components, damaged slats or panels, chain hoists, dock leveler parts; work at height from a scissor lift amid forklift traffic; occasional cutting, drilling or welding and field fitting on legacy, corroded assemblies.

Automatic pedestrian door repair at a retail, hospital or office entrance: replace worn carriers/rollers, drive belt, motor/gearbox, closer arm, harness or sensors on a sliding or swing operator inside the header, then re-tension, re-program the controller and adjust opening/closing speeds and forces to ANSI standards, working around public traffic behind barricades.

Bench work at the service shop: rebuild or refurbish an operator, gate opener, door closer or hardware sub-assembly removed from the field - disassemble the housing, replace worn gears, bearings, seals or boards, reassemble and bench-test before reinstallation.

Shop pre-assembly at the door company: cutting angle iron stock to length and bolting or welding hanger brackets onto horizontal track sections on a bench before the crew hauls them to the site.

Low, tight ceilings, obstructions, and non-standard legacy hardware.

New residential garage door installation (new construction or full door replacement): after sections and tracks are set, technician mounts end bearing plates, assembles and lifts the torsion tube with springs and drums into place above the opening from a ladder, threads cables and winds the springs. Site is a bare or partly finished garage on a construction/remodel job, with debris, uneven floors and other trades present.

Commercial sectional overhead door at a warehouse loading dock, retail bay, fire station or fleet garage: heavier multi-spring counterbalance mounted high above the opening, accessed with an extension ladder, scaffold or scissor lift; springs weigh 15-40 lb each; work performed inside an institution-controlled facility around traffic and dock operations.

Industrial high-lift / vertical-lift or rolling-steel door in a plant, parking structure or transit facility: counterbalance springs on a long shaft or inside a barrel, 15-25 ft up, reached by scaffolding or a lift; heavy hardware, tight ceiling clearances near ductwork and piping, custom legacy configurations.

sources.system: Hilti Jaibot

sources.claim: Hilti's Jaibot is the closest fielded construction robot for overhead work at height: it is positioned by a human operator with a remote control and then drills ceiling holes within reach automatically. It performs only drilling of anchor holes; it does not lift, hook, bolt or tension hardware such as counterbalance springs, and no source shows it installing any spring or cable assembly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = overhead drilling for MEP installation at height on jobsites. Transfer to this task FAILS: the objects (drill bit vs. 5-40 lb springs, torsion tubes, lift cables), the required manipulation (hole drilling vs. threading cables, hooking/tensioning springs, torquing set screws) and the mobility (operator-driven repositioning) are not comparable, so it cannot substantiate completing a spring-system installation at any tier.

No comparable cited system assembles garage-door-scale counterbalance hardware (heavy coil springs, torsion tube, drums, lift cables) even in such a cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = autonomous fixtured mechanical assembly. Transfer to this task FAILS: parts are 5 mm rigid moldings in dedicated nests, whereas installing a door spring system requires manipulating long heavy coil springs, routing flexible lift cables onto drums and winding springs to a torque/turn spec — none of which this or any cited cell demonstrates.

Commercial rolling steel curtain door or sectional dock door installed at an operating warehouse/loading dock: bolt or weld guide angles to masonry or steel jambs (drilling anchors), hoist a heavy coiled curtain and barrel into brackets, mount and wire an electric tube/jackshaft operator, install safety edge and photo-eyes, adjust limits and test cycling. Work at height from a scissor lift, around active facility traffic.

Automatic pedestrian door package installed at a retail, hospital, or office entrance: mount the header/operator to the existing storefront frame, hang sliding or swing door leaves, fit rails/guides and breakout hardware, mount and aim overhead presence sensors and door-mounted electronic-eye/safety beams, pull and terminate low-voltage wiring, program the controller and verify ANSI/BHMA 156.10 compliance with test equipment.

Retrofit/replacement of an opener, operator, or door closer at a home or small business: remove the old unit, mount the new opener or overhead concealed/surface closer to existing header and framing, add or relocate the electronic-eye brackets, run wiring, and adjust travel, force, and closing speed until it passes safety tests. Varied and often non-standard existing conditions.

Install of hollow metal door frames, rails, and dock/fire door hardware on an active new-construction or renovation jobsite: set and plumb frames in rough openings, anchor and grout, install rails/tracks and fire-rated rolling curtain with drop-test release, wire operators to temporary power. Unfinished floors, other trades working nearby, changing site layout.

sources.system: Schindler R.I.S.E.
sources.title: Schindler's Robotic Installation System for Elevators | Schindler Group
sources.claim: Schindler R.I.S.E. is a commercially deployed, fully autonomous installation robot that works inside elevator hoistways, but its scope is limited to drilling holes and setting anchor bolts (including for landing doors); human mechanics still mount rails, brackets, doors and their mechanisms.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: anchoring building-door and rail hardware to concrete. It shows the frontier of autonomous in-building installation is fastener-hole drilling/anchor setting only, not assembling, hanging, wiring or commissioning a door system.

sources.system: Hilti Jaibot

sources.claim: Hilti's Jaibot is a commercially deployed semi-autonomous jobsite robot that autonomously drills overhead holes from a BIM plan, but performs only the drilling/marking step of installation work and requires a worker to operate and to install the hardware.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: overhead anchor drilling on construction sites, a sub-step of mounting door rails and opener brackets. Cited to show no fielded jobsite robot goes beyond drilling to fitting, wiring and testing door hardware.

sources.system: Robotic door-hanging station (industrial arms with vision and nut runners) on automotive assembly lines

sources.claim: In fenced automotive assembly cells, robots autonomously pick a car door, align it to hinges with vision, and bolt it with nut runners with torque verification — a purpose-built, single-fastening operation on a fixtured body, not a multi-step door-system installation with wiring and sensor commissioning.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hanging a door on hinges in a purpose-built cell. Transfer fails: the objects (car door on a fixtured body, pre-drilled hinges) and scope (one bolting operation) differ from anchoring tracks/curtains to building structure and wiring, aligning and testing openers and photo-eyes.

sources.system: Automated door production/machining and assembly line
sources.title: Automated door production - machining & assembly | BETH
sources.claim: Automated door production lines use robots to feed and machine door leaves in a factory, i.e. manufacturing of door blanks, with no capability to install frames, rails, curtains, openers or safety-eye systems in an opening.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory door handling/assembly, the closest purpose-built (E1) analogue. It substantiates only material handling and machining of door leaves, not the installed, wired, tested door assembly the repairer must deliver.

tasks.label: Adjust doors to open or close with the correct amount of effort, or make simple adjustments to electric openers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential service call: technician adjusts torsion/extension spring tension on a homeowner's sectional garage door (winding bars, quarter-turn increments, set screws) so the door balances and lifts with correct effort; verified by lifting the door half-way and checking it holds. Cluttered private garage, ladder work, non-standard door weights and hardware.

Residential/light-commercial electric garage door opener: technician sets up/down travel limits and up/down force settings (screws, dials, or learn buttons on the opener head), adjusts chain/belt tension and arm linkage, then runs the door and performs the 2x4 safety-reversal and photo-eye tests until it opens/closes fully with correct force. Homeowner's garage, overhead work on a ladder.

Commercial automatic pedestrian door (sliding or low-energy swing operator) at a store, hospital, or office entrance: technician tunes opening/closing speed, check speed, hold-open time, and closing/opening force at the operator's control board (potentiometers, DIP switches, or menu buttons), adjusting belt/arm as needed, and verifies against ANSI/BHMA A156.10/A156.19 with a force gauge and stopwatch while the entrance stays in service.

Manual swing door with a surface or concealed closer in a school, office, hospital, or apartment corridor: technician adjusts sweep and latch speed valves, backcheck, spring power/size and arm preload so the door closes and latches properly and opens within the ADA 5 lbf limit; verified with a force gauge and timing the swing.

Commercial sectional or rolling steel door at a warehouse/loading dock: technician re-tensions the counterbalance springs (winding cones or tension wheel) and rebalances a heavy door so it can be operated with the correct effort and does not drift; heavy hardware, elevated work from a lift or ladder.

Industrial overhead or high-speed door operator: technician adjusts open/close limit switches, clutch/brake and, on high-speed doors, speed and reversing-edge sensitivity parameters so the door stops at the correct positions with the correct force; performed at the operator head in an active warehouse.

sources.system: KUKA LBR iiwa fog-light adjustment cobot (with Dürr headlamp aiming system, Ford)
sources.title: Ford automates fog light installation with KUKA LBR iiwa cobots
sources.claim: Ford, Dürr Assembly Products and KUKA deployed LBR iiwa cobots on vehicle assembly headlight test stands that autonomously locate and turn the hard-to-reach fog-lamp aim adjustment screws in the bumper, replacing the manual screw-turning adjustment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: setting headlamp/fog-lamp aim by turning a small recessed adjustment screw until an instrumented aim target is met. This is the same class of operation as turning a door closer's sweep/latch valve screw or an opener's travel-limit/force screw until a measured behaviour meets spec: comparable small adjustment hardware, comparable precision, closed loop against a measurement device, workpiece presented fixtured at a known position.

sources.system: KUKA LBR iiwa HRC headlight adjustment station

sources.claim: The camera-guided LBR iiwa headlight/fog-light adjustment cells are in series use at multiple headlight test stands on the production line, with the robot positioning an adjustment screwdriver on screws located behind bumper access holes.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (aim-screw adjustment to an instrumented target) and it establishes that the capability is a fielded production station, not a one-off, in a purpose-built end-of-line cell where the workpiece is presented in a known position.

sources.system: SEETECH DRAGON X15 Robotic headlamp aiming machine

sources.claim: SEETECH sells a robotic version of its DRAGON X15 end-of-line headlamp aiming machine in which a collaborative robot arm recognises and locates the adjustment screws and ... low-beam, high-beam and fog aim adjustment fully automatically in lights-out production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: closed-loop adjustment of a device (headlamp aim) by robotically finding and turning its adjustment screws until measured output is within tolerance — the same measure-adjust-remeasure loop a door technician runs on closer valves or opener force/limit screws, here in a fixtured end-of-line station.

sources.claim: Fori Automation supplies end-of-line cells in which robots mechanically adjust vehicle suspension hardware — turning tie rods with a socket gear head and cam bolts with a servo gear head — in closed loop until measured toe angle is within ±0.03 degrees.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robots turning a threaded mechanical adjuster (tie rod, cam bolt) while an instrument measures the resulting geometry, iterating to spec. Adjusting a door closer's spring power/arm preload or a door operator's limit nuts to reach a measured effort/travel target is the same adjust-and-verify loop on comparable threaded hardware in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: MATT smart device test automation robot
sources.title: MATT the Smart Device Test Automation Robot | Adapta Robotics
sources.claim: Adapta Robotics' MATT is a commercially sold test-automation robot that physically presses buttons and touchscreens on devices held in a fixture and verifies the device's response with cameras and sensors.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic actuation of a device's physical controls (buttons/keypads) in a fixtured test bench with sensed verification of the device response — the interaction needed to change speed/force/hold-open parameters on a modern automatic-door controller once the operator is presented in a purpose-built adjust-and-verify station.

sources.system: Spot Arm

sources.transferJustification: Closest field (E2) manipulation capability found: single constrained-motion actions under operator supervision, not diagnosis-and-adjustment of door hardware to a measured effort spec, so it cannot substantiate completion of any instance.

tasks.label: Set doors into place or stack hardware sections into openings after rail or track installation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New residential sectional garage door at a private home: after vertical/horizontal tracks are mounted, the installer sets the bottom section into the opening on the floor, shims and levels it, seats rollers into the vertical track, then stacks the remaining 3-4 insulated steel sections (each ~60-120 lb, 8-18 ft wide), bolting hinges and end brackets between them. Cluttered garage, uneven concrete slab, out-of-plumb jambs, no two homes alike.

Commercial sectional overhead door at a warehouse/loading dock or light-industrial building: heavier steel sections (150-350 lb each, up to 20+ ft wide) stacked into the opening on installed tracks, often using a two-person lift, forklift or panel lift, with hinges, struts and rollers fastened as the stack rises; work done inside an operating or newly finished facility with dock levelers and traffic nearby.

Rolling steel service/fire door at a commercial building: hoisting the assembled curtain-and-barrel coil (several hundred to over 1,000 lb) up onto the previously installed end brackets/guides above the opening, seating the barrel journals and pin, and squaring the assembly to the guides.

Automatic sliding or swing entrance door at a retail store, hospital, office or airport: after the header and track are installed, setting the tempered-glass sliding panels and sidelites into place, hanging the carriers/rollers on the track, plumbing the panels, and adjusting pocket/guide engagement so the operator can be commissioned.

Service call to re-set a door that has come off its tracks or to replace a damaged section: door partly hanging, cable off drum, rollers popped out, track possibly bent; worker secures the door, works the rollers back into the track, swaps a bent section, and re-stacks/aligns the door in the opening. Mostly homes and small businesses.

sources.system: Daifuku Door Auto Mounting System (Isuzu Fujisawa Plant)
sources.title: Enabling Flexible Manufacturing: New Door Auto Mounting System | DAIFUKU Square
sources.claim: Deployed multi-robot cell at Isuzu's Fujisawa Plant automatically mounts vehicle cab doors into the body opening: one robot holds and positions the door while another locates bolt holes by camera and drives the fasteners with a nutrunner; updated system installed summer 2022 in a live production line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hanging a door leaf into a prepared opening and bolting its hinge hardware. It is the same primitive as setting a door/section into an opening after track or hinge hardware is in place — grip a large panel, align it to an opening whose position is sensed by camera, engage the hardware, and torque fasteners — performed to automotive gap tolerances in a fenced production cell.

sources.claim: Vision-guided industrial robots insert windshield glass into the car-body aperture on production lines: the line PLC signals the ... the glass, on-arm 3D sensors measure the actual aperture position, and the robot corrects its path to place the panel into the opening despite body position variation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: placing a large fragile panel into a framed opening with sensed, variable location. Transfers to setting glass entrance-door panels and stacking door sections into an opening: same class of object (large flat panel), same requirement of millimetre alignment to an opening measured in situ rather than assumed.

sources.claim: A prefabricated-home manufacturer runs Kawasaki BX250L robots (250 kg payload) in an automated cell that lifts and places large, heavy OSB wall panels onto framed walls, replacing manual handling of oversized building panels.

sources.system: FANUC M-2000iA/2300

sources.system: Curtain-wall / facade panel installation robots (research prototypes, telescopic handler upgrades, cable-driven robots)
sources.developer: Various academic groups (e.g., Korea Univ. CWIR; EU cable-robot facade projects)
sources.title: Robot-based facade spatial assembly optimization - ScienceDirect

sources.transferJustification: Related task: installing large panels into openings in real buildings. Cited as the closest in-situ analogue; because it is prototype/assisted rather than autonomous worker-quality work, it does not substantiate completion of door setting at E2 or E3.

tasks.label: Assemble and fasten tracks to structures or bucks, using impact wrenches or welding equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential garage door replacement at an occupied single-family home: installer bolts together vertical/horizontal track sections and jamb/flag brackets, plumbs the vertical track against the wood buck and lag-screws it with an impact driver, then hangs the horizontal track and back-hangers from ceiling joists in a cluttered garage with parked cars and stored goods.

Garage door install at a new residential construction site (tract or custom home): empty garage, but bucks may be out of plumb, floor unfinished, other trades working nearby; installer shims, aligns and lag-bolts track and angle to the wood buck and ceiling framing.

Commercial sectional or rolling steel door at an operating warehouse/loading dock or industrial building: heavy track/guide angle held against a steel or masonry jamb, drilled and bolted or tack-welded in place, with work performed from a scissor lift alongside dock traffic.

Automatic sliding or swing door at a retail store, hospital or airport entrance: mounting the header/rail assembly and carrier track to storefront or steel framing, leveling and anchoring it, with the entrance partially barricaded during business hours.

Service call to repair a damaged track: bent vertical or horizontal track after a vehicle strike or door binding; installer removes fasteners, straightens or swaps the track section, re-shims and re-fastens to the jamb or hanger, checking alignment against the door sections and rollers.

sources.system: MWES Standard Ferris Wheel Robotic Welding Cell
sources.title: Robotic Frame Welding Automation | Midwest Engineered Systems
sources.claim: Commercially delivered robotic arc-welding cell with custom fixturing and a two-sided positioner welds large steel base frames autonomously once loaded, in a fenced industrial cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic welding of steel structural frames in a fixtured cell. It covers the 'welding equipment' path of this task — joining steel track/angle and brackets to a structural member at comparable weld precision — when the workpiece is presented fixtured as an E1 setting would present it.

sources.system: House of Design robotic truss systems (ABB robots)
sources.developer: House of Design Robotics / Builders FirstSource
sources.title: Video Showcase: Robots at the truss plant
sources.claim: Fully automated robotic systems handle long structural lumber members, position them in jigs and fasten them into finished roof and floor trusses in production plants of a major US building-products dealer.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic assembly and fastening of long, slender structural members into a fixtured frame. Objects (long steel/wood members), placement tolerances and powered fastening are comparable to bolting track sections and brackets onto a fixtured buck in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: WEINMANN WALLTEQ M-500 multifunction bridge
sources.title: WEINMANN WALLTEQ multifunction bridges (brochure)
sources.claim: Commercial multifunction gantry bridges automatically nail, staple or screw components onto timber wall, ceiling and roof frames held on fixtured production tables in prefabrication plants.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated powered fastening of components onto a fixtured wooden frame. This is the impact-driver/lag-screw path of the task — driving fasteners at planned positions into a wood buck — carried out in a purpose-built line.

sources.system: HRP-5P
sources.title: Development of a humanoid robot prototype, HRP-5P, capable of heavy labor
sources.claim: Humanoid robot autonomously handled and installed a large, heavy gypsum board against a wall frame at a simulated residential construction mock-up, using onboard perception and whole-body motion planning.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: lifting a large building element, positioning it against a frame and fastening it with a power tool. Shows the manipulation class needed for track placement, but only in a prepared mock-up, so it supports E1 rather than a jobsite tier.

sources.system: fischer construction robots (Züblin/STRABAG Frankfurt office project)
sources.title: Construction Robots Advance Frankfurt Office Build

sources.transferJustification: Same worksite class as commercial door installation. It substantiates only the hole-drilling sub-step; component handling, alignment and fastening remain human, so it cannot support completion of this task at E2 or E3.

sources.system: Hilti Jaibot
sources.title: Hilti Unveils BIM-Enabled Construction Jobsite Robot
sources.claim: Semi-autonomous mobile jobsite robot drills ceiling and wall holes to BIM data; it is driven between locations by an operator and performs only drilling and marking, not component installation.
sources.transferJustification: Closest commercially deployed jobsite robot to the drilling/anchoring element of track installation; it performs a sub-step only and is operator-driven, so it cannot substantiate completion of this task in human work facilities or unstructured sites.

sources.system: Robo-Buddy / Robo-Buddy Floor (Shimz Smart Site)
sources.title: Shimizu Deploys Robot for Installing Raised Floor Named "Robo-Buddy Floor"
sources.claim: Autonomous jobsite robots install standardized ceiling boards and raised-floor panels onto pre-built grids in high-rise construction, locating themselves from BIM and laser sensing.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: on-site robotic fastening of building components. Transfer to this task fails: it places flat standardized panels onto purpose-built grids/pedestals in cleared interiors, not multi-piece steel tracks that must be assembled, plumbed and lag-bolted to a door buck.

tasks.label: Inspect job sites, assessing headroom, side room, or other conditions to determine appropriateness of door for a given location.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential retrofit/replacement survey at an occupied single-family home: technician visits the driveway, enters an often cluttered garage, measures opening width/height, headroom to the lowest obstruction (joists, ductwork, lights), side room on each jamb, backroom depth, checks jamb/header condition and material, floor slope, power outlet location, water heater or storage in the side room, then decides which door, track (standard vs. low-headroom) and spring/opener package suits the location.

Jobsite visit to a house or light-commercial building under construction to verify the framed rough opening and surrounding clearances match the door already specified/ordered (opening dimensions, headroom, side room, backroom, obstructions from plumbing/electrical rough-in), and flag deviations from the plan before delivery.

Survey inside an operating warehouse, distribution center or manufacturing plant for a new or replacement sectional/rolling overhead or dock door: measure headroom, side room, backroom in the bay, note conduit, sprinkler lines, crane rails, dock levelers and racking, confirm mounting surfaces and power, and determine the suitable door type and mounting.

Survey of an automatic pedestrian entrance at a retail store, hospital, office lobby or airport vestibule with the public present: assess header/transom space, side room for sliding panels or swing arc, ADA clearances and activation/safety sensor zones, existing storefront framing and finishes, and traffic patterns, to determine whether a slider, swing or revolving unit fits the location.

Specialty/atypical sites: gate operators at parking structures and industrial yards, high-speed roll-up doors in food plants, fire/counter shutters, agricultural or self-storage doors — measuring clearances in unusual, sometimes outdoor or dirty settings with nonstandard framing and obstructions.

sources.system: Spot with Leica BLK ARC / Trimble X7 laser scanning payload
sources.title: 3D Laser Scanning Solutions & Autonomous Reality Capture | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics Spot carrying a laser-scanning payload (Leica BLK ARC, Trimble X7, FARO) runs autonomous reality-capture missions in industrial facilities, worksites and new construction, producing accurate as-built point clouds of the space.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous as-built laser scanning of a facility. Transfer: the measurement core of this task — capturing headroom, side room, backroom and obstruction geometry in a building bay — is exactly what these robot-borne survey-grade scanners produce, at millimetre-to-centimetre accuracy, in the same class of industrial facility.

sources.system: Spot with Leica BLK ARC
sources.title: Autonomous Reality Capture for Industrial Facilities | Boston Dynamics (webinar)
sources.claim: Point-cloud data captured by Spot on autonomous scanning missions in manufacturing facilities is used to confirm that a new installation will fit the existing space.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-captured scans used to verify a new piece of equipment will fit an existing location. Transfer: determining whether a door suits an opening is the same clearance-fit determination, on comparable geometry, inside the same kind of institution-controlled facility.

sources.system: Doxel autonomous lidar scanning robot
sources.title: AI Startup Using Robots and Lidar to Boost Productivity on Construction Sites - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Doxel's autonomous lidar-equipped ground robot scans live construction sites unattended and its software verifies whether the correct components are installed in the correct place, flagging deviations from the design.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous jobsite scanning plus automated as-built-vs-design conformance checking. Transfer: verifying that a framed opening and its surrounding clearances match the specified door is the same geometric conformance judgment, on building-scale features, on the same kind of construction jobsite.

sources.system: Doxel
sources.title: Top 10: AI Tools in Construction | Construction Digital
sources.claim: Doxel's robot continues to be described in 2026 trade coverage as autonomously scanning live construction sites and automatically comparing the lidar data with the BIM model to flag deviations.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as the IEEE Spectrum item: automated comparison of as-built geometry against a specified design is the machine analogue of checking a rough opening against the ordered door's clearance requirements.

sources.system: Exyn AL-4 autonomous lidar drone / Exyn Nexys
sources.title: Exyn Brings Level 4 Autonomy to Drones - IEEE Spectrum
sources.claim: Exyn's lidar drones reached Level 4A autonomy: given only a volume to map, the aircraft explores and maps a previously unknown GPS-denied space from takeoff to landing, and the technology is sold into mining, construction and AEC.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: one-off autonomous 3D capture of an unmapped interior. Transfer: a site survey is a single visit to a space with no prior map, so exploration-based autonomy (rather than teach-and-repeat) is what the measurement half of this task requires.

sources.system: Spot / quadruped scanning robots integrated with DroneDeploy
sources.title: How autonomous construction scanning creates a repeatable site record | DroneDeploy
sources.claim: Autonomous quadruped robots carrying laser scanners and 360 cameras are used commercially to walk routes across active construction sites and capture spatial data that teams compare against the BIM model.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous jobsite reality capture. sources.system: CALIPRI C12 / C12 Cobot inline gap-and-flush measurement system

sources.system: CUBE-R / MetraSCAN 3D-R robotic measuring cell
sources.title: R-Series Automated Inspection | 3D Scanners for Quality Control | Creaform
sources.claim: Turnkey robotic measuring cells with robot-mounted optical CMM scanners perform automated high-accuracy 3D dimensional inspection of parts presented in the cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional inspection of a fixtured workpiece against specification. Transfer: when the opening is brought to the machine, assessing whether its dimensions and clearances accept a given door is a specification-conformance measurement of the kind these cells run unattended.

tasks.label: Prepare doors for hardware installation, such as drilling holes to install locks.

instances.label: New commercial door installed/replaced in an occupied office, school or retail building: worker measures and marks from the hardware template, drills the 2-1/8" cross bore and 1" edge bore in a wood or hollow-metal slab, mortises the latch faceplate, and preps the frame for the strike, working in place at the opening around occupants.

Residential job at a private home: preparing a sectional garage door or the adjoining man-door for hardware - drilling/punching the stile for a T-handle or slide lock, drilling for opener/strut brackets, or boring an entry door for a lockset and deadbolt, in the driveway/garage with varied door construction.

Automatic swing or slide door installation at a hospital, airport or storefront entrance: drilling and tapping aluminum stile-and-rail door leaves, headers and jambs for pivots, operator arms, floor closers, exit devices and locks to the operator manufacturer's template, in an active facility.

Shop pre-prep before delivery: batches of door slabs and jambs on a bench or door machine in the contractor's/millwork shop, prepped for hinges, cylindrical locks, deadbolts and closers with jigs, routers and boring fixtures.

Retrofit/repair prep on an already-hung door at a business: enlarging an existing bore for an upgraded lock, adding a deadbolt above an existing knob, re-prepping and reinforcing after pry damage, matching existing strike and frame conditions.

tasks.label: Cut door stops or angle irons to fit openings.

Automatic sliding/swing door install or retrofit at a retail store, hospital, or office entrance: cutting aluminum jamb/stop trim, glass stops, or header cover to length (often with miters) to fit the existing rough opening, using a chop saw set up in the vestibule or on a cart in the lobby.

Commercial overhead/rolling steel door service or retrofit at an existing warehouse, dock, or fire station: cutting steel angle iron jamb/track angles and header angle to length with an abrasive chop saw or angle grinder, then drilling/punching mounting holes to suit the masonry opening.

Shop prefabrication at the contractor's own warehouse/fab shop: from field-measured dimensions on a work order, cutting bundles of wood stops or steel angle to size at a bench saw/chop saw before loading the truck for the install.

New commercial construction site: cutting angle iron and stops to fit door openings amid partial framing, dust, debris, and other trades, with the opening dimensions taken as found and cuts made on a saw stand in the shell of the building.

Odd-shaped or damaged-opening service call (older home, out-of-square or settled masonry opening, rotted stop replacement): cutting a filler or replacement stop piece with bevels/scribes, trial-fitting and trimming again to close the gap.

tasks.label: Remove or disassemble defective automatic mechanical door closers, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Interior commercial swing door (office suite, school corridor, hospital ward door): defective surface-mounted overhead closer. Tech works from a ladder in an occupied corridor, disconnects the spring-loaded arm, backs out 4-6 machine screws / sex bolts from door leaf and frame soffit plate, catches leaking hydraulic fluid, lowers the 6-10 lb cast body.

Exterior entrance door at a store, school, or clinic: weathered surface closer or low-energy swing operator. Corroded/painted-over fasteners, stripped heads, wind loading on the leaf, public pedestrian traffic through the opening while the unit is unbolted and taken down.

Commercial entrance with concealed hardware: overhead-concealed closer in the header or a floor closer in a cement case. Heavy glass/aluminum leaf must be taken off pivots first, cover plate and spindle broken loose, seized anchors cut or chiseled, unit pried out of the floor case.

Automatic sliding door at a retail or hospital vestibule: header cover removed, defective operator assembly (motor/gearbox, belt, carriage) unbolted from the header track; harness leads and controller connections disconnected before the unit comes out overhead.

Private residence, small apartment building, or unmanaged property: closer on a screen/entry door or a failed residential garage-door opener head. Cluttered, non-standard surroundings, no institutional control of the site, wood screws pulled out of soft or damaged jambs.

Service shop bench: a closer already removed from the field is disassembled for inspection or parts salvage - arm and shoe off, end caps and valves out, pinion and spring cartridge separated, parts sorted for rebuild or scrap.

New-construction or dock build-out: install bumpers, seals or shelters at multiple dock positions in a building still under construction — unfinished apron, temporary power, scaffolds or lifts, other trades working around, layout coordinated off drawings and field-verified dimensions.

Field repair/partial replacement on an installed unit at an operating facility: replace worn seal face wear pleats or torn vinyl covers, re-anchor a sagging head pad, add shims or backer blocks where the wall is out of plumb, refasten pulled anchors.

tasks.label: Lubricate door closer oil chambers, and pack spindles with leather washers.

instances.label: Scheduled preventive-maintenance lubrication of surface-mounted overhead door closers in an institutional building (school, office, hospital): technician works from a ladder, pops the cover, wipes the body, greases the pinion/spindle and arm pivots, tops up the hydraulic oil chamber on serviceable models, re-seals the fill plug, then adjusts sweep/latch valves and cycles the door.
