tasks.label: Position steel beams to support bedplates of machines and equipment, using blueprints and schematic drawings to determine work procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New production machine installed in an operating manufacturing plant (auto parts, packaging, food). From the foundation and layout drawings the millwright lays out beam lines off column lines/benchmarks, rigs steel support beams and soleplates with the overhead crane, chain falls and toe jacks, sets them on the concrete pad, shims and levels them, then bolts/welds them so the machine bedplate can be landed. Congested floor, adjacent running lines, utilities in the way.

Retrofit or replacement in a heavy-industry plant (paper mill, steel mill, mine concentrator, power house). Steel support beams/soleplates are threaded into an existing foundation pit or under existing equipment through tight access, set over anchor bolts, leveled to rotating-equipment tolerances (thousandths per foot) with shims and grout, hot, dirty, poorly lit conditions.

Greenfield/new-build industrial construction: working with a mobile crane and an ironworker crew, positioning structural steel beams on new concrete foundations and anchor-bolt patterns per structural and equipment layout drawings, before the equipment bedplates arrive. Unfinished building or open yard, weather, changing site layout and other trades.

Shop work: building or modifying a steel base frame/skid that will carry an equipment bedplate — cutting beams to length and positioning them on a layout table or jig per shop drawings, squaring, clamping and tack-welding, then finish welding and machining/drilling mounting pads. Fabrication bay of the employer's shop, overhead crane and standard fixtures available.

Field installation away from a production floor: setting support beams for a conveyor drive at a quarry or grain elevator, a compressor/pump skid on a rooftop or mezzanine, or equipment in a remote/agricultural facility. Access by forklift, boom truck or gin pole; improvised cribbing; uneven or sloped surfaces; positions scaled off simple drawings and field measurements.

Transfer holds for the E1 counterfactual of this task — steel beams and mating members presented clamped and located, positioned to drawing coordinates and secured — with comparable objects (rolled steel sections of several tonnes) and mm-level location accuracy.

tasks.label: Fabricate and dismantle parts, equipment, and machines, using a cutting torch or other cutting equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench/shop fabrication of flat parts to drawing dimensions from plate or sheet stock — machine sole plates, base plates, mounting brackets, gussets, guard panels, shim plates — laid out from a sketch or blueprint and cut with a hand oxy-fuel torch, plasma cutter, or track burner in the plant maintenance shop or contractor fab shop, then edges ground square.

Cutting stock to length and bevel in the shop: wide-flange beam, channel, angle, pipe, tube and round shafting cut for machine supports, frames, spacers, sleeves and lifting lugs, using torch, portable band saw, cold saw or abrasive chop saw, with weld-prep bevels where required.

In-situ dismantling inside an operating plant during a scheduled shutdown: torching out an old machine base, press frame, conveyor run, chute or tank, burning off seized anchor bolts, nuts and old welds, working overhead, at floor level and in confined spaces alongside live equipment, with fire watch, hot-work permit and rigging coordination.

Field cutting and fit-up during installation or relocation at an erection/construction site: trimming anchor bolts and embeds, burning holes and openings in decking, base plates and structural members, cutting grating, handrail and existing steel to clear the new machine, all sized to as-found measured conditions, frequently outdoors, at height or in a lift.

Sizing removed machinery into scrap-manageable pieces in a laydown or scrap area: gearbox and pump housings, castings, drums, tanks, sheaves and weldments cut apart by hand torch, cut locations judged by eye against the piece's as-found, rusty, painted and oil-coated condition.

Sizing removed regular stock into scrap or reusable lengths at a cutting station: beams, channel, angle and pipe salvaged from dismantled platforms, supports and guarding, cut into uniform lengths for the scrap bin or the rack.

tasks.label: Construct foundation for machines, using hand tools and building materials such as wood, cement, and steel.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cast-in-place reinforced concrete machine pad/plinth inside an operating manufacturing or process plant: lay out from drawings, prep subgrade, build lumber/plywood forms, tie rebar, place and vibrate concrete, screed and trowel, strip forms.

Set, shim and grout a machine baseplate/soleplate on a foundation: jackscrew/shim leveling to thousandths of an inch per foot, build wood grout dams, mix and place cementitious or epoxy grout, cure, torque anchor bolts, check final level and soft foot.

Fabricate a welded structural steel base, skid or equipment stand in the plant maintenance/fab shop from drawings: cut and fit channel, beam and plate, weld out, drill or punch mounting holes, clean up.

Set and secure a steel base/frame or sole plates at the machine location on the plant floor: position to layout lines, shim and level, weld or bolt to existing structure/embeds, final alignment before the machine goes on.

Install post-installed anchors in an existing concrete floor/foundation to receive a machine base: transfer hole layout from the equipment drawing or template, hammer-drill holes, clean, set adhesive or wedge anchors, tension.

Rough field/outdoor foundation work at a mine, quarry, mill yard or construction site: cut and stack timber cribbing, mats and mudsills on uneven ground, build board forms for a pier footing, place blocking and steel bearing plates in weather and dirt.

tasks.label: Operate engine lathe to grind, file, and turn machine parts to dimensional specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Plant maintenance machine shop: millwright chucks bar stock in the shop's engine lathe and turns a replacement shaft, sleeve or bushing to print dimensions (typically ±0.001-0.005 in.), checking with micrometer as cuts are taken, then filing/emery-polishing the finished diameter.

Fitting work: turning a bushing, sleeve or bearing spacer to a measured fit against a mating part the millwright has measured (press or slip fit), taking successive skim cuts and trial fits, then deburring, chamfering and polishing the part before assembly.

Reconditioning a worn removed component in the shop lathe: truing a coupling hub or sheave bore, dressing a scored shaft journal, or running a tool-post grinder to restore a bearing seat to a ground finish and size on a part whose starting condition varies.

Quick one-off shop-made items in the maintenance shop lathe: spacers, pins, studs, threaded adapters, shims cut from stock at modest tolerance, turned and filed to size while the equipment waits, often from a sketch rather than a print.

Field/on-site machining at the installed machine: portable lathe/turning attachment or in-place turning of a shaft end, flange or seat inside a plant on the erected equipment, in cramped, dirty, awkwardly-accessed conditions with the workpiece part of the installed assembly.

tasks.label: Install robot and modify its program, using teach pendant.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New robotic work cell in an automotive/metal-fabrication plant: millwright rigs a 300–1,500 kg six-axis robot into position with forklift or overhead crane per layout drawings, sets and shims the baseplate, drills and sets concrete anchors, levels and aligns to the cell datum within a few tenths of a millimeter, mounts the end-of-arm tool, routes power/dress packages to the controller, then powers up and jogs with the teach pendant to set the tool center point and touch up taught points until the cycle is accepted.

Relocation or re-installation of an existing robot during a plant shutdown or line retool: disconnect and unbolt the arm, move it a few bays, re-anchor and re-level on a new pedestal or riser, re-master/calibrate the axes, then use the teach pendant to re-teach or offset the taught positions to the moved fixtures and prove the program out before restart.

Light-payload cobot or small robot added to a machine shop or packaging line: bolt the robot to a pedestal or machine frame, mount gripper and sensors, run cabling and I/O to the controller/PLC, then hand-guide or pendant-jog waypoints (pick from tray, load chuck, place on conveyor) and adjust speeds and offsets until parts run without collision.

Program modification only, inside an existing fenced robot cell: after a gripper change, tooling wear, new part number, or palletizing pattern change, the millwright enters teach mode, jogs the robot on the pendant, edits and re-records positions, dry-runs at reduced speed, then returns the cell to auto and verifies production quality.

Installation in a difficult or non-standard setting: greenfield facility still under construction (open floor, other trades working, no finished utilities), a mezzanine or elevated steel platform, a washdown food plant, or a cramped retrofit into a legacy line where floor flatness and access are unknown until the crate is opened; includes fabricating shims/brackets on the fly and then teaching the program.

sources.system: FANUC lights-out robot assembly plant (Oshino, Japan)
sources.title: Lights-Out Manufacturing
sources.claim: FANUC operates lights-out plants in which robots assemble other robots unattended for extended periods — the closest existing capability to 'a machine putting a robot together' — but this is serial production of robot units inside a purpose-built assembly line, not rigging, anchoring, aligning and teach-pendant programming a robot into a customer's work cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic assembly of robot arms on a fixed production line. It involves comparable objects (robot castings, gearboxes) and precision, but the workpieces arrive fixtured on a dedicated line; it does not cover positioning a robot to a layout plan, setting concrete anchors, leveling/aligning to a cell datum, or creating and validating taught program points, so it does not transfer to the millwright installation-and-teach task.

sources.system: Hilti Jaibot

roles.title: Refractory Materials Repairers, Except Brickmasons
roles.description: Build or repair equipment such as furnaces, kilns, cupolas, boilers, converters, ladles, soaking pits, and ovens, using refractory materials.

tasks.label: Reline or repair ladles and pouring spouts with refractory clay, using trowels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel mill / large foundry: hot patch repair of a transfer or teeming ladle's working lining between campaigns at a ladle repair stand — worn slag line, barrel and bottom areas built back up with refractory repair mix, troweled/finished to profile while the vessel is still warm, before the ladle returns to the rotation.

Cold full reline of a large ladle in the relining bay: old lining demolished, safety and working lining bricks or castable installed, refractory clay/mortar troweled into joints and behind shapes, well block and nozzle seat bedded, spout rebuilt, then dried out.

Foundry medium pouring/transfer ladle (roughly 1–20 t): worn wear-face relined or patched with plastic refractory or castable, applied and troweled smooth in the foundry's ladle repair area, then dried before return to the pouring floor.

Small foundry hand ladles, bull ladles and shank ladles (under ~500 kg) plus small pouring cups: interior daubed with refractory clay/plastic mix by hand and trowel over a form or directly on the shell, edges struck off, then air- or torch-dried.

Rebuilding eroded ladle pouring spouts and lips: clay or plastic refractory packed into the washed-out spout channel and lip and troweled back to the original pouring profile in the ladle repair area.

In-situ patching of pouring spouts, launders and troughs on tilting furnaces, cupolas and pressure-pour units, daubed with refractory clay and troweled on the melt deck between heats, often hot and in cramped positions.

sources.system: VELCO stationary ladle gunning installation (ladle gunning manipulator type 208)
sources.developer: VELCO GmbH (Velbert, Germany), installed at Outokumpu Tornio, Finland
sources.title: Ladle gunning system - Velco.de
sources.claim: VELCO commissioned a fully automatic gunning installation ... steel ladles at Outokumpu Tornio; ladles are moved by rail carriage into a dedicated gunning hall with four gunning positions and programs that automatically gun the ladle bottom, side wall and spout with both permanent-lining and wear-layer material.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine gunning of refractory repair mix onto a ladle's wear lining and pouring spout instead of hand-troweling refractory clay. Same objects (steel ladle interior and spout), same material class and same accepted output — restored refractory thickness to profile — so performance carries over to relining/repairing ladles and pouring spouts.

sources.system: VELCO stationary ladle gunning installation
sources.title: Ladle gunning system - Velco.de
sources.claim: In the same deployed Outokumpu installation the human role is program selection; the gunning cycle itself then runs automatically, with manual joystick takeover only optional for spot work.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (machine application of refractory repair material to ladle lining and spout); this item establishes that execution is programmed and automatic rather than continuously teleoperated.

sources.system: MINSCAN-LS / LaCam / SCANTROL automated refractory maintenance system
sources.date: 2026-07 (product page retrieved; system in service since 2003)

sources.claim: Minteq/Ferrotron's Minscan-LS gunning manipulator coupled to LaCam laser measurement and Scantrol software repairs the refractory lining of an electric arc furnace by gunning fully automatically from the laser scan data, with no operator intervention needed; the concept has been in industrial use since a 2003 installation at Stahlwerk Bous.

sources.system: VELCO mobile lance manipulator for ladle gunning

tasks.label: Chip slag from linings of ladles or remove linings when beyond repair, using hammers and chisels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel melt shop relining bay: a 100–300 t teeming/hot-metal ladle whose brick working lining (MgO-C slag line, barrel, bottom) is spent is tipped or set on a stand and the whole working lining is broken out down to the safety lining, including breaking out the wellblock/porous-plug seats and prying loose bricks, using jackhammers, breakers and hand hammers and chisels.

Steel plant ladle prep bay, between heats: hot ladle (several hundred °C) is deskulled/deslagged — solidified steel skull and slag are chipped off the ladle lip and mouth ring, freeboard and slag line, and around the slide-gate/nozzle area, without damaging the still-serviceable lining; hand hammers, chisels and air tools, working under heat and time pressure.

Large monolithic (castable) lined casting/transfer ladle (tens of tonnes) in a foundry or steel plant repair bay: fused refractory and baked-on slag are removed from the inside wall so new refractory concrete will bond, taking off only the degraded layer and leaving sound refractory undisturbed; ladle stands upright, overhead crane available.

Iron/steel foundry ladle repair area: small hand, crane and treatment ladles (0.5–10 t) with rammed or castable linings — slag crust is chipped off the lining after use, and when the lining is beyond repair the old lining is knocked out at a bench or pit with hammer, chisel and air hammer, varied ladle shapes and sizes on the floor.

Nonferrous casthouse/crucible shop (aluminium or similar): solidified metal, bath and dross buildup is cut and chipped from the inside walls, bottom and spout of refractory-lined crucibles/transfer ladles to restore capacity, vessels delivered by handling vehicle or crane, sometimes still hot.

tasks.label: Mix specified amounts of sand, clay, mortar powder, and water to form refractory clay or mortar, using shovels or mixing machines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel mill, foundry or glass plant repair bay: worker batches refractory castable/mortar at the plant's mixing station — cuts and dumps 50-lb bags of premixed refractory into a pan or paddle mixer, meters water per the product data sheet, mixes to specified consistency, discharges into wheelbarrows or buckets for the crew. Fixed layout, plant-standard equipment, institution controls access.

Hand mixing small batches at the work face: mortar for laying brick, patching plastic or ramming mix blended with shovel, hoe, or drill paddle in a wheelbarrow, mortar box or bucket right beside or inside a torn-down furnace, ladle, boiler or oven — cramped, hot, dusty, rubble and scaffolding underfoot, consistency judged by eye and trowel feel.

Field/outage job at a customer site (power-plant boiler, cement kiln, incinerator, refinery heater): crew sets up a portable mortar/castable mixer or silo-fed mixing-pumping unit in a temporary staging area, often outdoors on uneven ground in variable weather, and mixes bulk quantities to feed pumps, buckets or the gun for hours.

Continuous supply during a reline or hot repair: worker keeps a gunning/shotcrete machine fed — dumping bags of dry gun mix into the hopper and controlling water addition at the mixer or nozzle so the material sprays at the right wetness, working in the plant's ladle/tundish/furnace repair bay for a whole shift.

Small precise batches of specialty material in the shop prep area: low-cement castable, mortar for thin-joint brickwork or a mold-cast shape mixed to a tight water tolerance in a small mixer, weighed on a scale, ball-in-hand or flow tested before use.

tasks.label: Measure furnace walls to determine dimensions and cut required number of sheets from plastic block, using saws.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Power/process-plant outage: worker enters a cooled boiler, incinerator or fired-heater chamber through a manway, works among scaffolding, dust and spalled lining, measures the panel areas between anchors and around burners/tubes with tape and laser meter, sketches dimensions, then cuts plastic refractory block into sheets with a hand or band saw at a staging area by the access door.

Steel mill or foundry vessel work in a relining/repair bay: worker measures the zone of a ladle, tundish, EAF sidewall or launder to be patched, allowing for anchors and existing lining thickness, and cuts plastic block sheets to fit on the bay floor with a portable saw.

Small industrial furnace, oven or kiln in a manufacturing plant (heat-treat furnace, forge furnace, aluminum holding furnace): worker measures wall and roof panel dimensions inside the small chamber, then cuts a modest number of plastic block sheets on a bench beside the furnace.

Refractory contractor field repair at a customer site (cement kiln hood, glass furnace port, incinerator wall): partly collapsed and irregular wall sections measured as found, often with weather exposure and no fixed layout; sheets cut from plastic block at a truck-side saw setup.

Contractor prep/fabrication shop: worker cuts a batch of plastic refractory block into sheets of standard panel dimensions taken from job drawings and a few field-verified measurements, boxes and stages them for shipment to the shutdown.

tasks.label: Dry and bake new linings by placing inverted linings over burners, building fires in ladles, or by using blowtorches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel melt shop / large foundry: a newly relined 20-150 t steel or iron ladle is brought by crane to the ladle drying-and-preheating station, coupled to the burner lid (vertical or horizontal), lit, and taken through a multi-hour ramp/soak dry-out and bake curve; worker watches for steam, spalling and burner faults and shuts down.

Foundry floor: newly lined small transfer/hand/pouring ladles and crucibles are dried by inverting them over a floor gas burner or building a fire in them, then baked to temperature; several ladles of differing sizes cycled through the day.

Bench or floor work on small relined or patched removable items (ladle lids and covers, spouts, launders, troughs, nozzle/well blocks, tundish inserts): worker plays a blowtorch or hand burner over the fresh refractory until the patch is dried and set.

Localized in-place patch drying: worker reaches or climbs into fixed equipment (furnace wall, cupola well, boiler tube wall, converter mouth, soaking pit) and torch-dries a small fresh patch on the standing lining, judging dryness by appearance and steam.

In-situ dry-out of a fully relined fixed unit (furnace, boiler, oven, kiln, large vessel) in the plant: temporary dry-out burner and thermocouples rigged into the unit, openings blanked, then a multi-day heat-up curve run and monitored to specification.

Field job at a customer site or a unit still under construction: portable burner rig or torches used to dry a newly installed lining, with scaffolding, temporary power/gas, weather exposure and site-to-site variation in access and layout.

sources.system: NUTEC Bickley ladle preheaters, heaters and dryers
sources.title: Ladle & Tundish Preheaters / Ladle Preheaters and Dryers - NUTEC Bickley
sources.claim: Commercial vertical ladle dryers and ladle/tundish preheaters supplied to steel and aluminum foundries dry and bake fresh refractory linings under programmable ramp/soak burner control, with hydraulic arms that position the burner lid onto the ladle at a fixed station.

sources.system: Hotwork refractory dryout service (excess-air burner)
sources.title: Hotwork Refractory Dryout Services | Hotwork

tasks.label: Remove worn or damaged plastic block refractory linings of furnaces, using hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outage/shutdown tear-out at a power, biomass or waste-to-energy plant: crew enters a cooled boiler or incinerator through a manhole, works from scaffolding, and removes large areas (tens to hundreds of m2) of worn monolithic/plastic refractory from walls and roof back to the studs, V-anchors and bare steel using pneumatic chipping hammers and hand breakers.

Steel mill / foundry vessel work in a relining bay: chipping out worn rammed-plastic or castable lining from ladle covers, tundish permanent linings, EAF roof deltas, launders, spouts, runners and cupola sections, working inside or over deep, hot, awkward vessels with pneumatic hammers and pry bars while protecting shells and safety linings.

Localized patch repair on a cooled-down furnace in place: cutting out a few square feet of damaged plastic block lining around a burner port, door jamb, arch or hot spot, squaring and feathering edges to sound material with hand hammer, chisel and small pneumatic chipper in confined, awkward access.

Refinery / petrochemical / cement turnaround: removing worn plastic and castable refractory from heater walls, cyclones, risers, transfer lines and duct interiors congested with tubes, hangers, hex mesh and anchors, in confined spaces under permit, using hand-held breakers and chipping guns.

Shop work on small or removable equipment: heat-treat furnaces, ovens, ladle covers, preheater lids, crucible furnaces and burner blocks brought into a maintenance shop, where the worn plastic lining is chipped out on the floor or a stand with hand and pneumatic tools.

Field job at an unstructured site: dismantling or repairing refractory in equipment taken as found — an asphalt-plant dryer, a small foundry cupola, mobile or decommissioned furnace being demolished — with ladders/lifts, variable access, debris and no fixed layout.

tasks.label: Climb scaffolding, carrying hoses, and spray surfaces of cupolas with refractory mixtures, using spray equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between-campaign gunning of a cupola/shaft melting furnace lining in an iron foundry melt shop: worker climbs the charge-door platform or an internal scaffold, drags the gunning hose up, and sprays refractory mix onto the worn melt zone, tuyere band and shaft walls of the fixed furnace. Hot, dusty, institution-controlled plant floor; the furnace is standard equipment in a known location.

Hot patch gunning of an electric arc furnace, converter or holding-furnace lining in a steel mill during a short break in production: hoses and lance are brought to the furnace platform, the worn banks/slag line are sprayed with gunning mix within a tight time window while the vessel is still hot.

Full spray relining of a transfer vessel (steel ladle, tundish, RH snorkel, treatment ladle) at a relining stand or preparation bay in a mill or foundry: vessel set in a known orientation, hoses run to the nozzle, whole working lining sprayed to specified thickness and finished.

Field refractory spraying during a customer-site turnaround inside large fired equipment (utility or waste-to-energy boiler, process heater, incinerator, rotary kiln, cyclone, transfer duct): scaffolding or a suspended platform is erected inside, worker climbs with hoses into a dark, confined, debris-strewn space and guns refractory over tube walls, anchors and hex mesh; layout and damage differ site to site.

Awkward patch spraying at height on ancillary equipment during a shutdown — furnace hoods, roofs, launders, ladle lips, burner throats, breeching and ductwork — reached by ladder or ad hoc scaffold with hose in hand, cluttered access, irregular small areas to be built back to profile.

tasks.label: Spread mortar on stopper heads and rods, using trowels, and slide brick sleeves over rods to form refractory jackets.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Steel/iron foundry ladle-prep shop, routine build: worker takes a clean steel stopper rod on a bench or vertical rod stand, trowels high-temperature mortar onto the stopper head and each sleeve mating face, and slides 3-8 standard clay-graphite brick sleeves down the rod to form a continuous refractory jacket, wiping excess mortar and setting the assembly aside to dry/preheat. Standard sizes, several assemblies per shift.

Large bottom-pour ladle stopper for a steel mill/large foundry: 2-4 m rod handled vertically in a stand or with a hoist, heavier and more numerous sleeves, mortar mixed to consistency on the spot, gooseneck/head threaded and mortared, and the finished jacket checked for straightness and seating against the nozzle before the ladle is teemed.

Rebuild of a used rod: worker strips spent, slag-soaked sleeves and baked-on mortar from a returned stopper rod, cleans and inspects the rod for warp, scale and thread damage, replaces the stopper head, then re-mortars and re-sleeves it. Condition of the incoming rod and residue varies heat to heat.

Work on the pouring floor / ladle pit: a stopper head or top sleeve is mortared or replaced on a rod at or near a hot ladle in the ladle stand shortly before pouring, with cramped access, radiant heat, dust, overhead crane traffic and other crew working nearby; must be finished in time for the pour.

Small job-shop foundry or captive shop with low volume and mixed work: stopper rods of several different diameters and sleeve types assembled on an improvised bench with hand-mixed mortar, sometimes one-off or custom-length builds for an unusual ladle.

sources.claim: REX-ROBO LSG is a commercial robot station in steel plants that automatically exchanges ladle slide-gate refractory plates and the lower nozzle, installs the upper nozzle, opens/closes the frame, attaches the hydraulic cylinder, lances the nozzle hole and analyses plate damage — i.e. it removes spent refractory ceramic pieces and seats new ones precisely.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: replacing refractory components on a ladle slide gate. It transfers to stopper-rod jacketing because the objects are the same class (heavy, brittle refractory ceramic pieces), the placement tolerance is comparable (a nozzle/plate must seat squarely on its mating face, as a sleeve must seat on the sleeve below it), and the robot removes spent pieces, installs new ones and verifies the result rather than merely handling them.

tasks.label: Dump and tamp clay in molds, using tamping tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shop/prep-bay fabrication of small molded refractory pieces: plastic fireclay or ramming mix is shoveled into steel or wooden molds on a bench, tamped down in layers with a hand or pneumatic tamper, struck off, and the mold stripped. Pieces include taphole/bott plugs, patch blocks, burner and tuyere surrounds, nozzle seats and test shapes. Clean, lit shop area inside the plant.

Relining a coreless induction furnace or cupola well on the melt deck: a steel former is set and centered inside the shell, dry vibratable/ramming clay mix is dumped into the annulus in ~2-inch layers, each layer forked/de-aired and tamped or vibrated to full density before the next; bottom rammed first. Repetitive, dusty, dimensionally critical, done to a fixed procedure in the plant's melt shop.

Monolithic lining or heavy repair of a ladle, tundish, spout, launder or runner in a relining/prep bay: vessel positioned, former or wooden form set inside, plastic refractory/ramming clay dumped into the gap and rammed or vibrated in lifts, top screeded, form pulled. Vessels are of a few standard sizes and the bay is a dedicated, institution-controlled work area.

In-place patch repair inside installed equipment (furnace wall or hearth, soaking pit, boiler, kiln, coke oven, ladle bottom well): a temporary form or mold is built or clamped over the eroded, irregular area amid rubble and residual lining, clay is dumped by hand and tamped into the cavity in a hot, confined, awkward-access space, then the form stripped. Geometry differs every time.

Field/shutdown work at a customer site (foundry, glass plant, cement plant, refinery heater): clay mixed on site, portable wooden molds knocked together on the spot, mix dumped and hand-tamped in awkward positions, sometimes overhead or at height on scaffold, under outage time pressure.

tasks.label: Transfer clay structures to curing ovens, melting tanks, and drawing kilns, using forklifts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine intra-plant transfer: moving palletized or base-mounted clay/refractory shapes (a few hundred lb to ~2 t) from the forming or drying area to a curing (drying) oven inside a refractory or glass plant. Flat concrete floor, marked aisles, fixed pick and drop stations, mixed pedestrian and lift-truck traffic.

Delivering clay structures / precast refractory shapes to the melting tank or furnace area of a glass or ceramics plant and setting them down at a marked staging spot. Hot zone with radiant heat, dust and cullet on the floor, narrow aisles beside operating equipment, crews working nearby.

Handling an oversized, unpalletized, fragile clay structure (e.g., a glass melting pot or large one-off precast block) with a special fork attachment, boom or slings; precise insertion into a pot arch / curing oven opening or placement on a kiln car for the drawing kiln. Cracking or chipping ruins the piece.

Plant yard work: unloading pallets/crates of clay shapes and refractory materials from flatbed trucks and moving them into the shop or covered storage, then feeding them toward the kiln area. Outdoors, uneven asphalt, weather, dunnage and strapping present.

Ad hoc forklift moves during a furnace rebuild or scheduled outage: a torn-down furnace hall (own plant or a customer's), scaffolding, hoses and rubble underfoot, temporary staging that changes hour to hour, crews signalling where to set each load.

tasks.label: Adhere to safety practices and procedures, such as checking equipment regularly and erecting barriers around work areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Setting up work-zone protection for a distribution job on a public street: reading the traffic situation, placing advance warning signs, coning a taper around the bucket truck/pole, and picking everything back up when the job is done.

Pre-use / periodic checking of the crew's equipment at the service center yard or staging area: air-testing and visually inspecting rubber gloves, sleeves and blankets, wiping and checking hot sticks, checking rigging, straps and hooks, and the daily walk-around/functional check of the aerial device or digger derrick.

Test-before-touch and grounding on a de-energized overhead distribution line: verifying absence of voltage on each phase with a detector on a hot stick from the bucket, then installing personal protective cluster grounds to conductors and system neutral/pole ground, and removing them afterward.

Barricading a hazard in a setting taken as found: caution tape or barricades around a downed conductor in a customer's yard, around an open pole hole or excavation in a parkway, or around equipment on an unpaved off-road right-of-way.

Personal protective equipment discipline before climbing or bucket work: inspecting and donning FR clothing, hard hat, rubber gloves and sleeves, inspecting the fall-arrest harness/climbing gear, and tying off at the work position.

tasks.label: Drive vehicles equipped with tools and materials to job sites.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine daytime run from the utility service center to a scheduled distribution job site in a city/suburb: bucket truck loaded with tools, reels and hardware; arterial and residential paved streets, traffic signals, school zones; ends parked at the curb/roadside next to the pole with cones set.

Longer drive on rural state highways and paved county roads to a remote distribution pole or transmission structure: 30-90 minutes, mixed speeds, farm traffic, sometimes at night; ends pulled onto a gravel shoulder or field entrance at the structure.

Off-pavement access: driving a line truck or digger derrick off the road onto right-of-way two-tracks, farm lanes, pasture and creek crossings, through locked gates, over mud, ruts and snow to reach a structure with no street address.

Dense urban / tight-quarters delivery of the truck: downtown streets and alleys, backing a heavy boom truck between parked cars, into an alley or a customer's driveway, working around lane closures, low clearances and pedestrians, under flagger or police traffic control.

Storm and emergency response: night driving in heavy rain, wind, ice or snow, roads blocked by downed trees, wires and flooding, detours around closed roads, often into unfamiliar out-of-territory areas in a mutual-aid convoy.

On-premises vehicle movements: repositioning trucks inside the service-center yard and material yard for loading, moving between staging areas, and driving through the fence line into a substation yard to unload.

tasks.label: Open switches or attach grounding devices to remove electrical hazards from disturbed or fallen lines or to facilitate repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Isolating a section of overhead distribution: at a roadside or urban pole the worker (or the system operator) opens pole-mounted switching devices — fused cutouts with a hot stick from a bucket, gang-operated air-break switches, reclosers/sectionalizers — to de-energize a section after a fault or for a planned repair, then verifies the open point. Public road/rear-lot setting, all weather, traffic and bystanders present.

Installing temporary protective grounds at an overhead distribution worksite: test for absence of voltage, clamp ground clusters onto each de-energized phase with a shotgun/hot stick from a bucket truck, bond the cluster to the pole ground or a driven rod, and remove the grounds after the repair. Roadside or backyard easement, variable pole framing and conductor sizes.

Storm/emergency response to a fallen or damaged conductor: crew finds the wire down in a street or yard amid tree limbs and debris, gets the section isolated, tests dead, and applies grounds on both sides of the break before making the repair. Wind, rain, darkness, uncontrolled public setting.

Underground work: opening load-break switches or pulling load-break elbows in a padmount switchgear cabinet or vault to de-energize a cable section, then installing grounding elbows or portable grounds on the de-energized cable before splicing or terminating. Pad on a street, parking lot, or easement; confined, sometimes wet vault.

Transmission line clearance: after the line is switched out, the worker climbs the structure or is lifted by bucket in the right-of-way and installs protective grounds (personal or bracket grounds) on the conductors and shield wire, then removes them at completion. Rough terrain, tall lattice or steel-pole structures, weather exposure.

Substation switching order: inside a fenced substation, open breakers and disconnect switches and apply grounds (close grounding switches or hang portable grounds) to clear a line or piece of apparatus for maintenance, then reverse the order to restore. Controlled access, standard bay layout, engineered clearances.

tasks.label: Climb poles or use truck-mounted buckets to access equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Roadside urban/suburban distribution: lineworker rides a truck-mounted insulated bucket up to a 4-35 kV pole to reach the conductors and work on them - connecting/disconnecting service drops and jumpers, tapping, installing tie wires and line hardware, energized or de-energized, with traffic beside the work zone.

Bucket access to pole-top apparatus for change-out: reaching a distribution transformer, cutouts, arresters, crossarm and insulators; boom-lifting heavy hardware into place and doing hand-tool/bolting work at the pole top on a street or rural roadside.

Free-climbing a wood pole with hooks, belt and hand line where a bucket cannot reach - rear-lot easement, backyard, alley, muddy field - on a pole of unknown condition with fences, guys, vegetation and animals around it.

Storm/emergency restoration access: climbing or bucketing to damaged structures at night or in wind, rain, cold or ice, over debris and soft ground, with broken poles, slack or downed conductors and time pressure.

Access purely to look: climbing or bucketing up to inspect, patrol or troubleshoot pole-top equipment and hardware (visual/thermal check of connectors, insulators, transformer, cutouts) after an outage or on a condition-assessment round, with no hands-on repair.

Transmission/rural structure access: climbing a steel lattice tower or wood H-frame, or booming up off-road, to reach insulator strings, dampers, spacers and structure hardware in a right-of-way far from paved access.

tasks.label: Install, maintain, and repair electrical distribution and transmission systems, including conduits, cables, wires, and related equipment, such as transformers, circuit breakers, and switches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Connection and small-component work on overhead distribution from an insulated bucket along streets and rural roads: making and removing hot taps and jumpers, installing connectors, clamps and grounding rings, replacing fuse cutouts and arresters, connecting new services on 4-35 kV lines, energized or de-energized, traffic and weather as found.

Pole-top and switchyard hardware changeouts that are bolted/clamped assemblies: swapping crossarms, pin/post insulators, brackets and bolted bus or terminal fittings on distribution poles and on disconnect switches in utility substations.

Heavy component work at height on in-service overhead lines: changing out pole-mounted transformers (150-700 lb), reclosers and regulators, splicing or replacing damaged conductor spans and service drops from a bucket or by climbing.

New overhead construction and rebuild along a route: digging holes and setting/replacing wood poles or steel transmission structures, framing them, stringing, sagging, clipping-in and dead-ending conductor across spans, installing switches and transformers.

Underground distribution: installing conduit and duct in trenches, pulling primary/secondary cable, splicing and terminating cable in manholes and vaults, setting and connecting padmount transformers and switchgear on residential and commercial sites.

Storm and emergency restoration: broken poles, downed and tangled conductor, blown transformers and cutouts, at night or in wind, rain, ice and mud, in backyards, roadsides and off-road terrain taken as found.

tasks.label: Inspect and test power lines and auxiliary equipment to locate and identify problems, using reading and testing instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled cycle inspection of overhead distribution circuits: pole, crossarm, insulator, connector, arrester and pole-top transformer condition assessed visually and with infrared, along streets, alleys, backyards and rural rights-of-way, in ordinary weather. Output is a list of located, identified defects (hot connections, cracked insulators, leaning poles, limbs on lines).

Transmission line and structure inspection patrols along corridors and easements (conductors, insulators, splices, hardware, corrosion, vegetation encroachment) using visual, infrared/corona and LiDAR instruments, plus post-storm/post-event damage assessment patrols of affected transmission and distribution lines in rough or debris-strewn terrain.

Outage/trouble response on a distribution circuit: patrol the line, read fault indicators, sectionalize and switch, test cutouts/fuses, reclosers, regulators and transformer secondaries with voltage detectors, ammeters and meters to locate and identify the fault, often at night or in bad weather, under restoration time pressure.

Hands-on contact testing and inspection of lines and pole-mounted auxiliary equipment from a bucket or climbing: hot-stick voltage detection and phasing before work, clamp-on load and voltage readings on transformers, capacitor banks and regulators, checking grounds and connections, plus groundline pole decay testing (sounding, boring, resistograph) and guy/anchor checks.

Underground residential/commercial distribution: locate cable faults and test cable and equipment with TDR, thumper, hipot, insulation resistance testers and cable identifiers at padmount transformers, pedestals, switchgear and manholes/vaults, including opening enclosures and connecting test leads.

Inspect and test equipment inside a fenced utility substation or switchyard: read transformer/breaker gauges and operation counters, check oil levels and insulator condition, infrared scan of bus, connections and transformers, ultrasonic/partial-discharge checks of energized apparatus.

instances.label: Planned distribution pole change-out on an energized 4–35 kV circuit along a public road: crew sets up traffic control, digs/augers a new hole beside the deteriorated pole with a digger derrick, sets and plumbs a 40–45 ft class-3/4 wood pole, frames it (crossarm, insulators, brackets), transfers energized primary and neutral, transformer, secondary and communications attachments, installs ground and guys, then pulls and hauls off the old pole and restores the surface.

Emergency storm restoration: broken poles with downed, possibly still-energized conductors, tangled comms lines and tree debris; work at night or in rain/mud on roadside or in yards, no prior survey, coordinating with tree crews and public safety, cutting and clearing wreckage, setting replacement poles and restringing to restore service under time pressure.

Straightening/plumbing a leaning pole after storm, soft soil or vehicle contact: excavate around butt, pull plumb with boom winch or come-along while conductors stay energized, backfill and tamp or add a stabilizer/rock, re-tension or install down guys and anchors, verify clearances.

Pole in a rear-lot easement, backyard, wetland, or steep off-road terrain with no bucket/derrick access: hand-dig or use a track machine/pole trailer, or set by helicopter; navigate fences, landscaping, sheds and property-owner constraints while transferring services to the new pole.

Transmission or sub-transmission structure replacement (wood H-frame, laminated or steel/concrete pole, 69–345 kV) on a right-of-way: outage-scheduled or live-line, crane or helicopter set, deep augured or drilled/backfilled foundation, heavy insulator strings and conductor transfer at height, matting and access-road work.

sources.system: RPD 35 (Robotic Pile Driver 35)
sources.title: Robotic pile driver faster than manual versions, says US startup – pv magazine International
sources.claim: Built Robotics' RPD 35 is a commercially offered, fully autonomous pile-driving machine that surveys, distributes, drives and inspects steel H-piles on utility-scale solar construction sites — the closest field-deployed autonomy to 'setting a vertical member in the ground', but limited to uniform new piles on graded greenfield sites.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: driving foundation piles. Transfer does NOT carry to pole replacement: the RPD 35 handles identical 12–16 ft, ≤200 lb steel H-beams on a surveyed, graded solar field with no existing structure to remove, no energized conductors, and no framing, hardware or service transfer at height. It cannot perform the whole instance.

sources.system: EPRI insulator inspection robot / Ti line-traversing robot
sources.title: Robots Take on Tough Tasks in Transmission and Distribution | EPRI Journal
sources.claim: EPRI's survey of transmission and distribution robotics shows the field is dominated by inspection robots (line-traversing inspectors, insulator crawlers, manhole/cable robots) that are still prototypes needing field maturation; no robot performs pole replacement or conductor transfer.

sources.system: 10 kV distribution-network live-working robots (Japan Phase II/III; State Grid 'Dawn'; insulated aerial-vehicle manipulator prototype)
sources.developer: State Grid / NARI / Tsinghua Tianjin Institute / Kyushu Electric (reviewed by Yin et al.)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: live-line manipulation on distribution poles. It bounds capability: even the on-pole manipulation step of a pole change-out is teleoperated and lab-stage, so it cannot substantiate autonomous completion of pole replacement.

tasks.label: String wire conductors and cables between poles, towers, trenches, pylons, and buildings, setting lines in place and using winches to adjust tension.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Overhead distribution conductor stringing along a street or rural road: crew hangs stringing blocks/travelers on crossarms of wood or composite poles from bucket trucks, pulls new primary conductor with a rope and puller/tensioner, sags to spec, dead-ends and ties in at insulators, and clips out the blocks — with traffic, trees, driveways and adjacent energized circuits present.

Transmission conductor stringing across a right-of-way between lattice towers or steel monopoles: pilot line placed by drone, helicopter or ground crew through travelers, sock line and pulling rope pulled in, bundled conductor pulled with a puller/tensioner while riding structures, sagged to sag charts, then clipped in and dead-ended; rough terrain, road/rail/line crossings requiring guard structures.

Service and secondary drops: stringing triplex/quadruplex from a distribution pole to a house, farm or small commercial building, attaching to the pole and to the building's service bracket, hand- or winch-tensioning for clearance over yards and driveways, then connecting at the weatherhead; varied building attachments and yard obstructions.

Underground cable installation in trenches and duct banks: rigging a capstan/winch and pulling grip at a manhole or vault, feeding and lubricating medium-voltage cable through conduit, monitoring pulling tension and sidewall pressure, then racking and training cable in the vault or laying and covering cable in an open trench on a street or subdivision site.

Conductor and cable installation inside a fenced utility substation or industrial plant yard: pulling control and power cable through cable trenches and trays, stringing bus/riser conductors between structures and equipment, tensioning and terminating — on premises controlled by the utility with standard layouts and access control.

tasks.label: Attach cross-arms, insulators, and auxiliary equipment to poles prior to installing them.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Framing a wood distribution pole on the ground at the job site: a 35-45 ft class pole lies on blocks along a roadside or rural right-of-way; the crew verifies/bores gains and through-holes, lifts an 8-10 ft wood or fiberglass cross-arm into position, drives a 5/8 in. machine bolt with washers, adds braces with lag screws, threads pin insulators onto pins (or bolts post insulators), and staples the pole ground wire. Uneven terrain, traffic, mud and weather; pole class and framing detail vary by drawing.

Attaching auxiliary equipment to a pole lying on the ground before setting: cluster/transformer mounting brackets, cutout and arrester brackets, riser conduit and standoffs, streetlight bracket, guy attachments, pole steps/bands, sometimes hanging a 300-1,500 lb transformer with the digger derrick while the pole is horizontal. Roadside or off-road job site, hardware picked from the truck body.

Pre-framing (dressing) poles in a utility service center or contractor laydown yard: a batch of identical poles on stands or racks, framed to a standard construction unit from stocked hardware, moved by forklift, then trucked to the job. Fixed yard layout, institution-controlled premises, standard equipment.

Shop/bench sub-assembly inside a service center: bolting insulator pins and pin/post insulators to cross-arms, assembling brace-and-bolt hardware kits and dead-end assemblies, bundling completed arms for delivery to crews. Indoor bench with power tools, torque specs, parts bins.

Transmission structure assembly on the ground at a tower site: bolting davit/cross arms to steel or concrete monopole sections, assembling lattice tower sections, hanging insulator strings with clevises, ball-and-socket links and cotter keys, before the crane erects the structure. Rough laydown area on the right-of-way.

It transfers to pole framing because the objects are comparable (heavy, long wood members positioned to drawing dimensions and joined with hardware at specified locations) and the required placement precision is similar; the demonstrated setting is a purpose-built fixtured cell, i.e., E1.

tasks.label: Dig holes, using augers, and set poles, using cranes and power equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine distribution pole set/replacement along a rural or suburban roadside right-of-way with a digger-derrick truck: locate and clear the spot, auger a 6-8 ft hole, rig and lift a 40-45 ft class 3/4 wood pole off the trailer, guide it into the hole, plumb it, then backfill and tamp in lifts. Work occurs feet from energized primary conductors, under traffic control, on variable soils and side slopes.

New-line or subdivision build in a cleared, staked corridor: a crew sets a run of several poles at surveyed stations in a day, open access for the derrick, no existing energized conductors overhead, repetitive holes and standard pole classes; soils and grades still vary station to station.

Urban/congested street pole set: dense buried utilities force potholing or vacuum excavation before augering, tight working radius between parked cars, sidewalks and building faces, pedestrians present, sometimes a crane rather than a derrick because of overhead clearance and reach limits.

Off-road / rough-terrain or transmission-class structure setting: cross-country right-of-way reached over mats or by tracked equipment, steep or rocky ground requiring a rock auger or drilled shaft, longer/heavier poles or laminated structures picked and set with a crane, rigging and tag lines handled by a ground crew.

Storm/emergency restoration pole replacement: broken poles and downed wire, mud, debris and standing water, improvised access across yards or fields, night or continuous-shift work, hole often dug beside the failed butt, urgency to restore service.

sources.system: RPD 35 / RPS 25 autonomous piling system
sources.title: Blattner Picks Autonomous Pile Drivers From Built Robotics for Solar Projects (ENR)
sources.claim: Built Robotics' RPD 35 autonomous pile-driving excavators install steel foundation piles on utility-scale solar construction sites unattended, carrying piles onboard, positioning to survey coordinates and driving them; Quanta subsidiary Blattner adopted them nationwide in September 2025.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous installation of vertical structural posts (solar foundation piles) into undisturbed ground. Transfer to pole setting: the same operation class on a heavy hydraulic excavator base - move to a surveyed point, take a vertical member from an onboard rack, place and hold it plumb in the earth - so with a pole presented in a purpose-built cradle/rack on prepared ground the setting cycle carries over. It does not cover augering a 6-8 ft hole, uprighting a 40-45 ft pole off a trailer, or backfill and tamping in as-found conditions.

sources.system: RPD 35 / RPS 25
sources.title: The World's First Autonomous Piling System for Utility-Scale Solar — Built Robotics
sources.claim: Manufacturer specifications bound the demonstrated capability: the RPD 35 handles piles up to 19 ft and 600 lb on grades up to 10%, far short of a 40-45 ft, 1,000-2,500 lb distribution pole, and it vibratory-drives piles rather than augering a hole, setting a pole and backfilling.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above; cited to bound the transfer - object size, weight, terrain limit and installation method differ from utility poles, which is why the transfer is credited only where the workpiece is presented and the ground prepared (E1) and not at E2/E3.

sources.claim: Epiroc Pit Viper surface drill rigs have drilled vertical blastholes fully autonomously for a decade at dozens of open-pit mines, tramming to planned hole locations and drilling to designed depth with improved spatial and depth accuracy.

Augering a pole hole is the same operation at smaller scale (position over a surveyed point, collar and drill a vertical hole to depth), substantiating the hole-digging half of this task where access is controlled and ground prepared; the rig places nothing in the hole.

tasks.label: Travel in trucks, helicopters, and airplanes to inspect lines for freedom from obstruction and adequacy of insulation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine ground patrol from a line truck along urban/suburban distribution circuits: driving the feeder route on public streets and alley/backyard easements, looking for tree limbs and brush against conductors, cracked, flashed or contaminated insulators, damaged crossarms and leaning poles; output is a patrol record and work orders.

Patrol of rural or off-road distribution and sub-transmission line segments across fields, pasture, woods and rough right-of-way reached by truck, ATV or on foot; checking span clearance, vegetation encroachment, insulator and hardware condition over many miles of sparsely travelled line.

Aerial patrol of high-voltage transmission circuits by helicopter or fixed-wing over long corridors and open country: visual plus infrared/corona survey of insulator strings, conductors, splices and hardware, and check of vegetation encroachment inside the ROW; findings logged by structure number.

Detailed close-up inspection of an individual structure flagged on patrol (from a bucket truck, by climbing, or by hovering aircraft): full-coverage look at insulators, arresters, splices, dampers and attachment hardware, including thermal/UV scan, with a condition report per structure.

Post-storm or trouble patrol of a damaged area: covering a feeder or corridor after wind, ice or hurricane to locate downed conductors, tree contacts, broken poles and burned insulators amid debris, often at night or in still-poor weather, reporting locations to dispatch and repair crews.

tasks.label: Identify defective sectionalizing devices, circuit breakers, fuses, voltage regulators, transformers, switches, relays, or wiring, using wiring diagrams and electrical-testing instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Outage/trouble call on an overhead distribution feeder: the lineworker patrols the circuit from a truck along roads and back-lot easements, then uses a voltage detector, clamp meter, fuse tester and hot stick from a bucket to determine which cutout fuse, pole-top transformer, switch or sectionalizing device failed. Live 4-35 kV, traffic, weather, night work, layouts differ pole to pole.

Underground residential/commercial circuit: worker opens pad-mounted transformers and switchgear or enters a vault, tests elbows and cable sections with a phasing/voltage tester, TDR or thumper to identify the faulted cable run, defective elbow, fuse or transformer. Confined pads in yards, easements and streets; wet, dirty, mixed vintages.

Routine or post-storm condition patrol of a distribution/transmission line: identify defective or deteriorating equipment (cracked arresters, open cutouts, damaged insulators, leaking transformers, overheated connectors) by visual inspection and infrared/corona imaging along rights-of-way and roadsides, producing a defect list for repair crews.

Thermographic and visual condition survey inside a fenced utility substation/switchyard: scan breakers, regulators, switches, bus connections and transformer banks with an IR camera and ultrasonic detector to find defective/overheating apparatus and report it. Fixed layout, utility-controlled access, standard apparatus.

Instrument testing of protection and control equipment in a substation or on a de-energized pole-top recloser/regulator: trace circuits on wiring/schematic diagrams, connect a relay test set, ohmmeter, insulation tester or breaker timer to terminal blocks, inject signals and judge whether the relay, breaker, regulator control or wiring is defective.

Bench testing of removed apparatus at the utility service center/shop: distribution transformers, voltage regulators, reclosers and switches are tested (turns ratio, winding resistance, insulation resistance, trip/close operation) against written test procedures to confirm whether the unit is defective before repair or scrap.
