tasks.label: Study technical manuals or attend training sessions provided by equipment manufacturers to maintain current knowledge.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Explain or demonstrate correct operation or preventive maintenance of medical equipment to personnel.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Unit-level in-service for nursing staff on a hospital floor after new infusion pumps or vital-signs monitors are deployed: the BMET gathers several nurses around a device, explains setup, programming, alarm conditions and common user errors, answering questions as they arise.

One-on-one instruction at the point of use (bedside, OR, ED) when returning a repaired device: the repairer explains why the fault occurred, shows the clinician the correct operating sequence or handling that avoids recurrence, and confirms the user understands.

Coaching clinical or facility staff on user-level preventive maintenance they are responsible for — cleaning/disinfection routines, battery conditioning, filter or circuit changes, leak checks, daily self-test logging — on ventilators, beds, sterilizers, or dialysis machines.
Instructing junior technicians or apprentices in the biomed shop on PM procedures, test-equipment use, safety-testing protocols, and documentation for a class of devices.

Formal or remote instruction: scheduled classroom/vendor-style in-service, competency sign-off session, or a virtual walkthrough with a satellite clinic on operating and maintaining imaging, lab, or ophthalmic equipment, including handing over written or recorded instructions.

tasks.label: Repair shop equipment, metal furniture, or hospital equipment, including welding broken parts or replacing missing parts, or bring item into local shop for major repairs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-place mechanical repair of patient beds, stretchers or gurneys on an occupied nursing unit: swap a seized caster, re-secure a side-rail latch, replace a broken brake pedal linkage, hand pendant or drive actuator, working around the bed in a patient room or corridor, then function-test and return to service.

Bench repair in the biomed/clinical-engineering shop of hospital equipment and metal furniture brought in for major work: strip the unit down with hand and power tools, diagnose the broken or missing hardware (wheels, bearings, hinges, fasteners, gas springs, motors), fit replacement parts from stock, reassemble, adjust and test.

Metal repair at the shop's weld/fab bench: re-weld a cracked steel tube joint on an equipment cart, stretcher frame or IV-pole base, or fabricate and weld on a replacement bracket, then grind, clean and refit.

Repair of fixed clinic, OR/lab furniture and shop equipment in place: exam-table hydraulics and casters, broken cabinet hinges and drawer slides, procedure carts and stools, plus the repairer's own bench tools and shop machinery, in clinic rooms and equipment rooms of the facility.

Taking an item out of service and moving it: unplug/disconnect and tag out a failed device or bed, load it onto a cart or wheel it out, swap in a loaner, and haul it through corridors and elevators to the biomed shop, or crate it for shipment to a depot.

Field service at a site taken as found: a home-care hospital bed, wheelchair or patient lift in a private residence, or equipment at a small independent clinic or long-term-care room with no controlled layout, using only the tools and parts carried in the van.

tasks.label: Solder loose connections, using soldering iron.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hospital/clinic clinical-engineering shop bench: resoldering a broken or cold joint on a patient cable or lead wire (ECG lead set, SpO2 sensor cable, pressure transducer cable) — strip and tin fine stranded wire, solder to connector pins or a small pad, add strain relief and heat-shrink, continuity-test.

Biomed shop bench: board-level resoldering of a cracked or cold joint on a PCB pulled from an infusion pump, patient monitor, or power supply — connector pin, transformer or battery lead, or a through-hole component; board on a bench mat, joint reflowed with iron and fresh solder, then inspected.

OEM or third-party depot repair/refurbishment facility: the same known failure joint (battery contacts, DC jack, connector pins) resoldered across many units of one model, boards handled in batches with jigs and standard process documentation.

In-situ repair at the point of use: resoldering a loose wire or terminal inside installed equipment — hospital bed motor harness, exam table limit switch, sterilizer heater lead, imaging gantry cable — with the unit partially disassembled in place, confined access, awkward posture, other equipment and staff nearby.

Fine micro-soldering at the bench under a stereo microscope: SMD pad, flex circuit, or fine-pitch connector on a small device (endoscope camera board, surgical handpiece, telemetry transmitter, probe cable), sub-millimeter pads and heat-sensitive parts.

Non-institutional setting: soldering a loose connection on home medical equipment (home ventilator, power wheelchair controller, home hospital bed) or in an EMS vehicle, working off an improvised surface in a residence or garage bay.

sources.system: Learning-Augmented Robotic Automation (cable insertion-and-soldering station)
sources.title: Learning-augmented robotic automation for real-world manufacturing (arXiv:2604.22235)
sources.claim: Neuromeka's Learning-Augmented Robotic Automation was deployed on a live electric-motor production line to autonomously insert deformable three-phase cables into PCB holes (0.3–0.6 mm clearance) and solder them, running 5 h 10 min unattended over 108 motors at a 99.4% product-level QC pass rate, with motors presented in random poses.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: production soldering of stranded wire ends into PCB/connector holes. It transfers to resoldering a loose connection because the objects (fine stranded conductors, PCB pads/pins), the sub-millimetre placement precision, the iron-and-solder-feed process, and the joint-quality acceptance criterion are the same; only the reason the joint is being made differs.

sources.system: Autonomous soldering robot for USB wires

sources.transferJustification: Related task: soldering multi-conductor cable wires to connector pads. Transfers to resoldering a broken patient-cable conductor: identical object class (fine deformable stranded wires and connector pads), identical tolerance, and the vision feedback handles the wire-pose variation that makes a repair joint differ from a production joint.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: selective point soldering of individual joints on a fixtured board, explicitly for high-mix work. A repair resolder is a single selective joint on a board; the object, tool (iron tip plus solder feed), and precision requirement are the same as the production case.

sources.system: Comau/ETNEO robotic soldering cell

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated joint-by-joint soldering with automated joint inspection. The inspection loop is what makes an unattended repair joint acceptable at worker quality, since the technician's own acceptance step is visual inspection of the finished joint.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: soldering medical-grade cable-to-connector joints in volume. Same physical joints a biomedical repairer remakes when a patient cable conductor breaks, and the medical-device acceptance standard is the same one the repair must meet.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: wire-to-terminal soldering in a fixtured cell where a human loads the work and the machine solders and verifies. This is exactly the E1 counterfactual for a bench repair: the loose connection is presented fixtured and the machine makes and checks the joint.

tasks.label: Compute power and space requirements for installing medical, dental, or related equipment and install units to manufacturers' specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dental office operatory build-out: technician computes electrical load (dedicated circuits, amperage), verifies air/vacuum/water line locations and clearances for a chair-mounted delivery unit, operatory light and intraoral/pan x-ray; anchors chair to floor, runs and connects utilities and low-voltage lines, levels, tests and calibrates to the manufacturer's install manual, then signs off with the practice.

Large capital imaging install in a hospital (CT, R/F room, mobile C-arm dock, cath lab monitor booms): pre-install site survey computing kVA/dedicated feeder needs, floor loading, ceiling structure, door/corridor ingress path and service clearances; then rigging the gantry/table into the shielded room, anchoring, cabling to the power distribution unit and network, and commissioning with the OEM field engineer.

Routine small/mid equipment installs across occupied hospital units: wall- or boom-mounted vital-signs monitors, telemetry receivers, exam lights, infusion pump docking stations, warming cabinets — checking receptacle/circuit loading and available wall space, locating studs/blocking, mounting brackets, plugging in and connecting to the clinical network, then electrical-safety testing and entering the asset in CMMS, all with staff and patients around.

Lab, pharmacy or sterile-processing equipment install: autoclave/washer-disinfector, chemistry analyzer, biosafety cabinet or pharmacy compounder — computing 208/480V three-phase power, breaker sizing, water/steam/drain and exhaust requirements and footprint/service clearances; moving the unit into the room, leveling, hooking up utilities, and validating operation to spec.

Field installs in unstandardized settings: home medical equipment (hospital bed, home dialysis machine, oxygen concentrator, patient lift) in a private residence, a small physician or vet practice in an older building, or a mobile imaging trailer — assessing unknown branch-circuit capacity and outlet condition, fitting the unit into whatever space exists, assembling and connecting it, and instructing the user.

instances.label: Hospital clinical engineering shop bench: technician makes a simple custom external part - a mounting bracket, adapter plate, spacer, protective cover or cart fixture - from a hand sketch or a verbal request from nursing/OR staff; cuts, drills, bends or 3D-prints stock, deburrs it, test-fits and bolts it onto the device, then checks the device still works.

Shop bench, obsolete or out-of-production device: an exact spare is unavailable, so the technician dresses down or reworks a substitute part (turns/files a shaft or bushing, enlarges or relocates holes, trims a panel or gasket), opens the legacy device, fits the reworked part inside, reassembles, and runs functional plus electrical-safety verification.

Shop bench: fabricates a one-off interface cable, adapter pigtail or small harness to connect equipment that was never designed to interconnect (monitor to gateway, transducer to recorder) - selects connectors, solders/crimps, applies shrink and strain relief, continuity/isolation tests, and terminates it into the devices.

University or hospital research lab: modifies clinical equipment for a study after discussion with investigators - adds sensor mounts, a custom enclosure or a fixture, taps signals, adapts a device to a bench or animal rig; cluttered lab benches, one-off requirements, iterative changes with the investigator.

On-site in a live clinical area (patient room, OR, imaging suite): field-measures installed equipment (booms, wall rails, beds, carts), fabricates or adapts mounting hardware, drills/bolts and routes cabling in place around staff, equipment and infection-control constraints, then verifies operation.

OEM or third-party depot/service center: applies a factory modification order or retrofit kit to a batch of identical devices - opens each unit, removes and substitutes boards, brackets or subassemblies per the modification instructions, reassembles, tests and documents.

A biomed shop's fabricated bracket, plate or spacer is geometrically simpler and looser-toleranced than aerospace components, and the input format (sketch or job order) matches the task statement, so part-making capability transfers within a fenced, fixtured cell.

roles.description: Repair percussion, stringed, reed, or wind instruments. May specialize in one area, such as piano tuning.

tasks.label: Adjust string tensions to tune instruments, using hand tools and electronic tuning devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Annual/semi-annual piano service call in a private home: technician sets a temperament and tunes ~220 strings on an upright or grand with a tuning lever, mutes/temperament strip and an electronic tuning device (Verituner/CyberTuner), setting each pin so the tuning holds; often a small pitch raise first; room acoustics, furniture and pets as found.

Piano tuning at an institution: school practice rooms, church sanctuary, university music building, recording studio or concert hall pre-concert touch-up; same lever-and-pin work, sometimes to a tighter standard and on a schedule, in a building whose premises and access are controlled by the institution.

Electric/acoustic guitar or bass at a repair bench or music-store shop: after restringing, neck/truss-rod or bridge work, the tech brings all strings up to pitch with a peg winder and clip-on/strobe tuner, stretches strings and re-tunes several times until stable and accepted for the setup.

Other geared-peg fretted instruments in the shop: banjo, mandolin, ukulele, 12-string, bouzouki; strings brought to pitch by hand after restringing or repair, re-tuned as they settle, checked against an electronic tuner.

Bowed strings and harp in a violin/harp shop: violin, viola, cello or bass tuned with wooden friction pegs and tailpiece fine tuners after new strings, bridge or soundpost work; or a pedal/lever harp brought up to pitch string-by-string with a tuning key on tapered pins.

Initial tuning on a production or refurbishment line: newly strung instruments presented in sequence on a bench or line at a manufacturer or high-volume rental/refurb facility, given a first rough tuning and repeated tunings as the strings and structure settle.

sources.system: Tronical Tune / Gibson Min-ETune (Roboheads)
sources.title: Tronical Tune (review) — Sound On Sound
sources.claim: Tronical Tune (sold factory-fitted by Gibson as Min-ETune/G Force) replaces a guitar's machine heads with motorised 'Roboheads' that sense each string's pitch and turn the pegs to bring all six strings to pitch automatically after the player strums; tuning accuracy is user-selectable down to ±1 cent.

sources.system: TronicalTune PLUS
sources.title: Guitar Tuner Fully Automatic TronicalTune® | Perfect Pitch Every Time
sources.claim: The Tronical system mounts on the guitar and drives the machine heads under closed-loop control, tuning all strings with no manual peg turning; it is marketed as a retrofit for a wide range of standard six-string guitars.

sources.system: SwivelAutotune (Swivel 2 mechatronic slide guitar)
sources.developer: Jim Murphy, Ajay Kapur, Dale Carnegie — Victoria University of Wellington (NIME 2014)
sources.title: Robot: Tune Yourself! Automatic Tuning for Musical Robotics (Zenodo record)
sources.claim: SwivelAutotune is a self-tuning procedure for the Swivel 2 mechatronic slide guitar: the robot actuates its own string, measures the pitch and drives the tensioning motor to the target frequency, closing the full excite–measure–adjust loop without a human.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: string-tension tuning on a purpose-built robotic string instrument rather than a customer's guitar. It transfers to E1 guitar tuning because the physical act is identical — sense pitch of a plucked steel string and drive a motor that changes its tension to a target frequency — at the same cent-level precision.

sources.system: Roadie 3 / Roadie Bass
sources.title: Roadie 3 | The New & Improved Automatic Guitar Tuner
sources.claim: Roadie is a hand-held motorised peg turner with closed-loop pitch (vibration) sensing that tunes instruments with geared machine heads — guitar, bass, ukulele, mandolin, banjo — but the user must position it on each peg in turn, and it cannot tune instruments with wooden friction pegs such ... violin and viola.
sources.transferJustification: Cited as supporting context on the actuation (motorised turning of standard geared machine heads to a sensed pitch) and as a limit for friction-peg bowed instruments; because a human must place it on each peg, it is treated as unclear autonomy and is not relied on for any positive judgment.

sources.system: Semi-automatic piano tuning system (stepper motor + Arduino + microphone)

sources.system: Yamaha piano-factory automated tuning systems
sources.title: Yamaha Piano Secrets Revealed – Cunningham Piano
sources.claim: At Yamaha's piano factory each piano is tuned four times; automated robotic tuning systems perform the first two (basic) tunings on the production line, while the final two tunings are done by human technicians.

sources.claim: Yamaha's own description of piano manufacture assigns the finish tuning — muting the outer strings of each trichord, tuning the centre string and matching the unisons — to an experienced senior piano technician, indicating the finished-quality tuning is not machine work even inside the factory.

tasks.label: Compare instrument pitches with tuning tool pitches to tune instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Piano tuning in a private home: technician arrives at a customer's house, opens an upright or grand, uses an electronic tuning device (ETD) or aural reference plus a tuning lever and mutes, sets a temperament and tunes roughly 220 strings to a stretched scale, setting pins so the tuning holds; room acoustics, piano condition and clutter vary house to house.

Piano tuning at an institution: school practice room, church, recital hall, piano dealer showroom or recording studio; same lever-and-ETD work on a known instrument, often to A440 concert pitch before an event, with the venue controlling access and layout.

Fretted-string instrument in a repair shop: after a setup, restring or fret job on a guitar, bass, ukulele, banjo or mandolin, the tech brings each string to pitch against a strobe/clip-on tuner at the bench, stretches new strings, retunes and checks intonation at the saddle.

Band instrument repair shop: after pad, cork or dent work on a flute, clarinet, sax, trumpet or trombone, the tech play-tests the instrument against a strobe tuner, compares note-by-note pitch, then adjusts tuning slide/cork position, key heights, headjoint or crown to bring intonation into spec.

Orchestral string instruments and harps: violin/viola/cello/bass brought up to pitch on friction or geared pegs and fine tuners in a shop or school instrument room after a soundpost, bridge or restring job; or a pedal harp's 47 strings tuned with a tuning key against an electronic tuner.

Percussion: tensioning timpani or drum heads rod-by-rod to an even pitch against a tuner, and tuning marimba/xylophone/vibraphone bars by removing material from the arch while checking the fundamental and overtones on a frequency analyzer, in a shop or school band room.

sources.system: Tronical Tune (Gibson Robot Guitar / Min-ETune)
sources.title: Tronical Tronical Tune - User review - Gearspace
sources.claim: Tronical Tune is a commercially sold robotic guitar-tuning system: servomotor-driven tuning pegs sense string pitch with piezoelectric sensors and turn the pegs to bring the strings to the target pitch.
sources.transferJustification: Same task as the instance: comparing sounded string pitch against a reference pitch and turning the tuning peg until they match, on the same objects (guitar strings and machine heads) a repair tech tunes.

sources.transferJustification: Establishes autonomy (no continuous human control) for the same pitch-comparison-and-adjust loop the repair technician performs.

sources.title: Gibson's stunning Robot Les Paul tunes itself in seconds - New Atlas
sources.claim: The servo tuners bring all six strings of a guitar to pitch in a couple of seconds, a shipped product rather than a laboratory demo.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (bringing strings to a reference pitch); speed and completeness of the whole six-string tuning cycle are what the shop instance requires.

sources.system: TronicalTune PLUS
sources.title: Tuner Guitar 2025 - Discover Why TronicalTune PLUS Is the Smartest Choice for Perfect Tuning
sources.claim: The current retrofit version of the robotic tuning system is sold for any six-string guitar and claims tuning accuracy of about one cent, comparable to or better than a technician working with a strobe tuner.
sources.transferJustification: Vendor specification of the same pitch-matching task; establishes the precision level and continued commercial availability of the robotic tuner.

sources.system: Roadie 3
sources.title: Band Industries Roadie 3 Automatic Guitar Tuner | Sweetwater
sources.claim: Roadie 3 is a commercial motorized tuner that senses string pitch and turns the peg to the target pitch, but a person must hold it, seat it on each peg in turn and pluck the string.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the task, but hand-positioned per peg by the worker, so it is a power tool in a human's hand rather than an autonomous system; cited to show the limit of general-instrument robotic tuning.

sources.system: Semi-automatic piano tuning system (Tuovinen/Välimäki, SMC 2019)
sources.title: Toward Automatic Tuning of the Piano - Aalto University's research portal
sources.claim: The most advanced published piano-tuning machine is a semi-automatic research prototype: an aluminium frame holding a stepper motor over one tuning pin with microphone feedback, intended to help a non-professional tune a grand piano, not to replace a tuner.

sources.system: Semi-automatic piano tuning system (CRI process)
sources.title: Toward Automatic Tuning of the Piano - Aalto University's research portal
sources.claim: The prototype's tuning still deviates from a professional tuning by 2.5 cents RMS in the lower range and 8.1 cents RMS above G#5, and the frame/motor assembly must be placed on each pin.

tasks.label: Play instruments to evaluate their sound quality and to locate any defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band-instrument repair tech play-tests a woodwind (clarinet, flute, alto sax) at the shop bench before/after repair: assembles it, blows through it, runs chromatic scales and long tones, and judges from response, stuffiness, airiness, buzz and intonation which pads leak, which keys are out of regulation, and whether tone is acceptable to return to the customer.

Repair tech play-tests a brass instrument (trumpet, trombone, horn) in the shop: buzzes and plays notes across registers with valves/slide, listening for stuffy or resistant notes from dents or leaks, rattles, sluggish valve response, and intonation problems, and reports what needs work.

Piano technician plays the piano during a tuning/regulation/service call in a private home, school room or church: strikes single notes, unisons, intervals and chords across the full compass, listening for beats, false strings, buzzes and rattles, sticking or noisy keys and uneven voicing, in a room laid out for people with the piano wherever the owner keeps it.

Fretted-string tech play-tests an acoustic or electric guitar/bass after a setup or fretwork in the shop, checking specifically for fret buzz, high or uneven frets, string action, nut slot height, neck relief and intonation up the neck.

Fretted-string tech plays a guitar/bass acoustically and through an amplifier to judge overall tone, sustain, dead notes, hardware rattles, and electrical noise from pickups, pots and jacks before returning it to the customer.

Luthier or percussion tech plays a bowed string instrument (violin, cello) or strikes drums/mallet percussion in the shop or a school band room, bowing or striking to judge tone, wolf notes, buzzes from open seams or loose fittings, and head/bearing-edge problems.

sources.system: Plek Station / Plek Pro
sources.title: What is a PLEK Machine and what can it do? – Andertons Music Co.
sources.claim: The Plek Station/Plek Pro is a commercial CNC machine into which a guitar is clamped as-is; it scans the fretboard and frets under real string tension and automatically identifies the instrument's setup defects (neck relief, nut and bridge/saddle problems, high or uneven frets) before machining them.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: diagnosing a fretted instrument's playability defects. A tech's play test of a guitar is aimed at finding fret buzz, action and intonation faults; the Plek locates exactly those causes (high frets, nut slots, relief) on the same objects to far finer precision, and shops/factories accept its report in place of the tech's by-ear/by-hand diagnosis.

sources.system: Plek Pro
sources.title: Plek Your New Guitar | Sweetwater
sources.claim: Plek machines are deployed in retail repair shops and factories as the accepted diagnostic-and-correction step for buzz and action problems, though a human tech still finishes the setup by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above: it substitutes for the buzz/action portion of the guitar play test, but the quote also shows a human still performs the final feel-and-tone judgment.

sources.system: OmniPianist
sources.title: [2511.02504] Dexterous Robotic Piano Playing at Scale
sources.claim: Bimanual robot hands can play a real piano autonomously, learning fingering and control without human demonstrations, in a laboratory setup; the work concerns performance, not evaluating a piano's condition.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic piano performance. It substantiates only the motor half of the instance (striking keys); nothing in it produces a technician-grade diagnosis of tuning, action or buzz defects.

sources.system: Waseda Flutist Robot WF-4RIV
sources.title: Development of Waseda flutist robot WF-4RIV: Implementation of auditory feedback system
sources.claim: The Waseda flutist robot plays a real flute with artificial lips and lungs and uses an auditory feedback control system to autonomously improve the sound it produces, but the evaluation is of its own performance, not of the instrument's defects.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic wind-instrument playing with acoustic self-monitoring. It shows a machine can blow and listen, but no published result maps the resulting sound to a located mechanical fault in the instrument.

sources.system: Waseda Anthropomorphic Saxophonist (WAS-2 / WAS-5)
sources.title: Development of the Waseda Saxophonist Robot
sources.claim: The Waseda saxophonist robot reproduces human saxophone playing with artificial lips, a tonguing mechanism, lungs and a 16-DOF hand, in a laboratory; performance is driven from stored scores.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic saxophone playing. Score-driven playback establishes the motor act only; it does not establish autonomous defect diagnosis, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.system: RIAM 2.0 – Reed Instrument Artificial Mouth
sources.title: RIAM 2.0 - Reed Instrument Artificial Mouth: A Blowing and Tonguing Device for Artificial Excitation of Single-Reed Woodwind Instruments
sources.claim: Artificial blowing machines (RIAM 2.0) can excite single-reed woodwinds with controlled blowing and tonguing in a laboratory, but they are research instruments for studying reed behaviour and sensors, not systems that diagnose faults in a customer's instrument.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine excitation of a woodwind. It covers blowing/tonguing under fixtured lab conditions but not key actuation over a full test scale nor conversion of the sound into a located repair fault.

sources.system: Robotized artificial mouth for brass instruments (LMA/PRISM)
sources.title: Robotized artificial mouth for brass instruments: automated experiments and cartography of playing parameters
sources.claim: A robotized artificial mouth can play brass instruments and run automated sweeps of playing parameters in a laboratory; it is an acoustics research rig, not a shop diagnostic system, and it does not operate valves or report faults.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine excitation of brass instruments. It demonstrates automated blowing/lip control on trumpets and trombones, but nothing about locating dents, leaks or valve faults from the resulting sound.

sources.system: BIAS (Brass Instrument Analysis System)
sources.developer: IWK Vienna / Artim, offered by Houghton Horns
sources.title: Brass Instrument Acoustic Analysis – Houghton Horns
sources.claim: Objective acoustic evaluation of a brass instrument's intonation and response (BIAS input-impedance analysis) is available as a commercial service, but a human operator must attach the measurement head and work through each valve combination.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instrumented evaluation of a brass instrument's acoustic quality. It shows the analysis exists, but the manipulation is done by a person, so no robotic system completes the instance.

sources.system: Aalto semi-automatic piano tuning system (CRI tuning)
sources.developer: Aalto University Acoustics Lab (Tuovinen, Hu, Välimäki)
sources.title: Toward Automatic Tuning of the Piano (SMC 2019)
sources.claim: The best-published piano tuning machine is semi-automatic: a motorized pin-turner with closed-loop pitch control mounted on a grand piano, still requiring a person to sound the keys and reposition the machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: evaluating a piano's tuning by ear. The system measures pitch and inharmonicity automatically, but a human must play the notes and move the device, so it does not complete the play-and-evaluate instance.

tasks.label: Disassemble instruments and parts for repair and adjustment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band-instrument shop bench: technician tears down a woodwind (student flute, clarinet, or saxophone) for repad/overhaul — unhook needle and flat springs, back out tiny pivot screws and rod screws, slide key stacks off posts in the correct order, remove old pads/corks, and organize parts for reassembly, on many makes/models arriving worn, bent, or with corroded screws.

Band-instrument shop bench: brass teardown (trumpet, trombone, French horn, tuba) — remove valve caps, pistons/rotors, springs and felts, pull stuck tuning and valve slides with pullers/heat, remove waterkeys, and unsolder braces or a lead pipe to free parts for dent work and cleaning.

Guitar/fretted repair shop: de-string an acoustic or electric, remove bridge pins, tuning machines, pickguard, control plate, knobs, pickups and desolder wiring, remove bolt-on neck or nut/saddle, and take off hardware ahead of fret work, refinishing, or electronics repair.

Piano technician: disassembly for repair/regulation, mostly on customer premises (homes, churches, schools) — remove fallboard, key slip, cheek blocks, upper/lower panels or grand action and keyframe, pull keys and key buttons, detach hammer shanks, dampers, trapwork; a share done in the shop for rebuilds (strings, plate, action stack).

Violin-family luthier shop: remove chinrest, tailpiece, strings, pegs, bridge and endpin; open the instrument by parting the glue seam and lifting the top plate; remove fingerboard or bass bar for crack repair or neck reset, preserving fragile aged wood and varnish.

Percussion repair bench: take a drum apart — loosen and remove 8–10 tension rods with a drum key, lift hoops and heads, unscrew lugs and mounting brackets, remove snare strainer/throw-off and hardware, or break down a kit's stands and pedals for repair.

sources.system: Panasonic autonomous disassembly workcells (Disassembly CPS)
sources.title: Appliance Manufacturer Uses Robots and AI to Disassemble Products | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: Panasonic has developed AI/vision-guided six-axis robot workcells that autonomously disassemble appliances: magnetic grippers lift covers, screwdrivers remove fasteners, other end effectors cut wires and remove components, with vision detecting screws even when dirty or rusty.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic teardown of fixtured consumer products. Transfer is limited to repetitive, accessible threaded fasteners and lifting a freed cover off a fixtured body — mechanically comparable to removing drum tension rods and lifting a hoop/head. It does not transfer to key-stack rod screws, needle springs, soldered brass joints, glued violin seams, or piano actions, which require preserving every part for reassembly across highly varied models.

sources.system: iDEAR e-waste disassembly robot
sources.title: Automated Electronics Disassembly — Fraunhofer research news
sources.claim: Fraunhofer IFF's iDEAR project robot autonomously performs disassembly skills (localizing, unscrewing, lifting, extracting, cutting) on electronic devices in a laboratory disassembly cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous non-destructive-ish teardown of electronic housings in a purpose-built cell. It substantiates vision-guided screw location plus removal on a fixtured object, which is the closest analogue to unbolting drum hardware; it does not substantiate teardown of spring-loaded woodwind key mechanisms, glued wooden instrument bodies, or piano actions.

sources.system: Automated e-waste unscrewing system (UR10e + mechatronic screwdriver)
sources.developer: Academic research group (published in Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing)
sources.title: Robotic system for automated disassembly of electronic waste: Unscrewing — ScienceDirect
sources.claim: A robotic unscrewing system for e-waste disassembly using a UR10e arm, RealSense D405 vision and a custom mechatronic screwdriver autonomously locates, identifies and removes screws from devices such as smartphones and computers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous fastener removal from small fixtured products. Supports the fastener-removal element of simple percussion hardware teardown in a purpose-built cell; provides no capability for spring unhooking, slide pulling, unsoldering, glue-seam opening, or wiring desoldering found in instrument repair.

sources.system: Daisy
sources.title: Meet Daisy and Taz: Apple's iPhone-Disassembling Robots | Supply Chain Digital
sources.claim: Apple's Daisy line, deployed in Austin, disassembles 23 iPhone models at 200 units per hour, separating components on a purpose-built automated line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: high-throughput product teardown on a purpose-built line. It shows the state of deployed disassembly automation is confined to a small set of pre-modeled, identical-condition products presented in fixtures for recycling, not to non-destructive teardown of varied, worn instruments whose every part must survive for reassembly.

tasks.label: Repair or replace musical instrument parts and components, such as strings, bridges, felts, and keys, using hand and power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band-instrument shop bench: technician disassembles a school-owned clarinet, flute, or saxophone, removes old pads/felts/corks, shellacs and seats new pads, replaces broken springs, straightens bent keys, solders posts, then reassembles and play-tests. Instruments arrive in varied condition and model; each key cup and tone hole is fitted by feel.

Music-store repair bench: guitar/bass/mandolin setup and part replacement — remove and replace strings, wind and trim at tuner posts, replace or reshape saddle and nut, replace bridge pins, tuners, or a cracked bridge, adjust truss rod, then intonate and play-test.

Piano work, in the customer's home or a church/school room: splice or replace a broken bass/treble wire, replace bridle straps, hammer or damper felts, key bushings and punchings, re-shape hammers, and regulate the affected notes in a cramped, non-standard space around furniture.

Violin/viola/cello shop: fit and carve a new bridge to the arching of a particular top, set or reset the sound post, fit and lubricate pegs, replace a nut or fingerboard, re-glue open seams, and re-string and adjust for tone.

On-site emergency repair at a school band room, marching-band field house, or performance venue: stuck valve, sprung key, popped-out pad, broken string, or loose brace fixed quickly from a portable tool kit before rehearsal or a concert.

sources.system: Robotic unscrewing system (UR10e + RealSense D405 + custom mechatronic screwdriver)
sources.developer: Academic research group (published in Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing)
sources.title: Robotic system for automated disassembly of electronic waste: Unscrewing
sources.claim: State-of-the-art autonomous manipulation for adjacent 'take-apart' repair work is limited to removing standard screws from flat electronic housings in a lab cell; it does not extend to fitting, gluing, and regulating delicate instrument parts.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic disassembly/unscrewing of consumer electronics. Cited as the closest autonomous tool-using repair-adjacent capability found; it does NOT transfer to instrument repair, since it only removes standardized fasteners from rigid, catalogued housings and performs no fitting of compliant parts (pads, felts, bridges) or reassembly to a playable, tone-tested standard.

sources.system: MusicMedic repair tooling and replacement pad/dent tools (hand tools, human-operated)
sources.title: The Dent Eraser | MusicMedic.com
sources.claim: Musical instrument part replacement is currently sold and performed as manual bench craft using hand tools (e.g., dent balls, pad sets, shellac), with no robotic offering identified.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (instrument part repair): shows the tooling ecosystem is entirely hand-operated, supporting the negative finding that no autonomous robotic system performs these repairs.

tasks.label: Reassemble instruments following repair, using hand tools and power tools and glue, hair, yarn, resin, or clamps, and lubricate instruments as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band-instrument shop: reassembling a clarinet, flute or saxophone after a repad/overhaul — remounting key stacks on rods and pivot screws, hooking needle and flat springs, seating pads with shellac/heat or glue, fitting corks and felts, regulating key heights and linkages, oiling the mechanism, and leak-testing until it plays evenly.

Brass repair bench: reassembling a trumpet, horn or trombone after dent work, valve rebuild or soldering — reinstalling pistons/rotors with correct port alignment, valve guides, springs, felts and corks, waterkeys and linkages, refitting slides, applying valve oil and slide grease, then play-testing for leaks and smooth action.

Stringed-instrument shop: closing up a violin, cello or guitar after repair — regluing top/seams or cracks with hide glue and spool clamps and cauls, refitting neck, bridge and soundpost, reinstalling guitar hardware/electronics, then stringing up and setting up to playing tolerances.

Piano shop/rebuilding bench: reassembling a grand or upright action after repair — hanging hammers/shanks and wippens, refitting keys to the keyframe, lubricating center pins, knuckles and key bushings, reinstalling the action and case parts, and checking regulation and touch.

Customer's home or church/school room: piano technician reassembling the instrument after in-place repair — putting the action back in, reinstalling fallboard, key slip, cheek blocks, pedal lyre and trapwork, applying lubricant to squeaky/sticky parts, working around furniture in a space not set up for the work.

Percussion, bow and accessory work: rebuilding drum hardware and mounting/tensioning heads, rewrapping mallet yarn, rehairing a bow with horsehair (combing, tying, wedging the hair into frog and head mortises, sizing and rosining), and reassembling small parts with glue and clamps.

sources.system: Epson SCARA robot assembly cell ("Foldy") at Taylor Guitars
sources.title: 2023 Assembly Plant of the Year: Hand Craftsmanship Meets High Tech at Taylor Guitars
sources.claim: Guitar maker Taylor Guitars runs an automated robotic cell in which four SCARA robots and machine-vision cameras build the ES2 piezoelectric pickup sub-assembly from parts fed by vibratory feeders and conveyors — new, identical parts in a fixtured purpose-built cell, not repair reassembly of a used instrument.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: assembly of musical-instrument components. It is the closest existing robotic instrument-assembly deployment, but it handles one new, standardized sub-assembly presented by feeders in a fenced cell; it does not demonstrate fitting, seating, springing, gluing/clamping or regulating heterogeneous used parts on a repaired instrument, so it does not transfer to the reassembly task.

sources.system: AgiBot Genie G2 humanoid
sources.title: Chinese humanoid robots deployed on assembly lines for precision tasks
sources.claim: Humanoid robots (AgiBot Genie G2) have been integrated into a consumer-electronics mass-production line in Nanchang, doing pick-and-place of materials from a conveyor into test boxes and final inspection over multi-hour shifts — the frontier of autonomous dexterous factory work, still on a standardized line with identical products.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: dexterous manipulation and precision handling in factory assembly. Cited to show the current ceiling of autonomous humanoid manipulation: repetitive pick-place and inspection of standardized parts, far below the multi-step tool use, gluing/clamping, spring hooking and regulation required to reassemble a repaired instrument.

sources.system: Compliant interactive peg-in-hole manipulation system (Rice University / NIST)
sources.developer: Rice University and U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.title: Robust Peg-in-Hole Assembly under Uncertainties via Compliant and Interactive Contact-Rich Manipulation (arXiv 2506.22766)
sources.claim: Autonomous tight-tolerance robotic insertion (peg-in-hole) remains an open research problem; a Rice University/NIST system demonstrated contact-based localization and compliant insertion in laboratory experiments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: precision parts mating, an elementary sub-step of instrument reassembly (rods through posts, pivot screws, valve guides). Cited as evidence of the state of the art: even this single rigid-part sub-step is a research challenge in the lab, so it cannot substantiate whole-instance reassembly at worker quality.

tasks.label: Inspect instruments to locate defects, and to determine their value or the level of restoration required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band/orchestra repair shop bench: a customer or school brings in a student woodwind or brass instrument (clarinet, flute, sax, trumpet). The tech handles and plays it, runs a leak light and feeler gauges over pads, checks key fit, spring tension, valve/slide action, solder joints, dents, cork and felt wear, then writes a defect list and a repair estimate.

Piano technician on site in a private home (occasionally a church or small studio): inspects an unfamiliar upright or grand before quoting work — checks pitch and tuning stability, tuning-pin torque and pinblock, soundboard and bridge cracks, hammer wear and voicing, action regulation, key bushings, case and finish, rust — and tells the owner whether it is worth tuning, repairing, rebuilding, or scrapping, with an approximate value.

Fretted-string shop bench: playability evaluation of an incoming guitar or bass for setup/fretwork — measure neck relief, string action and nut slot height, sight and check frets for wear, unevenness and buzzing positions, and decide whether a truss-rod/setup adjustment, fret dress, or refret is required.

String shop bench: full condition inspection of a used, damaged, or neglected guitar, violin, or cello — top and back cracks, open seams and loose braces, neck angle and joint, bridge lift, tuner and electronics function, finish damage — resulting in an itemized repair estimate and an opinion on whether restoration is economically worthwhile.

Fleet/rental inspection: technician goes through dozens of school-owned or rental-return instruments, either in a school band room or in batches on the shop floor, grading each one's condition, flagging playability faults and damage, and assigning each to clean-and-adjust, repair, or write-off.

High-value or vintage appraisal: an antique violin, vintage saxophone, or collectible guitar is examined for authenticity, originality of parts, prior repairs and over-varnish (sometimes with UV light, endoscope, or measurement of graduations), to produce a written valuation and restoration plan.

sources.system: Plek Station / Plek Pro (scan phase, Sensor Module)
sources.title: The Scan - Plek
sources.claim: The Plek Station/Plek Pro is a commercial computer-controlled luthier machine: the guitar is strapped into the machine under real or simulated string tension and its sensor module automatically scans the fingerboard, producing detailed measurements of nut, string action, fingerboard and frets accurate to about a thousandth of an inch, with recommended relief and fret curves plotted against actual values so out-of-spec frets and action are identified.

sources.system: Plek Station
sources.title: The Plek Station - Plek
sources.claim: Plek markets the machine's scan as the diagnostic step of a repair intake: the scan shows exactly what fretwork is needed, and viewing it lets the shop decide between a fret dress and a partial or complete refret by showing exact fret heights and projecting post-dress results.

sources.system: Plek Station
sources.title: Use Scenarios - Plek
sources.claim: Plek describes the repair-shop use case as using the machine to analyze a customer's instrument and identify problem ..., with the scan results shown to the owner to highlight those areas before any work is chosen.

sources.system: Plek Scanner
sources.title: The Plek Scanner - Plek
sources.claim: Plek has brought to production a dedicated inspection-only machine, the Plek Scanner, a touch-free laser system that scans a fingerboard in under two minutes for instrument evaluation in repair, quality control, and retail settings; the instrument is placed in the scanner and the machine produces the condition overview.

sources.system: Plek Station (Twin Town Guitars); Plek Pro in guitar factories
sources.developer: Plek GmbH / deploying shops and manufacturers
sources.date: retrieved 2026-07; shop service pages, deployment since 2000s
sources.title: PLEK Service at Twin Town Guitars in Minneapolis, Minnesota
sources.claim: Plek machines are in routine production and repair-shop use in the US and internationally: a Minneapolis repair shop's Plek Station scans the fingerboard, nut and frets under tension and the resulting digital reading is used to determine what adjustments and ... the instrument needs; large makers (Gibson, Taylor, Suhr, Martin) run Plek machines on production guitars.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (inspection of a fretted instrument to locate playability defects and set the level of work); this item establishes real-world deployment and that the scan output is what the shop's repair determination rests on.

tasks.label: Shape old parts and replacement parts to improve tone or intonation, using hand tools, lathes, or soldering irons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band-instrument shop, brass repair: technician reshapes existing parts on an assembled horn at the bench — rounding and burnishing a dented leadpipe or bell throat, filing/lapping valve ports and slide tubes, cutting or lengthening a tuning-slide crook and re-soldering braces/ferrules with a torch or soldering iron — then play-tests for tone and intonation and re-works as needed.

Band-instrument shop, woodwind repair (flute, clarinet, sax, oboe): leveling and undercutting tone-hole chimneys, shaping and fitting pads, corks and felts, filing key feet and regulation surfaces, reshaping a warped tenon or fitting a shaped replacement tenon cork — all on a delicate assembled instrument held in hand or a soft vise, judged by leak test and playing test.

Piano technician on site (home, school, church, concert hall) or in shop: filing/reshaping worn hammer felt back to profile, needling and lacquering shoulders and crown for voicing, easing/shaping hammer tails and string bearing points — iterating by ear across 88 notes until tone is even.

Fretted-string repair shop (guitar, bass): leveling, recrowning and dressing frets under simulated string tension; shaping a replacement bone/synthetic nut and cutting its slots; shaping a saddle and compensating it so the instrument plays in tune up the neck.

Bowed-string (violin family) shop: carving a new bridge blank so its feet match the belly arch and its top curve/thickness suit the instrument, shaping/fitting a sound post, dressing the fingerboard camber, thinning a patch or plate area — with knives, planes and files, judged by bowing the instrument.

Fabricating a replacement part from raw stock to specified dimensions on a lathe — e.g., a brass mouthpiece, a clarinet barrel, a ferrule, a slide tube, a bushing — with bore taper/throat sized to change tone or intonation, then finishing and fitting it to the customer's instrument.

sources.system: Plek Station / Plek Pro
sources.title: The Plek Station - Plek
sources.claim: The Plek Station is a commercial CNC machine sold to repair shops and builders that performs fret dressing, nut slotting/shaping and bridge slotting on guitars held in the machine.

sources.system: Plek Station fretcutter tool module
sources.title: Tool Modules - Plek
sources.claim: The Plek's cutting module removes fret height and forms the crown radius in one machine-controlled pass, i.e. the machine performs the shaping cut itself.

sources.system: PLEK Pro / PLEK Station in Gibson production and repair setups
sources.title: What are the major benefits of the Plek process at Gibson?
sources.claim: Gibson, a major manufacturer, states PLEK planes fingerboards, levels frets, shapes nuts and cuts nut slots to high precision, with repeatability comparable to the most experienced luthiers; some hand finishing still follows.

sources.system: PLEK machine in guitar repair shop service
sources.title: Plek Your Guitar | Peach Guitars
sources.claim: In a repair-shop deployment the Plek scans the strung, tuned instrument and then carries out the leveling and dressing cut automatically, under the machine's own control.

sources.system: CNC lathe mouthpiece production at Osmun Music
sources.title: Custom Mouthpieces – Osmun Music
sources.claim: A wind-instrument shop machines custom replacement mouthpieces (cup, throat, backbore geometry chosen to change tone) on a CNC lathe driven by CAD/CAM programs.
sources.transferJustification: Same task as the lathe instance: shaping a replacement instrument part to specified bore/taper dimensions in order to alter tone and intonation; comparable material (brass), comparable precision (thousandths of an inch).

sources.system: Tormach Duality Lathe / PCNC mill mouthpiece machining
sources.title: CNC Machined Trumpet Mouthpiece | Tormach
sources.claim: An independent maker turns and finishes stainless-steel trumpet mouthpieces of his own CAD design on a CNC lathe/mill, confirming CNC turning of instrument replacement parts is routine practice.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the lathe-fabrication instance: producing a replacement brass/steel instrument part whose internal geometry determines tone, at machinist tolerances.

tasks.label: String instruments, and adjust trusses and bridges of instruments to obtain specified string tensions and heights.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Full setup of an electric or acoustic guitar/bass at a repair bench in a music store: strip old strings, thread and wind a new set onto tuning posts, seat ball ends at bridge/tailpiece, stretch and tune to pitch, adjust truss rod for specified neck relief, set saddle/bridge height for specified action, set intonation, verify with feeler gauges and string-action rule.

Bowed-string instrument (violin/viola/cello) at a shop bench: fit or replace the bridge (carve feet to the belly arch, cut string slots, set specified string heights over the fingerboard), install strings through tailpiece and around pegs, wind pegs neatly, bring to tension, check soundpost and tune.

Piano string work by a piano technician: replace one or more broken strings or a full section, cut and coil wire onto tuning pins, thread around hitch pins and through agraffes/bridge pins, bring up to specified tension, seat and chip-tune to pitch in an institutional setting (school, church, dealer shop).

Bulk restringing and standardized setup of a school-district or rental-fleet batch of identical student guitars and violins in a band-and-orchestra repair shop: repetitive same-model work, spec sheet for action and relief, high throughput.

On-site string change and action adjustment away from the bench: customer's living room piano or harp, a stage or rehearsal room before a gig, a school band room — instrument in place amid furniture and clutter, variable lighting, no fixturing.

sources.system: PLEK (A+D Gitarrentechnologie)
sources.title: PLEK Machine - InSync | Sweetwater
sources.claim: The PLEK machine is a commercial 3-axis CNC that measures a guitar and mills frets, nut slots and saddles to set string heights — but it performs no string installation and no truss-rod adjustment.

tasks.label: Repair cracks in wood or metal instruments, using pinning wire, lathes, fillers, clamps, or soldering irons.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair shop bench: hairline-to-full-length crack in a grenadilla clarinet or oboe upper joint. Tech pulls keys, assesses crack depth under light/magnification, drills cross-holes and inserts pinning wire or carbon-fiber staples, wicks in thin CA or epoxy with wood dust, levels flush without altering the bore or tone-hole seats, refits keys and leak-tests the joint.

Repair shop bench: split seam, stress crack, or torn-out brace/valve-casing crack on a trumpet, trombone, or sousaphone. Tech cleans and strips lacquer, aligns and clamps the crack (sometimes fitting a shaped brass patch), applies flux and soft solder with torch or soldering iron, files/dresses and buffs the joint, then leak-tests and touches up the finish.

Luthier bench: top, back, or rib crack in a violin, cello, or acoustic guitar. Tech opens/cleans the crack, works hide glue in, closes it with cauls, clamps or magnets and cleats/studs the inside through the f-hole or soundhole, then levels and retouches the varnish to match.

Turned repair component for a cracked or split joint: tech measures the damaged tenon, socket, or valve-casing area, turns a metal sleeve, bushing, or wooden plug on a lathe to fit that specific instrument, then bonds or solders it in place and refits the mating parts to a leak-free fit.

On-site call at a home, school, or church: crack in a piano soundboard or bridge. Tech evaluates the crack with the piano in place, cleans and routs/tapers it, fits and glues a spruce shim or bridge cap section, clamps against the ribs, then levels, finishes, and re-checks bearing and tuning stability.

Percussion and miscellaneous: crack in a wooden or acrylic drum shell, split in a stave/segment glue joint, or a cracked wooden percussion bar. Tech opens the joint, glues, clamps with straps or cauls, reinforces if needed, and re-levels bearing edges or finishes the surface.

sources.system: Vision-based adaptive crack repair system (UR10e arm, RGB-D camera, laser scanner, extruder/pump)
sources.title: Vision-Based Adaptive Robotics for Autonomous Surface Crack Repair
sources.claim: An autonomous UR10e-based system detects and fills surface cracks in concrete/infrastructure specimens with an extruder and pump, validated on 3D-printed crack specimens in a laboratory setting.
sources.transferJustification: Closest published robotic 'crack filling' work. Transfer to this task does NOT hold: it deposits sealant on flat, rigid concrete surfaces at centimetre scale with no structural reinforcement step, whereas instrument crack repair needs sub-millimetre hairline detection in dark wood, cross-drilling and pinning, hide-glue/CA wicking, clamped closure, flush levelling that preserves bore and tone-hole geometry, and a leak-tight, cosmetically matched result on a curved, thin-walled, disassembled workpiece.

sources.system: Japan Unix robotic soldering systems (e.g., UNIX-DR/automated soldering robots)
sources.title: Robotic Soldering | Advanced Automated Soldering System | Japan Unix
sources.claim: Commercial robotic soldering cells perform programmed soldering with controlled thermal profiles on fixtured production parts (electronics/PCB and similar assemblies) in industrial cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is production soldering. Transfer to brass-instrument crack repair does not hold: these cells run taught paths on identical, fixtured parts with known joint locations, while a cracked cornet or trombone arrives with a unique crack path, needs lacquer stripping, crack alignment/clamping, possible fitted patch fabrication, torch heat judgment on thin brass to avoid burn-through, then filing, buffing and leak testing — none of which is demonstrated by these systems.

sources.title: Benefits of a Bar Feeder on a CNC Lathe
sources.claim: CNC turning centres with magazine bar feeders run unattended, producing turned metal parts automatically for entire shifts in a machine shop cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is unattended turning of parts. It covers only the lathe sub-step of a crack repair: producing a sleeve, bushing or plug from bar stock to a programmed dimension. It does not cover measuring the damaged instrument to derive that dimension, nor fitting, bonding/soldering and refitting the part to the specific cracked joint, which is the accepted output of the instance.

tasks.label: Polish instruments, using rags and polishing compounds, buffing wheels, or burnishing tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band-shop buffing station: brass/nickel-silver bodies, bells and slides (trumpet, trombone, sax) are cut- and color-buffed on motor-driven buffing wheels with compound after dent work or lacquer stripping, prior to relacquer or replate. Component-level work at a dedicated buffing motor with dust collection.

Final hand polish of a fully assembled instrument before customer pickup: rag/polishing cloth and lacquer or silver polish worked over the whole horn, around braces, valve clusters, key work, linkages and engraving, removing fingerprints and haze without snagging pads or springs.

Small-component polishing and burnishing: woodwind keys, rods, posts, trumpet valve casings, tuning slides, mouthpieces, and burnishing of slides/tone-hole rims — thin, delicate parts held against a wheel or worked with a burnishing tool, where excess pressure distorts the part.

Polishing lacquered/varnished wood instrument surfaces after finish touch-up: guitar bodies, violin varnish, drum shells — compound and cloth or buffing wheel to bring back gloss without burning through a thin finish.

Piano work on site (customer home, school, church): polishing the high-gloss polyester or satin case, key tops, and the brass/plated hardware and cast plate with rags and polish, working around furniture in a room not controlled by the shop.
Plated and percussion hardware: cymbals, drum lugs, hoops and stands, plus silver-plated flute/sax bodies — tarnish and corrosion removal by wheel buffing or hand rag with polishing compound.

tasks.label: Mix and measure glue that will be used for instrument repair.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Band/orchestral wind-instrument repair bench in a music store or independent shop: technician mixes a few grams of two-part epoxy (or measures/thins pad cement, shellac, contact cement) for one specific repair, proportioning by eye/weight on a mixing pad, stirring to homogeneity, and using it within pot life. Containers sit on a cluttered bench among tools.

Violin/guitar shop: luthier prepares hot hide glue - weighs granules, soaks in measured water to a chosen dilution (e.g., 1:1.5 to 1:2), heats in a glue pot to ~140-145 F, stirs, judges consistency by drip/string test and adjusts with water for the joint type (crack, seam, neck reset).

Piano shop bench: technician mixes/thins glue for action work (hide glue, PVC-E, aliphatic resin) - measuring small amounts, adding water or solvent to the working consistency needed for keytops, hammer shanks, bridle straps, or soundboard shims.

Field service call in a customer's home, church, school stage or band room: tuner/repairer mixes a small batch of glue (epoxy, hide glue from a portable pot, CA with accelerator) on site with a portable kit, on whatever surface is available, before making an on-site repair.

High-volume repair department (school-service shop, large retailer, manufacturer's repair line): repeated standard batches of the same adhesive to a written formula for repads, brace/crack repairs or drum-shell work, prepared several times a day at a dedicated glue station.

tasks.label: Align pads and keys on reed or wind instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Student-line clarinet or flute repad at a music-store / school-district repair bench: melt shellac or hot glue in each key cup, float and level the new pad so it seats leak-tight on the tone hole, verify with leak light and feeler gauge, then set key heights and adjust cork/felt so linked keys close simultaneously.

Saxophone pad alignment and key regulation at a shop bench: heat key cups, float larger pads, bend key arms/cups slightly to level a pad against a not-perfectly-flat tone hole, iterate against leak light or Magnehelic readings, and set regulation screws/cork so stacked keys close together.

Quick reseat / regulation fixes on rental-fleet or school-owned band instruments, done either at the shop check-in bench or on site in a school band room: free a sticking or tilted pad, tap or bend a key back into alignment, shim or shave a regulation cork so a linked key closes, all in a few minutes per horn.

Precision work on professional flutes, piccolos or oboes in a specialist shop: paper/mylar shimming of pads to sub-tenth-millimeter, checking impressions with feeler and light, adjusting key height, spring tension and regulation for even, silent, leak-free action on an expensive instrument.

Factory or dealer setup bench: on new or overhauled instruments, install and seat pads and regulate all keys to factory spec, then play-test before the instrument ships, with standard parts and a fixed station layout.

sources.system: Selmer Paris automated key-fit / tone-hole leveling machine
sources.title: How the BEST Saxophones in the World are Made – Selmer Edition
sources.claim: At Selmer Paris, one of the most automated woodwind factories, an automated machine measures key-post spacing, trims key metal and levels tone holes so keys fit; pad gluing, seating and regulation are still done by workers by hand with shellac and heat.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machining key fit and leveling tone holes prepares the surfaces that pads seat against, in the same instrument and same factory. It does not transfer to this task: the machine performs fixed subtractive machining on a rigidly held body and never places, floats, levels or leak-tests a pad, nor bends keys or sets regulation, which the same article shows workers doing by hand immediately afterward.

sources.system: Yamaha saxophone final assembly line
sources.title: How Yamaha Makes Saxophones (Mostly) By Hand
sources.claim: In Yamaha's saxophone factory — the most structured setting in which this task occurs — installing and regulating pads on the key stacks is performed by human technicians at manual assembly stations, with a human play-test before shipping.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (pad installation and key regulation) in a purpose-built production facility; cited as context showing the step remains manual even where the environment is maximally structured. It supports no positive judgment.

sources.system: Autonomous mobile robotic screwdriving system (UR-based, SINDy-model adaptive control)

sources.claim: State-of-the-art autonomous precision assembly demonstrated in manufacturing is fastener-level work: a mobile robot autonomously locating and driving screws under a few millimeters of pose uncertainty using force compliance — no comparable system performs adhesive pad seating, leveling against a tone hole, or leak-based iterative key regulation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fine, force-controlled small-part assembly in a factory. It does not transfer: pad alignment requires heating adhesive, floating a compliant leather/felt pad flat to a hand-lapped tone hole to a light-tight tolerance, judging seat quality from leak light or vacuum feedback, and elastically bending key arms — none of which this system or any cited system performs.

tasks.label: Solder posts and parts to hold them in their proper places.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench repair in a band-instrument shop: re-soldering a loose or broken brace/stay, ferrule, water key or bell-to-tube joint on a trumpet, trombone or tuba. Technician cleans off old soft solder, fits the flange, clamps/wires the part in alignment so slides and valves still move freely, torch-solders, then cleans flux and touches up lacquer.

Woodwind bench repair: re-attaching a post or key rib that has pulled off a saxophone or clarinet-body ligature/neck, positioning the post by trial fit of the key and rod so the mechanism runs straight and free, soft-soldering with a torch or resistance iron, then checking key action.

Fine hard/silver-soldering of small key parts: reattaching a broken key touchpiece, spatula, arm or a flute/piccolo post-and-rib on nickel-silver or sterling parts held in a third-hand or small jig, with heat controlled so adjacent existing joints do not let go.

Installing new hardware during an overhaul or customization in a shop or factory-service setting: soldering on new posts, guards, thumb rests, lyre boxes, saddles or replacement braces, using templates and positioning fixtures on a bench with soldering station and torch.

Field/mobile work: school-district route technician in a repair van or a band room, or backstage before a performance, re-soldering a loose post or brace quickly with a portable torch/iron and improvised holding, in a space not laid out for the work.

tasks.label: Remove dents and burrs from metal instruments, using mallets and burnishing tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench work in a band-instrument repair shop: a student trumpet or trombone bell with several small-to-medium dents and dings from drops and case damage. The tech mounts the bell on a bell mandrel/bell rollers, taps with a rawhide or nylon mallet, works each dent out with dent balls and rods, then burnishes the area smooth without stretching, thinning, or work-hardening the brass, preserving lacquer/engraving as far as possible.

Shop bench: dents in curved tubing — leadpipes, bows, tuning-slide crooks, French horn branches — that a straight rod cannot reach. The tech uses a magnetic dent-removal system, flexible/bent rods, or dent balls drawn through on a cable, sometimes unsoldering a branch to gain access, then burnishes and re-solders and blends the area.

Shop bench precision work: dented trombone outer/inner slide tubes or piston valve casings, where roundness must be restored to close tolerance so the slide or valve moves freely. The tech works the tube over a mandrel with dent rods, slide rollers and burnishers, then checks fit, straightness and free movement before reassembly.

Shop bench: dents in metal woodwind bodies — flute or piccolo tubes, saxophone bells, necks and bows — often near tone holes. The tech uses internal mandrels and dent rollers, light tapping and burnishing, taking care that tone-hole seats stay flat and level so pads still seal.

Shop bench/anvil work on severe damage: a crushed or deeply creased tuba, sousaphone or baritone bell or bow. The tech unrolls and hammers the metal out over stakes, anvils and bell mandrels with mallets, judges where the metal is fatigued or needs annealing, then burnishes, blends and polishes the repaired area.

Deburring and edge finishing incidental to other repairs: burrs on freshly cut or reamed tube ends, filed solder seams, mouthpiece receivers and trimmed slide tubes. The tech files/scrapes the burr and burnishes the edge smooth so parts fit and seal before assembly.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic edge deburring of metal parts. It transfers to the deburring/edge-burnishing portion of this task (instance 5) because the operation is the same — removing a raised burr from a metal edge and leaving a smooth surface — and the compliant spindle accommodates part-to-part variation once the part is fixtured. It does not transfer to dent removal, which requires reshaping thin, already-stretched brass from the inside.

tasks.label: Adjust felt hammers on pianos to increase tonal mellowness or brilliance, using sanding paddles, lacquer, or needles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential service call: after tuning a customer's upright or small grand in a living room, the technician voices a handful of harsh or uneven notes in situ — single-needle work between the strings on grooved, hardened hammers, occasional light filing — judged by ear against the owner's taste and the room's acoustics.

Institutional venue: voicing a grand at a school, church, or recital hall — evening-up or brightening/mellowing a full hammer set before a performance, often with the action pulled onto a bench beside the stage, matched to the pianist's request and the hall, under a deadline.

Shop bench work on a rebuilt/reconditioned piano: a new hammer set is hung, then pre-needled in the shoulders, shaped with sanding paddle/file, treated with lacquer or hardener where more brilliance is wanted, and iteratively test-played note by note until tone is even across all 88.

Dealer showroom / pre-delivery prep: voicing new or trade-in inventory to the store's tonal standard, or answering a customer complaint that a delivered piano is too bright — needling and light filing, judged by ear in the showroom or the customer's home.

Manufacturing plant hammer-prep station: deep-needling the shoulders of new hammer sets to a specified hardness/tension target on fixtured hammer rails, ahead of the final by-ear voicing done downstream in the voicing department.

tasks.label: Remove irregularities from tuning pins, strings, and hammers of pianos, using wood blocks or filing tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-home service call on a customer's grand or upright piano in a living room: technician pulls the grand action (or opens the upright), inspects hammer felt for string-cut grooves and flat/mated crowns, files and reshapes the worn hammers with sandpaper paddle/file, checks hammer-to-string mating and tone, reinstalls the action. Furniture-crowded, non-standard room; piano stays where it sits.

On-site service in an institution (school band/practice rooms, church, university, recital hall) under a maintenance contract: heavily played pianos with deeply grooved hammers; technician files/reshapes hammers on site, levels and seats strings, checks evenness across the scale, often between classes or rehearsals.

Shop/rebuild bench work: the action is removed and brought to the technician's shop; the full set of hammers is gang-filed or individually shaped on a bench or action cradle to restore crown and remove grooves, hammers squared to the string line, tone checked after re-installation.

Dealer showroom pre-delivery prep or concert-stage prep: new or recently traded piano is evened out — light hammer filing/shaping, string leveling, hammers mated to strings — so the instrument plays evenly before sale or performance.

String and tuning-pin specific irregularity work (mostly in homes and institutions, piano strung and standing): seating and leveling strings by tapping with a wood block and brass punch, removing kinks/false beats, dressing burrs on tuning pins and setting loose or protruding pins.

tasks.label: Strike wood, fiberglass, or metal bars of instruments, and use tuned blocks, stroboscopes, or electronic tuners to evaluate tones made by instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair-shop bench: a single wooden bar (rosewood/padauk marimba or xylophone bar) removed from its frame or a new blank is suspended on cord or foam, struck with a mallet, and the fundamental plus the 4th/10th partials are read on a strobe or electronic tuner to decide where material must come off; struck and re-read repeatedly through the tuning cycle.

Shop/factory bench: metal bar or tube instruments (glockenspiel/orchestra-bell bars, vibraphone aluminum bars, tubular chimes) placed on a test stand, struck, and each partial checked against reference pitch on an electronic tuner/strobe; includes new or replacement bars checked before installation.

On-site service call at a school, university or church: the assembled keyboard percussion instrument (marimba, vibraphone, bells) sits in its frame in a band room; the tech strikes every bar in sequence with a mallet, reads a clip-on/electronic tuner, and flags flat/sharp bars, dead bars, buzzes and cord or resonator problems, amid ambient room noise.

Final quality check in the shop after a repair or re-cord: the reassembled instrument is played across its full range, each bar struck and compared to tuned blocks/reference pitch, with judgment of evenness of tone, sustain and absence of rattles before the instrument is returned.

School music room / cart of educational Orff instruments: fiberglass and wood bar xylophones and metallophones; replacement bars and the existing set are struck quickly and compared to a tuned block or pocket tuner to confirm pitch and reject warped or cracked bars.

tasks.label: Wash metal instruments in lacquer-stripping and cyanide solutions to remove lacquer and tarnish.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Standard chemical clean of a disassembled student-grade brass horn (trumpet/cornet/trombone bell and slide sections) in the shop's chemical room: parts are racked/wired, immersed in a hot lacquer-stripping tank until the lacquer lifts, rinsed, dipped in an acid/cyanide brightening solution to strip tarnish, rinsed again and dried, ready for buffing and re-lacquer.

Batch of small metal parts (valve casings, pistons, slide tubes, braces, ferrules, water keys, sax keys) loaded into perforated baskets, run through stripper, rinse, cyanide/bright dip and rinse with agitation, then rinsed hot and blown/oven dried in the shop chem room.

Large low-brass instrument (tuba, sousaphone bell section, baritone) chem-cleaned in deep tanks: heavy awkward body hung on a rack or hoist, fully immersed in stripper and then bright dip, with extra rinsing of internal tubing and long draining/drying.

Silver-plated horn (silver trumpet, sax body, flute headjoint) with heavy tarnish: brief timed dip in cyanide-based tarnish-removal solution with careful dwell control to brighten the plating without attacking or removing it, followed by neutralizing rinse and dry.

Vintage or high-value instrument of unknown finish and condition (soft-soldered joints, engraving, worn plating, patches of original lacquer): technician watches the piece continuously in the tank, dips partially or spot-swabs areas, pulls it the moment the coating lifts, hand-brushes residue and re-dips selectively to avoid damage.
