automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Aircraft tube shop: set up a CNC/all-electric tube bender for a new part number that falls within the tooling already installed (multi-stack dies): load/verify the bend program, set feed/rotation/bend parameters, run a first article, measure it and apply springback/geometry corrections until the part is in ....

Aircraft tube shop: set up requiring a physical tooling changeover for a new diameter/bend radius — hoist and bolt on bend die, clamp die, pressure die and wiper, install and position mandrel and links, align and dial in the stack, then prove out the first article.

Aircraft tube shop: operate the bender through a production run of aerospace fluid lines (aluminum, CRES, titanium, 1/8 in.–3 in. OD) — load straight stock, cycle the machine through multi-bend programs, unload, and gauge/inspect parts periodically against the tube drawing.

Aircraft tube shop: operate cut-off saw/laser and deburring or chamfering machines to cut tube stock to developed length and remove internal and external burrs from tube ends before forming or welding.

Aircraft tube shop: operate bench/CNC end-forming, swaging, flaring and crimping machines — 37-degree double flares to AS specification, beads, reduced/expanded ends, swaged or crimped ferrules and fittings — then inspect the formed end for cracks, wall thinning and seal-surface quality.

At the assembly station or on the aircraft: hand-bend, tweak, or straighten a tube run so it fits the routing in a wing or fuselage bay, using a hand bender, straightening tool and portable deburring tool, working around installed structure and clamps in a confined space.

tasks.label: Set, align, adjust, or synchronize aircraft armament or rigging or control system components to established tolerances or requirements, using sighting devices and hand tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-situ rigging of a large transport/commercial aircraft's cable and pushrod flight-control system during final assembly: installing rig pins, adjusting turnbuckles and rod ends, pulling cable tension to spec with a tensiometer, checking surface travel with rigging fixtures/protractors, then safety-wiring and buying off the rig. Work is done from stands and inside wing and fuselage confined spaces, over long cable runs.

Hanging and aligning a movable control surface or its support fittings (flap, aileron, spoiler, elevator, rudder) on the airframe: positioning the surface to hinge-line, gap and step tolerances using sighting/measuring devices and laser or optical tooling, fitting shims, bolting up, and verifying free, symmetric travel.

Bench or fixture-level setting of control-linkage subassemblies before installation: setting pushrod/control-rod lengths and rod-end thread engagement, bellcranks, quadrants, and actuator/servo rigging to a dimensional spec, torquing and locking jam nuts, and verifying with gauges and go/no-go fixtures.

Military aircraft armament and aiming-system alignment: boresighting a gun installation, pylons, missile launcher rails and targeting/sight sensors to the aircraft reference datum with boresight/optical equipment, then shimming and adjusting mount hardware until readings fall inside harmonization tolerances.

Rotorcraft and light-aircraft rigging: setting swashplate/collective/pitch-link dimensions and control travel on a helicopter, making rotor track-and-balance pitch-link and trim-tab adjustments after run-up on the manufacturer's pad, or rigging aileron/elevator cables on a small general-aviation airframe.

sources.system: x-wheel / x-3Dprofile wheel alignment and toe setting stand

sources.claim: Duerr's x-wheel end-of-line stand measures chassis geometry optically and then adjusts the threaded tie-rod linkage to set toe angles to angle-minute tolerance with no operator present, i.e. an automated adjust-a-linkage-to-a-measured-tolerance cell.

tasks.label: Join structural assemblies, such as wings, tails, or fuselage.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial transport final/major body join: forward, centre and aft fuselage sections (and tail cone section) brought together in an assembly bay, aligned to a few thousandths with laser metrology and positioners, then splice joints drilled, countersunk, sealed and fastened with thousands of rivets/lockbolts; work done in a jigged station with crews inside and outside the barrel.

Structures-shop join of fuselage skin panels and shells into barrels/sections: longitudinal and circumferential splices, frames/clips and stringers joined to skins in fixed jigs; very high fastener counts, sealant, and bucking/collar work on the inner side of the skin.

Wing structural join: closing the wing box by joining upper/lower skin panels to spars and ribs in a jig, and joining wing sections / centre wing box; long straight-run fastening on large contoured panels with sealant and interference-fit fasteners.

Final-assembly mates requiring fit-up judgment: wing-to-body join, vertical/horizontal stabilizer attach, and military fighter/rotorcraft major mates — parts brought together, gaps measured, custom shims fabricated and installed, parts separated and re-mated, match drilling and bolt-up of fittings in confined interior spaces.
Business-jet / regional-jet series production airframe joins: lower rate lines (a few dozen aircraft a year) joining fuselage panels, shells and wing structures in dedicated jigs at a single site.

Small general-aviation, kit/experimental, prototype and repair-shop structural joins: wing spars, tail surfaces and fuselage sections hand-fitted, clecoed, hand-drilled and bucked or bonded, with improvised or simple tooling and frequent one-off configurations.

tasks.label: Capture or segregate waste material, such as aluminum swarf, machine cutting fluid, or solvents, for recycling or environmentally responsible disposal.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Capturing aluminum/titanium swarf produced while drilling and countersinking skins, frames, spars and control surfaces at the assembly position: running the vacuum shroud on the drill motor, emptying the chip canister into the designated metal-chip-only container, and clearing chips off the panel and jig before close-out. Aircraft assembly bay, standard tooling, chips must stay uncontaminated to keep recycling value.

Segregating chemical waste generated by cleaning, priming and sealing: solvent-soaked wipes (MEK/acetone/IPA), leftover sealant and adhesive cartridges, empty aerosol/solvent containers, placed into the correct labeled satellite-accumulation hazardous-waste containers, kept closed and logged per RCRA/EHS procedure.

Capturing machine cutting fluid and lubricants: catching drill lubricant and coolant drip from portable drilling/reaming equipment and bench machines with pans and absorbents, and transferring used fluid into the designated recovery drum or coolant-recycling tote rather than a floor drain.

End-of-shift and pre-close-out debris/FOD cleanup in and around the structure, including confined interiors (wing box, fuselage interior, control-surface cavities): vacuuming or sweeping metal chips, drill dust and cut-off fastener tails, and keeping recyclable metal debris separate from general trash.

Moving and staging filled scrap and waste containers: hauling chip bins, solvent drums and recycling carts from the work cell to the plant's central segregation/recycling accumulation area and returning empties, keeping each stream separated and labeled.

tasks.label: Position and align subassemblies in jigs or fixtures, using measuring instruments and following blueprint lines and index points.

instances.label: Major-component positioning at an OEM: a fuselage section, wing, or empennage subassembly is craned/rolled into a large join jig or positioner set, then aligned to tooling balls/index points against blueprint nominals using a laser tracker or indoor-GPS, iterating jack/positioner moves until in tolerance.

Medium structural details into a build jig: stringers, spars, ribs, frames, floor beams or skin planks lifted into a wing-panel or fuselage panel jig, seated on index pins/locators, clamped, and checked to blueprint lines with scales, trammels and gauges before drill/fasten.

Low-rate, high-mix work: prototype, legacy, spares, or repair/mod builds using hand-built soft tooling and mylars, parts lacking accurate digital definition, with fit-up iteration, shimming and rework judgment in a general assembly bay.

tasks.label: Layout and mark reference points and locations for installation of parts or components, using jigs, templates, or measuring and marking instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On the floor of an airframe plant, marking fastener/part locations on a large structural assembly held in an assembly jig: laying and clamping a drill template on a fuselage skin, wing panel or bulkhead, scribing/marking dozens to hundreds of hole, clip and stringer locations, cross-checking with tape, square and station/butt-line references; curved surfaces, some vertical or overhead, tolerances of a fraction of a millimetre.

Inside a fuselage/cabin on the assembly or systems-installation line: marking installation locations for interior and systems parts - seat-track positions on floor rails, bracket and clip positions on frames and floor beams, duct, tube and wire-harness support points - measured off station numbers and datum lines with tape, template and marker, working kneeling or in cramped access.

At a bench in a detail/subassembly shop: laying out a detail part or small subassembly (skin doubler, rib, angle, fitting) - transferring a template outline, applying layout dye, scribing trim, bend and drill locations with height gauge, dividers, scale and protractor before drilling or fitting.

Establishing reference datums and lines on a major assembly for alignment and rigging: marking waterline/buttline/station reference points on a wing, empennage or fuselage section, transferring positions from a master jig or optical/laser measurement, marking rig-pin and control-surface neutral reference points prior to installing rigging and control equipment.

In a hangar or modification line, laying out and marking on a built aircraft or replacement structure: matching an existing hole pattern for a replacement skin, marking an antenna, doubler or bracket location per drawing over painted, sealed, non-nominal existing structure using templates and measuring instruments.

tasks.label: Fit and fasten sheet metal coverings to surface areas or other sections of aircraft prior to welding or riveting.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-rate wing or empennage panel line at an airframer/tier-1: a machined or formed metal skin is laid in a long panel jig; the assembler locates stringers/spar chords to the skin off tooling holes and pilot holes, pulls the stack up with clamps and installs temporary bolts or Clecos along the runs before the automatic riveter or riveting crew makes the joint permanent. Standard parts, good two-sided access, repeatable geometry.

Fuselage shell and section work: skin panels offered up to frames and clips to build partial shells, and shells/sections brought together at longitudinal and circumferential lap joints in a large jig. Worker on platforms or stands aligns the skin lap and step, clamps, and installs temporary fasteners down the joint before riveting.

Smaller secondary structure at a bench or small jig: access doors, fairings, nacelle/pylon skins, control-surface skins, bulkhead and firewall coverings, and thin-gauge sheet parts fitted prior to spot or fusion welding. Parts held in loose tooling or by hand, cleco'd on pilot holes, checked for flushness and edge margin.

Fit-up that does not go together as drawn: the covering will not lie flush or the gap is out of tolerance, so the assembler trims and files edges, hand-forms or bumps the skin, adds peelable or liquid shim, or reworks clip/doubler position before cleco-ing. Also covers low-rate military and space-vehicle skins match-drilled off templates with frequent engineering changes.

Closeout coverings over already-built structure with one-sided or confined access: belly skins, lower wing panels over a closed box, tail-cone and bulkhead coverings. The assembler works overhead, behind structure, or lying inside the box, using single-sided temporary fasteners and long-reach clamps to hold the skin before riveting.

tasks.label: Verify dimensions of cable assemblies or positions of fittings, using measuring instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Structural sub-assembly check on the shop floor: after drilling/installing attach fittings, brackets or hole patterns in a rib, spar, panel, bulkhead or door frame held in an assembly jig, the assembler verifies feature/fitting positions and hole sizes with height gauges, micrometers, calipers, hole and depth gauges or a portable CMM against tooling datums, and records the results.

Large airframe check in the final-assembly bay: verifying positions of major fittings (wing-to-body attach fittings, landing-gear fittings, hinge and actuator fittings) on a wing, fuselage or empennage sitting in a large jig, using a laser tracker, photogrammetry targets, trammel bars or long-range gauges, working around scaffolding, tooling and other crews.

Cable/harness fabrication bench: verifying dimensions of a finished cable assembly - overall length between fitting bearing points, terminal/fitting orientation and position along the run, swage or crimp diameter/height with go-no-go gauges, micrometers, tape and gauge boards - before the assembly is released for installation.

In-situ rigging verification on the built-up aircraft: checking installed control-cable tension with a tensiometer, turnbuckle and end-fitting thread engagement/position, pulley and fairlead clearances, and control-surface travel with rig pins, protractors or inclinometers, reaching into wing bays, wheel wells and fuselage interiors.

Detail-part and first-article dimensional checks at an inspection bench: measuring machined fittings, bushings, brackets and swaged end terminals with calipers, micrometers, thread and bore gauges or a CMM before installation, and dispositioning out-of-tolerance parts.

tasks.label: Fabricate parts needed for assembly or installation, using shop machinery or equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the fab/assembly shop of an aircraft plant or MRO, the assembler makes small sheet-metal details called out on a drawing (clips, angles, brackets, doublers, filler strips, closeout plates): lay out or nest the blank, shear/nibble/rout it from aluminum sheet, form it on a brake or hand tools, drill/deburr, and check thickness, bend angle and hole pattern before it goes on the airframe.

Fabricating custom shims, packers and spacers to fill a measured gap in a structural joint (skin-to-frame, fitting-to-spar): measure or scan the gap, then cut/peel a laminated shim or machine/waterjet a solid shim to the required contour and thickness, trial fit and rework until the joint closes without pull-down.

Making rigid tube runs and hose assemblies for hydraulic, pneumatic, fuel or oxygen systems: cut aluminum/CRES/titanium tube to length, bend to the routing on a bender, flare or roller-swage end fittings, clean and cap, then fit-check the tube against the installed structure.

Fabricating flight-control cable and rigging hardware: cutting steel control cable to length from a reel, swaging or Nicopress-ing terminals and turnbuckle ends, making up push rods and bellcrank links, then proof-loading and inspecting the finished assembly before rigging.

Making small machined details on shop machine tools — bushings, spacers, sleeves, stand-offs, jig/tool details — turned or milled from bar or plate on a lathe, mill, drill press or CNC per blueprint, then reamed, tapped, deburred and dimensionally checked.

Fabricating non-structural details with shop equipment: cutting and crimping wire leads and harness branches, cutting composite plies, gaskets, seals, insulation blankets and plastic/phenolic details on a flatbed cutter or waterjet to a pattern.

tasks.label: Place and connect control cables to electronically controlled units, using hand tools, ring locks, cotter keys, threaded connectors, turnbuckles, or related devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Inside a fuselage or wing on the assembly line: route steel flight-control cables over pulleys and through fairleads, attach ends to quadrants/bellcranks and to electrically controlled trim/autopilot servo units, install and adjust turnbuckles to specified tension, and safety them with clips or cotter keys. Confined, overhead, blind-access work.

Avionics bay / equipment rack inside the airframe: place a pre-formed cable bundle along brackets, secure with cushioned clamps and ties, and mate threaded circular connectors (coupling-nut type) to electronic control units, actuator controllers and sensors, torquing and locking each connector per spec.

Subassembly held in a jig at a shop-floor workstation (wing spar section, empennage, flight-control surface, systems module): lay in cables/harness, connect them to actuators and electronic control units with threaded connectors and ring lugs, clamp and dress the run before the assembly moves to the aircraft.

Bench/form-board work in the harness or systems shop: lay out and route cable and harness assemblies on a board per drawing, terminate wires into connector inserts and backshells, install ring locks/retaining rings, and continuity-check the finished assembly.

Landing gear bay, pylon or engine area: attach control cables and sensor leads to units and clevis fittings, install clevis pins with cotter keys, torque and lockwire threaded connectors, working overhead in a cramped, greasy space around the gear structure.

tasks.label: Manually install structural assemblies or signal crane operators to position assemblies for joining.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-rate commercial final assembly line: mating major structural assemblies (forward/aft fuselage sections, wings, empennage) to the mid-fuselage — rigging the load, signaling the crane or positioner operator, aligning index/pilot holes to metrology targets, then pinning and temporary-fastening the joint.

Aerostructures panel/component line: loading and installing large flat or contoured structural parts into jigs — skins, stringers, spars, doublers — hoist- or crane-presented, clamped/tacked in the fixture ready for drilling and fastening.

Installing medium structural members into open jig-held structure: ribs, frames, bulkheads, floor beams, keel and door-surround fittings — hoisted into place, fit checked, shimmed, drilled and temporarily fastened while the structure is still open.

Installing small structural fittings inside or around closed airframe structure: brackets, clips, angles, doublers, intercostals in confined wing-box bays, fuselage crown and empennage interiors, with hand tools, sealant, liquid or peel shims and limited visibility.

Low-rate, high-mix work: military airframes, rotorcraft, business jets, prototypes and modification/retrofit lines, where fits vary part to part, tooling is manual, and structural assemblies are hand-fitted and crane-positioned to match drilled-at-assembly interfaces.

Space vehicle / missile structural assembly in a high bay or clean area: crane-rigged tank barrels, domes, rings, thrust structures and panels positioned to close tolerance and secured for welding or bolted joining.

tasks.label: Assemble prototypes or integrated-technology demonstrators of new or emerging environmental technologies for aircraft.

Integrating the technology demonstrator onto a ground test rig / iron bird: mounting motors, inverters, tanks and controllers on a steel test frame, connecting hoses, cables and plumbing, aligning shafts, per a one-off rig drawing.

Rework and modification during ground/flight test campaigns per engineering change: removing and reinstalling installed hardware, drilling out and replacing fasteners, re-shimming, re-routing lines in an as-built (not-as-drawn) demonstrator.

tasks.label: Install mechanical linkages and actuators, using tensiometers to verify tension of cables.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Transport-category final assembly (e.g., 737/A320-class line): routing flight-control cables through fuselage/wing/empennage over pulleys, fairleads and quadrants, installing bellcranks, pushrods and hydraulic/electromechanical actuators, adjusting turnbuckles and verifying tension with a tensiometer against temperature-corrected charts, then safety-wiring/cotter-pinning. Confined interior access, overhead work, multiple crews working the same airframe.

Light aircraft / business-jet assembly line: rigging aileron, elevator, rudder and trim cable systems in a small fuselage, installing control-column linkages and trim actuators, setting rig pins and travel stops, checking each cable run with a clamp-on tensiometer and re-adjusting turnbuckles until tension and surface travel both meet spec.

Component/subassembly shop: bolting actuators, rod-end linkages, bellcranks and drive fittings onto control surfaces, flap/slat or spoiler assemblies held in a bench fixture or jig; aligning close-tolerance clevis holes, inserting bolts, torquing to spec, adjusting rod-end length, functional check. Rigid parts, no cable rigging at this stage.

Rotorcraft assembly: installing swashplate control linkages, pitch links, bellcranks and hydraulic servo actuators; setting rig-pin dimensions, adjusting link lengths, tension-checking tail-rotor control cables with a tensiometer, and lockwiring the adjustments.

Missile / space-vehicle assembly in a high bay or clean room: installing fin or thrust-vector actuators and their mechanical linkages onto a fixtured section, mating connectors, torquing and lockwiring fasteners, verifying linkage travel; small lot sizes and configuration variation between units.

Rework and post-installation adjustment on the assembly line or in an adjacent hangar: replacing a rejected actuator, re-rigging a cable run after a structural rework, chasing an out-of-tolerance tension or travel reading, working in an airframe already partly closed out with limited access.

Motor rewind/repair shop, small-to-medium random-wound stator (roughly 5-150 HP, low voltage): after burnout and slot cleaning, worker cuts and inserts slot cells, then feeds shop-wound random coils into the slots one group at a time, adds phase insulation and wedges.

Motor rewind/repair shop, large and/or form-wound machine (200-2000 HP, medium voltage): worker fits slot cells into a large, sometimes distorted core, then lays taped form coils into open slots one at a time, springing tops, blocking and lacing end turns; every job a different frame, slot count and coil geometry.

Very large or one-off machine (hydro/turbo generator, large traction motor) built or rewound in a heavy shop or in the powerhouse: slot armor/cell material fitted and heavy stator bars or coils lowered into open slots, wedged and blocked, often by a crew with hoists.

tasks.label: Apply solutions or paints to wired electrical components, using hand tools, and bake components.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dip-and-bake varnish impregnation in an electrical equipment plant: worker racks batches of wound small stators, armatures, or bobbin coils, immerses or roll-dips them in an insulating varnish/resin tank, lets them drain, transfers the rack into a batch curing oven, sets time and temperature, then unloads and inspects for runs, voids, and varnish in unwanted areas.

Trickle/drip application of insulating resin to individual wound stators or armatures at a finishing station: part is preheated, resin is metered onto the winding ends and slots while the part rotates, then the part is gelled and cured under heat before cooling and inspection.

Bench-level selective application: worker uses a brush, syringe, or hand dispenser to apply epoxy, potting compound, insulating varnish, or lead-sealing solution to specific spots on small wound components (bobbins, toroids, small transformers, coil leads), masking or avoiding terminals, then places trays in a bench or tunnel oven to cure.

Spray application of insulating varnish or finish coat to larger wound assemblies (large stators, transformer coils and cores, field frames) with a spray gun in a booth or ventilated area, followed by a bake in a walk-in/tunnel oven; heavier parts moved by cart, hoist, or overhead conveyor.

Vacuum pressure impregnation of large or high-voltage coils and transformer windings: worker rigs and loads the winding into the impregnation vessel, runs the vacuum/resin fill/pressure cycle from a control panel, drains, then transfers the part to a curing oven for a long bake and unloads after cooling.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Motor repair/service center teardown: a field-return AC induction motor (roughly 5–250 hp) arrives dirty, oily and often rusted. The winder removes coupling/pulley and fan cover, breaks loose seized through-bolts and end-bracket fasteners, taps/pries off end brackets, lifts and withdraws the rotor with a hoist without scoring the stator bore, and pulls bearings with a puller or induction heat. Every unit is a different make, frame and vintage.

Motor repair/service center rebuild after rewind: heat/press new bearings onto the shaft, insert the rotor into the freshly wound stator without damaging coils or insulation, refit end brackets and shims, torque fasteners in sequence, check air gap and free shaft rotation, reconnect leads to the terminal box, and run/no-load test before shipping. One-off job, used and mixed-vintage parts.

Electrical equipment plant, repeating same-model work: assembling motors and wound components after winding — installing the wound stator/field into a frame or housing, fitting rotor, end shields and bearings, bolting and torquing with hand/air tools, connecting and soldering/fusing leads to terminals, on a line or bench with parts supplied in totes and fixtures.

Bench repair/rework of electrical components: a coil, transformer or small assembly comes back with a damaged lead, cracked terminal, chafed sleeving or loose connector. The worker inspects it, cuts away damaged wire and insulation, re-terminates (crimp/solder/braze), re-insulates with sleeving, tape or varnish, and verifies with meter/hipot. Defects and units vary.

Maintaining and repairing shop machinery parts with hand tools: servicing the winding/taping machines and tooling — changing wire guides, nozzles, tensioners, mandrels and forms, disassembling a jammed head, replacing worn belts, bushings or springs, adjusting and lubricating, and re-testing the machine on a sample part.

instances.label: Wire harness / cable assembly test in a harness shop: assembler hooks the finished harness to a test board or adapter set and runs continuity, resistance (including 4-wire), shorts/miswire and dielectric/insulation-resistance checks, then records pass/fail and readings on the traveler or in the shop system.

End-of-line functional/power-on test of a completed electronic unit (PCB assembly, controller, display board, power supply) at a bench test station in the plant: place unit in test fixture, mate test connectors, run the automated test sequence, verify operation, record results and route pass/fail.

In-process inspection and electrical checks of printed circuit assemblies at a workstation: visually check solder joints, component presence/orientation and workmanship, probe suspect nets with a DMM for shorts/opens and component values, log defects into the quality record.

Electrical test of larger assembled electromechanical equipment (motors, coils/windings, transformers, battery modules, control cabinets/panels): megger insulation-resistance, winding/contact resistance, hi-pot and a functional run, with numeric readings written to a test report.

Diagnostic/rework testing of a unit that failed test or of a one-off, non-standard or partially built assembly: read the schematic, open the enclosure, probe arbitrary points and terminal blocks with a multimeter or scope, isolate the fault, and write up findings.

Assembling support structures and casings: bolting or riveting sheet-metal frames, brackets, DIN rails, mounting plates and enclosure panels; setting rivets/clinch joints in housings and closing up the unit.

Low-volume, high-mix or one-off builds and modifications: prototype telemetry/test equipment, defense or medical units built from a traveler and drawing package, engineering-change rework and unit modification, with configurations that change unit to unit.

Prototype or low-volume run: fabricating a novel one-off part or structural member from a spec drawing or CAD file — laying out, sawing, drilling, tapping, filing and bending a bracket, standoff plate or coil form — then inspecting it against the drawing before it goes to assembly.

Rework/engineering-change work on an already-populated unit: drilling or enlarging a hole in an assembled chassis, trimming or notching a bracket, shortening a screw or standoff by hand tools so a part fits, working around installed wiring and boards and fit-checking as they go.

Cable and wire-harness work: positioning wires, terminals and connector housings — laying and routing wires on a harness board around pegs, inserting crimped terminals into connector cavities, dressing and clamping bundles so the ends can be terminated. Deformable wires, many branches, board-specific layout.

Low-volume, prototype, custom or rework build at a shared bench: the unit differs from the last one, the assembler works from drawings, re-seats or shims a part that does not fit, corrects a misalignment found at test, and adjusts fit by judgment before wiring.

instances.label: Component-level PCB rework at a bench in an electronics plant: a board flagged by ICT/AOI arrives with a defective SMT chip, QFP or BGA; the assembler removes the part with hot air, cleans residual solder from the pads, applies flux/paste, places and reflows a replacement, and verifies the site.

Solder-defect touch-up: boards flagged by inspection for bridges, cold, insufficient or open joints; the assembler reflows or adds solder at the named joint, wicks away a bridge, and re-inspects the corrected joint.

In-chassis wiring/harness rework: locating a mis-crimped, broken or mis-routed lead in a wire harness inside a motor, cabinet or telemetry chassis; extracting the terminal from its housing, re-stripping and re-crimping or replacing the lead, re-routing and re-lacing it, then continuity-testing.

Simple plug-in interconnect fix on a fixtured board or module: a connector, ribbon/FPC or plug-in cable that failed test because it was unseated or damaged is re-mated or swapped for a good one and re-tested.

Replacing a defective module/subassembly in a larger unit: unfastening screws or bolts, unplugging power/signal leads, swapping a failed power supply, board, motor, or battery block, reconnecting and re-running the functional test.

Adjusting a unit into specification: turning trim pots, tuning screws or alignment adjustments (or trimming a resistive element) while watching a meter, VNA or test set until the measured parameter meets the spec window, then locking and recording the result.

instances.label: Bench functional test of an assembled PCB or electronic subassembly at a test station in an EMS/OEM plant: assembler connects the unit to a bench supply and DMM/scope, applies specified input voltages, probes supply rails and output test points, turns a trim pot or writes a calibration value until the output is within spec, logs the result and passes or rejects the unit. Mixed-model work, boards arriving in ESD trays.

In-line or fixtured production test: assembler loads the board into an ICT/functional test fixture (bed-of-nails or flying-probe station), starts the program that sources and measures voltages against limits, unloads pass units, and re-runs or touches up flagged units. High volume, single product family per station.

Final alignment/calibration of a finished instrument or piece of test equipment in a QC or calibration area: connect the unit to a reference calibrator/standard, step through specified voltage points, adjust zero/span or trim (pot, screw, or digital trim) until readings meet tolerance, and produce the calibration record.

Voltage checks and adjustments on large or awkward assemblies — control/motor-drive panels, telemetry racks, power supplies, battery packs/modules: probe terminal blocks, connector pins or cell taps inside a cabinet or on a pack, measure rail and cell voltages, adjust setpoints or trim to specification, in cramped access among harnesses and heat sinks.

Verification and adjustment at an installed or staged system — customer site, integration bay, or a shipped unit set up outside a standard test station: assembler brings a meter to the equipment as found, measures voltages at accessible points and adjusts to specified values before sign-off.

tasks.label: Inspect, test, and adjust completed units to ensure that units meet specifications, tolerances, and customer order requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume end-of-line functional test of a completed electromechanical unit (small motor, actuator, gearbox/transfer case, pump, appliance subassembly) at a dedicated test station on the production line: the assembler places the unit in the test stand, makes mechanical and electrical connections, runs a scripted performance/insulation/NVH/leak sequence, records pass/fail, and routes failures.

Visual and dimensional inspection of a completed unit against the drawing: check for missing, reversed, or misaligned parts, damaged wiring or connectors, workmanship defects; gauge critical dimensions, gaps, clearances, and shaft runout with calipers, go/no-go gauges, or a scanner, in a plant inspection area.

Test-and-adjust to bring a unit inside tolerance: iteratively turn a trim screw, potentiometer, eccentric, or set screw, or add shims, while watching an instrument reading (voltage, RF response, torque, backlash, travel, timing) until the reading falls in spec, then lock the adjustment with thread locker or torque.

Final verification that the built unit matches the customer order/work order: correct model, options and accessories, correct nameplate, serial number and labels, correct connector/cable variants, then sign-off of the test record and traveler before packing, at a bench or final-audit station.

Low-volume, high-mix or custom units (aerospace actuators, gyros, servo drives, custom control assemblies): running a written customer acceptance test procedure at a bench with general-purpose instruments, judging marginal readings, and diagnosing and reworking units that fail — trace the fault, reseat/resolder/realign, retest.

tasks.label: Position, align, and adjust parts for proper fit and assembly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench assembly of small electromechanical subassemblies (servo motor, actuator, gyro, gear head): operator takes parts from kitted trays/bins, seats bearings on shafts, drops the rotor into the housing, meshes gears, aligns end caps and shims to spec, and checks that it turns freely before fastening. Factory bench, mixed models, sub-millimetre fits.

Line-station loading of a single part type: operator takes a part from a rack or bin and positions/aligns it into a nest, fixture, or mating chassis location at a fixed tolerance and takt (a few seconds to under a minute), so the next operation (weld, fasten, press) can proceed. Repetitive, one part family per station.

Multi-part build-up on a chassis or frame at a line station: positioning brackets, motors, gearboxes, covers and control linkages, aligning mounting holes and dowel features, nudging parts for clearance, then starting and running fasteners. Several different parts per cycle, mixed models on the same line.

Precision alignment and adjustment to tolerance: setting air gaps and end play, shimming, aligning encoders/optics/read heads or brake and linkage travel, measuring with gauges or test feedback, then re-adjusting until the reading is in spec and locking the setting.

Positioning and mating flexible/deformable parts: plugging connectors and flying leads into headers, dressing short cable runs, seating gaskets, O-rings and seals into grooves so the joint closes properly.

Positioning and aligning large or heavy components (stators into housings, motors/gearboxes into frames, battery or drive modules), typically with a hoist, balancer or lift assist, guiding the part onto dowels/pilots and aligning it before bolting.

tasks.label: Assemble parts or units, and position, align, and fasten units to assemblies, subassemblies, or frames, using hand tools and power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume repetitive station work on a motor/actuator/appliance line: the assembler takes housings and components from bins or kits at a fixed workstation, seats bearings, gears, armatures or covers on a base, aligns them, and drives screws to torque with a pistol-grip or in-line power driver at a fixed takt; hundreds of identical units per shift.

Mid-volume bench assembly of subassemblies (servo/actuator units, brakes, control linkages, small drives, control panels): kitted parts and work instructions, press-fits and shaft/bearing alignment, several fastener sizes, some connector mating and lead dressing, changeovers between models every few days.

Frame- or cabinet-level integration: heavy units (motors, gearboxes, drives, panels) are lifted with a hoist or by hand onto a frame, chassis or enclosure, aligned/shimmed to spec, and bolted with power tools and torque tools; sometimes two workers coordinate.

High-mix, low-volume or prototype precision assembly (gyros, dynamometers, custom actuators, instrument packages): unique or few-off parts built from drawings, tight tolerances and delicate components, custom fixtures, cable routing and connector attachment interleaved with fastening.

Rework, modification and final integration after test: partially disassemble a unit that failed test or needs an engineering change, realign or replace a part, re-fasten to spec, occasionally re-route or reconnect wiring, then return it to the line.

tasks.label: Connect cables, tubes, and wiring, according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At a production bench or line station, mate pre-terminated cable/harness connectors to their receptacles on a subassembly (motor, drive, PCB header, actuator) per the wiring diagram: pick the free-hanging connector, orient it, seat it until the latch clicks, tug-test.

Route and dress a multi-branch harness through a partially assembled chassis or enclosure: pull the bundle through grommets and openings, follow the specified path, snap clips into holes, add tie-wraps/tape, then land the branch ends on their devices.

Terminate individual conductors in a control panel / DIN-rail or terminal-block assembly of an electromechanical unit: take prepared (stripped/ferruled) wires, insert into the specified terminal, tighten screw or actuate push-in clamp, label and verify against the schematic.

Connect fluid/air lines on an appliance, actuator or hydraulic/pneumatic assembly: push tubing onto barbs or into push-to-connect fittings, thread and torque hose fittings, seat quick-connects, and check seating/leak-tightness.

Attach individual leads by soldering or crimping: tin and solder motor/coil leads to terminals, tabs or PCB pads, or crimp lugs/spades and attach them to studs per specification, with joint quality inspected.

tasks.label: Measure parts to determine tolerances, using precision measuring instruments such as micrometers, calipers, and verniers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process check at the assembly bench on a factory floor: assembler picks small machined/molded piece parts (shafts, pins, bushings, terminals, small housings) out of a tote or kit tray and verifies one to three drawing dimensions with a digital caliper or micrometer, judging pass/fail and noting the reading.

First-article or incoming-lot sampling inspection at a QC bench/inspection area: all or most drawing dimensions on a sample of parts are measured with micrometers, calipers, bore and depth gauges, and the readings are logged into an inspection report for the lot.

Dimensional check on a subassembly under build (motor/gearbox/actuator stack): stack height, shaft protrusion, bearing seat depth, axial end play measured with depth micrometer, height gauge or indicator while the unit sits in an assembly fixture on the bench.

In-situ clearance/gap check inside a partly assembled unit: feeler gauges or a dial indicator slipped into narrow gaps (brake shoe clearance, rotor-stator air gap, linkage backlash) on the assembly as built, requiring feel, access around wiring and adjacent parts, and a judgment call.

Measurement of larger or awkward items on the floor or bench: motor frames, gearbox housings, mounting plates, weldment brackets, actuator rod extension — checked with vernier calipers, large micrometers, depth and height gauges against print tolerances.

Measurement of compliant or odd small items: magnet wire and insulation diameter, gasket/O-ring cross-section, shim and spring free length, small stamped washers — measured with micrometers, optical comparators or laser micrometers, where gauge force and seating matter.

tasks.label: Attach name plates and mark identifying information on parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench work in an electromechanical assembly plant: applying pressure-sensitive nameplate/rating labels, serial-number and barcode decals, and UL/CE marks to housings of small-to-medium assembled units (actuators, gearmotors, drives, controllers). Label position specified by drawing; surfaces flat or gently curved metal/plastic; must be square, bubble-free, and legible.

Mechanically attaching rigid metal or plastic nameplates to housings and covers of motors, gyros, brakes, control panels: aligning the plate to pre-drilled or self-piercing locations and setting drive screws, pop rivets, or machine screws to spec without marring the finish.

Direct part marking of identifying information in the plant: loading a part or a blank tag into a dot-peen, laser, scribe or stamping marker, cycling it to apply serial/lot/date codes or data-matrix codes, and verifying legibility before the part moves on.

Routine in-process identification of subassemblies and wiring during build: printing and fitting wire markers/heat-shrink sleeves, cable and connector tags, and writing or applying the job/serial number on a subassembly per the traveler.

Ad-hoc judgment marks made during build, test or rework: match/orientation marks on mating parts, circling a discrepancy for inspection, noting a measured value or 'rework' on whatever surface is available at the point of the observation.

Labeling large or awkward finished equipment standing on the shop floor or in a rack (large dynamometers, tape-drive cabinets, enclosures): walking around the unit to apply several plates and labels at different heights and orientations, plus applying identification labels to the shipping crate/carton.

tasks.label: Disassemble units to replace parts or to crate them for shipping.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production rework at a bench on the assembly floor: a current-model electromechanical unit (servo actuator, drive assembly, small appliance) fails end-of-line test with a flagged defective module. The assembler removes housing screws/cover, unplugs a connector or two, pulls the bad motor/PCB/sensor, installs a good one from stock, refastens to torque, and sends it back to test. Repeatable, same model, defined part.

Teardown of high-mix, older-model, or field-returned units: unfamiliar internal layout, thread-locked, painted-over, corroded or stripped fasteners, adhesives, cable ties, potting, tape and shims. Worker works from exploded drawings, decides how far to strip, salvages reusable parts, bags and tags hardware, and reassembles with new parts.

Deeper mechanical rework: pressing out and replacing an internal bearing, gear, seal, brake pad or shaft, re-shimming and re-aligning linkages, re-lubricating, re-torquing and re-adjusting the unit until it meets spec. Requires feel, alignment judgment, press/puller tools.

Partial disassembly of a large assembled machine (dynamometer, drive train, control cabinet, tape-drive rack) so it will fit and survive shipment: drain/disconnect plumbing, label and disconnect wiring harnesses, unbolt subassemblies, rig them with a hoist or overhead crane, set them on skids and pallets, protect surfaces.

Packing and crating small-to-medium units and their removed parts: place unit into a foam-lined carton or crate, add inserts/dunnage and desiccant, bag and label removed hardware, close and seal or strap the container, apply shipping labels, stage for the pallet.

tasks.label: File, lap, and buff parts to fit, using hand and power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench deburring/edge-breaking of machined, cast or stamped metal parts (housings, brackets, actuator bodies) before assembly: worker uses hand files, needle files, small die grinder or belt sander to remove burrs, flash and sharp edges so parts seat and mate properly. Parts arrive in totes at a factory workstation; part types change through the shift.

Buffing/polishing part surfaces with a pedestal buffer, wheel or abrasive pad: removing tool marks, oxidation, scratches or plating defects on covers, housings, shafts and contact surfaces so mating faces slide/seal and cosmetic specs are met. Done at a bench or stand-mounted buffing wheel on the assembly floor.

File-and-try fitting of a loose component that is slightly oversized or misaligned: shaft to bore, key to keyway, pin to bushing, bracket to slot. Worker files/grinds a small amount, checks with the mating part or a gauge/micrometer, and repeats until the specified clearance or slip fit is achieved, then deburrs the reworked area.

Lapping mating or sealing surfaces to flatness and finish spec: valve/seal faces, brake plates, precision flats, or a bore lapped to size, using a lap plate or lapping tool with compound, checking with gauge or bluing until the required contact pattern/size is reached. Done at a dedicated bench or lapping station in the plant.

In-situ fitting on a partially assembled unit at the bench: a linkage, cover or interfering boss inside a servo, actuator or drive assembly binds; the worker files/stones/buffs the offending area in place inside the assembly, in a confined space, with hand tools, cleaning chips out afterwards and re-testing motion.

Field or customer-site fitting during installation or repair of installed equipment: worker files, grinds or buffs a bracket, shaft or contact surface to make it fit an existing machine, working in an unstructured location with portable hand and power tools.

tasks.label: Clean and lubricate parts and subassemblies, using grease paddles or oilcans.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production-line bench work: applying a measured film or bead of grease to bearings, gear teeth, cams and shafts of small motor, gearbox or actuator subassemblies with a paddle, brush or grease gun, dozens to hundreds of units per shift, to a written lubrication spec.

Oiling with an oilcan: placing drops of light oil on pivots, bushings, shafts and control-linkage joints of a partially assembled mechanism (brake, actuator, tape drive) at specified points, some recessed or inside bores, then wiping runoff.

Pre-lubricating seals before installation: coating O-rings, gaskets and seal bores with a thin film of grease or oil so they seat without twisting, at a seal-installation station on the assembly floor.

Cleaning parts and subassemblies before or between assembly steps: removing machining chips, swarf, coolant, oil residue, dust and fingerprints from housings, plates and mechanisms by solvent wipe, brush, compressed-air blow-off or parts washer at a factory cleaning station.

Large or awkward work: cleaning and greasing a bulky or already-built-up subassembly standing on a work stand or fixture bench (large gear racks, slides, housings, machine bases), reaching into the assembly to lubricate several points and wiping away excess grease.

tasks.label: Operate or tend automated assembling equipment, such as robotics and fixed automation equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume line in an electromechanical products plant: the assembler cyclically feeds components/subassemblies (housings, motors, gears, PCBs, brackets) from line-side totes into the nests of an automated assembly machine or robotic cell, presses cycle start, removes completed units and places them in trays/totes.

Tending the equipment while it runs: standing/walking the station, watching cycles and the HMI, checking indicator lights and counters, listening for abnormal sounds, noting heat/vibration or drifting behavior, logging output, and calling a stop or escalating when something looks wrong.

In-process quality verification of the automated equipment's output: pulling sample assemblies, checking critical dimensions or torque with gauges, doing a visual/functional check on a test fixture, segregating rejects, and signaling for a correction when readings drift.

Fault response: a part jams or misfeeds in an escapement, feeder track, or nest; the operator opens the guard, extracts the stuck or deformed part by hand or with pliers, checks the tooling for damage, clears the alarm, re-homes and restarts the equipment, escalating to maintenance if it recurs.

Changeover/setup for a new product or at shift start: swapping fixtures, nests, grippers or feeder tooling, calling up the correct program/recipe, loading the first parts, running and checking a first article, then releasing the machine to production.

Replenishment and housekeeping on the automated equipment: refilling screw hoppers, component feeders/reels or bowl feeders, topping up adhesive or lubricant, emptying scrap and waste-tape bins, and wiping down the cell between runs.

tasks.label: Operate small cranes to transport or position large parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: At an assembly station on the shop floor, the assembler uses a jib crane or chain hoist with a hook/sling to lift a heavy component (motor housing, base casting, gear case, transformer core, 100-800 lb) off a pallet, cart or shipping crate and set it on the workbench or build fixture, then unhooks it.

Precision mating with the hoist supporting the load: lowering a large part into or onto an assembly to tight alignment (stator into frame, gearbox onto motor face, rotor into bore, drive assembly onto base plate), inching the hoist while guiding the part by hand to line up pilots and bolt holes before releasing the load.

Using an overhead bridge crane (pendant or radio control) to move a large part or completed subassembly across the bay - from receiving/staging to the build area, or from the build area to test or shipping - traveling over aisles and equipment with people working nearby, controlling sway and setting the load down on a stand or pallet.

Rigging an awkward, irregular or unbalanced part before the lift: selecting slings, shackles, spreader bars or eyebolts, attaching to lift points, judging the center of gravity, test-lifting and adjusting, and using a tag line or hand guidance to keep the load from swinging or being damaged.

Using the crane/balancer as a third hand during assembly work: holding or suspending a heavy cover, frame or subassembly in position while it is aligned and bolted, or rotating/tilting a large assembly with the hoist to gain access to another face, then re-setting it.

tasks.label: Pack or fold insulation between panels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume appliance/consumer-product assembly line (dishwasher, range, HVAC unit): worker takes a preformed sound-deadening or thermal insulation pad from a stack, folds/bends it to the housing geometry and seats it between the outer cabinet panel and the inner shell before panels are closed. Standard model, fixed station, takt-timed.

Moderate-volume line or bench subassembly: worker packs a compressible fibrous blanket (fiberglass, mineral wool, ceramic fiber) into the cavity between an inner liner/shell and the outer sheet-metal panel of a standard unit (oven cavity, water heater, heater module), pressing and tucking it so it fills the gap without bunching, then fits the panel.

Low-volume or custom electromechanical cabinets and control enclosures: worker measures, cuts, folds and packs acoustic/thermal sheet insulation between panels, routing it around wiring harnesses, brackets, fans and components; geometry differs order to order and must be hand-fitted.

Large equipment build (generator enclosure, air handler, industrial oven casing, large actuator housing): worker packs heavy batts or boards into deep panel cavities, securing over pins/clips and around penetrations, often reaching or climbing into the partly built unit.

Rework, prototype or modification work: worker reopens a built or partly built unit, removes damaged/misfitted insulation and refits or folds new insulation between panels around already-installed wiring and hardware.

instances.label: High-volume powertrain plant: completed engine (or electric motor/e-drive) reaches end of line, is docked to a cold- or hot-test bench, spun/run through a test cycle while torque, pressures, vacuum, leak and NVH parameters are compared to limits; pass/fail and data record produced.

Final inspection station on the shop floor: worker checks a completed engine/machine for assembly completeness (fittings, plugs, brackets, torque marks), verifies key dimensions/clearances with gauges, checks fluid levels and surface damage, and signs the unit off against the build sheet or customer spec.

Test bay for mid-volume industrial machines (pump, hydraulic motor/pump unit, compressor, electric motor/generator, gearbox): unit is mounted on a test stand, connected to fluid/electrical services, run through speed and load points, performance curves and leak/insulation checks recorded and compared to customer specification.

Large or custom machine (big diesel genset, turbine package, paper/textile machine section, construction equipment, rebuilt engine) run-in on the floor or in a run-off bay: operate controls through all modes, watch and listen for leaks, vibration and abnormal noise, diagnose faults, adjust or rework, retest and document.

Testing/checkout away from a standard line: commissioning or functional checkout of the delivered machine at the customer's site or in a repair/service shop with variable layout, where the unit is tested in place under whatever conditions exist.

tasks.label: Set and verify parts clearances.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mass-production engine assembly line (auto/light-truck/diesel engine plant): at a line station the assembler reads or measures crank journal and block bore size grades with bore gauges/micrometers, selects graded main and rod bearing shells, installs them, and verifies the resulting oil clearance (Plastigage or gauge) before caps are torqued.

Valve-train clearance work on a built cylinder head or engine in a plant: measure cam-to-bucket/rocker-to-valve lash with feeler gauges or a gauge head, select and install the correct shim or tappet thickness (or turn and lock adjuster screws), then re-verify every valve to print.

Sub-assembly bench or short line for gearboxes, pumps, compressors and axles in a machine plant: measure stack heights and gaps with dial indicators/depth gauges, set tapered-bearing preload, shaft endplay, gear backlash or impeller-to-housing clearance with selected shim packs/spacers, and verify by re-measuring or rolling torque.

High-volume remanufacturing line for a known engine family (Reman/ReCon type): salvaged or restored standard-size components arrive in fixtures; assembler gauges bores and journals, select-fits bearings/shims to restore specified clearances, and verifies them before build-up.

Custom rebuild/overhaul in a jobbing shop: worn machine of mixed provenance and prior repairs; assembler measures wear, decides on oversize/undersize or re-machined parts, hand-fits or scrapes and shims to bring clearances into spec, verifying with feeler gauges, micrometers and dial indicators.

Large machine final assembly bay or field erection: setting and verifying turbine rotor-to-diaphragm/seal clearances, large compressor or gearbox axial and radial clearances, or paper-machine roll/doctor settings, using feeler and taper gauges, dial indicators and custom-ground shims while reaching into and around a multi-ton assembly.

tasks.label: Verify conformance of parts to stock lists or blueprints, using measuring instruments such as calipers, gauges, or micrometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production plant, line-side or receiving bench: assembler checks batches of machined components (housings, shafts, gears, covers, fasteners) against the blueprint/spec sheet with calipers, micrometers, plug/thread gauges before they go into the engine or pump build; known part numbers, tolerances roughly 0.01-0.05 mm, accept/reject and tag nonconforming parts.

In-process verification while building the engine/machine on the assembly stand or line: measuring bores and journals with bore gauges and micrometers, checking bearing clearances with feeler gauge/plastigage, checking shim and preload stack-ups, selecting matched or graded components, and recording results on the build sheet.

Kit/stock-list verification: confirming that a staged kit or pallet contains the parts called out on the stock list or BOM (correct part numbers, counts, sizes, left/right variants) with spot dimensional checks by caliper; mixed small parts in trays and bins at a staging bench.

Large machine work (turbine casings, paper-machine rolls, large gearboxes, engine bedplates) in a fabrication bay: verifying large castings, weldments, shafts and mating faces against blueprints with large micrometers, depth gauges, dial indicators, bore mics and straightedges, often measuring the component where it sits on stands.

Rebuild/repair shop: measuring worn or reconditioned parts (cylinder bores, crank journals, wear surfaces, bushings) against service limits and old blueprints; dirty, oily, one-off or legacy parts, judging taper, out-of-round, scoring and deciding reuse/rework/scrap.

Field/customer-site assembly or rebuild (mill, mine, plant floor of a customer, construction site): verifying part dimensions, shim thicknesses and clearances with handheld instruments in cramped, dirty, variable conditions against drawings brought to site.

tasks.label: Fasten or install piping, fixtures, or wiring and electrical components to form assemblies or subassemblies, using hand tools, rivet guns, or welding equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Engine/machine wiring: assembler lays the wiring harness over an engine or machine frame on a line pallet or assembly stand, routes branches around castings, snaps clips into brackets, plugs connectors into sensors, injectors, alternator and ECU, tie-wraps runs and torques ground lugs. Plant floor of an engine/machine assembly facility.

Bolt-on fixtures and accessories: mounting brackets, pump, alternator, turbocharger, covers and manifolds are placed on the engine/machine and fastened with hand torque tools or nutrunners to specified torque and sequence, with fastener verification. Indoor assembly line or bay in the plant.

Rigid fluid piping: fuel, oil, air or hydraulic tubes and pipe nipples are offered up to ports on the engine/machine, threaded fittings (flare nuts, banjo bolts, O-ring boss fittings) started without cross-threading, torqued, clamped to standoffs, and the circuit leak-checked. Plant assembly station.

Flexible hose installation: coolant, air and fuel hoses pushed onto barbed or beaded ports, routed around the machine structure avoiding hot or moving parts, and secured with worm or spring clamps and P-clips. Plant assembly station.

Permanent fastening of brackets, guards and panels: blind-riveting nameplates, sheet-metal shrouds, guards and covers onto a subassembly with a rivet gun, and MIG/TIG tacking or welding small brackets, tabs and mounts onto subassembly frames in the plant's weld area.

Machine control box / panel wiring: with contactors, relays and terminal blocks already fixed to the mounting plate, the assembler cuts wires to length, crimps ferrules, lands each conductor on the correct terminal to a torque spec, dresses the runs into wire ducts and labels them. Panel-build area of the plant.

tasks.label: Remove rough spots and smooth surfaces to fit, trim, or clean parts, using hand tools or power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench deburring of machined components before assembly in an engine/machine plant: breaking sharp edges and removing burrs from bores, bolt holes, ports and mating edges of housings, covers, gears and shafts using a hand file, deburring blade or air die grinder; several part numbers per shift, parts arriving in totes on carts, checked by eye and feel.

Removing casting flash, gate/riser stubs, weld spatter and rough spots from larger cast or fabricated pieces (engine blocks, pump/gearbox housings, frames, brackets) with a pneumatic disc grinder or belt sander at a grinding bench or booth in the shop.

Dressing or blending a specific surface to a stated dimension or finish: flattening/cleaning a sealing or mating face, blending a weld or a high area found at inspection, polishing a journal or port, verified with a straightedge, gauge or surface-finish comparator.

In-process fitting during assembly: trial-fit a part into the machine, find interference or high spots by feel, blueing or gauging, remove metal with a file, scraper or die grinder, reinstall and re-check, repeating until the part seats, aligns or turns freely.

Rebuild work: cleaning and smoothing surfaces of used parts on a teardown unit in the rebuild bay — scraping off old gasket material, carbon, corrosion and paint from flanges and housings with scrapers, wire wheels and abrasive pads before reassembly.

Field/on-site work at a customer plant or job site: a machine being rebuilt in place (e.g., paper-mill drive, crusher, large engine), where the assembler dresses or cleans a mating surface or removes rough spots with a portable grinder in cramped, as-found conditions.

tasks.label: Lay out and drill, ream, tap, or cut parts for assembly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production plant assembly station: assembler drills and taps holes in small-to-medium metal parts (brackets, covers, housings, mounting plates) during subassembly, using a drill press or hand/air tools at a bench, working from a drawing dimension or a hole template; standard fastener-hole tolerances and clean threads required.

Plant floor, large workpiece: assembler lays out hole positions on a heavy fabricated frame, base or housing with rule, square, scribe and center punch, then drills and taps with a magnetic-base or radial drill; part weighs hundreds of kilograms to tonnes and sits on stands or a floor plate.

Precision fitting during assembly: match-drilling and line/hand reaming of dowel-pin or fitted-bolt holes through two mated components already bolted together (gearbox housing to case, bearing cap, coupling flange) so the parts align; close diameter and location tolerance, hand-fit check.

Cutting and trimming parts to fit during assembly: cutting shim stock, gasket material, tubing, hose, conduit, spacers and bar stock to length or shape, then deburring the cut edges before installation.

Rebuild and field repair: on a used engine or machine in a repair shop or at a customer site, drilling out broken or seized studs, re-tapping stripped threads, drilling for thread inserts, and cutting away damaged parts; damage position and condition vary and are found as they come.

sources.system: Pioneer Industrial Systems robotic deflash/drill/tap cell (FANUC M-10iA)

sources.claim: A deployed FANUC M-10iA robotic cell performs the secondary machining of molded parts — deflashing plus drilling, milling and tapping of holes — inside an enclosed, light-curtained cell with a locating fixture; four such cells have been installed and each part cycle runs automatically after the operator loads it.
sources.transferJustification: The task's drilling and tapping of assembly parts is performed directly by this cell; the difference is that the parts are glass-filled molded composite rather than metal, but hole location, drilling and thread cutting are the same operations at the same class of tolerance.

tasks.label: Rework, repair, or replace damaged parts or assemblies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-line rework at an engine/machine assembly station: during build, a part is found damaged or wrongly installed (nicked sealing face, crushed O-ring, broken clip, cross-threaded bolt, scored bore). The assembler backs out fasteners, extracts the bad part, retrieves a good one, installs, re-torques to spec, and re-verifies. Mixed-model line, oily/greasy partial assemblies, damage varies case to case.

Off-line rework bay: a completed unit fails hot test, leak test, or functional test. The worker diagnoses the fault, partially disassembles the unit on a stand (harnesses, brackets, covers), replaces the failed component (injector, seal, gasket, sensor, turbo, pump), reassembles, and re-tests until it passes.

Rebuild/remanufacture of a returned or damaged assembly (diesel engine, pump, compressor, gearbox): full teardown of a dirty, corroded, sometimes seized unit; clean and inspect; salvage or replace worn/damaged internals such as bearings, bushings, seals, rings; reassemble to print with clearance checks.

Component-level repair instead of replacement: restoring a damaged or worn metal part to spec — blending out a nick or burr, grinding/dressing a damaged surface, weld or cladding build-up on a worn edge, then re-finishing to dimension and re-inspecting. Part can be taken to a bench/machine.

Large-assembly repair on the shop floor: a heavy sub-assembly of a partially built machine (turbine casing part, large gear/shaft, big housing) is damaged and must be removed and replaced using overhead crane, slings and heavy fixtures, with alignment, shimming, and often a second worker assisting.

sources.system: Acme Turnkey Aerospace Blade Repair System with Optomec CS-250 LENS laser cladding machine
sources.title: Optomec and Acme Manufacturing Showcase the Industry's First Fully Automated Work Cell for the Additive Repair of Turbine Parts
sources.claim: Optomec and Acme Manufacturing market a fully automated work cell that repairs worn/damaged titanium compressor blades: robotic blade-tip grinding, laser DED cladding and post-clad finishing, with automated pallet load/unload and tool paths generated automatically to accommodate part-to-part wear and distortion.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: MRO repair of damaged/worn engine airfoils. It transfers to an assembler's component-level rework because the objects are the same class of metal engine parts, the operation is the same (remove damage, build material back, re-finish to dimension), and it is performed on fixtured parts brought to the machine.

tasks.label: Assemble systems of gears by aligning and meshing gears in gearboxes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume powertrain gearbox/transmission line station in an engine or e-axle plant: kitted gears, shafts and carriers arrive on pallets at takt time; the assembler presses gears onto shafts, times/indexes the gear set, seats a planet carrier or shaft stack into the housing so the teeth mesh, and confirms free rotation before the unit indexes on.

Serial/batch production of small-to-medium standard gearboxes and gear reducers (industrial reducers, pump and transaxle drives, small marine/utility gearcases) built from a handful of recurring catalog models: install bearings, press gears onto shafts, drop shaft sets into a housing, mesh the gears, add shims to set preload/backlash to the build sheet, close and spin-test the box.

Large heavy gearbox assembly (wind turbine, mining, marine, paper-machine or turbine drives): housings, ring gears and shafts weighing hundreds of kilograms to several tons are set with an overhead crane or manipulator, guided by hand into mesh, checked with bluing contact patterns and dial-indicator backlash, and shimmed and re-checked iteratively.

Low-volume, prototype or custom gear-train build from blueprints (specialty machinery, textile/paper equipment, turbine accessory drives): unfamiliar part geometry, selective fitting, deburring or light rework of a part that won't seat, measuring backlash and center distances with indicators, and adjusting until the mesh meets print.

Rebuild/remanufacture of a used gearbox in a shop: tear down, clean and inspect worn gears and bearings, decide which parts to reuse, then reassemble a mix of new and used components and re-establish mesh and backlash.

On-site assembly or re-assembly of a gear drive at a customer facility or installation site: gearbox mounted on installed equipment, restricted access, alignment of gear coupling/pinion to the driven gear performed in place with portable tools.

sources.system: Force-controlled assembly robots (Ford AMTD with Fanuc Robotics, Kawasaki Robotics)
sources.developer: Ford Motor Co. / Fanuc Robotics North America

sources.claim: Ford's Advanced Manufacturing Technology Development Center, with Fanuc and Kawasaki, developed force-controlled robotic assembly for powertrain parts specifically because tasks such as clutch gear alignment and spline/gear meshing exceed positional-control robots; the work produced commercially available force-controlled assembly robots.

tasks.label: Set up and operate metalworking machines, such as milling or grinding machines, to shape or fabricate parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the plant's in-house machine shop, the assembler sets up a CNC mill or lathe for a batch of assembly parts (brackets, spacers, shafts): loads the program, installs vise/fixture and cutting tools, sets tool and work offsets, runs the cycle, deburrs and gauges parts with calipers/micrometers.

Grinding/finishing to fit during engine or machine build: surface grinder, pedestal or belt grinder used to remove stock, dress a mating surface, blend a weld, or bring a component to fit; iterative removal with measurement/fit checks against the assembly.

One-off or rework part made on a manual Bridgeport-type mill or engine lathe from a sketch, a worn original, or a mating part: the assembler measures the mating component, decides dimensions, dials in the work with an indicator, and cuts to a press or slip fit.

Repeat production run of a proven job on a semi-automated CNC in the shop: load raw stock, cycle start, unload, gauge to the traveler, deburr, and repeat for the required quantity with periodic offset tweaks for tool wear.

Field or customer-site machining while rebuilding installed equipment: portable milling, line boring a worn bore, or in-situ grinding of a flange or bedplate on a machine that cannot be moved, in a plant or outdoor setting taken as found.
Large casting or housing set up on a horizontal boring mill or large grinder: crane lift onto the table, block and clamp, indicate the part true, then bore/mill/grind bearing bores or mounting faces.

It is the 'operate the metalworking machine' half of this task - workpiece loading into the chuck/vise, cycle start, unload and post-process gauging - on the same milling and turning machines the assembler would run, with parts presented on a grid loading table.

sources.system: Hexagon AEON humanoid

tasks.label: Maintain and lubricate parts or components.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Engine build line or bench in an engine/powertrain plant or rebuild shop: assembler coats internal engine parts with assembly lube or oil as they go in - main and rod bearing shells, cam journals, piston rings and skirts, cylinder walls, valve stems, seals - using oil cans, brushes, swabs or grease from a tub, judging film thickness by eye and feel before the mating part is set.

Sub-assembly station: greasing or oiling smaller components before press-fit or joining - O-rings and lip seals, splines, bushings, gear teeth, thrust washers, pump internals - a metered dab or bead at several specified points, some hard to reach, with over- or under-application causing scrap downstream.

Large machine assembly bay (turbine, industrial pump, paper/textile machine, construction equipment): greasing bearing housings and zerk fittings with a grease gun, packing bearings, and filling gearcase/hydraulic oil reservoirs on a partly built machine standing on the shop floor or in a stand before test run and shipment.

Routine upkeep of the assembler's own tools, fixtures and station equipment inside the shop: oiling air tools, greasing press slides, fixture ways and conveyor bearings, wiping down and cleaning tooling, checking and topping lubricant reservoirs on a scheduled PM round.

Field or customer-site work: an assembler/field technician lubricates and services a machine after installation or rebuild at a mill, plant or construction site - locating fittings on equipment as found, clearing dirt, greasing, topping fluids, wiping and checking for leaks in cramped or dirty access conditions.

roles.title: Structural Metal Fabricators and Fitters
aliases: Structural and Ornamental Metalwork Metal Fabricator
Structural and Ornamental Metalwork Steel Fabricator
roles.description: Fabricate, position, align, and fit parts of structural metal products.

tasks.label: Verify conformance of workpieces to specifications, using squares, rulers, and measuring tapes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process fit-up check at a shop fitting bench or layout table: fitter sets a clip angle, stiffener, gusset or base plate on a beam/column, checks 90 degrees with a framing square and the location dimension with a tape/rule against the shop drawing before tacking; typical tolerance ~1/16 in.

Final dimensional inspection of a completed weldment/assembly (stair stringer, handrail, column with base plate, small frame) sitting on the shop floor or a table: overall length, diagonals for square, hole spacing and edge distances, plate squareness, checked against the shop drawing before shipping.

Checking cut and processed parts against the cut list at the saw/plasma/drill-line staging area: verifying member length, profile size, hole positions, bevels and miter angles on incoming pieces before they go to assembly.

Large fabricated assemblies (plate girders, trusses, long beams) in a shop bay: long-span tape pulls for overall length and diagonals, sweep/camber and web flatness checks, often two workers with the piece on horses or a fit-up line.

Field/erection-site verification: measuring existing conditions (openings, anchor bolt layouts, gaps between erected members) and checking fit-up of members in place, outdoors, sometimes at height or on a lift.
