tasks.label: Trim cured materials by sawing them with diamond-impregnated cutoff wheels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Boat/marine plant: after a hull, deck or liner is pulled from the mold, trim the excess cured laminate/flash back to the scribed sheer or flange line with a handheld pneumatic cutoff wheel (diamond blade), part sitting on a trim fixture or cart, heavy dust, 15-30 ft part, then dress the edge.

High-volume small/medium molded FRP parts (truck caps, RV panels, shower/tub and spa shells, golf cart body panels, SMC automotive panels): repetitive perimeter deflash/trim of the same part geometry to a net line at a bench or trim-fixture station in a plant.

Cut openings and holes in a cured part: hatches, windows, gimbal/jet-pump, instrument, dash and hardware cutouts laid out from a template or scribe, plunge-cut with a diamond cutoff wheel, then edges ground to the line.

Large one-off or low-volume cured parts (yacht components, tanks, wind blade sections, architectural panels): part supported on stands or still in the mold, long freehand trim lines, worker walks around and reaches over the part, geometry varies part to part.

In-place trimming on assembled units or at a field/customer site: cutting cured overlaminate or bonded-joint flash inside an assembled hull, trimming an installed FRP panel, tank or shower surround; confined access, no fixture, as-found conditions.
Bench cutoff work: cutting cured FRP stock, laminate offcuts, rods/tubes, test coupons or small components to length with a fixed diamond cutoff saw; short straight cuts, part held in a vise or jig.

roles.title: Timing Device Assemblers and Adjusters
roles.description: Perform precision assembling or adjusting, within narrow tolerances, of timing devices such as digital clocks or timing devices with electrical or electronic components.

tasks.label: Assemble and install components of timepieces to complete mechanisms, using watchmakers' tools and loupes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production-station assembly of quartz/electronic watch or timer movement modules in a plant (e.g. Shinola-style kitted Swiss parts): main plate in a holder, gear train, rotor and coil, circuit block, tiny screws, done under a loupe with tweezers and a micro-screwdriver, high repetition, tight cycle time.

Completing the timepiece: fitting dial and hands to the movement, seating the movement in the case with a casing ring, installing gasket and battery, closing the caseback, then function check — done at a bench in the plant on a defined model family.

Assembly of electronic timing devices/instrument clocks: mounting the PCB/quartz oscillator block, stepper motor and gear train into a housing, driving small screws, connecting or soldering leads, snapping on the mechanism cover, and function-testing the completed mechanism.

Bench assembly of a conventional mechanical calibre (100+ parts): fitting jewels, wheels, pallet fork, balance and hairspring, screwing bridges, oiling pivots, checking endshake and beat under the loupe, on mixed models in small batches.

Rework/repair completion: a mechanism that failed test or a serviced timepiece of a model no longer in production is opened, the defective part identified and replaced, and the mechanism reassembled and re-verified — one-off, non-standard sequence.

Assembling and installing the mechanism of a large timing device on site — tower/street clock movement, master-clock or synchronized-clock system — fitting drive, gearing and hand arbors to existing structures at a customer building.

tasks.label: Observe operation of timepiece parts and subassemblies to determine accuracy of movement, and to diagnose causes of defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production test of electronic timing subassemblies (quartz clock modules, digital clock/timer PCBAs): worker seats the unit in a test fixture, powers it, watches that it steps/counts/keeps time within spec, and identifies which stage or component is at fault on failures. Factory test station, standard product mix, high volume.

Rate/accuracy testing of an assembled mechanical or quartz movement: mount on a timing machine, run it in several positions, read rate variation, amplitude and beat error, and infer causes of out-of-tolerance readings (out of beat, low amplitude from friction, magnetism). Adjusting bench or final-inspection room in a watch/clock plant.

Observing subassemblies operate during assembly under a microscope: turning the gear train, checking free running, end shake, hand clearance and escapement action on partly assembled movements, spotting binding, burrs, bent pivots, misplaced parts. Assembly bench/line in a plant, repeating on a known calibre.

Final functional check of a completed timepiece or timing device (digital clock, wall clock, appliance/industrial timer): run the unit through its cycle, verify display/hands advance, alarm, chime or switching operate correctly, and determine what is wrong when it does not. End-of-line test bench.

Troubleshooting rejects and returns of unknown cause: a movement or timer that failed test or came back from the field, model and history vary, requires probing, partial disassembly and open-ended reasoning to find the root cause and report it. Rework/service bench.

tasks.label: Test operation and fit of timepiece parts and subassemblies, using electronic testing equipment, tweezers, watchmakers' tools, and loupes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production bench in a watch/timing-device plant: operator seats a quartz or electronic analog movement in a test holder, applies the electronic tester (current consumption, coil resistance, pulse/rate deviation, EOL), confirms hands step correctly, records pass/fail and routes rejects.

Rate testing and regulation of assembled mechanical movements/escapements: movement placed on a timing machine (acoustic pickup), measured in several positions for rate, amplitude and beat error, then regulator/index adjusted with watchmaker's tools and re-tested until within spec.

Loupe/stereo-microscope inspection and fit check of tiny parts and subassemblies (wheels, pinions, jewels, shock absorbers, screws, plates): handled with tweezers, checked for burrs, damage, seating height, end-shake and correct mesh/freedom of the train before or after assembly.

Functional test of electronic timing-device subassemblies (digital clock/timer PCBs with display, switches, buzzer, motor drive): board loaded to a test fixture, probed at test points, powered up, outputs and display verified, and checked for correct fit into the housing.

Service/repair, prototype or low-volume rework bench: an unfamiliar, worn or defective timepiece or subassembly is diagnosed — testing why it runs out of spec, trial-fitting replacement parts with tweezers under a loupe, re-testing iteratively until it performs to spec.

tasks.label: Replace specified parts to repair malfunctioning timepieces, using watchmakers' tools, loupes, and holding fixtures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mechanical wristwatch/pocket-watch movement that fails timing or run test: at a bench under a loupe, worker opens the case, strips the movement in a movement holder, removes the specified defective part (balance complete, mainspring/barrel, pallet fork, broken jewel, stem), fits the replacement, reassembles, oils and re-times it. Parts are sub-millimetre and hairsprings deform if mishandled.

Quartz/electronic wristwatch: open snap or screw case back, replace the specified part (cell, coil, circuit module, stem/crown, gasket), refit hands/dial if disturbed, close and reseal the case, pressure and function test. Case styles, back types and gasket fits vary watch to watch; done at a jeweler's or service-center bench.

Clock movement (wall, mantel, alarm or grandfather) brought to the bench: replace worn bushings, a cracked gear or pinion, suspension spring, hands, or a quartz movement module; parts are millimetre-to-centimetre scale, fits are made by hand feel, then the movement is run-tested and beat-adjusted.

Bare printed-circuit assembly of a digital clock/timer that failed in-circuit or functional test, presented at a rework bench with the defective component already identified: desolder and remove the part (crystal, capacitor, IC, coil), clean the pads, solder in the replacement, retest.

Complete electronic timing device (digital clock, time switch, industrial timer, timeclock) that malfunctions: open the housing, unplug/unscrew and swap the specified subassembly (display module, board, motor, contact block), reassemble the housing and retest the unit at the bench.

On-site work: replace parts in an installed timepiece or time system - tower/street clock movement, church clock, or master-clock/slave-clock system in a building - working from a ladder or in a clock chamber with hand tools and portable fixtures under found conditions.

tasks.label: Disassemble timepieces such as watches, clocks, and chronometers so that repairs can be made.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Complete teardown of a mechanical wristwatch movement at a service/repair bench in a watch manufacturer's service department: pop or unscrew the case back, extract movement from case, pull hands with a hand-lever, remove dial-foot screws and dial, let down the mainspring, remove balance with hairspring, pallet fork, bridges and wheel train, and lay ~80-130 parts out undamaged for cleaning and repair. Screws are 0.5-1.4 mm slotted; pivots bend at gram-level loads.

Disassembly of a quartz/electronic wrist watch to fix a fault: open a snap or screw-down case back with a case tool, release and pull the stem via a tiny setting lever, lift the movement out of the case ring, separate the circuit block, coil, rotor and battery from the plastic module without cracking the coil wire or scratching the dial.

Disassembly of a clock (alarm, mantel, wall or carriage clock) whose movement is faulty: remove hands and dial, unpin/unscrew the movement from the case, let down two mainsprings safely with a let-down key, remove plate nuts/pillar screws, separate plates and extract the wheel train, escapement and strike work without springing pivots.

Factory rework/repair of an electronic timing device (industrial timer, digital clock, timing instrument) that failed test: unscrew the housing screws, split the enclosure, unplug connectors and lift out the PCB or timing module subassembly intact so a defective component or module can be replaced. Known models, moderate-size fasteners, done on a production or rework bench.

Disassembly of a vintage, water-damaged or crash-damaged timepiece: rusted or seized screws, sheared case-back threads, broken stem, previous poor repairs, non-standard or one-off construction with no documentation; the technician improvises extraction (penetrating oil, custom stakes, screw extractors) while preserving irreplaceable parts.

On-site disassembly of a large clock at the customer's premises: a longcase/grandfather or tower clock in a home, church tower or public building - remove weights, pendulum, hands and dial, unbolt the movement from its seatboard or frame, and crate the parts for shop repair, working in a cramped, uncontrolled, variable space.

sources.system: Horosys Smart Micro Factory with Mecademic Meca500
sources.title: Smart Micro Factory Revolutionizing Watchmaking with Meca500 Robot | Mecademic Industrial Robotics
sources.claim: Commercial desktop robotic cells built around the Meca500 micro-robot perform watchmaking micro-operations (assembling, riveting, push-fitting jewels and other watch components) inside purpose-built fixtured modules with ~5 micron repeatability; the work is assembly of new, feeder-presented parts, not teardown of used timepieces.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: micro-assembly of watch components. Same objects and precision class as watch disassembly, but the cell handles new parts presented in fixtures/feeders in known orientation; nothing in the cited deployment removes screws, hands, bridges or a hairspring from an already-assembled, worn movement.

It shows machine capability only for a product purpose-designed for automation, with parts fed in known pose; it does not substantiate opening and dismantling an arbitrary used movement while preserving every part for repair.

Transfers to opening a housing and lifting out a PCB/module of an electronic timing device (similar fastener sizes, planar access, model-specific fixtures), but not to sub-millimetre horological parts or unknown/worn assemblies.

sources.system: Robotic unscrewing system for WEEE disassembly (UR10e + RealSense D405 + mechatronic screwdriver)
sources.developer: academic group, published in Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing
sources.title: Robotic system for automated disassembly of electronic waste: Unscrewing - ScienceDirect
sources.claim: A research robotic disassembly cell (UR10e arm, RealSense D405 depth camera, custom mechatronic screwdriver) autonomously locates and classifies screw heads on electronic devices and removes the fasteners, automating the unscrewing step of device teardown in a laboratory workcell.

tasks.label: Clean and lubricate timepiece parts and assemblies, using solvents, buff sticks, and oil.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-assembly batch cleaning in a movement/timing-device plant: trays of machined components (plates, bridges, wheels, screws, pinions) are loaded into cleaning baskets and run through solvent/ultrasonic cleaning, rinsing and hot-air drying cycles, then dried parts are inspected for residue before going to the assembly bench.

Oiling and greasing during assembly of a repeating caliber/timer model: applying microscopic metered doses of watch oil and grease to designated points (jewel holes, cap jewels and shock settings, pivots, escapement, barrel wall and arbor, keyless work) on the same part type over and over at a production station under a microscope, to a written lubrication plan.

Surface finishing of individual parts before assembly: burnishing/polishing pivots and small steel and brass parts, removing burrs, tarnish and handling marks with buff sticks, abrasive sticks and polishing wheels at the bench or on a polishing machine, then degreasing the finished parts.

Bench clean-and-lubricate of a varied, one-off unit in rework/service: a returned or failing assembled movement of a caliber that differs from unit to unit, with dried or contaminated old lubricant; the worker hand-cleans delicate parts (balance, pallet fork) in solvent, pegs out jewel holes with pegwood/buff sticks, judges which lubricants go where, and re-oils the reassembled movement.

Final-assembly cleaning and lubrication of assemblies: solvent-cleaning/defluxing electronic timing assemblies and printed-circuit clock modules, wiping fingerprints and residue off cased units, and greasing gaskets, plastic gear trains and setting mechanisms before closing the case.

tasks.label: Examine components of timepieces such as watches, clocks, or chronometers for defects, using loupes or microscopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production bench in a timing-device/watch plant: operator examines small precision mechanical components of a running lot (wheels, pinions, arbors, springs, plates, jewels) under a stereo microscope for burrs, cracks, chips, scratches and form errors, sorting good from bad into trays.

Electronics assembly area: operator examines timing-module electronic subassemblies under a microscope — PCB solder joints, tiny SMD parts, quartz crystal cans, coil/lead connections — for cold joints, bridges, missing/misplaced parts and cracks, before or after reflow.

Assembly line/finishing bench: loupe inspection of cosmetic and assembled items — dials, hands, cases, crystals, and completed movements/modules — for dust, marks, scratches, plating flaws and misaligned or missing parts.

Setup/first-article and periodic audit inspection: the worker checks the first pieces from a new run or a supplier lot under microscope against a drawing, measures critical features, judges borderline parts and records results on an inspection sheet.

Service/repair bench (factory service center or clock/watch repair shop): components of a used, often unfamiliar or vintage movement are examined under a loupe for wear, worn pivots, rust, broken teeth and fatigue to decide which parts must be replaced.

sources.claim: Keyence IM-8000 image dimension measurement systems inspect small precision parts automatically once the part is placed on the stage: one button measures up to 300 features in seconds with a 20 MP sensor, giving repeatable pass/fail results and inspection reports regardless of operator skill.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: microscope/optical-comparator dimensional inspection of small precision parts against a drawing. Same objects and magnification regime as first-article microscope checking, and it produces the accept/reject verdict and record the worker's inspection sheet supplies.

tasks.label: Bend parts, such as hairsprings, pallets, barrel covers, and bridges, to correct deficiencies in truing or endshake, using tweezers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Truing a hairspring at a watch manufacture or service-center bench: balance-and-hairspring assembly under a microscope, worker grips a 0.02-0.05 mm thick coil with fine tweezers and puts a local bend in it so the spiral runs flat and concentric, judging by eye and iterating.

Correcting endshake on a mechanical watch movement: a wheel has too much or too little axial play, so the worker lightly bends the bridge/cock arm or domes the barrel cover with tweezers, reassembles, re-checks the play (tolerance ~0.01-0.03 mm) and repeats until the wheel is free without shake.

Bending hardened-steel escapement parts of a watch movement (pallet fork guard pin, banking, lever arms) by a few microns with tweezers to correct lock, drop and safety action, judged by observing escapement function under a loupe.

Larger mechanical clock or spring-driven timer movements: bending brass plates, bridges, spring clips and levers with tweezers/pliers on the bench to correct wheel truing, endshake and lever alignment, tolerances on the order of 0.05 mm.

Electromechanical timing-device production/adjustment bench: bending contact springs, leaf blades and mounting brackets so contact gap, spring force and switching/timing points fall within spec, verified with gauges and a test set.

sources.system: Chronogrip
sources.title: How Robots Revolutionised Watchmaking - Talos Automation
sources.claim: The Chronogrip, the leading micromanipulation robot built for watch parts from a few millimetres down to thousandths of a millimetre, is a human-operated comanipulator rather than an autonomous system.
sources.transferJustification: Closest robotic system to this task's objects (hairsprings, pallets, bridges); it shows watch-part micromanipulation at this scale is still under continuous human control, so it cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.system: Horosys Smart Micro Factory with Mecademic Meca500
sources.title: Smart Micro Factory Revolutionizing Watchmaking with Meca500 Robot | Mecademic
sources.claim: A purpose-built desktop micro-factory cell built around a Meca500 six-axis robot (5-micron repeatability) autonomously assembles, rivets and press-fits jewels and other tiny watch components in production.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (watch-component assembly, riveting, press-fitting): establishes that watch-scale parts can be fixtured, presented and worked to micron precision by an autonomous machine in a purpose-built cell - the handling half of a fixtured bending correction.

sources.system: Load adjusting machine for magnetic disk drive head gimbal assemblies (US5297413)
sources.title: Load adjusting machine for magnetic disk drive head gimbal assemblies (US Patent 5,297,413)
sources.claim: Production machines measure the spring load of head-gimbal/suspension assemblies and correct it by plastically bending the load-beam spring region, holding gram-load and static-attitude tolerances finer than watch endshake.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: measure a mechanical deficiency of a thin (tens of microns) steel spring part held in a fixture, then plastically bend it into tolerance and re-measure - the same measure/bend/re-check loop the worker performs on bridges, covers and springs, at equal or finer precision.

sources.system: Gram load adjustment machine in suspension manufacturing line
sources.title: Method and apparatus for HDD suspension gimbal-dimple separation (contact) force measurement (US20050005425A1)
sources.claim: Gram-load adjustment machines are a standard in-line station in micro-suspension manufacturing: etched spring strips are fed to the machine, which forms and bends the spring region to the required load.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as the Hutchinson machine; this source shows measure-and-bend correction stations run inside high-volume production lines rather than only in the lab.

sources.system: Method and apparatus for the adjustment of contact springs in a relay (US4520254)
sources.title: Method and apparatus for the adjustment of contact springs in a relay (US Patent 4,520,254)
sources.claim: An automated relay adjustment apparatus measures each contact spring's position against the desired value, computes the deviation, and applies metered laser pulses that bend the spring by the required amount, re-measuring and repeating until in tolerance.
sources.transferJustification: Directly analogous task on the same class of part: thin contact springs of an electromechanical switching device are bent under machine control to correct a measured positional deficiency, which is what the worker does to contact springs and small levers of electromechanical timers.

sources.system: Galdabini automatic straightening systems
sources.title: GALDABINI - Straightening Systems (catalogue)
sources.claim: Commercial automatic straightening systems measure a workpiece's runout and form error and then apply controlled bending strokes to correct it, re-measuring afterwards, without an operator judging the correction.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: correcting a truing (runout) deficiency by machine-controlled plastic bending with closed-loop measurement; transfers to coarser clock-movement parts (brass plates, arbors, bridges, clips) whose tolerances (~0.05 mm) are well inside these machines' control.

tasks.label: Change timing weights on balance wheels to correct deficient timing.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Volume production at a movement/timing-device plant: balance assemblies of a single known calibre are run on a timing machine, and the assembler alters rim mass (timing screws, inertia weights, washers) to bring the rate into the specified tolerance; standard parts, fixtures/holders, batch work at a production bench.

Authorized service center or factory repair bench: a serviced modern mechanical wristwatch runs fast/slow, so the technician removes the balance, turns or swaps the free-sprung inertia weights (Microstella/Gyromax-type) per the factory procedure, re-poises, refits and re-measures on a timegrapher across positions.

Clock, marine/instrument timer or larger mechanical timing-device shop: a screwed balance wheel of 10-25 mm gets timing washers added or removed under rim screws, or screws moved/exchanged, to correct a daily-rate error; standard catalogue washers and screws, bench with timing stand.

Antique/vintage restoration or one-off repair in a workshop: an unfamiliar screwed balance with original, irreplaceable screws; the worker must judge and hand-fit or fabricate timing washers, preserve original parts, and iterate by feel and timing tests with no factory data or spare stock.

Adjustment of an installed device on site: tower or public clock movement, marine chronometer aboard a vessel, or a mechanical timer in operating machinery; the balance is reached in situ in cramped, non-standard surroundings and weights are changed with hand tools and a portable rate check.

sources.system: Sistem51 automated assembly and laser regulation line (ETA, Boncourt)
sources.title: Cheap Swiss watches made by robots - SWI swissinfo.ch
sources.claim: Swatch/ETA's Sistem51 mechanical movement is regulated without hands on a fully automated line: a laser sets the movement's rate to within +/-7 s/day, replacing the manual rate-adjustment step.
sources.transferJustification: Same task purpose: correcting a deficient rate by altering the balance's mass distribution. The machine removes rim material instead of moving screws/washers, but acts on the same workpiece to the same or tighter tolerance.

sources.system: Sistem51 automated production line (ETA Boncourt)
sources.title: Sistem51: a radical take on Swiss mechanical watchmaking - Europa Star
sources.claim: As of 2026 the Sistem51 line at ETA Boncourt still runs with no human hand touching the movement; rate ('accuracy') is set by laser on the inertia-regulated balance, with operators only supervising.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes autonomy (not teleoperation) and current deployment of the automated balance-inertia rate adjustment cited in evidence 0 and 2.

sources.system: Sistem51 laser balance-adjustment station
sources.title: Swatch Sistem51 - REVIEW - Monochrome Watches
sources.claim: In the Sistem51 the balance wheel's adjustment - normally a skilled watchmaker's job - is performed by a laser that removes material until the required chronometric rate is reached.
sources.transferJustification: Direct counterpart of changing timing weights: mass on the balance rim is altered under machine control to correct the rate of the oscillator.

sources.system: Factory computer-aided laser poising machines (watch industry production, Rolex imagery)
sources.title: In-Depth: Why the Position of a Watch Influences Accuracy | SJX Watches
sources.claim: New balance wheels are poised automatically by computer-aided laser machines during factory assembly, while balance work on watches returned for repair is still completed by hand by a watchmaker.
sources.transferJustification: Poising is the same operation family - adding or removing weight at chosen points on the balance rim - on the identical workpiece at the same precision; the same source states repair-side balance work remains manual.

sources.system: Industrial static balance-wheel balancing machines
sources.title: BALANCE WHEEL POISING TOOL - Horopedia
sources.claim: Industrial watch workshops use static balancing machines that automatically detect and correct balance-wheel mass defects at high speed, while hand poising tools remain the reference for artisanal and restoration work.
sources.transferJustification: The machine measures a balance wheel and corrects its rim mass distribution autonomously - the same measure-and-correct-weight loop as changing timing weights; the same source marks restoration work as still manual.

sources.system: CLAvissage / CLAastm automatic screwing stations for watch movements
sources.title: Controle chronometrique montres, vissage automatique - CLA - Clinical Laboratory Automation SA
sources.claim: A commercial benchtop automated screwing station handles the screws of watch movements, reaching all movement positions by rotation and translation, with precision removable fixtures supporting multiple part types.
sources.transferJustification: Changing timing weights or washers requires driving and removing watch- and clock-sized screws on a fixtured movement; this station performs that screw manipulation autonomously in a purpose-built holder.

sources.system: Horosys Smart Micro Factory with Mecademic Meca500
sources.title: Smart Micro Factory Revolutionizing Watchmaking with Meca500 Robot | Mecademic Industrial Robotics
sources.claim: A modular desktop robotic cell built around the Meca500 micro-robot assembles, rivets and press-fits jewels and other watchmaking components for Swiss manufacturers producing in low volumes.
sources.transferJustification: Demonstrates autonomous handling and fitting of watch-scale parts (jewels, small components) at micron precision in a fixtured desktop cell - the manipulation class needed to fit or exchange balance timing weights and washers.

tasks.label: Adjust sizes or positioning of timepiece parts to achieve specified fit or function, using calipers, fixtures, and loupes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Bench work in a small/medium instrument or clock plant: assembling an electromechanical or digital timing module (gear train, rotor/coil, contacts, cam) and adjusting the positioning of sub-millimetre parts — seating a pivot, shimming a plate, re-seating a contact — checking clearance and end-play with loupe, gauge pins and calipers until fit is right; batch of same model, standard fixtures on the bench.

Movement/timepiece assembly at a production bench or line: pressing jewels, shock springs and bushings to a specified depth to set end-shake, staking a wheel to height, and fitting/aligning hands on their pivots so they clear the dial and each other; uses a jeweling/staking fixture and press, verified under a loupe and with a height gauge.

Final calibration/adjustment of an assembled unit to hit the timing specification: measure rate/beat or timer interval on a test set and then move the regulating element (regulator index and stud, adjustable cam or contact, trimmer/position of a component) until the reading is inside tolerance; repeat and re-test on standard equipment at a fixed test station.

Rework of units failing QC or returned from the field, across a mixed model set: diagnose which part is out of position or out of size (rubbing hand, tight jewel, bent lever, out-of-spec shaft), disassemble as needed, then bend, file, burnish or re-seat the part to restore fit and function, re-test. One-off, non-repeating work at a bench with hand tools, loupe and calipers.

On-site adjustment of a large timing device at a customer building: tower/master clock, time-system slave dials or a large process timer — repositioning hands on the arbor, adjusting the escapement/pendulum drop or a switch cam, working on a ladder or in a plant room with hand tools and portable gauges, layout different at each site.

sources.system: Horosys Smart Micro Factory (Mecademic Meca500)
sources.title: Smart Micro Factory Revolutionizing Watchmaking with Meca500 Robot | Mecademic Industrial Robotics
sources.claim: Horosys' Smart Micro Factory modules built around the Meca500 micro-robot assemble, rivet and press-fit jewels and other watch components in 600x600 mm automated desktop stations equipped with cameras, feeders, presses and metrology, deployed at watch-component supplier Gimmel Rouages.
sources.transferJustification: Same object class and precision as the task: micron-level positioning of watch parts formerly handled under a microscope, with in-cell metrology, inside a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: stocoPRESS servo press (Exlar GSM20 actuator)
sources.title: Chassage automatisé pour l'horlogerie — Parkem AG
sources.claim: The stocoPRESS servo press, built by Stoco SA for a well-known watch manufacture, measures component height against a reference on the plate and continuously monitors force and position while pressing jewels, shock springs and pins to the required depth to better than 1 micron; lines run up to 15 presses producing twelve watches per minute fully automatically.

sources.system: Lecureux HSM1708 hands setting machine
sources.title: Hands setting machine HSM1708 - Lecureux
sources.claim: Lecureux's HSM1708 hands-setting machine fits watch hands on a movement, either semi-automatically at a workbench or fully automatically on an assembly line, centring each hand on its pivot with controlled driving force and video verification, including adjustment of off-centre hands.

sources.system: Witschi Retouche A2 / RMA (Retouche Mécanique Automatique)
sources.title: Système pour le réglage automatique de mouvements mécaniques — Retouche A2 (fiche technique)
sources.claim: Witschi's Retouche A2 with RMA units automatically regulates mechanical movements in series: fine pins enter the movement and move the regulator index and stud carrier while a microphone measures rate, iterating until the movement reaches the required accuracy; the unit can sit at a watchmaker's workstation or be integrated as a station in an automated production line.

sources.system: Averna Active Alignment system
sources.title: Active Alignment Camera Modules & Optical Devices | Averna
sources.claim: Averna's automated Active Alignment system assembles camera modules by dynamically adjusting lens position under real-time image feedback, reaching sub-micron accuracy in six degrees of freedom in a fully automated production cell combining machine vision, robotics and in-line ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: positioning an electronic/optical component and adjusting it until a measured functional output meets specification — the same closed measure-then-adjust loop, at finer precision than watch/timer work, in a purpose-built machine.

sources.system: Petitpierre connected decolletage production solution (lumen optical sensor + drop cleaning module)
sources.title: Petitpierre dans Le Temps - Petitpierre
sources.claim: Petitpierre's connected production solution for precision watch components measures each machined part with a high-precision optical sensor and software that analyses deviations and automatically sends the corrective adjustments to the machine tools without human intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: bringing watch-part dimensions to specified size through automated measurement-driven correction — the 'adjust sizes to achieve specified fit' half of the task, on the same components.

sources.system: Sinuowei quartz clock movement automatic assembly line
sources.developer: Xiamen Sinuowei Automated Science and Technology Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Quartz Clock Movements Full-automatically Assembling Machine Automatic Production Line
sources.claim: Xiamen Sinuowei supplies fully automatic assembly lines for quartz clock movements that assemble gears, motor and housing into complete movements.
sources.transferJustification: Same product family as the digital/electromechanical timing devices in this occupation; shows fixtured automatic stations set gear and motor positions in clock movements.

tasks.label: Mount hairsprings and balance wheel assemblies between jaws of truing calipers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Independent watchmaker / small repair shop bench: after fitting a new balance staff to a customer's watch, the balance complete with hairspring is mounted between the ruby jaws of a truing caliper to check truth in round and flat. One-off work, mixed brands and calibers (modern and mid-century), balance diameters 7-11 mm, pivots ~0.1 mm, jaws closed by feel until the wheel turns but not freely.

Brand or authorized service center bench (e.g., a Swiss brand's US service facility): the same mounting operation performed repeatedly on a limited, standardized set of in-house caliber balance completes removed from serviced watches; standard tooling, controlled parts flow, quality-audited output.

Vintage/antique restoration studio: bimetallic split balances, pocket-watch and chronometer balances, often with bent arms, worn or rusted pivots, screws missing; the assembly is mounted in a truing caliper (or hairspring truing caliper) with judgment about how much load the fragile pivot and spring can take.

Small-series manufacture or incoming component QC: trays of identical new balance completes for one caliber are mounted one after another between caliper/runner jaws at a bench or inspection station to verify concentricity and flatness before movement assembly.

Clock, timer and instrument work: larger platform-escapement, alarm-clock, marine-chronometer or timer balance wheels (12-25 mm) with their hairsprings mounted between caliper jaws at a repair bench; mixed, often obsolete types.

sources.system: Sistem51 automated movement assembly line
sources.developer: Swatch Group / ETA SA (Boncourt), with Nivarox-FAR
sources.title: The innovative "Sistem" powering the Royal Pop — Europa Star
sources.claim: Swatch Group's Sistem51 mechanical movement is assembled entirely by machines at ETA's Boncourt plant, including the escapement module containing the balance and Nivachron hairspring; operators only supervise. This shows automated pick-and-seat of a balance-and-hairspring oscillator on ~0.1 mm pivots inside a purpose-built line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated assembly of the escapement module, in which the balance-and-hairspring oscillator is gripped and seated on its ~0.1 mm pivots in jewel bearings. Same components and comparable micron-level precision as seating a balance complete between truing-caliper jaws, but only for one fixed, newly made part type presented by dedicated tooling.

sources.system: Smart Micro Factory (SMF) with Meca500 robot
sources.title: Smart Micro Factory Revolutionizing Watchmaking with Meca500 Robot | Mecademic Industrial Robotics
sources.claim: Horosys' Smart Micro Factory modules, built around Mecademic's Meca500 six-axis robot with cameras and feeders, run automated assembly, riveting and jewel push-fitting of watch components at benchtop scale, deployed at Swiss watch component supplier Gimmel Rouages.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: push-fitting jewels and assembling watch micro-parts to 0.01 mm positional requirements. Comparable object size and precision to placing a balance staff's pivots into caliper jaws, but the cell uses dedicated feeders and fixtures for a single known part.

sources.system: Percipio automatic micro-assembly machines (PiezoGripper-based platforms)
sources.title: Products | Percipio Robotics
sources.claim: Percipio Robotics supplies vision-controlled automatic micro-assembly machines that grip components down to 5 µm with ±0.5 µm positioning accuracy and run with only discreet human intervention; the company's expertise originates in watchmaking micro-assembly.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated micro-gripping and precision placement of horological-scale components. Establishes that micron-precision autonomous handling exists for fixed, characterized parts in purpose-built machines, not for arbitrary parts.

sources.system: Chronogrip micromanipulation robot
sources.title: How Robots Revolutionised Watchmaking — Talos Automation
sources.claim: Percipio's Chronogrip — the micromanipulation robot marketed specifically for watchmaking-style varied micro-assembly at a bench — requires a human operator and does not work autonomously, per the company's CEO.
sources.transferJustification: Directly relevant negative evidence: the one robot built for watchmaker-style micromanipulation of varied small parts is operator-controlled, so it cannot support a positive judgment for one-off repair instances.

sources.system: Vaucher balance assembly and poising stations
sources.title: Balances — The Naked Watchmaker
sources.claim: At Vaucher Manufacture's high-end balance production, balances arrive in soft plastic trays and are placed by an operator into the machine that checks the wheel for heavy spots; the press that fits the roller is automated but human-loaded.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mounting a balance into a poising/measuring fixture, the manufacturing analogue of mounting it between truing-caliper jaws. Shows that in low-volume high-end production this loading step is still performed by a human operator.

tasks.label: Estimate spaces between collets and first inner coils to determine if spaces are within acceptable limits.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Movement/hairspring plant, in-line or at-line QC: trays of new balance-spring (spiral-and-collet) assemblies arrive from the fitting station; the worker views each under a stereo microscope or projector and estimates the clearance between the collet body and the first inner coil, sorting pass/fail against a caliber tolerance.

Bench assembly of the balance complete in a manufacturing shop: after pinning/riveting the hairspring inner end to the collet, the worker holds the assembly in tweezers or on a staking-tool arbor under magnification and repeatedly estimates the collet-to-first-coil space between small tweezer corrections until it is inside limits.

Authorized brand service center overhauling standard modern calibers: the balance is removed from a cleaned used movement, the hairspring is examined under a microscope, and the technician estimates whether the inner coil clears the collet within factory limits before refitting.

Independent watch/clock repair bench: one-off vintage or unfamiliar movements, hairsprings often bent, rusty or replaced; the repairer eyeballs the collet-to-first-coil space under a loupe with no documented tolerance, judging acceptability from experience.

Factory metrology lab / first-article and sample audit: assemblies are set on a measuring microscope or optical comparator stage, the collet-to-first-coil gap is read against a scale or reticle and recorded on an inspection sheet for the caliber.

sources.system: Petitpierre drop + lumen (MVTec HALCON vision)
sources.developer: Petitpierre SA (Cortaillod, Switzerland) with MVTec HALCON
sources.title: Machine vision improves the measuring process of precision and micro components
sources.claim: Petitpierre's drop+lumen system, deployed at Swiss watch component maker KIF Parechoc, automatically cleans micromechanical watch-movement parts, transfers them to a telecentric optical station with a vacuum gripper, and measures diameters, concentricity, radii and angles with sub-micrometer, subpixel accuracy, exporting results to QC software.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional/geometric inspection of watch-movement micro components. The collet-to-first-coil space is a 2D edge-to-edge gap on a watch micro part; the cited system measures comparable features (concentricity, radii, lengths) on the same class of parts at sub-micrometer accuracy, far finer than the worker's visual estimate, in the same factory setting.

sources.system: Petitpierre drop + lumen at KIF Parechoc
sources.title: Clockwork Inspection (Cutting Tool Engineering)
sources.claim: Trade-press account of the same deployment: the contactless inspection and cleaning system serves a range of mechanical watch-movement components at KIF Parechoc, runs the whole measurement from a single operator click without manual adjustment, and was moved out of the clean room onto the production floor.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated optical metrology of mechanical watch-movement components in a production plant. Same object class and precision regime as the collet/hairspring gap check; shows the measurement decision is produced automatically and fed to quality control, i.e. an accept/reject output, not just an image.

sources.system: Kistler Automated Vision Inspection (AVI)
sources.title: Automated Vision Inspection systems for automated, precise and gentle inspection
sources.claim: Kistler's Automated Vision Inspection turnkey systems use an image-guided pick-and-place robot to take delicate parts from blisters or bulk, run several optical inspections checking seven dimensional parameters to 0.005 mm, and sort good/bad parts; several are in operation at industrial users.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-handled optical dimensional inspection of small, fragile parts with automatic pass/fail sorting. It demonstrates that presentation, measurement to a few microns, and the acceptance decision can be done without an operator, which is what estimating and judging the collet-to-coil space requires.

sources.system: RobotVIEW robotic vision inspection system
sources.title: Robotic Vision Inspection for Small Parts & Products
sources.claim: Sciotex RobotVIEW is a commercially offered, fully automated robotic inspection platform that singulates, presents and inspects small high-tolerance parts, using high-magnification telecentric optics for dimensional gauging plus 3D scanning and weighing, configured per part geometry.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional inspection of small precision parts in a purpose-built multi-station cell. Comparable object size and tolerance class to a balance-spring assembly; shows US-available commercial hardware that presents each unit itself and returns dimensional verdicts.

tasks.label: Bend inner coils of springs away from or toward collets, using tweezers, to locate centers of collets in centers of springs, and to correct errors resulting from faulty colleting of coils.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Watch service-centre bench (brand or authorized service workshop): after a hairspring is fitted to a new collet/balance staff on a standard modern caliber, the technician inspects the assembly under a stereo microscope and bends the innermost coil (~25-40 µm thick alloy ribbon) with fine tweezers so the collet sits concentric in the spring, then re-checks that the spring 'breathes' concentrically on the truing caliper and timing machine.

Independent watch-repair bench: vintage or damaged movement, unknown or obsolete caliber, aged/distorted steel hairspring with an off-centre collet from prior faulty colleting; the watchmaker must judge where to grip and bend the inner coils, working freehand under a loupe/microscope with high risk of permanent kinking or breakage of an irreplaceable spring.

Movement/timing-device assembly plant, final-adjustment bench: batches of balance-and-hairspring assemblies of one or two standard calibers fail a concentricity/flatness inspection; the operator corrects the inner coils with tweezers at a fixtured bench station under a microscope and returns each unit to inspection, at production cadence.

In-line rework station beside an automated colleting (laser-pinning) machine: high-volume single-caliber hairsprings whose collets came out slightly eccentric are re-centred by bending the inner coil, with a camera/inspection gauge confirming concentricity before the unit rejoins the line.

Clock / mechanical-timer work: platform-escapement or larger balance-spring assemblies (coarser wire, larger collet) in clock repair or mechanical timer assembly; inner coils bent with tweezers to centre the collet, with the assembly held in a movement holder on the bench.

sources.system: Chronogrip
sources.title: How Robots Revolutionised Watchmaking
sources.claim: Chronogrip, the micromanipulation robot purpose-built for watchmaking micro-parts (millimetre down to a few micrometres), is a cobotic station that requires a human operator and does not work autonomously.
sources.transferJustification: Chronogrip is the closest commercial system to this task (robotised watchmaker's tweezers under a microscope), but it is operator-driven via joystick/haptic controller, so it cannot support a positive judgment for autonomous hairspring coil bending.

sources.system: Chronogrip / Percipio automatic micro-assembly machines
sources.title: Products | Percipio Robotics
sources.claim: Percipio sells both cobotic tools (Chronogrip, driven by joystick/game controller/haptic device) and automatic micro-assembly machines gripping objects down to 5 ... with ±0.5 µm positioning under HD vision; the documented applications are micro-part gripping, placing and assembly, not plastic re-shaping of a coiled spring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated micro-assembly of watch-scale rigid parts. It does not transfer to bending a hairspring's inner coil, which requires controlled plastic deformation of a ~30 µm deformable ribbon judged against concentric 'breathing' of the spring; no such operation is documented.

sources.system: Smart Micro Factory (SMF) with Meca500 robot
sources.title: Smart Micro Factory Revolutionizing Watchmaking with Meca500 Robot
sources.claim: A commercially deployed desktop robotic micro-factory assembles, rivets and push-fits jewels and other watch components autonomously in 600 x 600 mm fixtured modules at 0.005 mm robot precision, installed at a supplier to luxury watchmakers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated precision assembly of watch components in a purpose-built desktop cell. It handles rigid parts placed in fixtures with pick-place and press operations; it demonstrates no manipulation or corrective bending of hairspring coils, so it does not substantiate this task even at E1.

sources.system: none (manual régleuse practice)
sources.title: The Hairspring: Soul of the Mechanical Watch
sources.claim: Industry commentary as of 2026 reports that final hairspring adjustment is still performed by a human under a ..., manipulating the spring micron by micron with tweezers, despite modern materials and machine tolerances.
sources.transferJustification: Not a robotic system; cited as context that hairspring shaping/centring operations of this kind remain a manual bench operation, consistent with the absence of any cited automated system performing them.

tasks.label: Turn wheels of calipers and examine springs, using loupes, to determine if center coils appear as perfect circles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Production bench at a watch/timing-device manufacturer: for each unit of a single current caliber, the assembler mounts the balance-and-hairspring assembly in a truing caliper, turns it, and inspects the center coils under a loupe for concentricity about the staff, passing or flagging the piece. High volume, identical known part geometry, fixtures and gauges provided.

Quality-control/metrology station at the same kind of plant: lot sampling or incoming inspection of purchased balance-spring assemblies. Parts arrive in trays, are placed in a caliper or holder, rotated and examined for round (concentric) center coils against a documented spec; results recorded and out-of-spec lots rejected.

Authorized service center bench: after cleaning, a balance staff change or a hairspring replacement on a modern movement, the technician mounts the balance in a truing caliper, turns the wheel, checks under a loupe whether the center coils run as true circles around the staff, and repeats after each correction. Caliber varies piece to piece within a known catalog.

Independent watch/clock repair shop: vintage, antique or unidentified movements. Hairsprings may be rusty, oily, previously mangled, of unknown original geometry, with worn pivots; the worker mounts what is there in a truing caliper, turns it under a loupe, and judges from experience whether the center coils are true and what deformation is present.

Mechanical clock/timer assembly plant: larger flat spiral or coil springs (clock balance springs, appliance/kitchen timer springs) checked on a caliper or arbor, turned by hand and viewed with a loupe for round, centered coils before assembly.

sources.system: Keyence IM-8000 Image Dimension Measurement System
sources.title: Keyence Launches IM-8000 Dimensional Measurement System
sources.claim: Commercial automated image dimension measurement system that measures roundness, coaxiality, run-out and flatness of a small part automatically, with a rotary unit for 360-degree measurement and ±2 µm camera accuracy — the same geometric determination ('are the center coils true circles about the axis?') the worker makes with a loupe and truing caliper.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated optical dimensional inspection of small precision parts (springs are a listed application). Transfer holds because the worker's judgment is geometric — circularity of the inner coils and their concentricity with the staff axis — which is exactly roundness/coaxiality/run-out measurement on a rotary stage at micron precision.

sources.system: Keyence IM-8000 Image Dimension Measurement System
sources.title: Keyence Launches IM-8000 Dimensional Measurement System
sources.claim: The same system begins measuring automatically as soon as the part is placed on the stage, needs no fixture set-up or operator skill, and returns hundreds of dimensions in about a second — the inspection verdict is machine-made, not operator-made.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above; establishes that the accept/reject determination is autonomous once the workpiece is presented, which is what the E1 counterfactual assumes.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated optical metrology of watch components (case concentricity, gear profiles, hairspring diameter). Same objects and precision class as the hairspring check in this task, done by a motorized stage plus vision instead of eye and loupe.

sources.system: Machine-vision flat spiral spring dimension inspection system (area-scan camera, bi-telecentric lens, vibration feeder)

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated dimensional inspection of flat spiral (coil) springs, the same object class as clock/timer spiral springs here; the system feeds, images and classifies springs without an operator, replacing the loupe-and-eye pass/fail judgment.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic measurement and classification of balance-and-hairspring assemblies in industry. Shows the exact workpieces of this task being fixtured and characterized by machine in a production/QC setting, though it measures physical properties rather than coil geometry.

sources.system: Chronogrip micro-assembly robot

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic micro-manipulation of watch components at a bench. Cited as negative evidence — the only bench-scale watchmaking robot found requires continuous human operation, so no E2 (human-bench) judgment is supported.

sources.transferJustification: Same task family (hairspring truing/inspection). Negative evidence bounding the E2 judgment: the industry standard for this operation at a human bench remains manual.

tasks.label: Examine and adjust hairspring assemblies to ensure horizontal and circular alignment of hairsprings, using calipers, loupes, and watchmakers' tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Movement-assembly bench at a watch/movement manufacturer: worker fits a balance-spring assembly (spring pinned to collet and stud) to a known caliber, examines the spring under a loupe or stereo microscope, and corrects flat (horizontal) and centering (circular) deviations with tweezers; the same caliber is repeated dozens of times per shift with fresh, in-spec components.

Final adjusting / QC rework station inside the same factory: a movement fails timing or positional checks, and the worker examines the hairspring in the assembled movement under the balance cock (coils touching, spring coned, off-centre between regulator pins, stud height wrong) and bends the spring or moves the stud/collet to restore flat and concentric development.

Mechanical instrument-timer or chronometer plant (aircraft clocks, mechanical timers, deck watches): worker builds and checks hairspring/balance assemblies in small batches against drawing tolerances, using fixtures, gauges, calipers and loupes, correcting alignment by hand before the escapement is closed up.

Service/overhaul department of a brand or company repair shop: cleaned, used balance-spring assemblies from many different calibres arrive with unpredictable distortions (kinked or bent coils, coning after mishandling, displaced collet, spring rubbing the balance arm); worker diagnoses the defect under magnification and trues the spring by hand.

One-off vintage restoration or prototype work: a replacement hairspring is selected and vibrated to the balance, the terminal curve is formed, and the spring is then trued flat and concentric; no two jobs are alike and no dedicated tooling exists for the calibre.

sources.system: SISTEM51 automated movement assembly line (Swatch Group / ETA, Boncourt)
sources.title: Swatch SISTEM51 — Swatch Group
sources.claim: Swatch's SISTEM51 mechanical movement — including its balance/hairspring oscillator — is assembled entirely by automated machines in a purpose-built line, with the oscillator's rate set by laser rather than by a human adjuster.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated build and adjustment of the balance–hairspring oscillator. It bears on this task because the machine line delivers, without hand work, the same accepted output the hairspring adjuster's examination and truing is meant to produce — an oscillator whose spring runs flat and concentric and keeps rate — on the same micron-scale components.

sources.system: SISTEM51 laser poising/regulation station
sources.title: Swatch – Hands-On with the Sistem51 Petite Seconde, an engineering marvel – the eclecticum
sources.claim: In SISTEM51 production the balance and hairspring subassembly is poised and regulated by laser during manufacture, so no manual adjustment of the oscillator is performed (or possible) afterwards.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine adjustment of the balance–hairspring assembly in place of the human régleur. Same component and tolerance class; it substantiates that a fixtured, purpose-built cell can bring a hairspring assembly to accepted output without a watchmaker's loupe-and-tweezer work.

sources.system: SISTEM51 assembly cells (robotic pick-and-place plus laser welding)
sources.title: Inside Swatch's Automated Watchmaking: How the Sistem51 Comes to Life
sources.claim: The SISTEM51 line uses robotic arms to pick the micro-components out of blister packaging and laser-welds the movement modules together in enclosed machine cells.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated micro-assembly of watch movement parts. Comparable objects (millimetre watch components) and a fenced, fixtured cell, showing the environment in which the oscillator assembly is produced without human handling.

sources.system: SISTEM51 movement

sources.claim: SISTEM51 remains in commercial production with an antimagnetic Nivachron hairspring and ..., holding a stated rate tolerance of -5/+15 seconds per ....
sources.transferJustification: Quality benchmark for the machine-adjusted oscillator: it shows the automated line's output is accepted commercially, which is what the 'worker quality' test requires for the volume-assembly instances.

sources.claim: Compact industrial robot arms with 5 µm repeatability are sold to and used by high-end watch manufacturers for micromanipulation and assembly of watch components a few millimetres in size.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fixtured micro-assembly of watch parts. It substantiates machine handling of watch-scale rigid components in a benchtop cell, but not the compliant bending of a hairspring, so it supports only the fixtured-assembly portion of the work.

sources.transferJustification: Directly this task's context: it identifies the flat-and-centring control as a discrete step in industrial hairspring production, with no indication that the correction is machine-performed.

tasks.label: Tighten or replace loose jewels, using watchmakers' tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Movement/mechanism assembly area of a watch, clock or timer manufacturer: on batches of identical current-production mainplates and bridges held in standard posages, the assembler sets ruby jewels (train, escape, balance, shock settings) and re-presses any jewel found loose or standing high, driving it to the specified depth so endshake and retention meet the caliber spec. Engineering specs, gauges and jewel stock by diameter are on hand.

In-process check/adjustment station in the same plant: a movement or subassembly fails an endshake, amplitude or height check; the adjuster traces it to a jewel that did not seat tight or sits at the wrong height, re-presses or swaps it on a jeweling press to the specified depth, and rechecks. Same caliber repeatedly, fixtures and reference dimensions available.

Repair/overhaul bench in a manufacturer's service department or authorized service center: a returned watch is stripped and a cracked or loose friction-set jewel is found; the watchmaker pushes the old jewel out with a Seitz/Horia jeweling tool, measures and selects a replacement, presses it to the correct endshake and verifies pivot freedom under a microscope. Mixed calibers arrive in unpredictable condition.

Independent, vintage/heritage or low-volume bespoke work, often at a one-person bench in a converted room or home workshop: jewels held in chatons or rubbed-in bezel settings are burnished/re-rubbed to tighten, or non-standard jewels are hand-fitted to unique or obsolete calibers with no drawings and no matching stock.

Assembly and adjustment of jeweled bearings in non-watch timing instruments at an instrument manufacturer (timers, chronometers, aircraft/marine clocks, meter movements): pressing ruby/corundum micro-bearings into frames or plates on fixtured parts, and tightening or reseating any bearing found loose so pivot endshake meets tolerance.

sources.system: stocoPRESS servopress (Stoco SA, with Exlar GSM20 electric actuator)
sources.title: Chassage automatisé pour l'horlogerie (Parkem AG application reference)
sources.claim: Stoco SA's stocoPRESS servopress automatically places small components, including ruby/corundum jewel micro-bearings, into watch mainplates and bridges on a watch manufacturer's production line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: production jewel-setting (chassage/empierrage). Same objects (sub-millimetre ruby jewels, watch plates/bridges), same tool action (press to a controlled depth) and same tolerance class as tightening or replacing a loose jewel, which is exactly a press to the correct seating depth.

sources.system: stocoPRESS servopress line (up to 15 presses)
sources.title: Chassage automatisé pour l'horlogerie (Parkem AG application reference)
sources.claim: The same automated jewel-pressing line drives each jewel to the required depth under continuous force and position measurement, to better than 1 µm, and runs the movement build fully automatically without manual watchmaker intervention.
sources.transferJustification: Depth control to <1 µm under force/position feedback is the same physical criterion a watchmaker meets when tightening or reseating a jewel (retention plus endshake), so the demonstrated capability carries over to the corrective press.

sources.system: Stoco SVS Workstation / SVS T / SVS TG / SVS XLFA / SVS TGA jewelling machines
sources.title: SVS series / Multi-composants – Chassage Garnissage Assemblage – Stoco SA
sources.claim: Stoco sells commercial jewelling machines (SVS series) that feed jewels from calibrated tubes, centre parts by camera and press jewels into mainplates and bridges with ±1 µm measurement repeatability; the XLFA/TGA variants add automatic plate feeding (~600 plates of autonomy).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: empierrage/garnissage of plates and bridges. Identical objects and precision to replacing a loose jewel; the machine selects the jewel from a feeder and presses it into the plate hole, which is the operative step of jewel replacement.

sources.system: Stoco Colibri servopress / SV1R2A assembly machine
sources.title: Machines et équipements de production Chassage Garnissage Assemblage – Stoco SA
sources.claim: Stoco's servopresses implement 'iterative press-fitting' with a probe in the press nose, applying 100% dynamic force-and-displacement control at ±3 µm and including retention (holding) checks — i.e. pressing a jewel to the exact height and verifying it is tight.
sources.transferJustification: Iterative pressing with a height probe is the automated equivalent of a watchmaker using a Horia/Seitz tool to push a jewel to the right depth; the built-in retention check ('contrôle tenue') detects the loose jewel the task is about.

sources.system: Smart Micro Factory (SMF) with Mecademic Meca500 six-axis robot
sources.title: Smart Micro Factories for the Watchmaking Industry (Mecademic case study)
sources.claim: Horosys' Smart Micro Factory, a 600 × 600 mm benchtop robotic cell built around the Mecademic Meca500 with cameras, feeders and presses, assembles, rivets and push-fits jewels and other watch components at 0.005 mm repeatability; it is in use at Swiss component supplier Gimmel Rouages.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic push-fitting and riveting of jewels in a purpose-built cell. Same jewels, same plates, 0.01 mm positional requirement — the physical act of fitting a replacement jewel is the demonstrated operation.

sources.system: Sistem51 automated movement assembly line
sources.title: Sistem51: a radical take on Swiss mechanical watchmaking – Europa Star
sources.claim: Swatch's Sistem51 mechanical movement has been assembled entirely by machines since 2013, with operators only supervising; jewel fitting is part of that fully automated movement build.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: complete automated assembly of a jewelled mechanical movement, including setting its jewel bearings; demonstrates that jewel seating to watch tolerances is achieved by machine in a purpose-built line.

roles.title: Team Assemblers
aliases: Delivery and Assembly Technician (Delivery and Assembly Tech)
roles.description: Work as part of a team having responsibility for assembling an entire product or component of a product. Team assemblers can perform all tasks conducted by the team in the assembly process and rotate through all or most of them, rather than being assigned to a specific task on a permanent basis. May participate in making management decisions affecting the work. Includes team leaders who work as part of the team.

tasks.label: Perform quality checks on products and parts.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-process visual/tactile check at the assembler's own bench or station: after building a subassembly (appliance chassis, wire harness, pump, medical device tray), confirm every component is present, seated and oriented correctly, fasteners engaged, no burrs, scratches or contamination; mixed models and frequent changeovers, parts lying loose on the bench or in a soft nest.

Repetitive single-feature check on each unit passing a fixed station of a moving line (automotive/large-appliance general assembly): confirm a seatbelt/door lock/connector is installed and seated, or sniff an air-conditioning circuit for refrigerant leak, on every unit at takt time, flagging failures to the line system.

Dimensional and fit verification on sampled parts or completed assemblies using calipers, go/no-go gauges, height gauges, feeler gauges or torque audits against the print or control plan; results logged on a check sheet, out-of-tolerance parts quarantined.

Functional test of the completed assembly at end of line: connect power/test harness or pneumatic-hydraulic interface, cycle switches and functions, run leak/pressure/electrical test, observe and record pass/fail, segregate failures for rework.

Screening of incoming or kitted parts before use: pull components from supplier bins/kits at line side, verify correct part numbers and counts, and inspect them one by one for damage, flash, short shots, bad plating or missing labels; segregate rejects into a scrap bin and notify the team lead.

Final cosmetic/finish and completeness inspection of the finished product (paint and trim surfaces, gaps, labels, decals) with defect disposition: mark or tag the defect, decide rework vs. scrap, and route the unit to rework while completing the inspection record.

tasks.label: Rotate through all the tasks required in a particular production process.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Vehicle final assembly (autos, light trucks, buses, RVs, heavy equipment): team member rotates through 4-10 stations on a moving line each week — installing seats, wiring harnesses and connectors, hoses, headliners, interior trim, torquing fasteners with DC tools, fitting doors/glass — at ~60-120 s takt with mixed models and options.

High-volume rigid-component subassembly at a Tier-1 automotive/industrial parts plant (e-motors, pumps, brake and steering modules, connectors, battery modules): rotation covers press-fit and staking, screw-fastening, adhesive/sealant dispensing, leak and functional test, marking/labeling, and pack-out.

Small consumer/electronic/medical device assembly: rotation covers feeding small parts, board and housing mating, snap-fit and screwdriving, ultrasonic welding, in-line functional and vision inspection, labeling and blister/carton packing, in a clean, high-volume line.

High-mix, low-volume assembly of machinery, aerospace structures/interiors, custom equipment or furniture: rotation covers many largely manual operations with hand tools from work instructions — fitting, shimming, sealant, drilling/riveting, harness routing, upholstery/soft goods, frequent changeovers between variants and short runs.

Process/machine-centered team cell (injection molding, stamping, packaging/consumer goods): rotation covers loading and unloading machines, degating/trimming, visual and gauge inspection, secondary operations such as pad printing or ultrasonic welding, boxing, labeling and palletizing.

tasks.label: Supervise assemblers and train employees on job procedures.

instances.label: Lead assembler on a manufacturing line observes team members during the shift, watches for technique errors or bottlenecks, and verbally coaches individuals to correct how they perform their station's operations.

On-the-job training of a new hire at an assembly station: walking through the written work instructions, showing the sequence of steps, then watching the trainee perform and giving corrective feedback until they are signed off as qualified.

Assigning and rotating team members among stations, monitoring pace and quality against takt/output targets, resolving who covers absences or breaks, and reporting personnel and throughput issues up to the production supervisor.

Training the whole team on a revised procedure, engineering change, or new product changeover: reviewing updated standard-work documents, explaining torque/inspection requirements, and confirming understanding.
Conducting safety and quality briefings (toolbox talks, PPE and lockout reminders, defect/scrap review), documenting attendance and training records for audit compliance.

tasks.label: Shovel, sweep, or otherwise clean work areas.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled/end-of-shift sweeping and scrubbing of the open floor: main aisles, the walkway bay alongside the assembly line, and open staging areas. Fine dust, cardboard bits, stray packaging and small debris on smooth sealed concrete in a plant with a fixed layout and traffic rules.

Detail cleaning of the immediate workstation: sweeping and dust-panning under and behind the bench, between fixtures and conveyor legs, around pallets, part bins, air hoses and power cords; tight corners, edges and the strip beneath the line where dropped hardware and trim collect.

Cleaning work surfaces and tooling: wiping bench tops, jigs, fixtures and hand tools free of dust, grease, adhesive squeeze-out and marker; clearing leftover fasteners, cut zip ties, film/wrap and reject parts into the correct scrap and recycle bins at the station (5S end-of-shift reset).

Mid-shift mess response: an oil, coolant, adhesive or solvent spill, or a dropped tote of small parts, in the work area. Worker cordons it, applies absorbent or degreaser, scoops/picks up the material, disposes of it, and dries the floor to a safe standard before work resumes.
Removing accumulated bulk waste from the work area: swapping and hauling full scrap hoppers, chip tubs, dunnage carts and cardboard bales from the line to the compactor or dumpster area of the plant.

Shoveling/scooping loose bulk material: swarf and turnings, spilled granulate, sand or blast media, broken pallet wood, or slush and snow tracked in at the adjacent dock door, moved by shovel and scoop into a container.

tasks.label: Provide assistance in the production of wiring assemblies.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Lead/cable prep at a wiring sub-assembly bench or semi-automatic press station in a factory: measure and cut wire to length, strip both ends, crimp terminals or ring lugs, apply seals and printed labels, insert terminals into connector housings, and bundle a batch of simple 1-3 wire cable assemblies for the line.

Building a multi-branch harness on a formboard/rotating carousel in a harness cell: reading the drawing, routing dozens of pre-terminated leads along the board, seating connectors in board fixtures, forming breakouts, applying tape, convoluted loom, cable ties and clips, then lifting the finished harness off the board.

Installing and connecting a wiring assembly into the product on the assembly line: routing the harness through a chassis, enclosure or frame, mating connectors to motors, switches and boards, landing ring terminals on terminal blocks or studs and torquing screws, securing clips and ties, and dressing the wires.

Bench termination work: tinning and soldering wire leads to terminals, lugs, pins or PCB pads, making and insulating splices, and applying/shrinking heat-shrink sleeving on small electro-mechanical sub-assemblies.

Verifying and finishing assemblies: docking the harness connectors onto a continuity/hipot test board, running the test, visually inspecting crimps, tape and labels, reworking defects found (re-crimping, re-seating a terminal, re-taping), then labeling, bagging and packing finished assemblies in the shipping rack.

Supporting the wiring cell: replenishing wire spools, terminal reels, seals, connectors and kitted components to the wiring workstations, staging kits for the next build, and moving carts/racks of completed assemblies to test, pack or the main line.

tasks.label: Maintain production equipment and machinery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: End-of-run / end-of-shift cleaning of the station's production equipment: blowing chips, scrap, dust, adhesive squeeze-out and coolant off fixtures, nests, tooling and machine surfaces, wiping down guarding and emptying scrap/chip containers on a plant assembly floor.

Replenishing consumables and lubricants on the line: greasing/oiling designated lube points, topping up coolant, adhesive, sealant or oil reservoirs, and reloading feeder consumables (screws, rivets, welding caps) at the machine.

Clearing jams, misfeeds and minor faults on assembly equipment (stuck part in a press or nest, deformed fastener in a feed tube, conveyor blockage, screwdriver or riveter misfeed), then resetting and restarting the line at rate.

Swapping worn consumable tooling at the machine: dull cutting tools/drill bits/inserts, welding electrode caps or tips, nutrunner sockets and bits — worn item removed and a fresh equivalent installed, with a check that the machine runs to spec.

Replacing wear parts that require disassembly with hand tools: drive belts, filters, seals, guides, worn guide rails or a failed sensor — remove guarding/fasteners, extract the old part, fit and align the new one, refit guarding.

Routine condition checks and reporting: walking the line's machines, reading gauges/indicators and temperatures, listening/looking for abnormalities, checking tool torque/air pressure, logging readings and writing up problems for the maintenance department.
Minor adjustments and small repairs with hand tools: re-aligning a guide or stop, tightening loose fasteners, adjusting a sensor bracket or air regulator, and re-verifying the machine's output.

instances.label: Supermarket / warehouse-club in-store bake-off: baker sets a preset program on a rack or convection oven, wheels a loaded rack or slides sheet pans of frozen or par-baked croissants, rolls and cookies into the hot oven throughout the morning, working in a customer-facing store back room with shared aisles.

Retail/artisan bread bakery: baker preheats a multi-deck or steam-tube oven, sets deck temperature and steam, and loads scored hearth loaves and baguettes onto the deck with a peel or setter board, judging placement and load density by eye.

Large wholesale/plant bakery: pans and peelboards of dough are conveyed into a tunnel or travelling oven; the baker sets zone temperatures and belt speed at the oven control panel and monitors the continuous charge of product into the hot oven.

Restaurant, hotel or café pastry kitchen: baker preheats a convection or combi oven and slides full and half sheet pans of pastries, cookies and breads onto racks at chosen heights, in a crowded shared kitchen with other cooks moving around the oven bank.

Specialty shop (cakes, pies, donuts, cupcakes): small batches of varied pan sizes and shapes — round cake pans, pie tins, muffin trays — set into a deck or convection oven at recipe-specific temperatures, with frequent product changeovers.
